papers.title: Synthesizing symbolic models of human and machine reasoning at scale
papers.abstract: Symbolic models offer a powerful account of cognition, but their scope has historically been limited by the need for hand-engineering and computational tractability. We show how advances in artificial intelligence (AI) can scale symbolic modeling and help overcome these engineering limitations. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS)---an approach for automated search of interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce behavior---and apply it to model both human and machine behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems. Analyzing these programs reveals that both people and machines tend to oversimplify, adopt rules that are partial explanations for their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features. These shared signatures are modulated by available resources, with reasoning effort predicting the extent to which machines simplify and explain their observations. Together, these results point to underlying mechanisms reminiscent of satisficing in both people and machines, and illustrate how BCSS offers a general approach for interpreting and comparing rule-based reasoning of humans and black-box AI systems.

papers.title: Instrumental Variables in Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes
papers.abstract: Causal questions often arise in systems that evolve in continuous time. While instrumental variable (IV) methods provide a principled approach to identify causal effects in static or discrete-time settings, even in the presence of unobserved confounding, they do not yet extend to continuous-time dynamics. In this work, we develop an IV framework for stationary continuous-time stochastic processes parameterized by stochastic differential equations (SDE), where the instrument itself takes the form of a stochastic process. We encode the structural sparsity and causal effects directly at the infinitesimal level of the drift, and contrast these assumptions with the IV assumptions on the discretized version of the same process. Based on these structural assumptions, we derive moment restrictions using path-valued instruments. We show how these restrictions simplify for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes and present an identification condition together with a corresponding consistent estimation method. Finally, we extend our estimation framework to nonlinear causal effects by expressing the path-based moment restrictions leveraging the signature kernel. Empirically, our method recovers causal effects in confounded continuous-time systems where maximum-likelihood-based estimation and discrete-time IV methods are systematically biased.

papers.intro:
Causal effect estimation under unobserved confounding is a central challenge in many scientific domains. In the presence of unobserved confounders, standard estimation techniques fail to distinguish between confounding and the true effect. This distinction is generally impossible from observational data without additional assumptions. The IV (IV) framework forms one of the most prominent settings in which principled strategies for cause-effect identification and estimation exist under certain assumptions. IV are exogenous variables that affect the covariates, are independent of the hidden confounders, and only affect the outcome through the covariates. IV methods have been thoroughly studied and are an established workhorse in the toolbox of econometricians (Sargan, 1958; Hansen, 1982; Staiger and Stock, 1997) and beyond. They also attracted renewed interest in the context of flexible machine learning techniques (Bennett et al., 2019; Hartford et al., 2017; Ailer et al., 2024).

papers.title: FlyingDrones: A Dataset and Benchmark for Optical Flow Estimation from UAV motion
papers.abstract: Optical flow is an important cue for drone analysis in aerial surveillance, airspace monitoring, and long-range target tracking, where motion remains informative when appearance is weak. Estimating the motion of small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, however, is difficult because distant targets occupy few pixels, have low contrast, and move against complex dynamic backgrounds. Standard optical-flow benchmarks emphasize large, object-centric motions and therefore do not characterize distant aerial targets well. We introduce FlyingDrones, a generated benchmark with dense ground-truth optical flow and segmentation masks derived from physically based rendering, and define resolution-normalized metrics (EPE Norm) that normalize flow by image dimensions. We evaluate 16 state-of-the-art model families on a motion- and size-stratified subset of 999 flow pairs at three resolutions. Every family recovers drone motion better than the zero-flow reference, but the gap between families widens with resolution: at 1920x1080, global-matching, recurrent, transformer, and short-window temporal models separate clearly from pyramid, classical, self-supervised, lightweight, and diffusion models. Within-family checkpoint spread is comparable to or larger than between-family spread, so the training curriculum is as important as the architecture. Two complementary studies test the benchmark beyond synthetic accuracy: a ground-truth-free motion-alignment evaluation on 21 cameras of real UAV footage shows that the synthetic ranking carries a moderate, significant signal about real-world performance (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.63 over 41 checkpoints) while the exact top ranks differ, and a fine-tuning study shows that 800 FlyingDrones pairs reduce held-out drone-region error by up to 37% and improve drone localization on the real footage for all four architectures tested.

papers.title: InnerLogic-Surg: An Open Surgical Foundation Model via Continual Pretraining
papers.abstract: Vision foundation models are the backbone of modern surgical image analysis, yet most surgical systems still rely on encoders pretrained on natural images or on specialist models trained from scratch on comparatively small datasets. Pretraining encoders on large amounts of surgery-specific data has the potential to generally enhance the performance of surgical image analysis methods simply by providing stronger backbones. Here we present InnerLogic-Surg, an open family of surgical vision encoders (21M--300M parameters) obtained by continually pretraining a transformer-based image encoder on millions of surgical images curated from 11,965 internet-sourced surgical videos spanning ~2,900 hours and more than fifteen procedure types. Our training recipe inherits DINOv3's pretraining stage to preserve representation ability after surgical adaptation, and additionally applies a learned feature-upsampling module for high-resolution dense prediction at low token cost. Across a benchmark covering workflow, instrument and anatomy recognition, segmentation, detection, and monocular depth, under the same architecture, the largest InnerLogic-Surg model achieves the best linear-probe performance in all 20 surgical tasks. We demonstrate that surgical continual pretraining yields transferable representations that generalize across procedures, anatomical regions, and task types, showing our surgical image encoders as a promising and scalable alternative to the procedure-specific representation learning approaches that have traditionally dominated surgical computer vision.

Surgical computer vision has traditionally been built around task-specific models trained on carefully annotated datasets. This paradigm has produced strong systems for individual surgical tasks such as workflow recognition, instrument segmentation, and anatomy understanding. However, extending these models to new tasks, procedures, or institutions often requires additional annotations and retraining, making it difficult to scale this approach. At the same time, surgical video is generated at a scale far beyond what can realistically be labeled, leaving most of its visual information unused.

Surgical computer vision has traditionally been built around task-specific models trained on carefully annotated datasets. This paradigm has produced strong systems for individual surgical tasks such as workflow recognition, instrument segmentation, and anatomy understanding. However, extending these models to new tasks, procedures, or institutions often requires additional annotations and retraining, making it difficult to scale this approach. At the same time, surgical video is generated at a scale far beyond what can realistically be labeled, leaving most of its visual information unused.

Foundation models seek to leverage this visual data at scale, and their success is driven largely by self-supervised learning (SSL), which enables reusable representations from vast collections of unlabeled images. Adapting such models to surgery, however, is not straightforward. Continued self-supervised training from general foundation models can erode spatial structure already present in the pretrained representations, creating a tension between acquiring surgical specificity and preserving the broad visual priors from general pretraining.

Recent work has begun to investigate surgery-specific foundation models. Self-supervised approaches, such as SurgeNetXL [1] and LemonFM [2], leverage increasingly large datasets of endoscopic videos to train domain-specific visual encoders. Concurrently, multimodal surgical vision-language pretraining models, such as SurgVLP [3] and PeskaVLP [4], exploit surgical lecture videos to align complex visual concepts with clinical text, showcasing powerful zero-shot capabilities. These models enable versatile downstream applications by fine-tuning massive architectures from scratch. However, they largely focus on learning representations within the surgical domain itself. Specifically, they omit the potential to continually adapt general-purpose foundation models to surgery while preserving the rich visual priors, generality, and spatial structure acquired during large-scale natural-image pretraining.

papers.title: Towards Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Whole-Slide Image Retrieval for Pathology Archives
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of digital pathology has rapidly expanded collections of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images, yet efficient navigation through these archives remains challenging, as metadata is often inconsistent or unavailable. Content-based image retrieval addresses this challenge by identifying similar cases directly from visual representations instead of manual annotations or metadata. Existing retrieval systems have demonstrated promising performance but largely rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, constraining scalability and generalization. Here, we present CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) as a scalable, diagnostic-driven slide-retrieval framework, validated on both public and clinical data. Using a fixed-length slide embedding, CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates with either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting. Newly processed cases are subsequently added to the expanding memory bank, allowing the retrieval archive to grow over time. On a comprehensive benchmark consisting of two public and one private clinical datasets representing four retrieval tasks, CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline, with gains on CAMELYON16 (3.10), BRACS-1 (2.75), BRACS-2 (1.95), and X-HER2 (3.75). Additional ablation and latency studies further examine the contribution of each component and highlight its potential for scalable deployment.

papers.intro:
Digital pathology archives are currently growing, thus complicating the retrieval of relevant slides for a particular query slide. Metadata-based searches are often hindered by inconsistent or incomplete databases. Alternatively, content-based image retrieval (CBIR) enables searching for whole-slide images (WSIs) directly from a query image, but requires a useful representation and similarity measure between slides. For this work, we assume that the main objective is to find diagnostically related cases in the archive. Such retrieval can support case-based review [15], education [5], and similarity-driven exploration [34]. However, WSIs are gigapixel-sized images that contain a variable number of heterogeneous tissue regions, making conventional methods inefficient and challenging to apply [16, 30, 31]. A retrieval system must therefore represent diagnostically relevant morphology in a form that can be efficiently stored and searched.

Alternatively, content-based image retrieval (CBIR) enables searching for whole-slide images (WSIs) directly from a query image, but requires a useful representation and similarity measure between slides. For this work, we assume that the main objective is to find diagnostically related cases in the archive. Such retrieval can support case-based review [15], education [5], and similarity-driven exploration [34]. However, WSIs are gigapixel-sized images that contain a variable number of heterogeneous tissue regions, making conventional methods inefficient and challenging to apply [16, 30, 31]. A retrieval system must therefore represent diagnostically relevant morphology in a form that can be efficiently stored and searched.

Existing CBIR approaches address the gigapixel scale by representing each slide with a selected set of local observations. Earlier systems used handcrafted color and texture descriptors [34]; recent WSI systems instead use learned patch features within mosaic-based retrieval [15], slide-level hashing [17], discrete-code indexing [5], or local patch matching [27]. While these approaches improve retrieval efficiency, they also involve trade-offs in how a slide is represented. The number of stored patches may depend on tissue content and sampling decisions, whereas stronger compression can remove diagnostically relevant details. In addition, visually similar slides are not necessarily diagnostically consistent.

For a scalable, searchable WSI archive, we argue that (i) the storage required for a newly indexed WSI should not depend on how many patches it contains, (ii) a WSI’s representation must preserve diagnostic evidence without relying on manually configured clustering or mosaic construction, and (iii) the search procedure must accommodate queries both with and without an available diagnosis. Motivated by these considerations, we recently conceptualized the diagnosis-aligned WSI retrieval framework CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) for growing clinical archives [1].

In this work, we review this concept and extend it with a grid-search strategy for improved hyperparameter selection, dedicated ablation and latency studies, and a clinical evaluation study. Following its initial overall structure, CLEAR-WSI can be formalized as shown in Figure 1. In a nutshell, it uses a diagnosis-aware, fixed-length slide representation that provides a constant per-slide storage footprint and predictable memory-bank growth, and integrates automated Self-Retrieval (SR) and label-available Class-Informed (CI) modes to support diagnosis-aligned search both with and without an available query diagnosis. We show on two public datasets (CAMELYON16, BRACS-1/2) and a private clinical X-HER2 cohort that CLEAR-WSI consistently outperforms representative state-of-the-art retrieval methods, making it a powerful tool for archival slide retrieval. CLEAR-WSI is openly available at Anonymized Git Repo.

papers.title: Reprogrammable polaritonic skyrmion and meron lattices based on the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$
papers.abstract: Optical topological quasiparticles such as skyrmions and merons consist of engineered electromagnetic fields which can be realized via the controlled interference of polaritons. The resulting polaritonic topological lattices offer a promising platform for on-chip information encoding and nanoscale light-matter interaction. However, realizing these functionalities requires active tailoring of the polaritonic topological lattice. Although previous works have achieved tuning of the size of the polaritonic lattice sites, these methods relied on cumbersome and time-consuming fabrication processes and do not allow reconfiguration of the topological invariant. Here, we demonstrate fast optical prototyping of reconfigurable hexagonal and square coupling structures for the generation of polaritonic topological lattices with hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN using the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$. As In$_3$SbTe$_2$ can be switched reversibly between its dielectric ($\varepsilon$>0) amorphous and metallic ($\varepsilon$<0) crystalline phase by laser pulses, metallic In$_3$SbTe$_2$ coupling structures can be optically programmed and reconfigured. Our approach enables tailoring the size of the topological lattice sites by tuning the incident frequency. Moreover, In$_3$SbTe$_2$ allows for tailoring the topological invariant by reprogramming the coupling structure. Our platform enables reprogramming of robust optical topologies within minutes, opening a route toward rewritable on-chip photonic computing based on robust and on demand reconfigurable topological states.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs
papers.abstract: Uncertainty quantification is crucial in scientific machine learning, where models inform safety-critical tasks such as flood forecasting, financial risk management, and thermal control in machines. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees, but in time-dependent settings common to physics and engineering, these guarantees can break down, leading to systematic undercoverage. We study this problem in the context of surrogate models for time-dependent physical systems described by partial differential equations. We prove that in a function space setting, distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, making exact coverage guarantees impossible. We further show that in discretized settings, the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast with the grid resolution, mandating restrictions on the spatial discretization to ensure coverage. Finally, for certain settings, we show how to use principled weighted conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.

papers.title: Training-Free Character-Length Control in Summarization with Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Summarization with a fixed character length is important for tasks such as headline and article preview generation, where text must fit an exact space. Autoregressive language models (LMs) struggle with precise character-length control: training-based methods require task-specific fine-tuning, while zero-shot prompting strategies achieve only approximate compliance. We propose DELTA (Diffusion Expected Length Targeting Algorithm), a training-free inference-time method for masked diffusion LMs that estimates expected character length at each denoising step and dynamically inserts or removes masked positions to steer toward a target length. DELTA requires no fine-tuning and is designed for off-the-shelf masked diffusion LMs. Across three summarization benchmarks, it reduces character-length errors by an order of magnitude compared to baselines while maintaining competitive summary quality in both automatic and human evaluation.

papers.intro:
Many summarization tasks require outputs that fit a precise character budget. In publishing workflows, for example, headlines and article previews are often produced for predefined display slots with fixed character capacities (Hitomi et al., 2019); similar constraints arise in notification previews, social media posts, subtitles, and UI text, where even a few extra characters can cause truncation or layout overflow. Existing approaches to length-controlled summarization operate within the constraints of autoregressive generation: training-based methods (Miculicich et al., 2023; Belligoli et al., 2025) modify the model or its objective to encourage a target length, while zero-shot strategies (Retkowski and Waibel, 2025; Xie and Lee, 2025) rely on prompting techniques or post-hoc filtering. Both approaches operate under standard left-to-right autoregressive decoding, where previously emitted tokens are not directly revised within the same generation pass. This makes it difficult to dynamically correct the decoded character length as generation proceeds.

This makes it difficult to dynamically correct the decoded character length as generation proceeds.

Masked diffusion language models such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream (Ye et al., 2025) offer a structurally different generation process. These models iteratively refine a buffer of masked tokens over multiple denoising steps, and are trained to generate across a range of output lengths. This means that occasional insertions or removals of mask tokens will not severely disrupt generation quality. We exploit this property with Delta, an inference-time method that estimates expected character length from both committed tokens and the probability distributions over remaining masks, then adjusts the buffer to steer toward a target. Delta requires no fine-tuning or architectural changes and is designed to apply to off-the-shelf masked diffusion LMs. Across three summarization benchmarks, it reduces character-length errors by an order of magnitude compared to all baselines while maintaining competitive summary quality.

papers.title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
papers.abstract: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

papers.intro:
Learned representations, commonly called embeddings, represent diverse data types (e.g., words, documents) as real-valued vectors, organized such that semantically similar items are positioned close together within the embedding space [1]. Since Word2Vec [2], embeddings have advanced further, notably with BERT [3], which marked a shift towards context-dependent embeddings, and with Sentence-BERT [4] and SimCSE [5], designed to learn embeddings for entire sentences. These representations then power a wide spectrum of downstream tasks, including classification, clustering, and retrieval [6]. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) [7] stands as a prominent example: a typical RAG pipeline involves chunking and embedding documents, retrieving relevant chunks based on similarity to a user query, and then generating a response from a large language model.

The use of embeddings at scale has two primary costs: (1) inference, which involves computing embeddings for new data, and is typically a one-time cost per element, as embeddings can be stored; and (2) downstream tasks, which often involve repeated comparisons between embeddings loaded into memory. An RAG index of one million chunks encoded as 1024-dimensional float32 vectors already occupies about 4 GB. Matryoshka Representations (MRs) [8, 9] offer hierarchical embedding storage, enabling the selection of representation size, and with 2D MRs also of the layer, during inference. Additionally, quantization techniques [10, 11] aim to reduce the bit precision of embedding values, resulting in a smaller memory footprint.

While these techniques have been investigated individually, their combined effect on embedding performance and efficiency remains an open question. This work seeks to address this gap, aiming to answer the following research question: RQ: “In the context of transformer-based text embedding models, can hierarchical representations and quantization be combined to improve the computational efficiency of embeddings while maintaining high performance on downstream tasks?” Our research is guided by four objectives: to evaluate the combined impact of hierarchical representations and quantization across a diverse set of tasks, identifying which task categories are most resilient to dimensionality reduction and precision loss; to quantify the efficiency gains in per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time; to determine configurations of dimensionality, numerical precision, and inference layer that balance performance preservation with resource efficiency; and to establish practical guidelines for resource-constrained environments.

papers.title: Why a Multi-Cycle Treasury Program is Essential to Maximize JWST's Scientific Contributions to Galaxy Formation
papers.abstract: The Genesis Initiative is an extragalactic community-wide effort to coordinate white papers in response to the STScI Multi-Cycle Treasury (MCT) concept call. Two of JWST's primary science goals are to discover and characterize the first stars and galaxies, and to understand how they evolved into the galaxies we see today - questions whose fundamental importance has been affirmed by the past three decadal surveys. JWST's first five years have surpassed expectations, revealing a bounty of unexpected discoveries about the early universe. Yet these discoveries have raised as many questions as they have answered, and key mission goals remain unmet. Transforming this excitement into a quantitative physical understanding of early galaxy formation requires a uniform, statistically controlled legacy dataset that the current portfolio of smaller, heterogeneous programs cannot provide. The history of the Hubble Space Telescope offers a clear precedent. Its most transformative extragalactic results came from large, coordinated surveys far exceeding what the standard time-allocation process typically approves, and these uniform datasets remain scientifically productive decades later. We argue that JWST is now poised for the same leap. Answering the field's central open questions demands coordinated, community-led surveys of ~1000-2000 hr, with uniform and well-characterized selection functions that are structurally impossible within single-cycle programs. Such an investment is time-critical while JWST's instruments remain at peak performance, and would maximize synergy with ALMA, Euclid, Roman, Rubin, and future facilities. We therefore urge STScI to open a MCT channel, enabling the bold, ambitious surveys needed to understand how galaxies evolve from first light to the present day.

papers.intro:
Two of the James Webb Space Telescope’s (JWST) primary science goals are “discovering and characterizing the first stars and galaxies”, and “understanding how these objects evolved into the galaxies we see in the nearby Universe” [39]. These questions – when the first galaxies emerged from the cosmic dark ages, how the first massive black holes formed, and how the heavy elements necessary for life were forged in the first stars —- together mark the genesis of our own Milky Way, and of the conditions that made life possible.

Two of the James Webb Space Telescope’s (JWST) primary science goals are “discovering and characterizing the first stars and galaxies”, and “understanding how these objects evolved into the galaxies we see in the nearby Universe” [39]. These questions – when the first galaxies emerged from the cosmic dark ages, how the first massive black holes formed, and how the heavy elements necessary for life were forged in the first stars —- together mark the genesis of our own Milky Way, and of the conditions that made life possible.

The fundamental importance of these questions has been called out by the past three Astronomy and Astrophysics decadal surveys, and formed the primary motivation for investing decades of effort and billions of dollars to making the JWST mission a reality. Most recently, the Astro2020 decadal identified “Cosmic Ecosystems: Unveiling the Hidden Drivers of Galaxy Growth” as a priority science area, stating: “An essential milestone on the pathway to revealing these drivers is a complete understanding of the formation and buildup of galaxies and their structures, stellar populations, metals, and central black holes over cosmic time. JWST is poised to revolutionize this subject by imaging and identifying galaxies out to some of the first generations during the epoch of reionization, and by obtaining deep redshifted ultraviolet–visible spectra for thousands of galaxies spanning the period from reionization to the present.” [78]. Other key questions identified by the Astro2020 science panels that JWST can address include: 1) What are the seeds of supermassive black holes and how do they grow? 2) How did the intergalactic medium and the first sources of radiation evolve from cosmic dawn through the epoch of reionization? 3) How do gas, metals, and dust flow into, through, and out of galaxies? 4) How do supermassive black holes form, and how is their growth coupled to the evolution of their host galaxies? [77]

JWST’s performance has been even better than expected, and the Universe has also cooperated by disclosing a bounty of unexpected discoveries. Despite the associated excitement, these discoveries have posed as many new questions as they have answered, and major goals of the JWST mission arguably remain un-achieved. A uniform, statistically controlled legacy dataset is now required to transform these discoveries into a quantitative physical understanding of early galaxy formation. Here we argue that this requires a coordinated and ambitious community-led strategy, demanding a significantly larger time allocation than has been approved through the standard TAC process to date. Over the past five years, the JWST user community has gained substantial expertise in designing observing strategies and in interpreting the resulting data. Now is the time for JWST to embark on the next phase of scientific discovery, by enabling these kinds of larger efforts.

papers.title: DOWSING, Dust Observations With SCUBA-2 In Nearby Galaxies: I. Dust in M81
papers.abstract: We present a resolved far-infrared/sub-millimetre study of dust in the nearby spiral galaxy M81 using Herschel PACS/SPIRE and JCMT SCUBA-2 observations from 70 to $850\,\mu\mathrm{m}$. We model the dust emission using both single-temperature modified blackbody (SMBB) fits and point process mapping (PPMAP), comparing pixel-by-pixel SED-fitting with image cubes of dust surface density as a function of position and temperature. For fixed $\beta = 1.9$ and a dust opacity of $\kappa_{350\,\mu\mathrm{m}} = 1.92\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}\,\mathrm{g}^{-1}$, SMBB gives an integrated dust mass of $(1.77 \pm 0.09) \times 10^{7}\,M_\odot$, while PPMAP gives $(2.65 \pm 0.13) \times10^{7}\,M_\odot$. The higher PPMAP mass is expected because real lines of sight contain dust over a range of temperatures, whereas SMBB assumes a single effective temperature and can underestimate the dust mass. Both methods show enhanced dust surface densities along the spiral arms and a radially declining dust temperature, with the warmest dust in the central region. Variable-$\beta$ fits indicate only moderate spatial variation in $\beta$ for well-constrained pixels, but the strong $T$-$\beta$ degeneracy motivates a fixed emissivity index for the main analysis. Combining the dust maps with HI data, we find a positive radial gas-to-dust ratio gradient, with $d\log_{10}(\mathrm{GDR})/dR = 0.065\,\mathrm{dex}\,\mathrm{kpc}^{-1}$. Comparison with M81's metallicity gradient implies a declining dust-to-metals ratio, potentially consistent with more efficient grain growth in the inner disc. The star formation rate is modest, $\sim 0.27\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, and is strongly concentrated along the spiral arms. These results suggest that the dust, gas, and star-forming structures of M81 are strongly shaped by its spiral arms, while the central region hosts the warmest dust in the disc.

papers.intro:
Dust in the interstellar medium (ISM) is crucial for various astrophysical processes, acting as a coolant in star-forming regions, heating the gas in photodissociation regions (Draine, 1978), facilitating molecular hydrogen formation (Gould and Salpeter, 1963), and indirectly supporting star and planet formation. Dust particles are produced from stellar outflows and supernovae, and they absorb and re-radiate about half of the universe’s emitted energy within the far-infrared (FIR) and sub-millimetre (Lagache et al., 2005, sub-mm;), making this wavelength range essential for studying the cold universe.

Dust in the interstellar medium (ISM) is crucial for various astrophysical processes, acting as a coolant in star-forming regions, heating the gas in photodissociation regions (Draine, 1978), facilitating molecular hydrogen formation (Gould and Salpeter, 1963), and indirectly supporting star and planet formation. Dust particles are produced from stellar outflows and supernovae, and they absorb and re-radiate about half of the universe’s emitted energy within the far-infrared (FIR) and sub-millimetre (Lagache et al., 2005, sub-mm;), making this wavelength range essential for studying the cold universe.

Continuum studies of FIR and sub-mm emission in nearby galaxies face strong observational limitations. Over most of the FIR regime the atmosphere is effectively opaque, making ground-based imaging impractical and space missions essential for sensitive surveys. In the sub-mm, by contrast, a small number of atmospheric windows permit ground-based observations; however, they remain technically demanding because atmospheric transmission is poor at these wavelengths, the sky background is bright and spatially extended, and low-surface-brightness discs require long integrations and careful removal of large-scale atmospheric fluctuations. Space-based facilities have therefore played a central role in building large FIR-to-sub-mm datasets. In particular, the Herschel Space Observatory (Pilbratt et al., 2010) provided sensitive imaging from 70 to 500 µ​m500\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}, substantially improving wavelength coverage over earlier space missions. It also delivered higher angular resolution, for example 6 ″6\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolArcsecond} at 70 µ​m70\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} with PACS compared to 18 ″18\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolArcsecond} with Spitzer MIPS. These capabilities also contributed to legacy data sets such as the DustPedia (Clark et al., 2026) database (Clark et al., 2018), which compiles multiwavelength observations of 875 nearby galaxies from a range of surveys. Nonetheless, although Herschel transformed FIR studies of nearby galaxies, its wavelength coverage ends at 500 µ​m500\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}, and the cold-dust-sensitive higher-wavelength SPIRE bands have poorer angular resolution than the shorter-wavelength PACS bands. These limitations motivate complementary ground-based sub-mm and mm observations (Li et al., 2020; Katsioli et al., 2023; Pantoni et al., 2026).

Longer-wavelength sub-mm data at 850 µ​m850\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} from instruments such as the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope’s (JCMT) SCUBA-2 camera (Holland et al., 2013) extend the wavelength coverage beyond Herschel’s 500 µ​m500\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} band, helping to constrain the long-wavelength slope more precisely and improving estimates of dust mass and temperature. This enables mapping of cold-dust properties on sub-kpc scales, even in galaxies beyond the Local Group, using pixel-by-pixel SED fitting. This approach reveals how dust physics and the interstellar radiation field (ISRF) vary across different galactic environments (Kennicutt et al., 2011; Davies et al., 2017, e.g.).

Radial variations in dust properties within nearby galaxies are shown in multiple resolved studies (Smith et al., 2012; Tabatabaei et al., 2014; Kirkpatrick et al., 2014; Galametz et al., 2016; Relaño et al., 2018; Chiang et al., 2018; Vílchez et al., 2019; van der Giessen et al., 2024; Park et al., 2024), but the physical origin of these variations remains uncertain. For example, radial analyses of the KINGFISH sample demonstrate that the dust temperature or equivalently the strength of the ISRF heating the majority of the dust generally decline with galactocentric radius, while the apparent emissivity index β\beta shows substantial diversity among galaxies, including decreasing, increasing, and non-monotonic radial behaviour (Hunt et al., 2015). Importantly, Hunt et al. (2015) argue that radial trends in β\beta do not uniquely imply intrinsic changes in grain emissivity: physically motivated dust models with fixed intrinsic emissivities can reproduce apparently shallow long-wavelength slopes, because temperature mixing and variations in the ISRF intensity distribution broaden the SED and can bias single-temperature modified blackbody (SMBB) fits toward low apparent β\beta, particularly in cool outer discs where the ISRF intensity is low. Consequently, spatial variations in β\beta are likely to reflect a combination of changing radiation-field conditions and genuine radial changes in grain chemical/physical properties (e.g. composition, structure, mantling) driven by gradients in ISM conditions, but the relative importance of these effects remains uncertain.

We address this through the Dust Observations with SCUBA-2 in Nearby Galaxies (DOWSING) survey, a new programme targeting 12 nearby, large-angular-size galaxies with existing Herschel continuum observations. The SCUBA-2 data complement these observations by providing higher-resolution imaging at 450 µ​m450\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} and extending the wavelength coverage to 850 µ​m850\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}, with effective beam FWHMs of approximately 9.8 ″9.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolArcsecond} and 14.6 ″14.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolArcsecond} (Dempsey et al., 2013), respectively. The main objectives of the survey are to study the causes of variations in the β\beta parameter, to measure the variation in the gas-to-dust ratio and the CO-to-H2 conversion factor in each individual galaxy, and to investigate the presence of CO-dark molecular gas (H2 that cannot be traced by CO, as expected where H2 survives but CO is photodissociated; Wolfire et al. 2010) in high-mass galaxies beyond the Local Group, where its contribution remains less well-constrained than in the Milky Way (Grenier et al., 2005; Planck Collaboration et al., 2011; Langer et al., 2014). SCUBA-2 has been obtaining deep images of these galaxies at 450 and 850 µ​m850\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} since 2020, and ∼\sim60% of the survey has been completed. When the survey is finished, SCUBA-2 images in combination with available Herschel images will be used to create high-resolution dust maps of these 12 galaxies.

papers.title: The ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST Survey: The Tully-Fisher Relation at $z = 4-6$
papers.abstract: The Tully-Fisher relation provides a fundamental link between galaxy mass and their kinematics. Although its evolution is relatively well constrained up to cosmic noon, observational probes at higher redshifts remain scarce. In this work, we investigate the stellar and baryonic Tully-Fisher relations (TFRs) at $z=4-6$ by analyzing JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of 18 main-sequence star-forming galaxies belonging to the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST survey. We apply a morpho-kinematic disk classification scheme, finding five disk-like galaxies and a survey disk fraction of $0.28\pm0.11$. These disk galaxies span stellar masses of $10^{9.5-10.5}\,M_\odot$, intrinsic rotational velocities of $91-127\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$, and intrinsic velocity dispersions of $66-129\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$. For both versions of the TFR, we find that the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST disks lie below the local relations and are likely offset from those reported at cosmic noon ($z\approx2.3$). By fixing the TFR slope to the $z=0$ value, we measure zero-point offsets for the stellar-mass TFR of $-0.96\pm0.18$ dex and $-0.50\pm0.18$ dex relative to the local Universe and cosmic noon, respectively. For the baryonic TFR, we find zero-point offsets of $-0.57\pm0.20$ dex and $-0.30\pm0.20$ dex with respect to the local Universe and cosmic noon relations. Our measurements are consistent with the redshift evolution of the zero-points of both TFRs being driven by the evolution of dark matter halo properties with cosmic time, modulated by a reduced contribution of dark matter to the dynamical mass on the galaxy scale.

papers.intro:
Understanding how galaxies assembled their mass and structure in the early Universe is a key goal of extragalactic astrophysics. During the first Gyr of cosmic history, typical star-forming galaxies were rapidly growing through gas accretion and mergers, while their internal structure was still settling (Madau and Dickinson, 2014; Dayal and Ferrara, 2018; Le Fèvre et al., 2020; Romano et al., 2021; Herrera-Camus et al., 2025). This early phase is key for studying how baryons assembled within dark matter (DM) haloes, and when rotationally supported galaxies began to emerge.

Understanding how galaxies assembled their mass and structure in the early Universe is a key goal of extragalactic astrophysics. During the first Gyr of cosmic history, typical star-forming galaxies were rapidly growing through gas accretion and mergers, while their internal structure was still settling (Madau and Dickinson, 2014; Dayal and Ferrara, 2018; Le Fèvre et al., 2020; Romano et al., 2021; Herrera-Camus et al., 2025). This early phase is key for studying how baryons assembled within dark matter (DM) haloes, and when rotationally supported galaxies began to emerge.

Gas kinematics provides a straightforward way to address the dynamical state of galaxies. For example, integral field unit (IFU) surveys observing the ionized-gas kinematics of galaxies at z≈1−3z\approx 1-3 revealed a diverse galaxy population, including turbulent rotating disks, dispersion-dominated systems, and mergers (Förster Schreiber et al., 2009; Wisnioski et al., 2015). These galaxies were found, on average, exhibiting larger velocity dispersions and lower rotational support compared to their local counterparts (Wisnioski et al., 2015; Genzel et al., 2017; Price et al., 2020). However, the magnitude of this evolution remains debated and appears to depend on the gas tracer. Measurements based on cold gas generally show lower velocity dispersions and higher rotational support than ionized-gas measurements, implying a milder evolution of disk turbulence and rotational support with redshift (Girard et al., 2021; Rizzo et al., 2021; Roman-Oliveira et al., 2023; Rizzo et al., 2024). Extending such analysis to earlier epochs is crucial to determine when stable rotating disks become common, how disk settling proceeds with cosmic time, and how this process is connected to the build-up of stellar mass (M⋆M_{\star}) within galaxies.

Extending such analysis to earlier epochs is crucial to determine when stable rotating disks become common, how disk settling proceeds with cosmic time, and how this process is connected to the build-up of stellar mass (M⋆M_{\star}) within galaxies.

In this context, a useful way to study the connection between the mass of a galaxy and its dynamics is the Tully-Fisher relation (TFR). Originally defined as a relationship between the luminosity and rotation velocity of systems (Tully and Fisher, 1977), it is now commonly studied in terms of their stellar mass and/or baryonic mass (MbarM_{\rm bar}) versus a characteristic circular velocity (e.g., McGaugh et al. 2000; Reyes et al. 2011; Swinbank et al. 2012; Lelli et al. 2016). The stellar-mass TFR (sTFR) and the baryonic TFR (bTFR) provide a powerful framework for testing how disk-like galaxies assemble their mass within dark matter halos. The cosmic evolution of both the sTFR and bTFR can place constraints on gas fractions, star-formation efficiency, feedback, and the relative contributions of baryons and dark matter on galaxy scales (e.g., Übler et al. 2017; Tiley et al. 2019; Birkin et al. 2024; Sharma et al. 2024).

The cosmic evolution of both the sTFR and bTFR can place constraints on gas fractions, star-formation efficiency, feedback, and the relative contributions of baryons and dark matter on galaxy scales (e.g., Übler et al. 2017; Tiley et al. 2019; Birkin et al. 2024; Sharma et al. 2024).

Observationally, the cosmic evolution of the TFR has been studied extensively up to z≈2z\approx 2, with mixed results reported in the literature depending on the redshift range, sample selection, and galaxy population. Some studies report little or no evolution in the sTFR out to z≈1−2z\approx 1-2, suggesting that the sTFR was already in place for massive star-forming disks at relatively early times (Conselice et al., 2005; Miller et al., 2011; Di Teodoro et al., 2016; Tiley et al., 2019; Birkin et al., 2024). In contrast, other studies report negative offsets with respect to the local relation, indicating that galaxies at fixed stellar mass show higher circular velocities at earlier cosmic times, possibly due to an evolution in the efficiency of gas-to-star conversion within growing dark matter halos (Puech et al., 2008; Vergani et al., 2012; Übler et al., 2017; Harrison et al., 2017). Overall, there is currently no clear consensus on the cosmic evolution of the sTFR. The disagreement among the studies can arise from observational and methodological differences in the derivation of galaxy kinematics, stellar masses, and data quality (Übler et al., 2017; Pelliccia et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2024; Espejo Salcedo et al., 2025; Mancera Piña et al., 2026). Compared to the sTFR, the bTFR cosmic evolution remains less constrained because robust measurements of gas masses are required, which remain challenging at high redshift. In the local Universe, adding the gas mass into the mass budget for dwarf galaxies moves these systems into a single baryonic mass TFR (McGaugh et al., 2000; Lelli et al., 2016). At high redshift, accounting for gas mass becomes increasingly important for massive systems because galaxy gas fractions increase toward earlier cosmic times (Tacconi et al., 2020).

papers.title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.

papers.intro:
Rising mobility demand puts pressure on urban transportation systems [1], motivating Mobility-on-Demand (MoD) services aimed at utilizing existing infrastructure more efficiently [2]. Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) represents the next evolutionary step of these services and is moving from concept to operational reality. By replacing human-driven vehicles with fully compliant autonomous vehicles under centralized fleet control, AMoD operators can steer supply by continuously rebalancing idle vehicles without relying on driver participation [3] and influence demand through dynamic pricing without accounting for driver-side incentives [4]. However, profit-oriented operators may use centralized control to concentrate service in high-revenue regions [5, 6] and capture consumer surplus through price discrimination [7, 8], motivating regulation that aligns AMoD operations with public-sector objectives [9].

Designing such regulatory frameworks is complex, as regulators must balance citizen satisfaction, operator interests, and sustainability goals [10]. Interventions may also be limited by the temporal mismatch between operators’ frequent operational decisions [11] and medium- to long-term regulatory adjustments [12]. At the same time, requirements for sharing dynamic mobility data [13] together with the algorithmic controllability of AMoD fleets make adaptive regulation a practically relevant alternative to fixed instruments.

papers.title: Coordinated Space and Ground Monitoring of Accretion Bursts in a Protoplanetary Disk: MIRI and iSHELL observe the long-term modulation of gas within a small inner disk cavity
papers.abstract: DQ Tau is a TTauri eccentric binary with pulsed accretion bursts regulated by its $\sim 16$-day orbital period. We have monitored this system with seven instruments from ground and space over 40 days. We present results on molecular gas variability from nine JWST-MIRI and nine IRTF-iSHELL epochs over three sequential accretion bursts with accretion luminosity pulses increasing by factors of $\sim 9$-80. A fundamental new measurement from this analysis is the line broadening of CO (from iSHELL) and H$_2$O (from MIRI) lines, which we use to estimate Keplerian radii and their variability in parallel to the line luminosity. This unprecedented dataset clearly shows that the molecular emission does not react like HI and the 5-$\mu$m continuum with each accretion burst: the line luminosity and width of all hot molecular gas tracers decrease over $\sim30$-35 days, consistent with an emitting region decreasing in temperature and mass as it recedes to larger radii within the $\sim 0.2$-0.4 au inner cavity perturbed by the binary. The infrared molecular spectrum of DQ Tau is affected more by disk dynamics then by chemical changes triggered by variable accretion, supporting model expectations for chemical relaxation timescales that are much longer than the duration of these accretion bursts ($\gg 10$ days). The variability observed in all tracers in this study is consistent with a scenario where gas mass builds up near the disk edge to modulate the burst peak intensity and gas density in the inner cavity every $\sim4$-5 orbital periods. The origin of this modulation is still unclear.

papers.intro:
The chemical composition of gas and dust in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks has been proposed to evolve during planet formation through multiple processes. With inner disks being largely shaped by radial and vertical gradients in temperature and density, a number of factors may impact disk chemistry beyond what is expected in a static, smooth disk geometry: disk structures like radial or azimuthal over-densities and gaps [4, 15], gas dispersal through disk winds [2, 79], planet formation [38], irradiation conditions that slowly evolve over Myr timescales [69], and even the sudden irradiation changes produced by episodic accretion outbursts [13, 42]. While during the T Tauri phase the average accretion variability is about a factor of 2–3 (0.3–0.5 dex) over timescales as short as days and as long as years [31, 102], episodic “bursters” have been observed to change by factors of 10–100 over timescales from days to weeks and in exceptional cases up to several months [42, the EX Lup outbursts and V1647 Ori outbursts,]. These stronger events, while shorter and still moderate in comparison to the FU Ori-type outbursts happening at earlier stages, have been observed to significantly change the dust and gas emission from inner disks during the planet formation phases at ∼1\sim 1 Myr [1, 17, 93]. In fact, the increased UV and X-ray irradiation during outbursts is expected to alter the inner disk chemistry, with potential longer-term impact on planet formation. These effects include: UV photo-dissociation of molecules, increased molecular formation in a warmer disk region, ice sublimation during higher accretion events [29, 74, 107, 112, 55, 87, 93]. All these effects can have an observable impact by increasing or decreasing the emission from a given molecule, depending on the case.

While episodic accretion bursts are thought to be common in young stars as they assemble their mass, their low frequency and unpredictability make them hard to use for studies of inner disk chemistry during planet-formation in the Class II phase of solar-mass stars, which have so far been rare and limited to a few epochs. Pulsed accretion in disks around binary systems offer an alternative predictable experiment to monitor inner disk chemistry as a function of variable irradiation conditions. However, these systems also have complex inner disk dynamics where accretion onto the stars is regulated by the interactions between the inner disk and the binary orbit, producing asymmetric and highly variable structures at the inner edge [8, 75, 91, 39, 53, 36, 94]. The interactions between physics, chemistry, and variable irradiation conditions in these inner disks are still mostly unexplored.

DQ Tau is a spectroscopic equal-mass binary system in Taurus at a distance of 196 pc (see Table 1). This system has long been studied as a prototype of “pulsed accretion” triggered by the interaction between the stellar orbits and the inner disk [8, 71], also observed in UZ Tau E and TWA 3A [58, 98, 99]. The two stars in DQ Tau have roughly equal mass of ∼0.6\sim 0.6 M⊙M_{\odot} for a total dynamical mass of 1.21±0.26​M⊙1.21\pm 0.26M_{\odot}, with a binary period of ∼15.7\sim 15.7 days and eccentricity of ∼0.55\sim 0.55 [71, 34, 3]. The circumbinary disk is relatively compact, with an outer size of 37 au (including 90% of the millimeter flux) and possibly a narrow unresolved substructure at ∼15\sim 15–16 au [66, 117, 115, Long et al. in prep.]. The disk inclination from ALMA data in 2016 is 19.6±0.119.6\pm 0.1 deg [115], confirmed by new higher-resolution ALMA data (F. Long, priv. comm.). The binary orbit has recently been updated in Alqubelat et al. [3] as part of the coordinated observing campaign described in this work. It is expected by dynamical models that the resonant gravitational torques from the binary should produce a low-density inner disk region out to ∼2\sim 2–4 times the semi-major axis aa [8, 81, 73]. This corresponds to ∼0.3\sim 0.3–0.6 au using semi-major axis estimates reported in Table 1, where we adopt the intermediate value of 3​a3a. In this work, we refer to this inner region as the inner disk “cavity” produced by the binary dynamics, which we remark it is not expected to be fully devoid of gas, azimuthally symmetric, nor stable in time [75, e.g.]. Near-infrared interferometry detected dust emission from inside this inner cavity edge [23], and previous spectrally-resolved MM-band CO lines also showed large velocities of 70–80 km/s (FWHM), indicating CO emission extending well within this cavity down to ∼0.1\sim 0.1 au [27].

papers.title: Using Structure Functions to Characterize Protoplanetary Disk Velocity Residuals
papers.abstract: Protoplanetary disks, the birthplace of planetary systems, are highly dynamic environments. High angular and spectral resolution observations have revealed non-Keplerian motions in nearly every source studied, indicative of (magneto-)hydrodynamical instabilities or planet-disk interactions. However, these velocity perturbations rarely exhibit ordered structure, limiting our ability to attribute them to a specific mechanism. We propose the second-order structure function as a tool for recovering structural properties of velocity perturbations in the presence of significant noise. Using morphological models, we demonstrate how easy-to-calculate heuristics and parametric model fits together identify structure in noisy data and recover its properties, including correlation lengths, their radial scaling where genuinely present, and the anisotropy. We further outline a workflow to de-noise the data and to build a matched null model against which inferences are compared. Applying the framework to one numerical simulation each of the gravitational, magneto-rotational and vertical-shear instabilities, we recover their structure at high significance and the structural heuristics separate all three pairs, with the gravitational and vertical-shear instability simulations remaining the hardest to distinguish once observationally degraded. As a demonstration on real data, 12CO observations of TW Hya reveal azimuthally elongated velocity structure that persists once the large-scale m=1 component is removed. We also delineate where a Gaussian description breaks down for coherent features such as spiral arms, and how inclination affects the recovered heuristics. The methodology is implemented in the eddy package and provides a foundation for statistically characterizing turbulent velocity structure in high-resolution disk observations.

papers.intro:
It is now clear that the gas dynamics in protoplanetary disks exhibit substantial deviations from a simple Keplerian-like velocity profile [27, e.g.,]. While for some sources the perturbations form a clear structure, easily attributable to known (magneto-)hydrodynamical processes, such as the multi-armed spirals indicative of the gravitational instability in AB Aur [28], for many sources the structure is far less interpretable [11, e.g.,]. This is particularly true of the velocity signatures expected from (magneto-)hydrodynamical turbulence, which are predicted to be stochastic and spatially correlated rather than to form large-scale, coherent, easily parameterized morphology [14, 5, e.g.,]. Characterizing such fields calls for statistical descriptors of the correlation structure of the residuals rather than the fitting of individual features.

In this paper we explore the use of the second-order structure function, S2S_{2}, as a way to identify and characterize structure in an apparently noise-dominated velocity map. First introduced in Kolmogorov’s description of the inertial range of incompressible turbulence [20], the structure function is a standard descriptor of turbulent and geophysical flows and is widely used in terrestrial applications such as the study of atmospheric and oceanographic turbulence [23]. It has likewise seen extensive use in astronomical contexts, most prominently in characterizing turbulence in the interstellar medium and molecular clouds, including the size–linewidth relation of Larson [21], the velocity structure of molecular gas [25, 15] as well as in recovering the underlying velocity statistics from line-of-sight velocity centroids [9] and in quantifying fluctuations in the solar wind and magnetized astrophysical plasmas [6].

Given the long-standing assumption that protoplanetary disks exhibit some level of turbulence [22], our goal is to establish what the structure function can and cannot reliably recover from a disk velocity field, before applying it to real data. To this end we work with synthetic, correlated Gaussian random fields drawn natively on the disk polar grid, for which the true correlation structure is known by construction. We introduce a set of empirical heuristics together with a complementary parametric fit, and we build a noise-aware pipeline that de-noises at the level of S2S_{2} and assesses the significance of each measured quantity against matched noise-only null ensembles. With this machinery, implemented in the eddy package [32], we quantify the biases intrinsic to the method and determine which properties of the field remain recoverable in the presence of noise.

The layout of this manuscript is as follows. We start in Section II by describing the models we will use for the demonstration of this methodology. In Section III we introduce the structure function and build intuition through application to simple models. These models are extended in Section IV where we consider the impact of finite angular resolution and noise in our characterization. In Section V we apply the complete pipeline to velocity fields from numerical simulations of (magneto-)hydrodynamical instabilities, testing whether the velocity fields of these simulations can be identified and distinguished from one another. In Section VI we illustrate what the method recovers from real data, using observations of TW Hya, and in Section VII we discuss how it extends to inclined disks. We summarize our findings in Section VIII.

papers.title: Double Neutron Star Mergers and Fast Blue Optical Transients: A Circumbinary Disk Connection
papers.abstract: Post-common-envelope evolution (CEE) circumbinary disks (CBDs) form when part of the ejected envelope remains bound and circularizes around the stripped core and its companion. Leveraging results of scale-free hydrodynamical simulations, we develop a framework to model the effect of such disks on subsequent binary evolution, and implement it in the population synthesis code COMPAS. Applying our framework to double neutron star (DNS) merger progenitors, we find that CBDs generally induce substantial orbital shrinkage, changing the merging DNS population and lowering the overall merger rate. We explore an extensive grid of binary-evolution and disk models, and find that CBD interactions reduce the DNS merger rate by up to $28\%$, primarily through 'premature' mergers between the neutron star (NS) and the giant's core. These mergers may power luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs), occurring at a fiducial rate of $\simeq11 \:\rm Gpc^{-3} \rm yr^{-1}$. Our results indicate that natal kicks contribute little to LFBOT offsets, and that they should be associated with young stellar populations, though not necessarily active star-forming regions. Since LFBOT progenitors would otherwise produce short-delay DNS mergers, CBDs further challenge DNS mergers as the source of early r-process enrichment. For surviving DNS mergers, accretion from the disk leads to higher chirp masses, potentially explaining the puzzling mass of GW190425. Our framework provides a general tool for studying CBD-binary interactions in post-CEE systems.

Binaries are common across astrophysical scales, ranging from galaxy pairs to stellar and sub-stellar systems. In gas-rich environments, binarity often leads to the formation of circumbinary disks (CBDs), in which material settles into orbit around the binary as a whole rather than around either component individually (e.g., Dutrey et al. 29; Akeson et al. 3; Hoard et al. 56; Ragusa et al. 110; Liao et al. 81; Gallardo Cava et al. 38). The exchange of angular momentum and mass between the CBD and the binary through gravitational and accretion forces affects the binary’s evolution (e.g., Artymowicz and Lubow 5; Artymowicz and Lubow 6), driving either orbital decay or expansion.

The formation of CBDs around stellar binaries and their effect on the subsequent evolution of orbital separation and eccentricity has been extensively studied in recent years, with growing interest in CBDs around post-common-envelope evolution (CEE) binary systems (e.g., Kashi and Soker 66; Dermine et al. 24; Chen and Podsiadlowski 15; Izzard and Jermyn 61; Gagnier and Pejcha 37; Vetter et al. 150). If a binary survives dynamically unstable mass transfer, a fraction of the envelope material may remain bound to the system and fall back towards the inner binary. Since this gas carries substantial angular momentum, it cannot be re-accreted directly onto either component. Instead, it circularizes at radii comparable to a few times the post-CEE orbital separation, forming a rotationally supported CBD that can persist while it viscously spreads and is slowly accreted (e.g., see Pringle 109; Lai and Muñoz 76 for reviews).

For binaries that involve a neutron star (NS) or a black hole (BH), the interaction with a CBD formed around the compact object and exposed core of its companion after CEE (see Fig. 1) could affect the formation and merger rates of double compact objects (e.g., Vetter et al. 151; Wei et al. 160; Unger et al. 145). If angular momentum is transferred from the binary to the disk, the orbit shrinks, potentially bringing its components into the gravitational-wave (GW)–driven merger regime, or shortening the merger timescale in systems that were already supposed to merge. If the compact object and core of the giant get even closer due to their interaction with the CBD, they may ultimately merge, producing energetic transients such as luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs; e.g., Soker 125; Metzger 92; Tuna and Metzger 143; Cohen and Soker 19) and Ibn/Icn supernovae (SNe; e.g., Wei et al. 160); see Grichener 51 for a recent review. Conversely, if the binary system extracts angular momentum from the disk, the orbit widens, driving the two components further apart. This orbital widening can delay or even prevent the merger of double compact objects that would otherwise coalesce within the age of the Universe through GW emission.

papers.title: Prescribed Color Patterns in Tight Hamilton Cycles and Spanning Trees
papers.abstract: We compare transversal and pattern thresholds for two spanning structures. For every fixed $k\ge 3$ and $\alpha>0$, we prove that every sufficiently large $n$-vertex $k$-graph collection with minimum codegree at least $(1/2+\alpha)n$ contains a tight Hamilton cycle with any prescribed color pattern. Hence the transversal and pattern thresholds for tight Hamilton cycles coincide asymptotically. For spanning trees, we show that for every $\alpha>0$ there exists $c=c(\alpha)>0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph collection with minimum degree at least $(1/2+\alpha)n$ contains every $n$-vertex tree with maximum degree at most $n^c$ and any prescribed color pattern. On the other hand, we construct spanning trees of maximum degree $\sqrt n+1$ whose pattern threshold exceeds their transversal threshold by a positive linear term.

papers.title: MetricTrail: Revisiting the Power of Metric Depth and Local Optimization for Long-Sequence Streaming 3D Reconstruction
papers.abstract: We present MetricTrail, a streaming system for accurate camera motion estimation and dense reconstruction from long monocular videos. To keep inference efficient over long sequences, we revisit DPVO's sparse local estimator. We find that single-image metric depth substantially improves its trajectory accuracy, without retraining the correspondence network or enlarging the optimization window. Metric predictions initialize patch depths and remain as soft constraints during optimization. We further improve correspondence estimation through learned adapters that augment matching features and recurrent context with frozen DINOv3 representations. The correspondence estimator and adapters are trained on diverse short clips without additional long-sequence training. This modular design also allows the depth provider to be independently upgraded and supports supplied camera intrinsics and calibrated stereo observations without retraining. Under the reported RGB-only protocols, MetricTrail achieves the lowest average trajectory error among evaluated methods on KITTI, Oxford Spires, and VBR. Pairing the estimated poses with single-image depth predictions also produces strong dense reconstruction on indoor and outdoor benchmarks and coherent reconstructions of in-the-wild videos. With supplied intrinsics, the system processes KITTI-02 at 12.70 FPS with 3.21 GB peak GPU memory.

papers.intro:
Streaming 3D reconstruction turns thousands of monocular observations into a coherent geometric model of the world. For robotic navigation and large-scale mapping, this model must remain consistent as the camera moves through new environments and revisits familiar places. Over long trajectories, camera-motion and scale errors can accumulate, misaligning observations of the same scene. Maintaining consistency with manageable computation and memory is a central challenge for long-video reconstruction.

CUT3R [1] maintains a persistent recurrent state, but accumulated drift remains a challenge on very long sequences. LingBot-Map [2] structures attention memory to retain geometric information across time; for extremely long inputs, its windowed mode introduces alignment errors that can accumulate across window boundaries. Optimization-based camera estimation provides a complementary way to enforce multi-view consistency. ViPE [3] combines learned correspondences and metric-depth regularization with local tracking and global bundle adjustment (BA). However, its original pipeline performs global BA over all retained frames, including a final refinement after processing the full video, increasing memory and computation as the sequence grows.

papers.title: Data-Driven Configuration of Protective Separation Zones in Collaborative Robot Cells from Operator Occupancy
papers.abstract: The protective separation zone of a collaborative robot cell is commonly dimensioned for a worst case that disregards where the operator is actually present during the task. This paper presents a camera-based, data-driven method that configures this zone from observed operator occupancy. Operator positions accumulated over several production shifts are aggregated into an occupancy heatmap, from which a protective field is derived that trades off the achievable robot velocity against the required safety distance, following the speed and separation monitoring principle of ISO/TS 15066. The resulting configuration is advisory, that is, reviewed within the risk assessment rather than applied autonomously to the robot controller. The method, which builds on a pose-based perception pipeline with activity recognition, was evaluated in two operational cells at two industrial partners, where the protective field could be reduced by approximately 17% and a productivity increase of 9% was measured. However, adoption proved to depend on more than the demonstrated gain alone.

papers.intro:
Collaborative robots promise to combine the repeatability of automation with the flexibility of the human operator, and they have consequently attracted considerable attention as a means of automating tasks that resist full automation, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises [1, 2, 3]. Realising this promise in production, however, requires the shared workspace to be kept safe without sacrificing the very productivity that motivates the deployment [4, 5]. The present work is concerned with this tension in cells that implement speed and separation monitoring in the sense of ISO/TS 15066 [6].

Realising this promise in production, however, requires the shared workspace to be kept safe without sacrificing the very productivity that motivates the deployment [4, 5]. The present work is concerned with this tension in cells that implement speed and separation monitoring in the sense of ISO/TS 15066 [6].

The contribution of this work is twofold. First, a data-driven method for configuring the protective separation zone of a collaborative cell is presented: operator positions observed over time are aggregated into an occupancy heatmap, from which an optimised size of the protective field is derived that trades off the achievable robot velocity against the required safety distance, following the speed and separation monitoring principle of ISO/TS 15066. The result is advisory, that is, it is provided as a proposal reviewed within the risk assessment before adoption rather than applied autonomously to the robot controller. Second, the perception pipeline from which the occupancy is obtained is described, comprising pose-based person tracking and an activity recognition step that distinguishes interaction with the cell from unrelated traffic. Unlike prior fluency and safety approaches that are validated in simulation or in the laboratory under idealised perception (e.g., [7]), the proposed approach was developed and evaluated together with industrial partners in a real production setting, where occupancy estimation and activity recognition must contend with the occlusions, layouts and operator behaviour encountered on the shop floor.

papers.title: Distributed Optimization Involving Non-Lipschitzian, Linear Composite Functions: Unified Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well as globally coupling constraints including affine equality and nonlinear inequality. The terminal goal is to minimize the sum of local non-differentiable convex functions and proximable nonsmooth convex composite terms attached to linear operators, over networked multi-agent systems. This formulated framework not only applies in complex practical problems but also reduces to existing distributed optimization structures. To cope with technical issues caused by local linear mappings, potential multiple nonsmooth functions and coupling nonlinear constraints, we first derive a new local first-order condition, and further present a novel fully distributed optimization algorithm based on variable decompositions and proximal operators. Specifically, the proposed algorithm allows each agent to update states via local information exchange and through {locally fixed step-sizes}, and to find inexact solutions of subproblems without loss of convergence speed. In contrast to existing tailor-made algorithms for the bounded gradients of objective functions or affine constraints, our algorithm is capable of solving more practical cases involving general convex functions and nonlinear constraints. Under mild assumptions, the convergence rate $o(1/k)$ in terms of the optimality and successive-difference metrics is achieved, by constructing the equivalent variational inequalities of the proposed algorithm. Finally, numerical experiments on practical application problems illustrate the theoretical results.
