To date, a variety of efficient distributed algorithms have been explored for different optimization problems. In [3], the distributed subgradient method was first developed to solve unconstrained consensus optimization problems. After that, many gradient-based variants have appeared for such unconstrained problems in the literature, including the linearly convergent first-order method [4], proximal gradient algorithms for nonsmooth objectives [5], asynchronous distributed algorithms [6, 7], and another insightful approach [8] for time-varying networks. With the consideration of local constraints arising in consensus problems, the distributed stochastic algorithms for local feasible constraints [9, 10], the quasi-Newton method for linear (in)equality constraints [11], and distributed continuous-time algorithms [12, 13] for potential nonlinear constraints characterized by convex functions were successively proposed. However, the above methods do not cope well with global coupling constraints. Fortunately, these advancements [14, 15, 16, 17, 18] have made it possible to crack this difficulty. To be specific, a distributed method of multipliers was produced in [14] via the combination of dual lifting and operator splitting approaches, the discrete-time primal-dual algorithm based on region partitioning in [15] and proximal Jacobian alternating direction method of multipliers in [16] were further presented for linear coupling constraints. But [14] required two rounds of communication at each agent, and [16] used a coordinated step-size that is dependent on the number of agents. For the purpose of coping with coupling inequalities, a projected subgradient dynamics and modified Lagrangian function were integrated in [17] to produce distributed primal-dual methods in continuous-time setting, while a static penalty method was introduced in [18] for seeking approximate solutions to original problems. However, there still exist several challenges for distributed algorithm development and convergence analysis. First, practical objective functions may comprise multiple nonsmooth terms coupled with local linear mappings, making distributed proximal algorithms [5, 19, 20] designed for single nonsmooth terms computationally demanding. Although subgradient methods handle nonsmoothness, their oscillatory behavior necessitates additional conditions to ensure convergence, such as subgradient boundedness [3, 18], and local constraint boundedness [12, 13]. Second, the (weighted) Laplacian matrix is widely adopted to handle consensus and global coupling constraints [21, 15, 22, 19]. However, for convergence proofs, estimating the global Laplacian’s largest eigenvalue becomes challenging in large-scale networks, which also forces conservative step-size selections. Additionally, many distributed methods rely on specifically tailored Lyapunov functions for convergence analysis [15, 12, 13, 17], hindering the development of a unified framework capable of accommodating diverse objective and constraint structures. Third, while intricate optimization problems are tackled by efficient distributed algorithms, certain centralized computations remain unavoidable, such as solving local minimization subproblems [1, 23]. Moreover, consensus-based and non-consensus distributed problems are typically studied in isolation [19, 24]. Algorithms designed for one cannot be readily reused for the other due to the presence of edge-based equality constraints, local nonlinear constraints, and global coupling constraints. Finally, from a centralized perspective, general nonsmooth convex problems can be solved with sublinear convergence using first-order primal-dual methods [25], whereas NAMA [26] and SuperMann [27] respectively achieve linear and superlinear rates under strong convexity or metric subregularity. However, these methods operate in a centralized manner and are incapable of directly offering a distributed solution for the entire constraint structure inherent in problem (1).

papers.title: Graph Symbolic Distillation: Decoding Graph Data into Interpretable Formulas across Materials and Chemistry
papers.abstract: Graph data provide a natural representation of the interconnected structures and interactions underlying many chemical and materials systems. Graph neural networks (GNNs) can learn complex relationships from such data, yet translating these representations into interpretable descriptors and scientific insights remains challenging. Here we introduce graph symbolic distillation (GSD), a framework for decoding graph data into interpretable symbolic formulas. GSD identifies task-relevant message-passing architectures and distills their learned transformations while preserving graph connectivity and aggregation operations. Across three case studies spanning bulk materials, molecules, and surfaces, GSD not only recovers expert-defined descriptors from elementary node and edge features, but also reveals relationships emerging from their organization in complex graphs: extremal local geometric descriptors for band gap variations in $\gamma$-CsPbI$_3$, a local polarity--size relationship underlying hydration free energy, and site-specific electronic--connectivity coupling in multidentate adsorption. GSD thus provides a general route from graph data to interpretable descriptors and new, testable scientific insights.

papers.title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
papers.abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

Protein motif scaffolding asks whether a generative model can build a foldable protein scaffold around a prescribed set of functionally important residues. This task is central to the emerging field of generative protein design [24, 26], making benchmark quality especially important. A useful benchmark should reveal not only whether a model can reproduce a static motif geometry, but also which functional motifs are scaffoldable, which models fail systematically, and whether nominally successful designs remain stable under physically realistic conformational fluctuations [4].

This task is central to the emerging field of generative protein design [24, 26], making benchmark quality especially important. A useful benchmark should reveal not only whether a model can reproduce a static motif geometry, but also which functional motifs are scaffoldable, which models fail systematically, and whether nominally successful designs remain stable under physically realistic conformational fluctuations [4].

Existing motif-scaffolding benchmarks rely on static structure-level metrics: they evaluate a single predicted protein structure rather than its conformational behaviour over time. Standard evaluations ask whether a generated design can be refolded to recover the target motif in this single structure and whether the resulting scaffold is novel with respect to known proteins. While these are sensible and computationally scalable criteria, they do not assess whether the recovered motif remains stable under thermal fluctuations. Consequently, designs that satisfy conventional static benchmark criteria may nevertheless lose the required motif geometry during their natural conformational dynamics, potentially compromising their functional plausibility. This distinction is particularly important for catalytic and binding-site motifs, whose function depends on maintaining the correct geometry throughout their conformational dynamics rather than in a single predicted structure [28, 11, 1].

A central challenge in benchmarking protein scaffold generation is that evaluation protocols implicitly define what is considered a “successful” design, by the choice of metrics used. Here, we focus on the MotifBench [34] benchmark as a representative case study for scaffold-design evaluation. MotifBench adopts a now widely used evaluation paradigm that emerged from earlier generative modeling efforts such as RFDiffusion [29], FrameFlow [33], and Genie2 [14], and is increasingly reused in broader benchmarks including ProteinBench [32] and GeomMotif [23]. This paradigm is based on an inverse-folding plus refolding oracle, where candidate backbones are sequence-designed using ProteinMPNN [5] and subsequently validated via single-sequence structure prediction with ESMFold [15] (or, in earlier work, AlphaFold2 [31]). MotifBench develops this into a standardized and reproducible benchmark with fixed sampling protocols, success thresholds, and aggregation metrics, thereby reflecting its emergence as a de facto community baseline.

Here, we revisit the validity of this evaluation paradigm by assessing the dynamical stability of MotifBench “solved” designs. To cover the variety of state-of-the-art generative models for protein design and build upon previous benchmarks [34], we chose diffusion models, namely RFDiffusion [29] and Genie2 [14], the flow-matching models FrameFlow [33] and Proteina [10] and for the Protein Language Model domain DPLM2 [27] and ESM3 [12]. In this study, molecular dynamics (MD) analysis across diverse generative models indicates that many nominally “solved” cases exhibit substantial scaffold instabilities, with only a minority remaining fully stable under dynamical evaluation. These results suggest that the ProteinMPNN+ESMFold pipeline primarily captures self-consistency under a single folding model and tends to emphasize local motif reconstruction over global structural stability.

A larger and more systematically derived benchmark is therefore valuable even if it preserves the original ranking structure, because it reduces dependence on a narrow set of canonical cases and increases statistical resolution.

In this work, we introduce BILBY (Benchmarking Interactions, Landscapes, Backbone fidelity, and dYnamics), comprising two complementary resources for functional motif-scaffolding evaluation. First, BILBY-PRO is a systematically constructed benchmark of 220 functional motif-scaffolding problems derived from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries linked to experimentally resolved structures. Constructed independently of the original MotifBench dataset, BILBY-PRO adopts a compatible task representation and evaluation protocol. Second, we evaluate six recent scaffold-generation methods on both the original MotifBench panel and BILBY-PRO, revealing model-specific trade-offs between target coverage and unique-solution yield. Third, BILBY-MD provides a reference-based, dynamics-aware evaluation framework using explicit-solvent all-atom MD to assess motif geometry, scaffold stability, contact preservation, and conformational ensemble agreement. Here, we apply BILBY-MD to designs evaluated on the original MotifBench panel. Together, these contributions separate benchmark composition, static design success, and dynamical fidelity, demonstrating when static motif recovery does, and does not, translate into dynamically credible scaffold behavior.

papers.title: Online Optimization for Controlling HVAC Systems
papers.abstract: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems account for a significant portion of buildings' energy consumption, motivating the design of energy- and cost-efficient control strategies. However, conventional strategies employ simple, reactive control, without incorporating a model. Therefore, in this paper we adopt an economic model predictive control framework and focus on designing online algorithms to solve the control input design problems with a limited computational budget. In particular, we propose two tailored online algorithms based on projected gradient descent, with a custom projection routine, and the projected primal-dual method. We discuss the pros and cons of both algorithm designs, focusing in particular on computational efficiency. We further compare them through numerical experiments simulating the control of an HVAC system over the course of a day. The results show that computationally efficient online solvers for HVAC systems control are indeed possible. Moreover, the performance closely matches that of a baseline algorithm with unlimited computational budget, in terms of reference temperature tracking and comfort temperature range enforcement.

However, these methods are primarily reactive, as they do not exploit a model of the system’s evolution and predictions of future disturbances, which include fluctuations in outdoor temperature, occupancy , and solar irradiance [5, 6, 7]. Therefore, model predictive control (MPC) has been proposed as an alternative framework for controlling HVAC systems [8]. Beyond operational efficiency and user comfort, energy cost is also an important factor. For this reason, the economic MPC (E-MPC) framework has been further proposed to control HVAC systems [9, 10]. Indeed, E-MPC allows incorporating the time-varying price of electricity directly in the objective function alongside temperature control goals and constraints. In this paper, we thus adopt the E-MPC framework.

In this paper, we thus adopt the E-MPC framework.

Despite the advantages of the E-MPC framework, in practice it requires solving constrained optimization problems at every sampling instant. The resulting computational burden therefore can become a practical limitation, especially in light of two important factors: thermal inertia and hardware resources. Buildings, indeed, might be characterized by high thermal inertia, which means that the application of control inputs only very slowly regulates the temperature. It is therefore important to reduce the ratio between computation time and control input application as much as possible, so that temperature can be more effectively regulated during sampling intervals. The second factor are the computational resources available to implement HVAC systems controllers. These resources are in fact often limited, and computation-heavy control input design might not be possible [11], especially if the computation time exceeds the sampling interval. Therefore, in this paper we focus on designing efficient solvers for the HVAC E-MPC problem.

From an optimization perspective, HVAC E-MPC consists of a sequence of constrained optimization problems whose parameters change over time in response to fluctuations in energy prices, occupancy, outside temperatures, and past control inputs. The E-MPC problem therefore can be interpreted naturally as an online optimization problem [12, 13], and more specifically as feedback optimization [14]. Unlike static optimization problems, in online optimization the computational time is limited to the interval between the formulation of consecutive problems. The challenge then is to design algorithms that can approximate the problems’ solutions well, but in a limited time.

papers.title: Multi-epoch monitoring of the faint northern component in 3C 84 during 2016-2021
papers.abstract: We present the results of multi-epoch very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations of the sub-parsec-scale northern jet component of 3C 84 (known as the N1 component) at 7 mm from 2016 to 2021. The peak position of the N1 component exhibits positional variations of approximately 0.2 mas at a distance of about 2.5 mas from the central radio core (C1) throughout the observation period. Although a linear fit yields a small proper motion of $\mu_{\rm{Dec}}=0.054\pm0.019~\rm{mas}~\rm{yr}^{-1}$, corresponding to an apparent velocity of $\beta_{\rm{app}}=0.062\pm0.021$, this displacement is comparable to the observed positional scatter, and the hypothesis that N1 exhibits systematic motion is not statistically supported. In contrast, the peak flux density varies by approximately a factor of two on timescales of several months. We propose two possible explanations for the observed behavior of N1. One is that N1 is the counterpart of the southern hotspot C3, but its motion has been halted by a collision with a compact and dense cloud along its path; in this case, the flux variability may be caused by changes in the free-free absorption opacity of the non-uniform cloud. The other possibility is that N1 is part of the northern jet that is heavily obscured by foreground free-free absorption and is observed through a gap in the absorbing medium; in this case, the variability may reflect intrinsic changes in the jet and its interaction with a non-uniform ambient medium. These results provide new constraints on the physical origin of N1 and on the circumnuclear environment of 3C 84.

papers.intro:
Relativistic jets launched from active galactic nuclei (AGNs) can transport energy and momentum from the vicinity of the central supermassive black hole into their surrounding environment, and are an important channel of AGN feedback (Fabian, 2012, e.g.,). At the same time, the propagation and morphology of jets are affected by the physical conditions of the surrounding medium. Very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) provides a unique means of resolving the parsec- and sub-parsec-scale structures of these jets, where their propagation and interaction with the circumnuclear environment can be investigated (Zensus, 1997, e.g.,). Multi-epoch VLBI observations can further trace the motion and evolution of individual jet components, providing important constraints on their kinematics and on the medium through which the jets propagate.

The compact radio source 3C 84, hosted by the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1275, is located at the center of the Perseus cluster (z=0.0176). Thanks to its proximity, 3C 84 is one of the best laboratory to explore the central parsec-scale region of AGN in detail. The C3 component (see Figure 2 for component designations), which is located about one parsec south of the central radio core (the so-called C1 component), is a newborn approaching hotspot associated with the radio outburst that started in 2005 (Abdo et al., 2009; Nagai et al., 2010, and the references therein). Recent VLBI observations of C3 have revealed that the jet trajectory is disturbed by the interaction between the jet and the surrounding material (Nagai et al., 2017; Kino et al., 2018; Kino et al., 2021). The behavior of the C3 component revealed by these observations is consistent with results from a study employing the regularized maximum likelihood (RML) imaging method to achieve super-resolution (Foschi et al., 2025). These observations suggest that the ambient matter in the central parsec-scale region of 3C 84 is highly non-uniform.

Regarding the northern counter-lobe component, it is generally considered to be dimmed by free-free absorption (FFA) in the ionized gas associated with the accretion disk (Walker et al., 2000). Although the counterpart of C3 was undetectable for about 10 years between 2005 and 2015, a new component named N1 was detected in December 2015 (Fujita and Nagai, 2017; Wajima et al., 2020). Foschi et al. (2025) also report the detection of diffuse emission to the north of C1, which is consistent with the N1 component. At the time of its discovery at the end of 2015, N1 was naturally interpreted as the counter hotspot propagating at approximately the same speed as C3, since their distances from C1 are comparable.

We focus on 43 GHz VLBI observations for following reasons. First, the high angular resolution and imaging capability at 43 GHz enable us to resolve the sub-parsec-scale structure of 3C 84 and to isolate the relatively faint N1 component from the surrounding emission. Moreover, the 43 GHz VLBI arrays provide relatively stable and well-established observing capabilities over a wide range of observing epochs, which is important for long-term monitoring of the faint and diffuse N1 component. Second, FFA is less severe at 43 GHz than at lower frequencies, allowing us to probe the northern side of the source that is strongly obscured at lower frequencies. At the same time, the absorption is not necessarily negligible at 43 GHz, making this frequency particularly useful for investigating the interplay between the intrinsic jet structure and the foreground absorbing medium. Thus, 43 GHz offers a useful balance between angular resolution, and reduced FFA, enabling us to investigate both the kinematics of N1 and its possible connection to the absorbing circumnuclear medium.

papers.title: Design and Commissioning of the BURSTT-256 Main Antenna Array for the Fast Radio Burst Survey in the Local Universe
papers.abstract: The Bustling Universe Radio Survey Telescope in Taiwan (BURSTT) is a radio interferometer array designed for surveying fast radio bursts (FRBs) in the nearby Universe with a wide instantaneous field of view (FoV) of $\approx$6000 deg$^2$ and precisely localizing them with sub-arcsecond angular resolution. The first phase of BURSTT, BURSTT-256, consists of a main antenna array comprising 256 log-periodic dipole antennas (LPDAs) observing at 400-800 MHz for real-time beamforming and FRB search, currently with 256 beams covering $\approx$ 3200 deg$^2$ FoV, together with several smaller outrigger stations with 16-64 antennas and separated by $\mathcal{O}(10^2 - 10^3)$ km baselines for joint observations to localize FRBs using very-long baseline interferometry. This work presents the design, deployment, and commissioning of the BURSTT-256 main array, including site selection, radio-frequency (RF) background characterization, receiver antenna array and RF front-end, as well as real-time, factorized digital beamforming backend that currently generates 256 beams. The system's on-sky performance, sensitivity, and beamforming fidelity have been calibrated through observations of bright celestial calibrators. The antenna array in the initial phase using commercial LPDAs has a system equivalent flux density of $\approx$11 kJy, and is expected to achieve $\approx$4 kJy using custom-design LPDAs after optimization in late 2026. BURSTT-256 serves as a critical pathfinder for future expansion of the array to 2048 elements and beyond, operating at 300-700 MHz with $\approx$6000 deg$^2$ FoV. It establishes the framework required to discover and localize nearby FRBs with sub-arcsecond precision. By substantially increasing the number of well-localized nearby FRBs, BURSTT will facilitate multi-wavelength and multi-messenger counterpart identification, helping to unveil the elusive origin of FRBs.

papers.intro:
Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients of extragalactic origin, detected from 110 MHz110\text{\,}\mathrm{MHz} [43] up to 8 GHz8\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz} [16], with immense energy output of isotropic equivalent energies of 1028​–​103610^{28}\text{--}10^{36} erg\mathrm{erg}) [54]. As these coherent radio pulses traverse the intervening ionized astrophysical plasma, they undergo frequency-dependent dispersion which induces a characteristic quadratic arrival-time delay, Δ​t∝D​M⋅ν−2\Delta t\propto DM\cdot\nu^{-2} [54]. The magnitude of this delay is quantified by the dispersion measure (DM≡∫ne​𝑑l\mathrm{DM}\equiv\int n_{e}dl), representing the integrated column density of free electrons along the line of sight. FRBs typically exhibit DMs of 𝒪⁡(102​–​103)\mathcal{O}(10^{2}\text{--}10^{3}) pc/cm3\mathrm{pc}\text{/}{\mathrm{cm}}^{3}, with substantial excesses over the Galactic plasma contribution that confirm their extragalactic nature [15]. Their coherent pulses propagating over cosmological distances, currently confirmed up to redshift z≈2z\approx 2 (Caleb et al. 8), can potentially serve as a new cosmological probe, e.g., mapping the baryon distribution of the Universe [25, 20, 21]. For comprehensive reviews of the field, readers are referred to [41, 15, 42, 54, 55].

Since the first discovery in 2007 (Lorimer et al. 30, Lorimer et al. 31), more than 4000 FRBs have been discovered to date, with the vast majority (3641 unique sources) contributed by the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) FRB project (CHIME/FRB Collaboration et al. 9). The estimated all-sky FRB rate is ∼1000\sim 1000 per day for fluence above 5 Jy ms5\text{\,}\mathrm{Jy}\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} (CHIME/FRB Collaboration et al. 13). Despite the large number of samples, the precise physical origins of FRBs remain elusive. For example, a key phenomenological division exists within the population: while most FRBs appear as one-off events, about dozens of FRB sources emit multiple pulses and thus are called as “repeaters”, suggesting their non-catastrophic origin. Repeaters are found to exhibit emission properties distinct from non-repeaters, such as wider temporal durations and narrower spectral bandwidths [44]. This dichotomy prompts debate over whether repeaters and non-repeaters originate from distinct astrophysical populations or multiple progenitor formation channels, e.g., [19, 53]. It could be possible that repeating FRBs appear as one-off events due to the lack of a comprehensive FRB survey so far. To address this issue, a wide field-of-view instrument is important because it allows long-term continuous monitoring for each FRB source.

Local environments of FRB sources provide insightful implications for constraining the progenitor types. To scrutinize local environments of FRBs and fully characterize FRB’s intrinsic properties, localizing FRBs with arcsecond angular resolution or beyond is necessary to identify their host galaxies and even to the region within, and to facilitate coincident multi-wavelength and multi-messenger follow-up observations. To date, only more than a hundred of FRBs have been precisely localized to their host galaxies [31, 50, 11], revealing a highly diverse range of environments. However, most of localized FRBs are distant, with only a few exceptions within ∼\sim100 Mpc100\text{\,}\mathrm{Mpc} distance, e.g., one Galactic FRB 200428 which is associated with the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 [1, 6] with a coincident multi-wavelength (X-ray) counterpart observed [33, 26, 48]; and FRB 20200120E localized in a globular cluster in the nearby M81 galaxy (Kirsten et al. 22); repeating FRB 20181030A hosted by NGC 3252 at ∼\sim20 Mpc20\text{\,}\mathrm{Mpc} distance [5]; and FRB 20231229A at ∼\sim90 Mpc90\text{\,}\mathrm{Mpc} distance [11].

The lack of well-localized FRBs in the local Universe is mainly because most, if not all, of existing telescopes discovering the FRBs are not specifically designed for FRB surveys. Traditional large-aperture single-dish telescopes — such as Parkes, Green Bank, and FAST telescopes — offer high sensitivity to detect fainter bursts at farther distances to probe larger cosmological volumes. However, they alone do not have adequate angular resolution to localize FRBs to their host galaxies, and their small field of view (FoV) limits their ability to monitor the sky with high cadence or for a long time, and consequently, repeaters may get misclassified as one-off events. Telescopes consisting of arrays of dish antennas, either ones dedicated to FRB survey, e.g., Deep Synoptic Array-110 (DSA-110; Law et al. 24, Sharma et al. 50), or those in commensal mode, e.g., CRAFT at Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP; Shannon et al. 49), MeerTRAP at MeerKAT (Rajwade et al. 47), and SPOTLIGHT at Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT; Panda et al. 39), improve the localization capability with the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique, but their FoV is still limited to 𝒪⁡(10)\mathcal{O}(10) deg2{\mathrm{deg}}^{2}. However, the FoV is still narrow for long-term monitoring or for covering a substantial amount of the full sky. All of these highlight the necessity of a dedicated telescope which has both wide FoV and localization capabilities.

papers.title: Learning Robotic World Models with Semantic and Visual Feedback
papers.abstract: Robot world models predict action-conditioned future visual states to support robotic planning and decision making. However, visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation alone provides limited constraints on fine-grained visual errors, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback. We present RoboImagine, a framework for post-training autoregressive robotic world models through candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback. Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared visual observations, action sequences, and task instructions. A frozen multimodal evaluator provides task-relevant semantic preferences through pairwise video comparisons in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback that constrains local structural and appearance errors. These signals drive policy optimization through group-relative advantages. Fixed initial context and branch-specific rolling histories support long-sequence generation with bounded context and consistent conditioning between candidate generation and policy optimization. Experiments with separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa cover real-world and simulated manipulation. On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts, and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show that diverse search improves prediction quality and that combined semantic and visual feedback yields higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Rolling histories further improve long-horizon prediction. These results support improving visual fidelity, task relevance, and long-horizon prediction through candidate comparison and complementary feedback.

papers.intro:
Robot world models predict how scenes evolve under actions, enabling robots to assess potential outcomes before execution [1, 2, 3, 4]. As learnable internal simulators, they support planning, policy evaluation, and long-horizon reasoning [5, 6, 7, 8]. Unlike generic video generation, which primarily emphasizes visual quality, robot world models must capture action-induced state changes, object contacts, and interactions to provide reliable guidance for manipulation decisions [9, 10]. Visual observations describe the current scene, action sequences specify the execution process, and natural-language instructions provide task goals; together, they form the multimodal context for understanding and predicting robot interactions. Prediction quality therefore depends not only on visual fidelity, but also on how accurately the model captures physical evolution under the given actions and its relationship to the task goal [11, 12].

Prediction quality therefore depends not only on visual fidelity, but also on how accurately the model captures physical evolution under the given actions and its relationship to the task goal [11, 12].

However, evaluating predicted futures remains a central challenge in training robot world models. Existing methods typically use maximum-likelihood, reconstruction, or perceptual objectives [10, 13, 14, 15]. These objectives provide effective visual supervision, but visual similarity alone does not fully capture task-relevant changes. For example, a prediction that preserves scene appearance may still miss action-induced object displacement or changes in contact. Conversely, multimodal semantic evaluation assesses visible task progress using instructions and scene context, yet may be insufficiently sensitive to local structural distortions and fine-grained appearance errors. As Figure 1 illustrates, visual fidelity and task semantics provide complementary perspectives on prediction quality. Aligning robot world models therefore calls for both forms of feedback: constraining visual detail while assessing whether predicted state transitions are plausible under the given actions and task conditions.

Prior work explores reward-based post-training for robotic world models [16]. RLVR-World rewards action-conditioned forecasts using visual prediction metrics [10]. RoboAlign-R1 [17] distills a vision–language judge into a lightweight reward model that scores individual generated videos. Such semantic feedback motivates a broader question: how should alternative futures be constructed and evaluated to provide informative learning signals? Absolute video scores require calibration across scenes and tasks, whereas futures generated under shared observations, actions, and instructions can be compared directly for visible task progress. However, nearly identical candidates provide little basis for comparison, and semantic preferences alone may overlook local visual errors. Effective comparative learning must therefore address both candidate construction and feedback design. We investigate how diverse candidate futures and complementary semantic and visual feedback jointly shape the learning of robotic world models.

papers.title: PlayGen2: Learning Real-Time Playable Worlds with Explicit 3D State
papers.abstract: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties these requirements to view-dependent appearance synthesis, making it difficult to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generation and interaction. We present PlayGen2, a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering. PlayGen2 maintains a persistent world memory comprising static geometry represented by a volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed 3D states for the player and other entities. Within a fixed-size local region, its world-state model jointly learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery, committing updates to a persistent world memory. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction. Using Doom as a testbed, we demonstrate that the model successfully learns world dynamics including geometry-aware player motion and player--NPC interactions. The framework is computationally efficient, enabling the complete simulation and rendering pipeline to achieve approximately 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. These capabilities demonstrate the transferability and extensibility of the learned game-world model. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.

papers.intro:
Playing in a generated world requires more than a sequence of plausible images. A player expects a corridor to remain in place after turning away, a wall to constrain movement, and nearby entities to evolve while controls remain responsive. These expectations concern a world that persists and changes under interaction, not merely the appearance of its next frame. Building a playable world model therefore requires bringing together low-latency control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions (Yang et al., 2024; Garcin et al., 2026; Duan et al., 2026).

Playing in a generated world requires more than a sequence of plausible images. A player expects a corridor to remain in place after turning away, a wall to constrain movement, and nearby entities to evolve while controls remain responsive. These expectations concern a world that persists and changes under interaction, not merely the appearance of its next frame. Building a playable world model therefore requires bringing together low-latency control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions (Yang et al., 2024; Garcin et al., 2026; Duan et al., 2026).

Action-conditioned video generation offers a compelling route toward this goal (Bruce et al., 2024). Systems such as GameNGen (Valevski et al., 2025) and PlayGen (Yang et al., 2024) demonstrate that neural models can simulate gameplay and support real-time interaction directly from visual histories. However, when generated frames serve as the sole recurrent world representation, the model must use the same view-dependent signal to preserve geometry, track entities, predict their interactions, and synthesize appearance. Information outside the current view must be recovered from visual memory (Garcin et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026), and errors in generated visual histories can propagate through autoregressive prediction (Valevski et al., 2025). Moreover, a pixel-based interface does not directly expose entity states for editing, participant composition, or rule-based interventions (Po et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). To address these problems, recent work has begun to separate simulation from rendering (Garcin et al., 2026; Duan et al., 2026; Po et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). This separation, however, does not by itself determine how to learn a persistent game world that both evolves under interaction and expands through exploration.

Information outside the current view must be recovered from visual memory (Garcin et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026), and errors in generated visual histories can propagate through autoregressive prediction (Valevski et al., 2025). Moreover, a pixel-based interface does not directly expose entity states for editing, participant composition, or rule-based interventions (Po et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). To address these problems, recent work has begun to separate simulation from rendering (Garcin et al., 2026; Duan et al., 2026; Po et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). This separation, however, does not by itself determine how to learn a persistent game world that both evolves under interaction and expands through exploration.

Inspired by the explicit world state maintained by traditional game engines, we organize learned game-world simulation around two complementary processes. State transition predicts how the player and other existing entities evolve, conditioned on player actions and the current world state. Incremental world generation completes previously unknown geometry and introduces newly encountered entities. These processes are coupled through a shared, persistent 3D state: newly generated geometry provides context for subsequent state transitions, while the resulting player motion determines which previously unknown regions need to be generated next. We therefore seek to jointly learn incremental world generation and action-conditioned state transitions, while keeping appearance synthesis separate.

Inspired by traditional game engines, we organize the world state into static geometry and dynamic entities. Static geometry is represented as a volumetric occupancy grid, while dynamic entities have identity-indexed states describing their 3D bounding volumes, semantic classes, and motion attributes. papers.title: Responsible GenAI Use During Active Armed Conflict: Evidence from Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms
papers.abstract: Armed conflict can increase the value of Generative AI (GenAI) while undermining the conditions required for its responsible use. Yet the perspectives of community-based humanitarian responders working under these conditions remain underrepresented in responsible AI research. We examine GenAI use in Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), a community-led humanitarian network, through an exploratory survey of 89 respondents and 15 semi-structured interviews with GenAI users and non-users. War reconfigures GenAI's role, making it most useful where its outputs are hardest to verify. ERR responders turned to GenAI when conflict made human expertise difficult or dangerous to reach. However, participants cautioned that GenAI could not independently establish rapidly changing local conditions, and that relying on its outputs could lead to harmful decisions when human verification was difficult. Risks arose before GenAI was used. For some volunteers, carrying a phone or accessing the internet could expose them to danger. Others were concerned that sharing sensitive beneficiary or operational information with GenAI could put people at risk. Participants feared that AI-assisted reports could undermine their credibility with donors, whose funding sustains the food and medical aid ERRs provide. Access to GenAI was uneven, and volunteers using it sometimes relied on colleagues with relevant expertise or local knowledge to verify its results. Our findings show that responsible use of GenAI during conflict depends not only on model performance or individual adoption, but also on whether responders can safely access these tools, verify their outputs against local conditions, and recognize when limiting or avoiding GenAI is the more responsible choice.

papers.intro:
Armed conflict affects civilians by causing harm, death, displacement, and limiting access to basic needs such as food, water, and health care. Its effects are widespread; in 2025, 117.8 million people were forcibly displaced, including 68.7 million displaced within their countries (International Committee of the Red Cross, 2026; United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, 2026). In Sudan, since fighting started in April 2023, 9.3 million people have been displaced within the country, and 4.3 million have crossed into neighboring countries. In 2026, 33.7 million people there require urgent humanitarian assistance, and 37% of health facilities are non-functional (World Health Organization, 2026). International humanitarian organizations have faced access and capacity constraints, increasing the importance of locally led mutual aid like Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), a community-led volunteer network that provides humanitarian assistance during the war in Sudan (Carter and Satti, 2026). The term “Rooms” refers to the WhatsApp group chats through which volunteers initially organized their emergency response activities (Olson et al., 2024).

papers.title: Angle Estimation for Initial Access in True-Time-Delay Systems: Communication and Sensing Tradeoff
papers.abstract: In joint communication & sensing (JCNS) the data signal is used to obtain parameter estimates. An example is the angle of arrival (AoA) which can be used to solve the initial access problem of beam selection. true-time delay (TTD) arrays are attractive for this purpose, as their frequency-dependent response encodes the angle information in the receive signal power spectrum. This work investigates the tradeoff between angle estimation accuracy and achievable data rate for uplink signals in a TTD array. The Fisher information (FI) for the angle is used to find the bayesian Cramer-Rao lower bound (BCRLB) under the assumption of a raised cosine distributed angle prior. Maximization of the FI under a data rate constraint is solved by waterfilling power per frequency bin dependent on sensing weights. Compared to a frequency flat signal, the optimized power allocation increases the FI \approx 4.9 dB at 5% rate loss for prior width of \pm 10{\deg}. Numerical simulations show that the derived BCRLB can be attained by a maximum likelihood (ML) estimator above an signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) threshold, confirming that the FI underlying the waveform design is attainable.

papers.intro:
In 6G systems, JCNS will play an important role by transforming cell infrastructures into perceptive networks [1]. Parameter estimates such as the AoA, derived from sensing, are key enablers of smart, context-aware mobile communication systems [2]. They can be used for beam selection, localization, object tracking, and for the synchronization and calibration of increasingly large antenna arrays in MIMO (MIMO) systems [3].

TTD arrays apply a frequency-dependent phase shift, resulting in a frequency dependent beam. Recently, they have regained interest for fast beam training [4] in initial access procedures. The property of frequency selectivity makes TTD arrays attractive for sensing, as the AoA information is contained in the frequency response of the combined receive signal. Angle estimation methods for TTD systems include OMP (OMP) and ML based estimation [5], LMMSE (LMMSE) [6] or correlation- and model-based estimators [7].

In JCNS, the waveform serves a dual purpose of communication and sensing. Existing works on waveform design optimize the tradeoff between communication rate and sensing metrics such as the CRLB (CRLB) [2], and characterize the fundamental limits of this tradeoff for Gaussian channels [8]. In the case of TTD arrays, the sensing information and communication performance depend both on the power allocation over frequency bins. To the best of our knowledge this tradeoff has not been studied for TTD arrays. In an uplink sensing scenario, the BS (BS) configures pilot and data allocation for the UE (UE), so that the waveform design choice is a scheduling decision at the BS.

papers.title: GuidedWAM: Training-Free Energy Guidance for World Action Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.

The generative model learns the driving policy simultaneously with a visual world model, where the policy inherits the physical and visual knowledge of a large video prior, and the model can imagine the future driving scene [29, 37, 25, 31]. Recent WAMs reach planning scores above 90 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 [8, 29, 37].

Despite these advantages, WAMs come with their own drawbacks. By training as a whole, the driving objectives freeze once the training is finished and cannot be extended at will. In practice, a driving policy has to serve objectives that change with the operating context during deployment: a wider margin to the road edge on a narrow street, a larger clearance around vulnerable road users, a temporal speed limit, or a passenger’s comfort preference. A WAM learns its driving behavior mainly from driving data. Sampling-time condition is only possible if such driving objectives are available in the data during training. Adding one means collecting supervision for it and retraining a billion-parameter model, which has to be repeated for every new objective. What is missing is a control channel that acts on the frozen model at sampling time.

papers.title: How Generative AI Redefines Personalization and Diversity in the Newsroom
papers.abstract: The tension between news personalization and information diversity has traditionally been understood as a matter of different content reaching different people, with diversity evaluated by the range of sources, topics, and perspectives to which audiences are exposed. Generative AI outdates this understanding, since it transforms personalization in two ways: how journalists adapt news to audiences and how the AI tools journalists use personalize content production to their own preferences. Drawing on 16 semi-structured interviews with media professionals across public service, commercial, and state-affiliated news settings, we examine how these practices reshape editorial judgment and the conditions under which news diversity is produced. We find that participants negotiate AI integration by maintaining authority over meaning while delegating aspects of content presentation. Yet the tools they adapt for their own work also mediate which sources and perspectives become available, introducing diversity-relevant decisions that remain largely invisible to organizational oversight. While participants anticipate diversity risks in audience-facing personalization, they predominantly interpret diversity-imposed limitations in their own tools as technical problems. As a result, decisions that shape news diversity increasingly occur before publication and across multiple versions of a story, where neither evaluation of published items nor human approval can readily observe them. Journalists thus remain formally responsible for outcomes shaped by decisions they cannot fully see or control. Our findings highlight that safeguarding news diversity requires looking beyond published content to the professional practices, infrastructures, and distributions of control that shape it.

papers.intro:
Personalization and diversity are central to how news media serve the public, yet balancing them is a longstanding challenge (Van den Bulck and Moe, 2018). Personalization can make news more relevant and accessible to individual audiences, while tailoring news to individual preferences can narrow exposure to information beyond those preferences and fragment shared public knowledge (Helberger et al., 2018). Research on digital news personalization has primarily examined how news services select and distribute existing stories (Thurman and Schifferes, 2012; Bodó, 2019). Drawing on Napoli’s distinction between source diversity (who produces news), content diversity (what is produced), and exposure diversity (what audiences encounter) (Napoli, 1999), much of this work addresses exposure diversity: whether recommendations broaden or narrow what audiences encounter (Möller et al., 2018), how diversity can be measured in recommendations (Vrijenhoek et al., 2021), whether personalization fragments publics (Nechushtai and Lewis, 2019). These approaches generally take the news item as its unit of analysis, assuming a relatively stable piece of journalistic content that can be selected and distributed to different audiences.

These approaches generally take the news item as its unit of analysis, assuming a relatively stable piece of journalistic content that can be selected and distributed to different audiences.

Generative AI (GenAI) challenges the assumption of a relatively stable news item as the unit of analysis. News personalization no longer involves only selecting which stories reach different audiences; the stories themselves can also be adapted. A single report can take different lengths, languages, formats, and emphases for different audiences, potentially changing which facts, contexts, and perspectives each reader encounters. At the same time, GenAI expands where personalization can occur. Journalists and other newsroom practitioners can configure general-purpose AI tools to suit their professional needs and workflows. As these individually adapted tools support research, sourcing, and drafting, they may shape which sources, information, and perspectives practitioners encounter and draw upon in producing news. We conceptualize these developments as two-way personalization: tool personalization, which shapes the information and tools through which reporting is produced and audience personalization, which shapes how reporting reaches different readers.

GenAI does not merely introduce new biases into journalism; it changes where diversity-relevant decisions occur and whether conventional evaluation and oversight can observe them. Existing approaches to news diversity have provided important ways of examining who produces news (Voakes et al., 1996), what information is published (Masini et al., 2018; Loecherbach et al., 2020), and which news items audiences encounter (Helberger et al., 2018; Möller et al., 2018; Vrijenhoek et al., 2021). However, evaluating published output alone overlooks two consequential forms of AI mediation. Before publication, individually configured AI tools can shape which sources and perspectives become available for editorial consideration, leaving relevant omissions invisible in the resulting report. After publication, generative adaptation can produce multiple versions of the same story that retain its overall subject while differing in essential claims, evidential qualifications, or context. These extend familiar concerns about source bias and inaccurate rewriting, but they arise where conventional evaluation does not look. They reveal the limits of treating finished news items as sufficient objects of diversity evaluation, and human approval as sufficient evidence of editorial control. Governance increasingly rests on the latter: the EU AI Act, for example, exempts AI-generated public-interest text from disclosure when it has undergone human review or editorial control and a person holds editorial responsibility (European Parliament and Council, 2024). We make the following contributions:

An empirical account of two-way personalization. We show how practitioners adapt news for audiences and AI tools to their work (Figure 1). They regard changes to news form as more readily delegable to GenAI than changes to meaning, yet this boundary is difficult to maintain in practice. They also exercise editorial judgment through personally configured tools that may fall outside organizational oversight. Practitioners frame the risks of these two forms of personalization differently: they anticipate diversity risks in audience personalization, while treating limitations in their own AI-assisted sourcing primarily as accuracy problems that better prompting or more capable models could resolve.

papers.title: MUSS: A Multi-scale and Sequence-based Model for Single-cell Gene Regulation
papers.abstract: Modeling gene regulation in single cells requires jointly representing DNA sequence, chromatin accessibility, and gene expression across regulatory scales. Sequence-based models capture DNA-level regulatory grammar but often lack cell-level resolution, whereas many single-cell omics models represent genes and peaks as fixed-vocabulary tokens without their underlying sequence. Here, we present MUSS, a sequence-based multi-scale model for single-cell gene regulation that preserves both DNA-level and cell-level resolution. MUSS derives peak- and gene-level representations from DNA using a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder and integrates them through peak-peak self-attention and distance-biased peak-gene interactions. Peak masked language modeling followed by training on paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq aligns these representations with cell-specific regulatory states. Across gene expression prediction, enhancer-gene linking, motif-guided regulatory prioritization, and zero-shot cell clustering, MUSS achieves strong performance against sequence-based and single-cell omics baselines. It further predicts expression for genes and peaks unseen during task training. These results support sequence-grounded, multi-scale representations for decoding cell-type-specific regulatory programs. Code, datasets, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/MUSS_neurips26.

Transcription factors (TFs) bind specific DNA motifs in accessible regulatory regions and influence target genes through combinatorial interactions spanning kilobases to megabases [27, 34, 20]. Modeling this process requires both the sequence content of regulatory elements and the cell-specific chromatin state in which they operate. Paired single-cell chromatin accessibility (scATAC-seq) and expression (scRNA-seq) measurements provide an opportunity to connect these scales, while large-scale genomic and single-cell models supply transferable representations [11, 50, 33, 9, 49].

Existing approaches capture complementary aspects of regulation. Sequence-to-function models such as Borzoi and AlphaGenome predict functional readouts within genomic windows, while GET combines sequence-derived features with accessibility [28, 2, 16]. These approaches do not directly integrate the genome-wide accessibility state of each individual cell with a shared representation of its peaks and genes. Recent work, notably scooby, does extend sequence-based prediction to single-cell resolution using a cell-specific decoder [22]. In parallel, single-cell omics models learn cell-state-dependent gene or peak representations from expression and accessibility data [38, 9, 21, 44, 24, 8]. However, fixed-vocabulary representations do not by themselves provide sequence-grounded embeddings for previously unseen regulatory entities. The remaining challenge is to unify DNA-derived peak and gene representations with cell-specific context across regulatory scales.

We propose Muss (Figure 1), which derives both peak and gene embeddings from a frozen DNA sequence encoder. A multi-scale encoder models dependencies among accessible peaks through self-attention and exchanges information between peaks and genes through distance-biased cross-attention. Peak masked language modeling learns accessibility context, and subsequent supervision on paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq connects this context to gene expression. A genomic region absent from task training can still be encoded from its sequence and processed by the same interaction layers. Our contributions are: • Unified multi-scale regulatory modeling. A shared sequence-based representation links DNA, chromatin accessibility, and cell-state-dependent gene expression through peak–peak and peak–gene interactions. • Generalization beyond the training vocabulary. Held-out-region experiments across four paired datasets demonstrate expression prediction for unseen genes and peaks, alongside transfer to unseen cell types. • Reusable regulatory representations. Enhancer–gene linking, motif-guided prioritization, zero-shot clustering, and few-shot adaptation assess transfer beyond expression prediction. Additional baselines and cross-task ablations distinguish these gains from those of sequence embeddings alone. Related work is discussed further in Appendix A.

papers.title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.

papers.intro:
Three-dimensional (3D) computed tomography (CT) data possess an intrinsic, multi-scale hierarchical structure where local voxel-level textures are nested within anatomical organs, which in turn follow a natural spatial arrangement within the body. Clinical text mirrors this hierarchy, as reports are typically organized into organ-specific findings and global impressions. Unifying these domains requires learning joint representations that bridge fine-grained anatomical details with holistic bodily context, a balance that remains a key challenge for medical vision-language models.

While recent progress in vision-language (VL) models has revolutionized natural image understanding, standard 3D medical approaches often treat volumes and reports as flat sequences, effectively discarding these essential structural inductive biases [19]. The MambaHoME architecture [36] recently introduced hierarchical routing, but solely for vision inputs, and the challenge of jointly modeling vision-language cross-modal hierarchies in a unified representation remains an open problem. Existing medical VL models have largely focused either on global alignment [7] or localized patches [52]. More recent efforts introduce anatomy-aware priors [47, 41, 10], yet they frequently treat image and text hierarchies as separate or auxiliary concerns. To the best of our knowledge, no previous work has unified the hierarchical routing of 3D vision tokens with the semantic hierarchy of clinical reports into a single, differentiable framework for image analysis.

To bridge this gap, we introduce MedHiVE, a Medical Hierarchical Vision–Language Experts framework, designed to exploit multi-scale structural priors. We encode each CT volume and its report into global and anatomy-level representations, using a long-context text encoder [28] for the report and voxel-wise organ masks for the volume. We propose a hierarchical multimodal encoder with two-level, slot-based Soft MoE routing over global tokens and anatomy-level representations from both vision and text. Global vision tokens and paired global text tokens are softly grouped and processed by global experts, while anatomy-level image and text representations are handled in parallel by local experts. These global and anatomy-aware slots are concatenated and routed through a second SMoE layer with shared experts for joint vision–language processing. To enrich learned representations, we apply a contrastive loss to align vision-language representations on both local and global scales. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. Hierarchical vision–language architecture operating on anatomy-level representations and global tokens from both vision and text, using slot-based SMoE routing through anatomy-specific and global vision and language experts. 2. Local-global vision–language contrastive learning that jointly optimizes scan–report and anatomy–snippet objectives, aligning representations across global and anatomical scales. 3. Anatomy-aware supervision that combines organ masks with automatically extracted organ-specific report snippets, enabling organ-level alignment without sentence-level labels.

papers.title: A diameter-one set in $\mathbb{R}^5$ that cannot be covered by six diameter-one balls
papers.abstract: We construct a compact set of diameter $1$ in $\mathbb{R}^5$ which cannot be covered by six Euclidean balls of diameter $1$. Its convex hull is a full-dimensional convex body satisfying the same property. Moreover, a finite subset of diameter $1$ cannot be covered by six closed balls even when their radius is increased to $0.50001$. The compact set is the quadratic image of the unit sphere in the space of symmetric $3\times3$ matrices of trace zero. A hypothetical cover leads to twelve spherical ellipses covering ${\mathbb S}^2$ and arranged in six antipodal pairs. Using Euler's formula, we replace them by twelve pentagonal regions contained in the ellipses. An area estimate then gives a contradiction.

papers.title: Optical Network Digital Twin: From Digital Coherent Transmission to Intelligent Network Operations
papers.abstract: Optical Network Digital Twins (ONDTs) are emerging as a key framework for representing, synchronizing, and utilizing the physical state of optical networks for quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, optimization, and intelligent operation. This survey provides a comprehensive view of ONDTs, spanning digital coherent transmission and physical-layer observability to intelligent network operations. We systematically organize ONDT technologies from ecosystem, functional, control, and implementation architecture perspectives and review the enabling technologies required to construct, synchronize, and utilize digital representations of physical optical networks. As a unifying framework to describe both ONDT design and validation, we introduce a categorization based on the following figures of merit: Fidelity, Dynamicity, and Deployability (FDD). In particular, we emphasize fit-for-purpose Fidelity, where modeling effort focuses on the physical effects of components rather than solely maximizing model accuracy, favoring scalability and generalizability. Furthermore, experimental and field validations are examined to evaluate the practical applicability of ONDT technologies. We further examine experimental and field validations, from physics-based QoT estimation and measurement-informed model refinement to field synchronization, service provisioning, multi-domain observability, and infrastructure characterization. Finally, we discuss the complementary roles of ONDTs and AI agents toward autonomous optical networks and identify key research directions for practical deployment.

papers.intro:
Digital twin (DT) technology collects real-world data and enables simulation, prediction, optimization, fault location, predictive maintenance, condition monitoring, process control, and performance evaluation. It is emerging as a means to manage the inherent complexity and uncertainty of large-scale physical systems. Recently, the emergence of Physical Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increased the need for reliable digital representations of real-world systems. DT technology is increasingly recognized as a key enabler for achieving secure and reliable Physical AI systems. In this perspective, it is essential to clearly articulate the value gained after DT adoption in terms of the initial investment costs required to develop and build DT. To this end, one important requirement is Fidelity, referring to the ability of a DT to capture and faithfully reproduce the behavior of the target physical system. Sufficient Fidelity for target applications enables reliable analysis, optimization, and operational decisions about physical systems. This feature is particularly important in scenarios where potential impact of actions must be evaluated and explained beforehand, such as cases in which a potential impact can affect multiple users or spread between interconnected systems or in which system restoration would require a relatively long time.

The second important requirement here is Dynamicity. Dynamicity appropriate to target applications can provide greater operational benefits and a clearer return on investment. While the advantages of Dynamicity depend on the application targeted by DT, high Dynamicity can open the way to new applications and even enable fundamentally new operational formats that could not be achieved without the benefits provided by a DT architecture. Fig. 1(a) shows DT application mapping along the axes of Fidelity and Dynamicity. The emergence of new connectivity demands driven by datac enter interconnects (DCI) and AI infrastructures has created new opportunities for Optical Network Digital Twin (ONDT) adoption, especially in applications that require both high fidelity and fast synchronization. The third important requirement is Deployability. Fig. 1(b) shows the design space for practical ONDT deployment. The horizontal axis represents the extent of infrastructure reuse and associated capital expenditure (CAPEX), while the vertical axis represents operational impacts such as changes to operation/business support systems, operational workflows, and workforce training. High deployability is achieved by maximizing infrastructure reuse while minimizing operational impact, as highlighted in Fig. 1(b). Especially, deploying ONDT to support emerging DCI/AI services over existing carrier optical line systems represents an important practical use case. ONDT deployment does not inherently require the addition or replacement of physical network elements. It is also important that ONDT can be easily applied to upgrading existing infrastructure, such as carrier line systems, because deploying new optical-fiber infrastructure requires not only equipment and materials but also large-scale civil engineering work and labor, resulting in substantial costs and deployment time. Historically, carrier optical networks have evolved as the base layer of carrier-grade infrastructures supporting a huge number of users on Fiber to the Home (FTTH) and cellular services, so they have had to be highly reliable and robust. Meanwhile, carriers must continuously extend, upgrade, and maintain the infrastructure while satisfying the Service Level Agreement (SLA) for an ever-increasing number of users.

Coherent transponders can provide rich physical-layer telemetry and standardized management interfaces that can be leveraged by ONDT applications without requiring changes to the underlying line system (see Sec. II-A2). Leveraging their existing observability and programmability provides a practical entry point for ONDT-based operations while minimizing changes to the existing infrastructure. Digital coherent transmission also simplifies optical network design by enabling receiver-side chromatic dispersion (CD) compensation using digital signal processing (DSP) and eliminating the need for dedicated optical dispersion compensation elements. Gaussian Noise (GN) models reduce the computational complexity of estimating fiber nonlinear impairments and enable network-level design and optimization. The digitalization of coherent transceivers (TRxs) has also accelerated the standardization of management interfaces and data models, enabling telemetry and software-defined network operations as described later in Sec. Conventional optical networks have traditionally been designed and deployed based on long-term traffic forecasts and capacity planning. Once deployed, their physical configuration typically remains relatively static for long periods of time and changes primarily due to increased traffic and network failures [1]. However, with the rapid growth of AI and cloud computing, the factors that determine connectivity demand are beginning to change. In distributed computing infrastructures for AI, machine-to-machine traffic is increasingly influenced by constraints such as regional power availability, where data must be stored and processed, and data sovereignty requirements, in addition to the placement and utilization of computing resources. These constraints are driving the geographical distribution of compute and data resources across hyperscale, regional, and on-premises datacenters. Of particular relevance to coherent optical transport networks is the emergence of scale-across connectivity, which interconnects geographically distributed AI computing resources. Although large-scale AI training across multiple data centers has not yet become a widely deployed commercial use case, advanced demonstrations are already emerging [2]. Moreover, this evolution involves not only the spatial distribution of computing and data resources but also temporal variations in their utilization. Measurements from production hyperscale cloud data centers have demonstrated clear daily periodicity, including traffic peaks and valleys over the course of a day, as well as application-dependent traffic distributions. Real traffic is also highly non-uniform and can exhibit hot spots, motivating monitoring-based bandwidth allocation and network reconfiguration [3]. Also, concerns about data security and privacy are driving governments and enterprises to adopt distributed sovereign cloud architectures [4]. Given this trend, the geographical distribution of DCs is accelerating, and as a result, the demand for large-capacity and flexible DCI networks is rapidly increasing [5].

papers.title: Spin supersolid in triangular lattice easy-axis spin-1/2 antiferromagnet: a fermionic parton perspective
papers.abstract: We study the supersolid order of the spin-1/2 easy-axis XXZ antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice using a fermionic parton mean-field theory built on the $\pi$-flux Dirac spin liquid, with the mean-field order generated by an on-site spinon interaction term and nearest-neighbor (anisotropic) spin couplings. The collective modes are obtained using the random-phase approximation (RPA). In a finite parameter region, we find the Y state as a self-consistent solution, together with the competing Y' state, which is a $90^\circ$-rotated Y state inside the order plane. The mean-field energy favors Y', even though the two states are exactly degenerate in the classical limit. However, the Y state can become lower in energy when higher-order corrections due to the fluctuations of the collective modes are considered. The Y state can also be stabilized on the mean-field level by applying small external fields, which we do in two different ways: moment-aligned local field and uniform field along the easy axis. In both cases, the RPA calculation for the stabilized Y state gives a roton minimum at the $M$ point in the excitation spectrum. A gapped pseudo-Goldstone mode above the gapless Goldstone mode is obtained as well, which has also been observed experimentally. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of tuning the spinon interaction strength and the anisotropy in spin couplings in our phenomenological model. Comparison with the recent numerical and experimental results is also discussed.

papers.intro:
A supersolid breaks lattice translations and a continuous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry at the same time. One of the cleanest lattice realization is the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice with easy-axis exchange anisotropy. Mapped onto hard-core bosons, SzS^{z} becomes the boson density and S±S^{\pm} create and remove bosons. In this language the model describes bosons with nearest-neighbor repulsion and hopping, and its ground state is a supersolid [37, 12, 25, 36, 19, 13, 40, 28]. In spin language it is the Y\mathrm{Y} state, where the magnetic orders on each triangular plaquette form a coplanar Y\mathrm{Y}-shaped pattern. The SzS^{z} components form a three-sublattice density wave, and in-plane order breaks the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry about the easy axis. Classically, Y\mathrm{Y} is degenerate with other coplanar states, among them the Y′\mathrm{Y}^{\prime} state, a 90∘90^{\circ}-rotated Y\mathrm{Y} state inside the order plane [8], and quantum fluctuations select Y\mathrm{Y} as the true ground state [26, 21, 31, 8].

Cobalt-based triangular magnets have made the model experimentally accessible. Na2BaCo(PO4)2 [29, 9, 30] and K2Co(SeO3)2 [44] both realize it, where the latter is closer to the Ising limit [2, 45]. Its low-energy spectrum is dominated by a broad continuum with roton-like minima at the MM point [46, 45, 2]. Above the gapless excitation at the KK point, it contains a pseudo-Goldstone mode with a gap of about 0.060.06 meV, and no coherent magnon is resolved within the continuum [45]. Polarized neutron scattering analysis has recently shown that the transverse ordered moment is small and that the low-energy dynamics is predominantly longitudinal [47].

These experimentally measured spectra cannot be described by linear spin-wave theory, which has neither the continuum nor the minimum at MM [2, 24, 23]. Quantum Monte Carlo reproduces the measured spectrum of K2Co(SeO3)2, including the MM point minima [45]. Tensor network simulations find two low-energy branches: a gapless one, carried by fluctuations out of the plane of the order, and a gapped pseudo-Goldstone branch, carried by in-plane fluctuations. Both branches have nearly degenerate minima at MM [10, 4]. These studies attribute the minima to the magnon–Higgs scattering mechanism [4, 27]. Nonlinear spin-wave theory in the strong easy-axis limit fails to produce the minimum or the small pseudo-Goldstone gap [24]. Ref. [7] combines DMRG and several different analytical approaches, demonstrating robust roton feature at the MM point. A roton-like minimum at MM is also found in the isotropic triangular antiferromagnet [42, 43, 17, 22]. Its interpretations range from magnon interactions [3, 35] to proximity to a spin liquid with spinon excitations [11, 6, 41].

The natural parent state for a fermionic parton theory is the π\pi-flux Dirac spin liquid [16, 32]. Its Dirac nodes sit at ±𝑴/2\pm\bm{M}/2, so 𝑴\bm{M} is the momentum of inter-valley spinon pairs. Building on this, Ref. [18] described the supersolid of Na2BaCo(PO4)2 as a precursory Dirac spin liquid at the mean-field level. For the isotropic model with 120∘120^{\circ}-order, Ref. [41] obtained the roton-like minimum from level repulsion between the magnon and the spinon continuum, in a fermionic RPA treatment with an on-site Hubbard-type term. There are also other similar fermionic parton constructions in the literature [14, 18, 1]. The readers can refer to a recent review article on this topic [15].
