In this work, we use a fermionic parton mean-field theory built on the π\pi-flux state, to find the magnetic order self-consistently, and obtain the collective modes with RPA calculations. In the parameter regime of interest, the mean-field theory has two self-consistent solutions, Y\mathrm{Y} and Y′\mathrm{Y}^{\prime}, with Y′\mathrm{Y}^{\prime} slightly lower in energy. However, including higher order corrections due to fluctuations makes Y\mathrm{Y} the stable ground state. On the mean-field level, the Y\mathrm{Y} state can be stabilized by adding small external fields, after which the excitation spectra can be calculated using RPA. We use two different types of external field: moment-aligned local field and a uniform field along the easy axis. Both cases show stable excitation spectra with a roton minimum at the MM point. The former shows a gapped Goldstone mode at the KK point due to the explicitly broken U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry, whereas the Goldstone of the latter remains gapless because the uniform field preserves the U⁡(1)U(1) on the Hamiltonian level. On top of the gapless Goldstone from the transverse channel, there is also a gapped pseudo-Goldstone from the longitudinal channel. Other than the collective modes at low energy, the parton construction also naturally gives rise to continuum in the excitation spectra. Since the parton theory proposed here is a phenomenological model, we also investigate the effects of tuning the parameters—the on-site spinon interaction strength and the anisotropy in spin coupling—on the calculated excitation spectra. Comparisons with existing numerical and experimental works are also made.

Note that the parton theory is not derived from the original spin model, and should be regarded as a physically motivated phenomenological model with symmetry considerations. We remark on the approximations made in this treatment. First, the single-occupancy constraint is imposed only on average and the trial state is not Gutzwiller projected. The trial state therefore contains spinon density fluctuations outside of the physical Hilbert space, and the gauge fluctuations of the parton theory are also ignored. Second, with allowed spinon density fluctuation, a Hubbard-like on-site spinon interaction UU is introduced, which penalizes double-occupancy and generates magnetic orders as well as their fluctuations for the trial state. As a consequence, the couplings in the model Hamiltonian are phenomenological parameters for the trial state, and should not be directly compared with couplings in the original spin model. Finally, the roton minimum and the continuum in the excitation spectra do not necessarily imply the existence of fractionalized spinons. The purpose here is to provide another possible perspective to the observed physics. Within these limits, the theory gives a self-consistent description of the supersolid order and its low-energy excitation spectrum.

papers.title: SDSS-V LVM: Spatial Resolution Effects on Diagnostic Diagrams in the Magellanic Clouds
papers.abstract: We investigate how spatial resolution affects emission-line diagnostics in the interstellar medium (ISM) of the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds (SMC and LMC) using SDSS Local Volume Mapper (LVM) data obtained at and degraded to 19, 42, 170 pc (for the SMC) and 17, 68, 272 pc (for the LMC), respectively. We compare the distributions of strong emission-line ratios through 1D and 2D Kolmogorov Smirnov tests. We deduced that diagnostics involving ionization and density sensitive ratios such as [OIII]{\lambda}5007/H\b{eta}, [SII]{\lambda}{\lambda}6717+6731/H{\alpha} and [NII]{\lambda}6584/H{\alpha} are the most strongly impacted by resolution loss in this order. The SMC shows significant deviations even from intermediate scales (42 pc), whereas for the LMC, the coarsest resolution (272 pc) remains relatively stable, indicating that the SMC is intrinsically more affected by spatial mixing. Resolution degradation produces a marked homogenization effect: extreme values present at the finest scales are progressively diluted, causing diagnostic diagrams to converge toward their mean loci. Diffuse ionized gas is particularly sensitive to this mixing, while H{\alpha} selected ionized regions exhibit more robust behavior across resolutions. The sensitivity of diagnostic diagrams involving emission-line ratios, equivalent widths, and kinematic properties varies with both spatial resolution and galaxy, with the SMC generally showing stronger changes than the LMC. Our results demonstrate that sub-50 pc resolution is required to resolve the detailed structure of low-metallicity galaxies, and they highlight at least the need for careful interpretation of line-ratio diagnostics in extragalactic studies where coarse spatial resolution is unavoidable.

papers.intro:
Ionized gas plays a central role in understanding galaxy evolution, providing crucial insights into feedback processes and the physical conditions of the interstellar medium (ISM). Over the past decade, there has been increasing reliance on strong optical emission lines, both recombination lines (RLs) such as Hα\alpha and Hβ\beta, and collisionally excited lines (CELs) such as [OIII]λ\lambda5007, [SII]λ\lambdaλ\lambda6717, 6731, [NII]λ\lambda6584, and [OI]λ\lambda6300 as diagnostic tools for probing and identifying ionization conditions in extragalactic HII regions (Berg et al., 2015; Sánchez et al., 2015a; Shapley et al., 2025). A major challenge arising from the rapid improvement in spatial resolution is the proper interpretation of diagnostics in a spatially resolved manner, as these were originally developed and calibrated using data with much coarser resolution (Kewley et al., 2001; Kauffmann et al., 2003; Cid Fernandes et al., 2011; Sánchez et al., 2024). This issue is particularly relevant when attempting to differentiate between the various ionization sources of the ISM (Espinosa-Ponce et al., 2020).

In the wavelength range covered by the optical regime, the major advances have been driven largely by modern integral-field spectroscopic surveys or programs. These include observations of nearby galaxies with the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE), such as those from the All-weather MUse Supernova Integral-field of Nearby Galaxies survey (AMUSING++; López-Cobá et al., 2020), the Physics at High Angular Resolution in Nearby Galaxies program (PHANGS-MUSE; Emsellem et al., 2022), mosaicking of large targets (Feltre et al., 2026), the Measuring Active Galactic Nuclei Under MUSE Microscope survey (MAGNUM; Venturi et al., 2021; Mingozzi et al., 2019), and, more recently, by the Local Volume Mapper (LVM; Drory et al., 2024). The LVM, a key program of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-V; Kollmeier et al., 2026), maps approximately 4300 square degrees of the sky, covering the southern Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds (MCs), and other Local Group systems. LVM is a wide-field integral-field spectroscopic survey providing optical spectroscopy over a wavelength range of 3600–9800 Å, with 35.3" diameter science fibers and an IFU field of view of approximately 0.5’ in diameter. The high spatial resolution provided by the LVM (on the order of 0.1 pc for Milky Way objects and on the order of tens of parsecs for the Magellanic Clouds) reveals small-scale structures and allows us to distinguish ionization sources that would appear mixed or blended at degraded resolutions (Drory et al., 2024). Its capabilities enable detailed studies of star-forming regions (e.g. Kreckel et al., 2024; Villa-Durango et al., 2025; Sattler et al., 2025; Hilder et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2026), supernova remnants (Sarbadhicary et al., 2025), Wolf–Rayet stars (González-Torà et al., 2025), the planetary nebulae (Sánchez et al., 2026), among other topics.

These include observations of nearby galaxies with the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE), such as those from the All-weather MUse Supernova Integral-field of Nearby Galaxies survey (AMUSING++; López-Cobá et al., 2020), the Physics at High Angular Resolution in Nearby Galaxies program (PHANGS-MUSE; Emsellem et al., 2022), mosaicking of large targets (Feltre et al., 2026), the Measuring Active Galactic Nuclei Under MUSE Microscope survey (MAGNUM; Venturi et al., 2021; Mingozzi et al., 2019), and, more recently, by the Local Volume Mapper (LVM; Drory et al., 2024). The LVM, a key program of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-V; Kollmeier et al., 2026), maps approximately 4300 square degrees of the sky, covering the southern Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds (MCs), and other Local Group systems. LVM is a wide-field integral-field spectroscopic survey providing optical spectroscopy over a wavelength range of 3600–9800 Å, with 35.3" diameter science fibers and an IFU field of view of approximately 0.5’ in diameter. The high spatial resolution provided by the LVM (on the order of 0.1 pc for Milky Way objects and on the order of tens of parsecs for the Magellanic Clouds) reveals small-scale structures and allows us to distinguish ionization sources that would appear mixed or blended at degraded resolutions (Drory et al., 2024). Its capabilities enable detailed studies of star-forming regions (e.g. Kreckel et al., 2024; Villa-Durango et al., 2025; Sattler et al., 2025; Hilder et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2026), supernova remnants (Sarbadhicary et al., 2025), Wolf–Rayet stars (González-Torà et al., 2025), the planetary nebulae (Sánchez et al., 2026), among other topics.

High spatial resolution observations also offer critical benchmarks for interpreting the unresolved emission of distant galaxies (Carnall et al., 2023; Carniani et al., 2024), including those at high redshift revealed by the James Webb Space Telescope (Arellano-Córdova et al., 2022; Arellano-Córdova et al., 2025; Rogers et al., 2024; Rogers et al., 2025; Stanton et al., 2025). By studying the ionized ISM in a spatially resolved manner in the local Universe, we can better understand the physical processes that influence the diagnostic tools applied to extragalactic systems where spatial resolution is inherently limited. Understanding the capabilities and limitations of emission-line diagnostics in nearby, well-resolved environments is therefore essential for bridging the gap between local and distant galaxy studies.

Among extragalactic systems, those with low metallicities, such as the Magellanic Clouds with metallicities of Z << 0.5 Z⊙{\odot} for the LMC and Z << 0.2 Z⊙{\odot} for the SMC; Russell and Dopita, 1992), are particularly important for understanding the processes that drive galaxy evolution, since their chemical composition resembles that of galaxies at early cosmic epochs (Izotov et al., 2024). The integral-field spectroscopy provided by the LVM enables detailed studies of their properties, particularly how emission-line diagnostics change when the gas exhibits lower cooling efficiencies, a harder ionizing radiation field, and complex interactions with the underlying stellar populations. These galaxies, situated at distances of approximately 50–60 kpc (Scowcroft et al., 2016; Pietrzyński et al., 2019), are the most massive dwarf satellite galaxies of the Milky Way. Owing to their proximity and respective spatial orientations or inclinations (estimated using red clump stars), with iLMC≈23.4∘{}_{\rm LMC}\approx 23.4^{\circ} (e.g., Choi et al., 2022) and iSMC≈35.4∘{}_{\rm SMC}\approx 35.4^{\circ} (e.g., Tatton et al., 2021), they offer the unique advantage of resolving individual stars (Gochermann and Schmidt-Kaler, 2002; Mucciarelli et al., 2023) as well as key structures of the interstellar medium, such as molecular clouds (Paradis et al., 2019; Saldaño et al., 2024) and regions shaped by stellar feedback (McClure-Griffiths et al., 2018; Grishunin et al., 2024), including HII regions (Lopez et al., 2014) and supernova remnants (Toribio San Cipriano et al., 2017; Maggi et al., 2019).

papers.title: Asymptotic analysis of the dynamical field-field correlation function of the impenetrable Bose gas
papers.abstract: We study the long-time, large-distance asymptotic behaviour of the two-point correlation function of fields of the impenetrable Bose gas in equilibrium states characterized by a quasi-momentum distribution (or filling fraction). This includes, in particular, the cases of Gibbs and generalized Gibbs ensembles. The overall structure of the asymptotic expansion depends on the number of Fermi points, those points for which the quasi-momentum distribution takes the value $1/2$. The leading asymptotic behaviour is determined by a relaxation rate, a logarithmic correction term and an amplitude for which we provide simple and explicit expressions. In the case of two Fermi points the first sub-leading correction is calculated as well.
papers.intro:
Repulsively interacting Bosons confined to one spatial dimension never condense. Under any kind of external conditions they always form a gas. The idealized case of point-particles with ultra short-range pairwise interactions, modeled by a delta-function potential, is referred to as the (Lieb–Liniger) Bose gas [1] or the non-linear Schrödinger model (NLSM). In the limit of infinite repulsion strength it turns into the impenetrable Bose gas, also known as Tonks–Girardeau gas [2, 3]. Astonishingly enough, even this extreme case can nowadays be realized and studied in cold atom experiments [4, 5, 6].

The idealized case of point-particles with ultra short-range pairwise interactions, modeled by a delta-function potential, is referred to as the (Lieb–Liniger) Bose gas [1] or the non-linear Schrödinger model (NLSM). In the limit of infinite repulsion strength it turns into the impenetrable Bose gas, also known as Tonks–Girardeau gas [2, 3]. Astonishingly enough, even this extreme case can nowadays be realized and studied in cold atom experiments [4, 5, 6].

The infinite repulsion prevents any two impenetrable Bosons from occupying the same point in space, which makes them appear much like Fermions. Thermodynamically they form, in fact, an ideal Fermi gas. However, their correlation functions may be quite different from those of free Fermions. This holds, in particular, for the correlation function of fields considered in this work and can be partially attributed to the fact that the relation between the Bose fields and their Fermi-field counterparts is non-local and partially to the different boundary conditions (periodic and anti-periodic) for the effective Fermions in sectors with odd and even particle numbers [3].

The field-field correlation functions of the impenetrable Bose gas can be represented as Fredholm minors of certain so-called integrable integral operators [7, 8, 9]. For the static case this was established in the 60s in seminal works by Schultz [10] and Lenard [11, 12]. In 1990 Korepin and Slavnov [13] generalized these works to the dynamical finite-temperature case. Nowadays determinant representations of special functions of the type derived by those authors are considered numerically efficient [14]. Still, they are rather non-intuitive. For the use in applications and also for an understanding of the qualitative behaviour of the correlation functions explicit asymptotic formulae are preferable.

The asymptotic analysis of Fredholm determinants as functions of their parameters (such as distance, time, or temperature in the case of correlations functions) turned out to be challenging. It took many years until appropriate methods were developed. The static field-field correlation function in the ground state, which is equivalent to the reduced density matrix in the sense of Landau and Lifshitz [15], was first analyzed by Lenard [11], who proved that it goes to zero asymptotically for large distances. Later it was studied in detail by Vaidya and Tracy [16] and by Jimbo et al. [17]. The static finite temperature case was considered by Riemann–Hilbert techniques in [18, 19]. Riemann–Hilbert techniques then made it possible to attack the most general finite-temperature dynamical case in a tour de force by Its et al. in [7] (for a review see [20]). This work is our main reference point.

Recently we have employed modern Riemann–Hilbert techniques [21, 8, 22] to perform a long-time, large distance asymptotic analysis of the Fredholm determinant associated with a generalized free Fermion model [23, 24]. The main motivation for that work was to prepare for the asymptotic analysis of the Lieb–Liniger model at finite positive interaction strength. This will be the subject of a subsequent publication. Here we shall apply our new asymptotic results to the simpler special case of the impenetrable Bose gas. We shall approve, extend and improve the analysis of [7]. Our analysis will not be restricted to the case of thermal equilibrium. We rather consider stationary density matrices characterized by a filling fraction (or quasi-momentum distribution). This includes the cases of thermal equilibrium and of generalized Gibbs ensembles [25, 26, 27] and also applies to more general stationary states which may occur as a consequence of relaxation after an interaction quench (see e.g. [28, 29]). We believe that such kind of extension would have been possible for the authors of [7], but those days there was no experimental motivation for it.

papers.title: Winding-Pack Quench Simulation of Stellarator Coils: Hydraulic Field-Network Coupling and Transverse Heat Conduction in OPENSC$^2$
papers.abstract: Quench propagation in cable-in-conduit conductors is thermo-hydraulically driven, yet existing 1D models treat a conductor as one straight adiabatic cable with prescribed pressure and mass-flow boundaries, so secondary quenches and flow redistribution between windings cannot be resolved. We extend the open-source code OPENSC$^2$ with transverse heat conduction between turns, a 3D field resolving the current-sharing temperature, induced losses, and a lumped hydraulic network coupled to the conductors by a mass-flow formulation. Validated against the 2006 W7-X coil tests, it predicts the quench site, cuts the outlet-temperature error from 55 K to 12 K, and reproduces the neighboring windings' heating as flow reversal through the coil inlet.

papers.intro:
Stellarator-type fusion reactors are currently regarded as a very promising route to practically inexhaustible carbon-free energy [43]. Within such a reactor, the magnet system, consisting of inherently three-dimensional superconducting coils, plays a central role: physically, as the source of the magnetic confinement of the plasma, and economically, as a major cost driver of the reactor [42, 26]. Quench protection is therefore a crucial aspect of the design of these coils. Future fusion power-plant magnets will store magnetic energy on the order of gigajoules, so an uncontrolled quench would have disastrous consequences. Stellarators in particular cannot afford damaged coils, since replacing their geometrically complex three-dimensional windings would be practically impossible without dismantling major parts of the machine, shutting down the entire power plant for several months, or even longer if the affected coil had to be re-manufactured.

Cable-in-conduit conductors (CICCs) are a class of superconducting cables that are particularly attractive for high-field and high-current applications such as fusion reactor magnets [31, 3, 24]. CICCs are characterized by a conduit enclosing either superconducting strands, in the case of low-temperature superconductors (LTS), or a number of high-temperature superconductor (HTS) stacks, together with the coolant, which is confined within the cable. The coolant is forced through the CICC along one or more flow channels, wetting and cooling the superconductor either directly or indirectly through a former. Figure 1 shows, as an example, the CICC used in the Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) fusion experiment at the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Greifswald, Germany. In this conductor, superconducting NbTi strands are enclosed by an aluminum jacket, and supercritical helium is forced through the void between the strands, cooling them directly. The conduit gives CICCs a high robustness against thermal and structural loads and simplifies the insulation of adjacent turns, permitting large potential differences between them. This makes CICCs intrinsically better protected against quench than other superconducting cable types such as Rutherford cables.

Numerical simulation tools have become indispensable for studying quench behavior and for designing quench protection systems. Most of these tools originated in the accelerator magnet community. LEDET, for example, employs a lumped-element electro-thermal model to simulate the superconducting coil in the event of a quench and to analyze the performance of quench protection systems, representing the physical phenomena in terms of electric circuits and thermal networks [28]. ROXIE, the workhorse of the magnet design for the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, instead offers high-fidelity magneto-thermal quench simulation based on a reduced magnetic vector potential approach combined with a finite-element-boundary-element coupling [35]. FiQuS is a more recent tool that supports both 2D and 3D quench simulation, employs advanced numerical techniques and is built on the open-source meshing and finite-element (FE) tools Gmsh and GetDP [41, 14]. What most accelerator magnet simulation tools such as LEDET, ROXIE and FiQuS have in common is that they solve a coupled electro- or magneto-thermal problem in order to simulate quench propagation in a superconducting coil. This is appropriate because accelerator magnets typically use Rutherford cables cooled by a static helium bath. In the event of a quench, the helium evaporating at the quenching conductor can escape freely and is immediately replaced by fresh helium, as sketched in figure 2a. The fluid behavior of the helium is therefore irrelevant for the quench, whose propagation is driven purely by heat conduction within the cable. The cooling can be reduced to a Robin boundary condition representing the heat transfer between the cable and the surrounding helium at a fixed temperature.

In a CICC, by contrast, the heated helium is confined inside the conduit and causes a hydraulic pressure rise (see figure 2b). The warm helium is expelled along the winding, carrying its heat into coil sections that have not (yet) quenched. Quench propagation in a CICC is therefore thermo-hydraulically driven, so the helium hydraulics cannot be neglected. Depending on the topology of the hydraulic network, warm helium from the initially quenched winding may even redistribute into adjacent windings and trigger secondary quenches. Dedicated software tools for CICCs that account for the hydraulics do exist. THEA, for example, is a commercial code written in Fortran that solves the full set of electric, thermal and hydraulic equations [10]. 4C [33] and VINCENTA [7] are both proprietary codes that perform thermo-hydraulic simulations of CICCs and have been used for the simulation of the toroidal field coils in ITER.

papers.title: SHARP(ening the) view of unresolved globular clusters in ultra diffuse galaxies
papers.abstract: Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies (UDGs) challenge current galaxy formation models within the {\Lambda}CDM framework, particularly regarding their dark matter content and formation histories. Globular Clusters (GCs) serve as excellent tracers for probing the halos of these faint systems; however, current spectroscopic facilities struggle to reach the depth required to fully characterize GC populations beyond the local neighborhood. In this work, we present the scientific potential of NEXUS@SHARP, a near-infrared multi-slit spectrograph proposed on the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). We demonstrate that NEXUS is uniquely positioned to overcome current observational limitations by combining high spatial resolution with efficient multiplexing. We show that NEXUS can efficiently help to characterize the GC population in UDGs across diverse environments out to 60 to 70 Mpc - with a few hours of ELT time. These capabilities will allow for precise measurements of radial velocities and stellar populations, enabling robust dynamical mass estimates and distinguishing between competing UDG formation scenario.

papers.title: Black Hole Seeds and Little Red Dots: Connecting Formation and Growth with a JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Program
papers.abstract: JWST has revealed an abundant population of faint active galactic nuclei and a new class of compact, high-redshift sources known as Little Red Dots (LRDs), whose physical nature remains debated, with accreting massive black holes among the leading explanations. The emerging demographics of early black holes, with their high inferred number densities and, in some systems, the apparent excess of black hole mass relative to stellar mass, challenge simple scenarios of black hole seeding and growth. Despite these observational breakthroughs, the origin of early massive black holes remains uncertain, because "black holes have no memory": current samples cannot separate the imprint of seeding from subsequent growth. This white paper identifies the multi-cycle JWST observations needed to revolutionize our understanding of early black hole growth by: (i) distinguishing seeding pathways, (ii) constraining early black hole growth mechanisms, (iii) resolving the physical nature of broad-line emitters and LRDs, and (iv) testing black hole-galaxy co-evolution. These tasks require uniformly selected samples extending to low black hole and host-galaxy masses, allowing self-consistent measurements of black hole mass functions, Eddington-ratio distributions, and host properties. Grating spectroscopy, deep MIRI imaging, and variability analysis through repeated observations of the same fields would provide complementary tests of black hole formation and growth, their connection to host-galaxy evolution, and the nature of newly discovered populations of LRDs. In this white paper, we argue that these joint tests require a coordinated JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program; such a program could provide the depth, uniformity, and time baseline needed to place substantially stronger, complementary constraints on early black hole formation, growth, and their connection to galaxy evolution.

papers.title: The JWST Early Release Science Program for Direct Observations of Exoplanetary Systems IX: A Multi-Wavelength Framework for Source Characterization in JWST Coronagraphic Imaging of the HIP 65426 System
papers.abstract: We present an updated analysis of the JWST coronagraphic imaging data of the HIP 65426 system. We aim to search for and characterize potential planetary companions as well as provide updated astrometry and photometry for the known exoplanet HIP 65426 b following updates to the JWST and spaceKLIP pipelines. Our measured photometry and astrometry show significant differences to those in Carter et al. (2023) but are consistent to within $2.2{\sigma}$ in separation, $1.5{\sigma}$ in position angle, and $3.7{\sigma}$ in flux. Our results indicate that pipeline updates have changed the photometry and astrometry significantly in some filters, especially in terms of observed flux. We see the greatest changes in separation in F444W and F1550C, position angle in F250M, and flux in F250M, F300M, F410M, F1140C, and F1550C. The SED of HIP 65426 b remains consistent with a young, giant planet best fit by models with a cloudy atmosphere and an effective temperature estimate of ~1436 K. Using both NIRCam and MIRI data, we identified 21 candidate companion sources in addition to the known planet. Of the 21 sources, 13 were attributed to astrophysical sources with eight background stars, four galaxies, one unknown, and zero planets. While one of these sources was detected in Chauvin et al. (2017), the remaining point sources were undetected in previous ground-based observations, which makes this work an initial epoch of astrometry for these objects. High-contrast imaging is a key technique used to observe faint targets, such as exoplanets or disks, in close proximity to their bright host stars. JWST Early Release Science Program 01386 [32] was designed to test and demonstrate JWST’s capabilities for both high-contrast coronagraphic imaging and spectroscopic observations of widely-separated exoplanet companions. papers.title: On the importance of medium-resolution continuum spectroscopy for JWST's extragalactic legacy
papers.abstract: We argue for a significant investment of JWST time into an extremely deep medium-resolution NIRSpec MSA survey targeting a large, representative sample of high-redshift $(z>1.5)$ galaxies, specifically intended to obtain high-SNR continuum detections. This is only possible with JWST, and no planned future instrumentation has similar capabilities, meaning that obtaining such observations with JWST must be urgently prioritised. The vast majority of existing archival NIRSpec observations are not deep enough for continuum science, being focused on the detection of emission lines. Deeper continuum data opens up the ability to constrain a much wider range of key galaxy physical parameters, including stellar population ages and metallicities, stellar kinematics and neutral gas physical properties, inflows and outflows. Such measurements will provide crucial insight into quenching physics, galaxy dynamical masses, merger histories, pristine early star-formation, reionization and the physics of Little Red Dots, as well as enabling all of the emission-line science that can be achieved with shallower observations. To facilitate future survey planning, we present an empirically derived relationship between rest-optical continuum SNR in JWST NIRSpec medium-resolution data, rest-optical apparent magnitude and exposure time, which we show to be independent of redshift (and hence the grating used). We then provide a 1000-hour sketch survey plan based on achieving the continuum SNR $=20$/pixel necessary to constrain key physical properties and scaling relations for a large galaxy sample at $z>1.5$. We finally discuss NIRSpec sky subtraction strategies, which are of critical importance for continuum SNR.

papers.title: Dust Survival in Lensed Quiescent Galaxies at $z>1$ Depends on How They Quench
papers.abstract: The interstellar medium of massive quiescent galaxies holds key clues to how they quench, yet remain poorly understood. Although dust is expected to be depleted rapidly ($\lesssim$100 Myr) after quenching, some quiescent galaxies host substantial dust reservoirs, raising the question of whether dust survives quenching or is replenished afterward. We present ALMA Band 6 continuum observations ($\lambda_{\mathrm{rest}}$$>$250$\mu$m) of eight strongly-lensed, spectroscopically-selected quiescent galaxies at z$\sim$1-2.5 from the COOL-LAMPS and REQUIEM surveys, plus five archival REQUIEM systems. The sample spans more than two orders of magnitude in dust-to-stellar-mass ratio ($f_{\mathrm{dust}}<10^{-5}$ to $>10^{-3}$), and two galaxies host extended, resolved dust. Comparing $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ with time since quenching, roughly half the sample, preferentially at higher redshift, is consistent with rapid quenching and harsh dust destruction, while lower-redshift, more slowly quenched systems are consistent with milder destruction, possibly reflecting an evolving dominant quenching mode. The two most dust-rich galaxies exceed even the mildest model destruction tracks, with J1201-3952 retaining the highest $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ $\sim$1.8 Gyr after quenching. If these systems are truly quiescent, their dust masses approach maximum stellar yields, pointing to ISM grain regrowth and/or TP-AGB dust production. However due to our single-band continuum data, $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ is uncertain ($\pm$0.3 dex systematic uncertainty from the unknown dust temperature) and we cannot rule out obscured star formation in these two galaxies. Our results suggest that dust survival depends on how galaxies quench: rapid, harsh quenching efficiently destroys dust, while slower, milder quenching can leave dust reservoirs that persist or are replenished long after star formation ceases.

papers.intro:
In the current picture of massive galaxy evolution, a large fraction of massive galaxies exhibit low star formation rates [89, 54, 136, 29, SFRs; e.g.,], compact, bulge-dominated morphologies [28, 140, 139, e.g.,], and red colors from old stellar populations [66, 148, 143, 145, 90, e.g.,]. These quiescent galaxies are thought to evolve from star-forming disk galaxies, but the physical processes through which star formation shuts down and the origin of their compact morphologies is unclear [142, 9, 10, for recent comprehensive reviews, see]. Proposed quenching mechanisms must either heat, remove, consume, or expel reservoirs of cold molecular gas, which serve as the fuel for star formation, either over rapid (<<1Gyr) or slower (>>1Gyr) timescales [17, 100, 41, e.g.,]. Therefore, the joint analysis of star formation histories (SFH) and cold dust and gas content in quiescent galaxies can reveal how, when, and where quenching happens.

Several studies have sought to study molecular gas in quiescent and post-starburst galaxies, primarily utilizing CO spectroscopy [51, 124, 149, 150, 152, 40, 119, 113]. However, a challenge of this approach is the long integration times required to detect CO, particularly in systems that are expected to be intrinsically gas-poor if quenching has occurred through gas depletion. Consequently, CO has been detected in only a handful of quiescent galaxies, limiting robust constraints on the molecular gas content of the population. Beyond total gas content, spatially-resolved gas measurements can identify specific quenching mechanisms and elucidate how stellar mass assembles across different regions of a galaxy. For example, centrally depleted gas reservoirs could indicate inside-out quenching driven by AGN feedback or morphological quenching, consistent with the suppressed central star formation and older central stellar populations seen in resolved studies of massive galaxies at cosmic noon [132, 94, 131, 5]. Similarly, gas displaced from the stellar body or swept up in outflows would point to environmental stripping or ejective feedback [125, 7, 39]. However, such resolved CO observations are prohibitively expensive for most quiescent galaxies at z>1z>1.

Dust is injected by supernovae and the winds of evolved stars and is subsequently reprocessed in the ISM, where grains grow in dense gas and are shattered into smaller grains in diffuse gas [109, 93, 99]. Once star formation ceases, these sources fade, with Type II supernovae ending within ∼\sim40 Myr, dust production by asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars declining over the following several hundred Myr to ∼\sim2 Gyr as progressively lower-mass stars reach this phase, and grain growth stalling as cold, dense gas is consumed, heated, or expelled. Destruction, by contrast, can be rapid, through thermal sputtering in hot gas, supernova shocks, astration, and outflows [72], with sputtering alone destroying grains within ∼\sim1-10 Myr in hot halos [37, 58, 59, 52]. Quiescent galaxies are therefore naively expected to lose their dust shortly after quenching. Yet observations of quiescent galaxies with substantial dust reservoirs [51, 48, 8, 67] suggest that removal may be prolonged in some quiescent systems, or offset by replenishment through grain growth or asymptotic giant branch (AGB) production [32, 74, 34].

Dust is injected by supernovae and the winds of evolved stars and is subsequently reprocessed in the ISM, where grains grow in dense gas and are shattered into smaller grains in diffuse gas [109, 93, 99]. Once star formation ceases, these sources fade, with Type II supernovae ending within ∼\sim40 Myr, dust production by asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars declining over the following several hundred Myr to ∼\sim2 Gyr as progressively lower-mass stars reach this phase, and grain growth stalling as cold, dense gas is consumed, heated, or expelled. Destruction, by contrast, can be rapid, through thermal sputtering in hot gas, supernova shocks, astration, and outflows [72], with sputtering alone destroying grains within ∼\sim1-10 Myr in hot halos [37, 58, 59, 52]. Quiescent galaxies are therefore naively expected to lose their dust shortly after quenching. Yet observations of quiescent galaxies with substantial dust reservoirs [51, 48, 8, 67] suggest that removal may be prolonged in some quiescent systems, or offset by replenishment through grain growth or asymptotic giant branch (AGB) production [32, 74, 34].

Beyond the timescale of dust destruction, a second confounding factor is the diversity of SFHs among quiescent galaxies, which encode a wide range of quenching timescales and times since quenching. While only <10<10% of quiescent galaxies at z∼1z\sim 1 are predicted to be recently quenched, this number rises to ∼50\sim 50% at z∼2z\sim 2 [e.g., 142, and references therein]. If dust destruction proceeds more slowly than quenching, recently quenched galaxies may retain dust formed before quenching, or sustain enough residual star formation to continue producing it. Thermally pulsing asymptotic giant branch (TP-AGB) stars add a further channel: they are expected to be prominent in quiescent galaxies with intermediate-age stellar populations (∼\sim0.3-2 Gyr), particularly at z∼1z\sim 1, and could produce dust long after quenching, which would trace the intermediate-age stars rather than the dense core [76].

papers.title: Thorium and Europium production in the early Galaxy: Implications for nucleocosmochronology
papers.abstract:
The ages of the oldest stellar populations can be investigated through nucleocosmochronology, with the thorium-to-europium abundance ratio providing a promising chronometer. We assess the reliability of log(Th/Eu) as an age indicator by testing whether thorium and europium were co-produced in a constant ratio in metal-poor stars, and evaluate the uncertainties affecting stellar ages.
  We present new Th and Eu abundance measurements for eight TITANS reference stars observed with UVES at the VLT. Combining these measurements with homogeneous literature samples, we investigate the behaviour of log(Th/Eu) as a function of metallicity. We derive ages adopting a theoretical initial r-process production ratio and assess the effects of observational uncertainties and sample statistics.
  At low metallicity, the observed Th/Eu ratios show no significant dependence on metallicity after excluding stars with anomalous actinide abundances, supporting broadly uniform Th and Eu co-production in the early Galaxy. The derived ages are consistent with expectations for an old, metal-poor halo population, although individual uncertainties remain substantial. Higher spectral resolution is needed to improve Th measurements, while combining stars in coeval populations can provide additional statistical gains.
  Nucleocosmochronology offers an independent approach to dating the oldest stellar populations. Homogeneous samples of coeval stars, particularly in globular clusters, observed with future high-resolution multi-object spectrographs could provide stronger constraints on the early formation history of the Milky Way and the age of the Universe.

papers.intro:
The study of heavy-element nucleosynthesis provides fundamental insights into the origin of the oldest stellar populations and the chemical evolution of the Galaxy (Mishenina et al. 2022, see, e.g). Elements with Z≥30Z\geq 30 are mainly produced through neutron-capture processes, among which the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) is responsible for a significant fraction of the heavy-element inventory (Burbidge et al. 1957; Cameron 1957), particularly for the production of lanthanides (Z=57Z=57–71) and actinides (Z≥90Z\geq 90) (Goriely and Arnould 2001, e.g.). Although neutron star mergers (NSMs) are currently the only observationally confirmed astrophysical sites of r-process nucleosynthesis (Drout et al. 2017; Cowperthwaite et al. 2017; Watson et al. 2019; Domoto et al. 2025), other potential contributors, such as neutron star–black hole mergers, collapsars, and rare classes of core-collapse supernovae, are still under investigation (Cowan et al. 2021; Siegel et al. 2022; Soker 2026, see, e.g.,). Observational evidence from metal-poor stars suggests that elements belonging to the second r-process peak, around A=130, and the third r-process peak, around A=195, including the lanthanides, generally follow a nearly universal abundance pattern, consistent with production through a common r-process channel (Sneden et al. 1996; Honda et al. 2006; Cowan et al. 2021, e.g.), but see also Alencastro Puls et al. (2025) for the third r-process peak challenges. In contrast, the actinides show significant star-to-star variations, most notably in the so-called actinide-boost and actinide-deficient stars (Hill et al. 2002; Holmbeck et al. 2018, see, e.g.). These groups demonstrate that the production of the heaviest r-process nuclei depends sensitively on the physical conditions of the enrichment event, and it remains unclear whether such variations reflect multiple astrophysical sites or intrinsic diversity within a single class of r-process events (Schatz et al. 2002; Eichler et al. 2019; Farouqi et al. 2022; Wanajo et al. 2024; Racca et al. 2025; Jeong et al. 2026, see, e.g.,). Despite this diversity, thorium (Th) often broadly follows the abundance pattern of the lighter r-process elements, particularly those associated with the second and third r-process peaks, such as europium (Eu). Among metal-poor r-process-enhanced stars, approximately 15% exhibit an actinide boost (Shah et al. 2026, see, e.g.,). However, they represent only a small fraction of the overall metal-poor stellar population. Both estimates are affected by strong observational biases, particularly those associated with the detectability of Th lines (Hill et al. 2002; Roederer et al. 2009, e.g.).

The radioactive nature of Th makes it particularly valuable for stellar-age estimates. papers.title: Cepheid Metallicity in the Leavitt Law (C-MetaLL) survey: X First spectroscopic characterization of Galactic Type II Cepheids and calibration of the Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity relations
papers.abstract:
Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are Population II pulsating stars that serve as distance indicators through their period--luminosity relation. Along with RR Lyrae stars and the tip of the red giant branch, they offer an independent route to the Hubble constant, helping assess systematic uncertainties in its determination.
  We aim to investigate the impact of chemical composition on T2Cs' period--luminosity relations by building a homogeneous spectroscopic sample of Galactic T2Cs with iron and oxygen abundances.
  We observed 80 Galactic T2Cs with UVES at the ESO Very Large Telescope. For 74 stars, we derived stellar parameters and iron and oxygen abundances through a self-consistent spectroscopic analysis based on equivalent widths of absorption lines. This sample nearly doubles the number of T2Cs with spectroscopic metallicity measurements available in the literature.
  We used these abundances to test theoretical predictions for the instability strip and, together with $Gaia$ parallaxes, to derive Period--Wesenheit--metallicity (PWZ) relations. In agreement with theoretical predictions, the metallicity coefficient ($\gamma$) is small and statistically consistent with zero in all relations, ranging from approximately $-0.02$ to $+0.17$ mag dex$^{-1}$. We also estimated distances to 22 Galactic Globular Clusters hosting T2Cs, finding agreement within uncertainties with independent literature estimates.
  Our results show that metallicity has, at most, a minor impact on T2Cs' pulsation properties and distance scale, supporting their reliability as Population II distance indicators.

In the last century, H0H_{0} measurements based on both early and late universe observations have become more accurate and precise, resulting in the so-called "Hubble tension" (Di Valentino et al., 2021; H0DN Collaboration et al., 2026, see e.g.). The tension arises because of a 5-7 σ\sigma difference in the H0H_{0} values coming from two most accurate direct and indirect determinations (Di Valentino et al., 2025): the first one is based on Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation observations analysed together with the Lambda Cold Dark Matter model of the Universe (Planck Collaboration et al., 2020), the other is a direct measurement of Type Ia Supernovae in the Hubble flow calibrated with Classical Cepheids (CCs) distances in the Local Universe (Riess et al., 2022). Evaluating the significance of this tension warrants the use of alternate distance tracers and independent approaches often involving multiple probes to control systematic uncertainties (H0DN Collaboration et al., 2026, e.g.,). Population II distance indicators, such as RR Lyrae (RRL) stars and Type II Cepheids (T2Cs), together with the tip of the Red Giant Branch (TRGB), offer the possibility of providing an alternative route to H0H_{0} (Beaton et al., 2016; Bhardwaj, 2022; Cruz Reyes et al., 2026).

T2Cs, being older and less massive than CCs, populate various environments: the Galactic Bulge (Soszyński et al., 2011; Soszyński et al., 2017; Matsunaga et al., 2013; Braga et al., 2019, see e.g.), the Galactic Globular Clusters (Matsunaga et al., 2006; Ngeow et al., 2022, GGCs, see), the Galactic halo (Ripepi et al., 2023), and the Magellanic Clouds (see e.g. Ripepi et al., 2015; Soszyński et al., 2018; Sicignano et al., 2024, hereinafter S24). T2Cs are brighter by more than 0.2 dex than RRL and, according to their pulsation period, are classified into three sub-groups (Soszyński et al., 2008; Bono et al., 2020; Bono et al., 2024, see e.g.): BL Herculis (BLHer) stars with periods longer than RRLs (1 day) and shorter than four days; W Virginis (WVir) stars with periods between four and twenty days, RV Tauri stars with periods longer than twenty days. However, these period boundaries are only approximate and vary with the metallicity of their host stellar system. Moreover, a subsample of WVir stars showing peculiar light curves and brighter magnitudes is suspected to have a binary origin (Soszyński et al., 2008).

papers.title: ProtoGestalt: Interpretable Prototypes for Facial Phenotyping and Diagnosis of Rare Genetic Disorders
papers.abstract: Rare genetic disorders are difficult to diagnose due to their diversity and overlapping clinical features. Facial morphology can provide diagnostic clues, yet most diagnostic models offer limited interpretability and are not designed to support broad screening for undiagnosed disease. We present ProtoGestalt, an interpretable prototype-based framework for facial phenotyping, rare-disease screening, and syndrome identification. The method extends prototype learning by constraining learned visual features to select facial regions, allowing predictions to be explained through localized and additive evidence. We assess ProtoGestalt's ability to distinguish syndromic from unaffected faces on multiple control datasets and class prevalence values. We further evaluate it's diagnostic performance on syndromes observed during training. The learned prototype-based representations provide significant separation between syndromic and case-matched control images and retain useful performance as the proportion of controls increases. The framework also demonstrates the ability to differentiate among syndromes. Although reasonably accurate specialized models for facial classification of rare disorders already exist, ProtoGestalt offers an interpretable alternative that links predictions to anatomically meaningful facial regions, potentially supporting clinical decision-making and the discovery of phenotype-gene associations.

Rare genetic disorders affect more than 6% of the global population. There are an estimated 7,000–10,000 known rare diseases, approximately 80% of which have a genetic etiology (Marwaha et al. 2022), while fewer than 10% have an approved therapy (Halley et al. 2022). Due to the large number of disorders, extensive phenotypic heterogeneity, and overlapping clinical presentations, the median time to diagnosis is 4-7 years (Heuyer et al. 2017; Molster et al. 2016).

A necessary step toward a rare disease diagnosis is referral for genetic testing by a front-line clinician. This referral, however, is usually substantially delayed relative to symptom onset because clinicians do not consider rare diseases in their initial assessments. This is partly because two-thirds of clinicians significantly underestimate the prevalence of rare diseases, considering them to be 50 to 500 times rarer than the standard definitions used in the U.S. and Europe (Rohani-Montez et al. 2023). Additionally, rare diseases exhibit complex, variable phenotypic presentations that may overlap with those of more common conditions, further delaying evaluation. Indeed, prior studies indicate that many clinicians may not recognize rare disease phenotypes and report a lack of knowledge of rare disease symptoms as a barrier to diagnosis (Rohani-Montez et al. 2023; Budych et al. 2012). Even after rare conditions are considered, the existence of thousands of phenotypically complex rare conditions, many with overlapping features, presents a significant challenge to determining a specific diagnosis.

A necessary step toward a rare disease diagnosis is referral for genetic testing by a front-line clinician. This referral, however, is usually substantially delayed relative to symptom onset because clinicians do not consider rare diseases in their initial assessments. This is partly because two-thirds of clinicians significantly underestimate the prevalence of rare diseases, considering them to be 50 to 500 times rarer than the standard definitions used in the U.S. and Europe (Rohani-Montez et al. 2023). Additionally, rare diseases exhibit complex, variable phenotypic presentations that may overlap with those of more common conditions, further delaying evaluation. Indeed, prior studies indicate that many clinicians may not recognize rare disease phenotypes and report a lack of knowledge of rare disease symptoms as a barrier to diagnosis (Rohani-Montez et al. 2023; Budych et al. 2012). Even after rare conditions are considered, the existence of thousands of phenotypically complex rare conditions, many with overlapping features, presents a significant challenge to determining a specific diagnosis.

Computational methods could assist with early recognition of individuals with undiagnosed rare disease (i.e., those for whom rare disease has yet to be considered in diagnostic planning) and subsequent disease specific diagnosis. Surprisingly, there has been only limited work on identifying patients with undiagnosed rare diseases, with most existing studies focusing on screening for a single disease. For example, Bhasuran et al. developed a machine learning pipeline to identify patients with acute hepatic porphyria (Bhasuran et al. 2025). While potentially useful, this approach would require a separate model for each rare disease, making this paradigm impractical as a general screening strategy. In contrast, the ThinkRare model uses a rule-based approach applied to structured EHR data to identify pediatric patients with any undiagnosed multisystem rare genetic disease who are eligible for exome sequencing (Ediae et al. 2025). However, the rule-based design encodes fixed expert-defined clinical eligibility criteria, limiting adaptability across institutions with different documentation conventions or patient populations.

These methods rely on detailed phenotypic information about the patient, typically using a controlled vocabulary such as the Human Phenotype Ontology (Köhler et al. 2021), and, optionally, genetic sequence data. This phenotype labeling requirement poses a substantial challenge as ontologies such as the HPO are complex. Indeed, the current HPO version (v2026-06-23) contains over 20,000 terms. Additionally, it includes many subjective terms that are difficult for non-experts to apply in practice. For example, the term midline nasal groove is described as “an abnormal groove on the midline of the nose that may extend to the nasal tip.” Finally, none of these systems have been adapted to the problem of identifying individuals with an undiagnosed rare disease.

The facial gestalt, or overall facial morphology, is often a characteristic clinical feature indicating presence of an undiagnosed rare disease, with certain features associated with specific diagnoses (Kirchhoff et al. 2025). Approximately 30–40% of genetic disorders include facial dysmorphology features (Ferry et al. 2014). In this paper, we introduce ProtoGestalt, a prototype learning model to support both identification of individuals with undiagnosed rare diseases and disease diagnosis for individuals suspected of having a rare disease. ProtoGestalt is an extension of PIP-Net (Nauta et al. 2023b) which learns latent-space prototypes that represent characteristic portions of objects, in our case facial regions. We extend this approach by enforcing anatomical constraints on the prototype learning process using facial landmarks. The primary advantage of our approach is that the model predictions are inherently explainable through visualization of the matching prototypes for a given input. Additionally, prototypes that are consistently present across individuals with the same condition can potentially be used to objectively characterize the disease, which may help support rare disease research. papers.title: The HST-Hyperion Survey: X-ray AGN Enhancement in the Hyperion Proto-supercluster
papers.abstract: Dense environments can influence both galaxy evolution and supermassive black hole growth, but whether they enhance or suppress (or both) active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity at high redshift ($z\gtrsim2$) remains uncertain. As one of the most massive structures identified in the early universe, the Hyperion proto-supercluster at $z\approx2.5$ provides a unique opportunity to investigate this connection during an epoch near the peak of both cosmic star formation rate and AGN activity density. To examine the impact of galaxy environment on AGN activity, we measure the fraction of X-ray-selected AGN in Hyperion as a whole, its highly overdense peaks, and its outskirts, comparing these measurements to a coeval field sample. We identify X-ray AGN using the deep Chandra COSMOS-Legacy Survey and combine optical/near-infrared (NIR) photometry and photometric redshift information from COSMOS2020 with extensive ground-based spectroscopy and HST-grism observations. Redshift information is incorporated statistically using a Monte Carlo framework. We find a higher X-ray AGN fraction in Hyperion ($7.4^{+3.2}_{-1.8}\%$) than in the coeval field ($3.2^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\%$), corresponding to a $\sim2.3\sigma$ difference. Strikingly, this enhancement is concentrated in the overdense peaks, where the X-ray AGN fraction reaches $12.3^{+5.5}_{-3.4}\%$ ($15.0^{+6.9}_{-4.4}\%$ in the most massive peaks versus $6.2^{+11.9}_{-2.1}\%$ in the less massive peaks), while the lower-density Hyperion outskirts ($2.1^{+3.6}_{-1.1}\%$) show no evidence of enhancement relative to the field. These results add to the limited but growing evidence for enhanced AGN activity in high-redshift protostructures, suggesting that the dense environments at these epochs may preferentially trigger AGN during the early stages of cluster assembly.

papers.intro:
Galaxy properties vary strongly with environment in the lower-redshift, local universe, from late-types typically found in low-density field regions to the prevalence of early-types in dense galaxy clusters [17, e.g.,]. Gas accretion can regulate the supply of material available to galaxies [65, e.g.,], while environmental processes such as ram-pressure stripping can remove gas from galaxies [24, 6, 71, e.g.,]. At higher redshifts, galaxy interactions increasingly provide a mechanism for redistributing gas [56, 53, 57, e.g.,]. Specifically, interactions and mergers can drive gas toward galaxy centers, potentially triggering active galactic nuclei (AGN; e.g., 61). Once triggered, AGN can suppress star formation and contribute to galaxy quenching, working with environmental effects to enhance gas removal [18, 48, e.g.,]. AGN feedback may also augment environmental processes that remove or limit gas in dense environments [5, e.g.,]. Enhanced AGN activity in dense environments may therefore influence both host galaxies and the surrounding large-scale structure, motivating measurements of its environmental dependence.

papers.title: A physics-based adaptive low-rank method for 6D Vlasov simulations
papers.abstract: The numerical simulation of kinetic plasma models in six-dimensional phase space poses significant computational and memory challenges, particularly when considering modern high-performance computing architectures. In this work, we propose an adaptive dynamical low-rank approach for the efficient solution of the 6D Vlasov--Poisson system. Our strategy is an extension of the projector-splitting dynamical low-rank integrator. The algorithm changes the rank based on physical observables (e.g., the electric field and energy) as opposed to controlling the error in the distribution function. Our approach is memory efficient in the sense that only rank $r$ objects are required to implement the scheme. This makes the algorithm suitable for performing high-dimensional computations on graphic processing units. Comparisons with rank adaptive Basis-Update & Galerkin integrators exhibit both significant memory savings and reduction in run time. We show, by presenting a variety of 6D benchmark experiments implemented in the C++/CUDA low-rank framework Ensign, that our technique allows us to run simulations with a significantly smaller rank, while still preserving the physical fidelity. Thus, the approach substantially reduces memory footprint and computational cost and enables simulations that are prohibitively expensive for full-rank or less memory-efficient low-rank schemes.

Despite the utility of kinetic equations, exact analytical solutions are rarely available due to the inherent mathematical complexity of these models. Developing reliable and efficient numerical methods capable of yielding accurate solutions is therefore of paramount importance [10]. In this context, a major bottleneck in simulating complex physical phenomena is the so-called curse of dimensionality, that is, the vast number of degrees of freedom in the discretized system renders standard integrators computationally prohibitive in terms of memory demands and execution times. This is particularly critical in kinetic modeling with three-dimensional spatial and velocity domains (i.e., d=3d=3), which yield a six-dimensional phase space. Such problems remain feasible only, if at all, on large clusters, i.e., on supercomputers (see, e.g, [2, 23, 15]).

A recent yet promising approach to mitigate this challenge are low-rank approximations of the phase space (see, e.g., [12] for a review). We consider the dynamical low-rank (DLR) approach here, see [22] or Section 2 for more details. In this framework, the distribution function is approximated on a rank-rr manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} (with rr much lower than the number of degrees of freedom) by constraining the dynamics to the tangent space of ℳ\mathcal{M}. The primary advantage of this methodology is that computations are performed in a significantly lower-dimensional space, while preserving the fundamental features of the system. A non-exhaustive list of contexts in which the DLR approach has been successfully applied includes matrix DEs [20, 4, 25], the Vlasov equation [13, 16, 3], radiation transport [26], biochemistry [27, 14], the Schrödinger equation [20, 8], and uncertainty quantification [24].

In the simplest case, the rank of the manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} is kept constant throughout the entire time integration. This facilitates theoretical analysis and reduces coding effort. However, a fixed-rank approach is clearly suboptimal in general. In fact, the minimal rank required to achieve a prescribed accuracy is rarely known a priori and can vary significantly over time as the system evolves (for instance, during transitions between linear and nonlinear regimes). In this context, rank-adaptive DLR algorithms offer a clear advantage over fixed-rank strategies by using an error estimate which dynamically adjusts the rank to meet accuracy requirements without wasting computational resources. Such DLR methods have been derived and studied, e.g., in [5, 7, 6, 21, 20, 19].

This is the case for both step-and-truncate type methods (see, e.g., [11, 18]) and the so-called rank-adaptive Basis-Update & Galerkin (BUG) dynamical low-rank integrators (see, e.g., [5, 7], although not for the parallel BUG integrator in [6]). This is especially an issue on the more memory constraint graphic processing unit (GPU) based systems now commonly used in high-performance computing (HPC) systems.

papers.title: On the Topology of the Set of Nonnegative Forms That Are Not Sums of Squares
papers.abstract: We study the topology of the normalized space of real nonnegative forms of degree $2d$ in $n$ variables that are not sums of squares. Whenever it is nonempty, we prove that it is path-connected but not acyclic, and in particular not contractible. We give explicit bounds on the degrees in which its reduced homology can be nonzero. In the two minimal nonempty cases, we show an embedding of an exterior algebra into the cohomology ring, and prove containment of the binary octahedral and binary icosahedral groups, respectively, in its fundamental group.
papers.intro:
A basic problem in real algebra is to relate global nonnegativity of polynomials, a condition on all real points, to algebraic representations such as sums of squares. The two notions agree in some cases but not in general. Hilbert’s 1888 theorem gives an exact classification: every nonnegative homogeneous form of positive even degree is a sum of squares only in one of the following three cases of families: quadratic forms in any number of variables, forms in two variables, and ternary quartics [16]. A decade later, Hilbert’s 17th problem asked whether every polynomial that is nonnegative on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} can be expressed as a sum of squares of rational functions [17]. Artin answered this affirmatively in 1927 [1].

papers.title: When GeoFMs Meet VHR: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Very High Resolution Earth Observation Imagery
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are a widely adopted starting point for remote sensing tasks. Most are pretrained on Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery at a ground sampling distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. Many applications instead rely on very high resolution (VHR) imagery, where individual buildings, roads, and amenities are resolved. We study which pretraining regimes transfer well to this scale. We introduce VHR-Bench, a benchmark suite of ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer spanning five task families, eight application domains, and both satellite and aerial platforms. We evaluate twelve encoders in three pretraining tiers with frozen backbones at two training-data fractions. We find that both pretraining on large natural-image collections and VHR-specific pretraining transfer effectively to VHR tasks, with complementary strengths. SkySense leads when labels are scarce; at the full label fraction the web-pretrained DINOv3 ViT-L edges ahead, with the two close together there. Encoders pretrained only on Sentinel-scale imagery transfer least well under RGB input. Guided by these complementary results, we continue the self-supervised pretraining of DINOv3 ViT-L on 1.02 million held-out VHR tiles and evaluate the resulting encoder without changing the downstream protocol. The continued model gives a clear improvement over the released backbone when labels are scarce and a modest one at the full fraction, at no increase in inference parameters or compute. These findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: already strong, broad natural-image pretraining can be further improved by a short VHR continuation stage while preserving its general visual features.

papers.intro:
Self-supervised pretraining on large satellite archives has made Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs), also referred to as Earth Observation Foundation Models (EO-FMs), a common backbone for remote sensing tasks. Most rely on Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery, which is openly available on a global scale with high temporal revisit, at a Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. This large amount of medium to high-resolution data has driven substantial progress in broad-area scene analysis, but leaves an important resolution regime largely unaddressed: Very High Resolution (VHR).

Self-supervised pretraining on large satellite archives has made Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs), also referred to as Earth Observation Foundation Models (EO-FMs), a common backbone for remote sensing tasks. Most rely on Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery, which is openly available on a global scale with high temporal revisit, at a Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. This large amount of medium to high-resolution data has driven substantial progress in broad-area scene analysis, but leaves an important resolution regime largely unaddressed: Very High Resolution (VHR).

We focus on the practical demand that lies in this regime. Applications from disaster response to infrastructure mapping depend on VHR imagery, acquired from satellite platforms such as WorldView, Pléiades, and SPOT, or from aerial and drone surveys. At such resolutions, fine-grained features such as buildings, roads, amenities, and tree crowns are discriminated at the pixel level, enabling spatially precise tasks including building footprint extraction, road mapping, post-disaster damage assessment, canopy height regression, photovoltaic panel detection, tree species classification, and many more. Many disaster tasks are time-critical and demand object-level accurate spatial outputs.

Whether existing GeoFMs transfer well to this resolution regime has not been systematically evaluated. Our first hypothesis is that pretraining on medium to high-resolution Sentinel archives may be insufficient at VHR, given the substantial scale mismatch between pretraining and inference conditions. Conversely, we hypothesize that computer-vision models pretrained on large RGB natural image corpora may transfer well to optical VHR imagery: beyond sharing the same three-channel representation, VHR imagery is closer to natural images than Sentinel-2 imagery in terms of spatial scale, texture, visual diversity, and fine-grained detail. We therefore investigate whether GeoFMs without VHR pretraining underperform on VHR tasks and whether generic RGB models provide a strong alternative to VHR-specific pretraining.

We make three contributions. First, we introduce VHR-Bench, a benchmark of ten VHR datasets spanning five task families and covering eight application domains on both satellite and aerial optical sensors, under one common evaluation framework. Second, we evaluate twelve encoders organized into three pretraining tiers under a fixed protocol at two training-data fractions (10 and 100%). Third, as a design direction derived from the benchmark’s results, and to test whether label-free adaptation can improve an already strong natural image encoder on the VHR domain, we assemble 1.02 million VHR tiles from seven open sources and use them to continue DINOv3 ViT-L’s self-supervised pretraining. We will release11 1 upon acceptance. the resulting model and its pretraining corpus. Together, VHR-Bench and this evaluation give the community a shared reference for how well current GeoFMs transfer to the VHR regime. The evaluation shows that generic natural-image and VHR-pretrained encoders achieve the strongest performance, while Sentinel-only encoders consistently lag behind under RGB input. These findings challenge the assumption that geospatial pretraining is inherently preferable for VHR imagery, and provide a basis for assessing the additional value of VHR-specific pretraining.

papers.title: Chiral-vibration-induced magnetism and circular dichroism in organic molecules
papers.abstract: We investigate the vibrational inverse Faraday effect and transient vibrational circular dichroism in benzene, coronene, and methane at the single-molecule level. We combine density-functional tight-binding calculations with damped normal-mode dynamics. Circularly polarized light excites suitable degenerate infrared-active modes, driving chiral nuclear motion that produces effective magnetic moments. Reversing the pump helicity reverses the vibrational chirality and the sign of the transient dichroic response. These results support a writing-readout scheme in which circularly polarized pumping prepares a chiral vibrational state and transient vibrational circular dichroism probes its handedness. We further examine how molecular symmetry shapes the light-induced chiral response across the three molecular systems. This work provides a valuable platform for exploring all-optical control of magnetism and chiroptical probing at the molecular scale.

papers.intro:
Chiral phonons carrying nonzero angular momentum have attracted considerable attention in recent years. Studies now span transport, nonlinear optics, and ultrafast dynamics, establishing chiral phonons as an emerging research field.[1, 2] One particularly promising direction is the interaction between chiral phonons and electronic orbital degrees of freedom. In conventional transition metals, orbital angular momentum can be generated through charge-to-orbital[3, 4] or spin-to-orbital[5, 6] conversion. Chiral-phonon–orbital coupling instead offers the possibility of generating orbital currents without a net charge current, providing a basis for low-power orbitronics. Chiral phonons can also possess appreciable effective magnetic moments, in some systems approaching the scale of the electronic Bohr magneton.[7, 8, 9] They may therefore mediate vibration-driven magnetism.

Circularly polarized excitation of suitable helicity can induce effective magnetic fields or magnetization through chiral phonons, an effect commonly termed the phonon inverse Faraday effect (phonon IFE). Related electric-field-driven dynamical multiferroicity has also been reported.[10] Recent work has addressed both its microscopic mechanism and its magnitude. Luo et al.[11] observed large effective magnetic fields associated with chiral phonons in rare-earth halides. Shabala and Geilhufe[12] analyzed electron–phonon coupling pathways to clarify the dynamical origin of the phonon IFE and its connection to electronic structure. Lopez et al.[13] subsequently considered a magneto-opto-phononic framework. The conditions for generating chiral phonons, and chiral vibrations more broadly, can be less restrictive than circularly polarized driving alone. Ren et al.[14] showed theoretically that periodic linearly polarized excitation can produce coherent chiral phonons and nonzero steady-state magnetization in a paramagnet through nonlinear spin–phonon coupling and spontaneous symmetry breaking. The concept also extends beyond crystalline phonons: Feng et al.[15] investigated vibrational angular momentum in thermally driven chiral molecular systems. These developments motivate the study of nonequilibrium chiral nuclear motion at the molecular scale.

Experimentally, chirality is manifested by different responses to left- and right-circularly polarized light in absorption, refraction, and scattering. Vibrational circular dichroism (VCD) measures the difference in mid-infrared absorption between the two helicities and is the vibrational counterpart of electronic circular dichroism.[16, 17] Following its initial observation in the 1970s,[18, 19] theoretical descriptions developed from classical treatments of optical polarization in molecules[20] to the non-Born–Oppenheimer electronic transition-current-density formulation of Nafie.[21] Polavarapu[22] reviewed quantum-mechanical calculations of VCD, vibrational Raman optical activity, and vibrational optical rotation. VCD has since become an established tool in physical and analytical chemistry.[16, 17] Advances in instrumentation and experimental sensitivity[23, 24] have broadened its use in studies of short-lived intermediates and nonequilibrium optical properties.[25, 26] Pollok et al.[23] combined matrix isolation and VCD spectroscopy to identify the stereochemistry of conformational states. Dutta and Helbing[24] reported an actively stabilized interferometric arrangement for ultrafast chiral and achiral infrared spectroscopy. Studies by Sato et al.[25] and Taniguchi et al.[26] further examined intermediate states in gelation and the evolution of helical supramolecular systems. Together, these studies motivate time-resolved optical probes of molecular and supramolecular chirality.

A microscopic dynamical description connecting chiral molecular vibrations to magnetism remains an important objective. Most phonon-IFE studies have focused on crystalline condensed-matter systems,[11, 12, 13] where the lattice environment complicates the relation between nuclear motion and magnetic response. Here, we develop a molecular framework for the vibrational inverse Faraday effect (vibrational IFE), using isolated organic molecules to resolve the buildup and evolution of vibration-induced magnetism. Molecular point groups, including D6​hD_{6h}, TdT_{d}, and more broadly C5C_{5}, provide a range of symmetry settings for examining degeneracy and chiral motion. A molecular description also permits atom-resolved analysis without the additional complexity of a crystal lattice. We investigate an optical writing-readout scheme: circularly polarized light (CPL) prepares one of two vibrational states of opposite chirality in an initially achiral molecule, and transient VCD probes the resulting handedness. In the proposed scheme, the pump helicity, the direction of vibrational rotation, and the sign of the VCD response are directly related. In addition, the early oscillatory buildup of the magnetic moment provides a time-domain feature that can distinguish it from the initially linear growth of electronic orbital magnetization reported in Ref. 27.

We investigate an optical writing-readout scheme: circularly polarized light (CPL) prepares one of two vibrational states of opposite chirality in an initially achiral molecule, and transient VCD probes the resulting handedness. In the proposed scheme, the pump helicity, the direction of vibrational rotation, and the sign of the VCD response are directly related. In addition, the early oscillatory buildup of the magnetic moment provides a time-domain feature that can distinguish it from the initially linear growth of electronic orbital magnetization reported in Ref. 27.

papers.title: GUARDTs: Decentralized Access Control for Replicated Data Types
papers.abstract:
Replicated data types providing strong eventual consistency offer a principled foundation for developing decentralized software. Yet existing approaches to programming such data types leave access control unresolved: they either provide none at all, delegate it to a trusted coordinator, reintroducing the centralization they were designed to avoid, or tie it to specific data-type constructions, while typically assuming non-Byzantine replicas and static policies.
  We present GUARDTs: Guarded Unforgeable Algebraic Replicated Data Types, which embed fine-grained permissions directly into the application data model, operate without a central authority, support dynamic policy evolution, and tolerate Byzantine replicas. We formally prove that GUARDTs guarantee confidentiality, integrity, and availability and show empirically that their access control adds negligible overhead on top of the cost of Byzantine-resilient replication itself.

Distributed applications increasingly rely on centralized, cloud-based infrastructure to synchronize state across components and to enforce access control. The appeal is clear: centralization hides the complexities of distribution and provides a single source of truth for permissions. Yet it concentrates control in a third party, raising concerns about data ownership, privacy, and security; it imposes uniform policies ill-suited to the diverse needs of individual applications; and it introduces a single point of failure that undermines availability and increases latency.

First, decentralization: the access-control mechanism operates without a central authority; a trusted coordinator that manages permissions would reinstate the very single point of trust that decentralized architectures are designed to eliminate. Second, generality: the mechanism neither is tied to specific data-type constructions nor treats application data as opaque; instead, it is applicable to arbitrary application data types while still being able to inspect their specific structure to enforce fine-grained policies in which read and write privileges differ across replicas and across sub-components of the data types. We leverage their algebraic, tree-like structure to define fine-grained permission trees, tightly integrating access control into the data model. The authorization state is replicated as a HashDAG (Kleppmann, 2022b) among all replicas, providing each with converging, tamper-evident evidence for local authorization decisions. papers.title: Gelfand numbers of Schatten class embeddings in the quasi-Banach range
papers.abstract: We prove Conjecture 1.4 of Prochno and Strzelecki [J. Approx. Theory 277 (2022), 105736] on Gelfand numbers of embeddings between finite-dimensional Schatten classes. For $0<p\le1$ and indices bounded away from the ambient dimension by a fixed proportion, we obtain the conjectured lower bound, uniformly in the target exponent $2\le q\le\infty$. Together with the known upper estimate obtained by Hinrichs, Prochno and Vyb\'iral [Math. Ann., 380(3-4):1563-1593, 2021], this gives the exact asymptotic order in the previously unresolved range. As a consequence, we obtain a complete all-index description by combining our result with the estimates of Hinrichs, Prochno and Vyb\'iral and of Prochno and Strzelecki. The proof is deterministic and is based on Hilbert--Schmidt projections on rectangular matrix spaces.
