papers.title: When, Where, How: Active In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) adapt to a new task only through the labeled rows in their context. However, labels are expensive to acquire in real-world scenarios due to the need for highly specific domain knowledge to ensure high-quality data. Active in-context learning transfers classical acquisition rules to this setting, in which the model that guides acquisition changes with every label added. We ask how the value of diversity, predictive uncertainty and target-aware information gain changes as a frozen TFM acquires more context. For that, we study Target-Aware Nearest Neighbor (TANN) acquisition and the Expected Predictive Information Gain in Context (EPIC) and evaluate them against classical rules. Our study across twenty benchmarks with two well-established TFMs and classical GBDTs highlights three findings: (i) When: diversity-based acquisition is best during the first acquisition iterations; (ii) Where: labeling pool rows that serve the target inputs via a simple target-aware nearest-neighbor rule matters substantially; (iii) How: EPIC yields the best models at the label budget, retains on average 80--87% of the chance-corrected full-data performance with only 5-10% of the pool labeled on the eight benchmarks with the largest pools, and selects labels that also improve the predictive performance of gradient-boosted decision trees.

papers.intro:
Tabular foundation models (TFMs) like TabPFN (Hollmann et al., 2023; Hollmann et al., 2025) and TabICL (Qu et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2026), pre-trained on a large corpus of synthetic tasks, solve new tasks by in-context learning (Dong et al., 2024). The frozen models are given labeled rows together with the query rows and return predictions in a single forward pass. The labeled rows are therefore the only information that adapts a TFM to a new task, and they have a decisive influence on its predictive performance. This, however, presupposes access to labeled data that can be fed to the model. In many real-world applications, labels are the bottleneck (Chai et al., 2022; Tharwat and Schenck, 2023; Li et al., 2023): they are the costly resource, as they require expert annotation, measurement or time, while unlabeled data are abundant. The choice of the rows to label is therefore a central lever and a question in its own right.

Recently, active in-context learning (AICL) has emerged as a paradigm to dynamically grow the context of a frozen TFM from an unlabeled pool. Tab-AICL (Treerath and Pittorino, 2026) transfers conventional acquisition like margin-, core-set- and hybrid-based rules (Settles, 2009; Sener and Savarese, 2018) from classical active learning to TFMs. A key finding is that no rule dominates across datasets and that the gains are concentrated in the cold start. Their analysis also makes the assumption that the rules applied remain unchanged throughout acquisition, yet a frozen TFM changes with every acquired label. The quantities that acquisition rules rely on, the model’s uncertainty and its view of which rows are similar, change accordingly as more labels are acquired. Moreover, existing rules score a candidate by its own uncertainty or by its distance to the labeled set, and ignore where the model will be used. In classical active learning, the dependence of the best strategy on the budget has been documented (Hacohen et al., 2022), and prediction-oriented criteria have been proposed that target the inputs of interest (Yu et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2023); for frozen TFMs, neither aspect has been examined.

A TFM removes both obstacles: its prediction already approximates a posterior predictive distribution, and conditioning it on a hypothetical label amounts to appending one row to its context. We introduce the expected predictive information gain in context (EPIC), which is assessed on the target inputs through the model’s in-context conditioning and evaluates all candidate-label hypotheses of a round with a single fit. Moreover, we define a target-aware nearest neighbor (TANN) approach, a simple rule that labels, for the targets on which the model is least certain, their nearest pool rows. Together with diversity- and uncertainty-based rules from prior works, these instruments separate three aspects of acquisition.

Our evaluation on the twenty benchmarks of Treerath and Pittorino (2026) supports three findings: • When: acquisition should change as the context grows. Moreover, the labels it selects also improve classical GBDTs, XGBoost and CatBoost, over their own acquisition rules (Section 4.4).

papers.title: Resolving Tusn\'ady's Problem
papers.abstract: We prove a lower bound of $\Omega_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ for the worst-case combinatorial discrepancy of $N$-point sets with respect to anchored boxes in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$. Together with Nikolov's upper bound of the same order and Wei's planar lower bound, this settles Tusn\'ady's problem: the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. The proof combines smoothed product test functions, sampling discretization, and an entropy argument for conditioned Gaussian vectors.

papers.title: Joint Higher-Order Low-Rank Tensor Decompositions for Multichannel Acoustic System Compression
papers.abstract: Multichannel room impulse responses (RIRs) in acoustics are often long and therefore the sample count becomes large if seen as finite impulse response (FIR) filters, making storage and real-time convolution costly. Pole-zero (PZ) models are an established way to represent RIRs compactly as infinite impulse response (IIR) transfer functions. We show that a PZ model implies a low-rank canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) of tensorized RIRs: the early reflections form a sparse rank-1 sum, while the late reverberation admits a CPD with factors determined by the poles. This motivates higher-order-tensor-based compression of RIRs via the block term decomposition (BTD), a generalization of the CPD. We propose two multichannel compression schemes: (i) a stacked multichannel block term decomposition (SMCBTD) applied to a (D+1)-mode tensor of RIRs, and (ii) a joint multichannel block term decomposition (JMCBTD) that shares subsets of factors across channels discovered by spectral clustering on factor-subspace affinity graphs. Both are optimized by an alternating higher-order orthogonal iteration (HOOI) procedure. On simulated rooms as well as measured datasets, the proposed methods achieve consistently lower reconstruction error at equal compression ratios compared to separate single-channel decompositions and a generalized low-rank approximation of matrices (GLRAM) baseline. The largest gains occur with scalar cores (i.e., CPD), supporting the PZ-to-CPD modelling link. We also find D = 3 to be a practical sweet spot, offering most of the achievable gain at moderate compute/memory cost. The compressed models enable efficient downstream multichannel convolution.

papers.intro:
In room acoustic signal processing, the room impulse response (RIR) is a fundamental concept that describes the point-to-point acoustic path from a sound source to a microphone within a room [1]. It captures the effects of the room’s geometry, materials, and potentially interior furnishings on the sound propagation, including reflections, diffractions, and absorptions. They are of great importance in various applications aiming to measure, evaluate, model or compensate for the acoustic properties of a room, such as in source localization [2], speech enhancement and source separation [3], room geometry estimation [4], or dereverberation [5].

In room acoustic signal processing, the room impulse response (RIR) is a fundamental concept that describes the point-to-point acoustic path from a sound source to a microphone within a room [1]. It captures the effects of the room’s geometry, materials, and potentially interior furnishings on the sound propagation, including reflections, diffractions, and absorptions. They are of great importance in various applications aiming to measure, evaluate, model or compensate for the acoustic properties of a room, such as in source localization [2], speech enhancement and source separation [3], room geometry estimation [4], or dereverberation [5].

The RIRs are typically modelled as either infinite impulse response (IIR) filters (e.g., [6, 7]) or finite impulse response (FIR) filters, depending on the application and the desired properties of the model. The FIR model is often preferred due to its simplicity, with the drawback of requiring a large number of parameters. For an average-sized room, the RIR can be several thousands of samples, while for large spaces, such as concert halls or churches, a RIR can be several tens to hundreds of thousands of samples long. This can lead to issues with storage and computational complexity, especially when multiple RIRs are considered. This is particularly relevant in applications that aim to reproduce the room in a virtual environment, such as virtual reality or augmented reality, where a potentially large number of RIRs measured within the acoustic space are needed. While IIR models are compact and can represent long RIRs with few parameters, they tend to be more difficult to work with, e.g., due to numerical stability issues. The pole-zero (PZ) model [6] is a common approach to model RIRs as IIR filters. It enables a mathematical representation of the room modes, the resonances of the room, through its poles. The room modes are shared by all RIRs in a room [8]. The method proposed in [9] takes advantage of common poles in a distributed estimation algorithm. Other literature uses the common-pole model for spatial interpolation of RIRs [10] by estimating modal parameters. In this paper, we show that there is a clear connection between the PZ model and low-rank tensor approximations by means of modal factorization of RIRs.

The need for compact representation of RIRs has led to the development of various compression techniques, with recent ones focusing on low-rank decompositions of RIRs. The truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) is a well-known method for low-rank approximation of matrices, which has been applied to matricized RIRs [11]. In [12], a generalized form of the SVD, the generalized low-rank approximation of matrices (GLRAM) [13] is used to jointly compress a set of matricized RIRs. We use the term ”matricized” to describe the arrangement of consecutive RIR segments of appropriate length as columns of an appropriately sized matrix; the analogue term we use for higher-order tensors is ”tensorized”. Higher-order decompositions, such as the Kronecker product decomposition or the canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) have been applied to individual RIRs arranged in tensor form [14, 15]. All these methods focus on compact representations that allow efficient downstream uses of the compressed RIRs, mainly described in [14, 12] where the decompositions yield fast convolution algorithms. Other compression approaches for multichannel acoustic systems include [16] where neural audio codecs are applied. Although this approach is effective in terms of compression, the particular application does not consider joint compression of multiple RIRs nor does the compact representation yield more efficient downstream applications. While an effective approach, it does not consider the same requirements and is not considered in our comparisons.

We extend these low-rank compression approaches to a joint multichannel setting by introducing tensor-decomposition-based models for sets of RIRs. Our framework is based on the block term decomposition (BTD), which provides a convenient umbrella model for several standard low-rank tensor decompositions. In particular, the Tucker decomposition (TD), also known as low multilinear rank approximation (LMLRA), is the natural extension of matrix low-rank approximations such as GLRAM [12] to arbitrary DD-mode tensors. The CPD can be viewed as a restricted TD model with a superdiagonal core whose dimensions are all equal to the CPD rank [17]. The block term decomposition (BTD) further generalizes these models by representing a tensor as a sum of block terms, where each block is itself a TD model with its own core and factor matrices. This hierarchy allows us to treat CPD, TD, and intermediate BTD models within a common framework. It is particularly useful in the present context because the PZ-based analysis suggests a low-rank tensor structure for tensorized RIRs, but does not determine a priori whether scalar-core, single-core, or multi-block structures are most parameter-efficient in practice. By comparing CPD, TD, and BTD models experimentally, we assess which member of this decomposition family best matches measured and simulated RIRs. As shown in Section 5, scalar-core BTD, i.e., CPD, provides the most parameter-efficient representation in many of the considered scenarios, supporting the proposed connection between the PZ model and low-rank CPD structure.

papers.title: The Geometry of Simulated Perspectives: Dissociating Representation and Behaviour in a Multimodal Language Model
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models can simulate different observers, yet it remains unclear how assigned perspectives reshape their internal representations and whether these changes govern their judgements. Here, we investigate the representational geometry of persona-conditioned visual interestingness in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Across 100 images and 53 prompting conditions, we systematically vary persona content and the linguistic framing used to introduce it, while recording behavioural ratings and layer-wise hidden states. We observe a systematic reorganisation of representational geometry across processing depth: early layers primarily encode image identity, whereas persona-specific structures emerge in later layers. Strikingly, prompt framing reshapes internal representations more strongly than persona identity, whereas persona content has a greater impact on behavioural judgements. This dissociation is further illustrated by minimal identity statements that alter representations even without changing responses. These findings demonstrate that representational distance does not necessarily reflect behavioural relevance. More broadly, they reveal how simulated perspectives emerge as distinct structures within the representational space of artificial cognitive systems, highlighting a fundamental distinction between the geometry of internal representations and their functional consequences.

papers.title: Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting for Online Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a scene during capture: each keyframe spawns primitives once and refines them for only a few dozen iterations, leaving little chance to fix poor initialization or missing detail. Gaussians are also inherently soft, needing many overlaps for solid surfaces. We present Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting (HIBS), which brings beta kernels to incremental reconstruction. Their shape parameter interpolates between a soft, Gaussian-like profile and a flat-topped, near-opaque surfel, acting as a confidence dial for geometry. Our confidence-aware spawning uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to initialize both opacity and shape, producing solid primitives where geometry is verifiable and soft, correctable primitives where it is not. As online densification, error-driven relocation recycles stale primitives into photometric-error hotspots. Bounded beta kernel support enables exact tile culling and faster rasterization, and a closed-form, shape-preserving merging formulation provides a level-of-detail (LOD) hierarchy for fast optimization and real-time rendering. On Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol, HIBS improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB while reducing optimization time by up to 40%. Project page: https://linus-franke.com/hibs/

This leaves little room for gradient-driven clone/split densification, opacity resets, or long optimization schedules to repair poorly initialized primitives. papers.title: Adapters as Data: The Latent Space of LoRAs
papers.abstract: LoRA adapters are usually treated as finished artifacts rather than as a data modality. Prior work has shown that LoRA adapters populate a low-dimensional manifold that a linear PCA basis already organizes well enough to support different operations such as sampling, editing, and inversion. We ask what a learned, nonlinear latent adds beyond this. We train a transformer autoencoder on the same population of LoRA identity adapters, mapping each into a latent space and compare every operation against the identical operation applied directly to the raw adapter weights. The latent preserves the capabilities already available in weight space, sampling diverse identities and editing individual attributes. Beyond preservation, we show that the latent is far more robust to displacement than weight space, degrading into distorted but still valid faces rather than texture. Fixed-dimensional weight-space representations cannot natively host adapters of more than one rank, so we extend our sequential autoencoder to hold mixed-rank adapters within one shared latent. papers.title: Bearing, heading and the perceptual geometry of collective motion
papers.abstract: Traditional models of collective motion commonly assume that animals turn to match their neighbours' directions of travel. In the harmonic theory, decisions follow from a neural representation of direction, and a neighbour enters only as a stimulus at a bearing, the direction in which it lies. Here we show that a neighbour's spatial extent allows its orientation to enter through projection geometry alone, and the theory generates a matrix of coupling coefficients indexed by the neighbour's bearing and aspect. Responses to bearing alone form one edge of this matrix, and classical heading matching is a special case on its diagonal, one ray through a two-parameter family. Independently, an animal that responds only to neighbour position, perceived with a delay, acquires an alignment coefficient set by the slope of its distance-weighted attraction profile, so that it can align, anti-align or reverse sign. Alignment need not be a rule to be measured. In schooling fish and walking pigeons with body orientation measured independently of travel, social responses are recovered, including bearing responses in the fish. Heading excess depends on how turning is measured, appearing in the fish with forward but not centred responses and remaining unresolved in pigeons. Controls show why neither outcome identifies a direct alignment rule. In fish recordings with motion-assigned body polarity, heading-dependent structure departs from Vicsek form and fails the coefficient test for a common angular potential. Whether animals align thereby becomes a measurable question, with geometric, perceptual and behavioural origins that can be distinguished.

papers.intro:
For half a century, the movement of animal groups has been modelled by assuming that individuals turn to match the directions of travel of their neighbours [1, 2, 3, 4]. In the Vicsek model it is the only interaction [3, 5, 6], in the hydrodynamic theories built on it the alignment term supplies the symmetry that makes long-range order possible in two dimensions [7, 8, 9], and in zonal models it is one of three concentric rules [4, 10]. Whatever else these models differ on, they assume that a moving animal steers towards its neighbours’ directions of travel.

The evidence comes from inferring interaction rules directly from tracked trajectories [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17], by regressing an individual’s turning onto its neighbours’ relative positions and velocities. Two directions matter here: an animal’s heading, the direction its body faces, and its direction of travel. In almost all such datasets the heading is not measured but reconstructed from the displacement of the centroid between frames, so the two are identical by construction and any response to a neighbour’s motion is interpreted as a response to its heading.

Golden shiners show no evidence of explicit matching of body orientation [12], and mosquitofish turn in response to a neighbour’s position with only weak evidence of a response to its orientation [13]. Marching locusts are captured by a ring-attractor model that represents each conspecific solely by its bearing, the direction in which it lies [18], and that orders globally only when those bearings are held in an allocentric frame [19]. Models without access to neighbours’ headings also produce collective order [20, 21]. Collective order establishes neither the presence nor the necessity of a heading-matching rule.

At first sight the test is obvious: measure body orientation independently of the direction of travel and decompose the observed turning into a component driven by where neighbours are and one driven by which way they face. It is harder than it looks. The two channels can be separated only where they predict different turns. In a polarized group the bearing and heading predictors become collinear, and in a disordered group they separate but there is little signal to attribute. Identifiability and estimability pull in opposite directions.

What makes the question tractable is a result that at first seems to make it worse. Suppose an individual responds only to neighbour position but perceives that position with a finite delay. A lagged pursuer steers toward where its neighbour used to be. Depending on how its attraction falls off with distance, it appears to anti-align, to align, or to switch from one to the other with range. Measuring alignment therefore cannot falsify a bearing-only theory. We show that the discriminating content lies one level down. A delay adds two corrections to the bearing response, one following the change in a neighbour’s distance and one following the drift of its bearing, and the measured attraction profile and its slope fix their ratio, a constraint we call the coefficient lock. A genuine alignment rule has its own gain and no reason to obey it.

papers.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
papers.abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

papers.intro:
Polymer informatics, which leverages data-driven approaches to predict polymer properties, has advanced significantly in recent years, driven by developments in machine learning, high-throughput computation, and the growing availability of materials data. Early efforts, such as the Polymer Genome project Kim et al. (2018), established foundational datasets comprising hundreds of organic polymers with both computed (e.g., bandgaps and dielectric constants) and experimental properties (e.g., glass transition temperatures), enabling the development of multi-task machine learning models. In these initial studies, polymer representations were typically constructed using handcrafted descriptors or fingerprints based on chemical intuition. For instance, neural networks trained on such features demonstrated reasonable predictive performance across multiple properties Kim et al. (2018). However, these approaches rely on expert-designed representations, which can be computationally expensive to generate and may limit their generalizability.

papers.title: Trilemma: How Agents choose between Honesty, Confidentiality, and Task Completion
papers.abstract: Personal AI agents often act on underspecified instructions and draw on context such as their user's messages and calendar to decide how to proceed. This context can contain private preferences that interfere with the task, with other people's interests, or with confidentiality norms. Prior work has studied deception under goal conflicts and the leakage of private information, but largely as separate problems. We study both problems together in a simulated company Slack workspace in which four employees delegate sprint staffing to personal agents. Two agents learn from private messages that their employee avoids working with a particular colleague. Because the other agents request justifications for task preferences and the only true justification is confidential, the agents cannot simultaneously remain honest, preserve confidentiality, and complete the staffing. We evaluate seven open-weight models and Claude and GPT models. Of the 135/140 open-weight agents that pursue the avoidance preference, 107 either make false claims about task fit or logistics or cite a true consideration as if it were their actual reason. In a three-model comparison, confidentiality instructions reduce disclosure of the preference from 83% (none) to 31% (medium) to 2% (strong). However, the task is often not completed anyway; in the main experiment (medium confidentiality instructions), only 16 of 70 runs end with a valid staffing. In their reasoning traces, agents frequently acknowledge evidence against their claims and still conclude that the claims are not false; they engage in motivated reasoning. Our results indicate that agents can strategically make false or misleading claims in a day-to-day task without being instructed to; the environment provides a controlled testbed for studying how agents resolve such conflicts and for developing deception monitors.

papers.intro:
Personal AI agents must often act on instructions that leave important decisions unspecified (Qian et al., 2024; Yi et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2026). An AI agent asked to organize a project may consult previous conversations, existing commitments, and preferences expressed privately. This context helps it act on its user’s behalf, but does not always determine a unique course of action, particularly when the task conflicts with the user’s preferences or with external norms and rules, such as confidentiality obligations or access authorizations. The agent must then decide, on the user’s behalf, how to resolve the conflict. In a widely reported case from August 2026, a user asked his agent whether it could move him up a gym-class waitlist. The agent did so by canceling another member’s reservation through an unsecured API, an action the user had never requested and the agent could not undo (Wilson & Hobbins, 2026). An AI agent asked to organize a project may consult previous conversations, existing commitments, and preferences expressed privately. Prior research has demonstrated deceptive behavior under goal conflicts and in simulated company settings, sometimes without instructions to deceive (Scheurer et al., 2024; Järviniemi & Hubinger, 2024; Lynch et al., 2025). We characterize the choices agents make under conflicting demands, the strategies they adopt as others respond, and the reasoning they express about those choices. Agents frequently try to maintain both their employee’s avoidance of working with Bob and the confidentiality of that preference. To defend their position publicly, many offer misleading explanations based on task fit or scheduling that contradict the available evidence, or misdirect by presenting another true consideration as their decisive reason. This pattern appears in 107107 of the 135135 agents that pursue the avoidance preference. Agents sometimes acknowledge evidence against a claim, then reinterpret it or narrow their definition of honesty to justify the message they send. papers.title: Formamide formation on forsterite and Mg(OH)$_2\cdot$H$_2$O
papers.abstract: Context. Formamide formation in the Universe has been the subject of debate due to its importance as a precursor to amino acids and RNA. Current studies focus on the gas-phase and icy grain formation routes. However, formamide formation on bare silicate surfaces or hydrated Mg-bearing molecular models remains largely unexplored in environments relevant to protoplanetary disks. Aims. This study presents a quantum-chemical investigation of formamide formation on an Mg center and a silicate surface. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the bare (010) forsterite ($Mg_2SiO_4$) surface, used as an analog of a bare dust-grain surface, may promote formamide formation via $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. Methods. I employed density functional theory (DFT) to study the addition of $NH_2$ to $H_2CO$ with an isolated $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ molecular model and on the forsterite (010) surface. First, I benchmarked various theoretical methodologies. I then examined the ability of $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the forsterite (010) surface to promote formamide formation. Finally, for the case with an entrance barrier, I computed unimolecular rate constants and half-lives to assess its kinetic behavior. Results. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ promotes proton transfer within the $NH_2$-$CH_2O$ intermediate via the O-H group coordinated with Mg following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$, whereas on the forsterite, a barrier-less addition pathway is found when $NH_2$ is initially physisorbed close to the formaldehyde center, followed by proton transfer leading to formamide formation. Conclusions. The Mg-bearing model systems considered here can promote rapid proton transfer following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. For the $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ model, the reaction step from the pre-reactive complex is predicted to occur on nanosecond timescales at temperatures approaching 300 K. The present work provides kinetic data for astrochemical models.

papers.intro:
The Universe serves as the cradle where organic molecules can form and develop, eventually becoming incorporated into planetary systems where life can begin (Tielens 2013). This is evident from the rich organic inventory found in carbonaceous chondrite meteorites; they are ancient materials formed under protoplanetary disk accretion and believed to have preserved the chemical conditions of the early Solar System (Sephton 2002). Isotopic analysis of these meteorites suggests that organic molecules likely have extraterrestrial origins (Sandford et al. 2001). Most of the organic precursors of life are thought to have originated under interstellar medium (ISM) conditions, where they are further chemically processed in protoplanetary disk environments, allowing them to be directly incorporated into forming planets (Ehrenfreund and Charnley 2000).

Isotopic analysis of these meteorites suggests that organic molecules likely have extraterrestrial origins (Sandford et al. 2001). Most of the organic precursors of life are thought to have originated under interstellar medium (ISM) conditions, where they are further chemically processed in protoplanetary disk environments, allowing them to be directly incorporated into forming planets (Ehrenfreund and Charnley 2000).

There are two hypothesized pathways for the formation of interstellar complex organic molecules, which are important precursors to building blocks of life such as amino acids. The "bottom-up" approach suggests that interstellar complex organic molecules form through the hydrogenation of CO on interstellar dust in the cold ISM, gradually building molecular complexity by adding a few atoms at a time. The "top-down" approach proposes that large carbonaceous molecules, such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), fragment, releasing smaller molecules that can increase molecular complexity (Tielens 2013). Finally, the products from the bottom-up and top-down processes are further processed during the evolutionary stages of the ISM, where they chemically evolve under protoplanetary disk and planetary conditions (Ehrenfreund and Charnley 2000).

During the bottom-up phase, the hydrogenation of CO leads to formaldehyde formation, which is known to be a reactant of the so-called Strecker amino acids reaction (Aponte et al. 2017). However, for this reaction to occur, a high temperature and a liquid water environment, where equilibrium chemistry can occur, are necessary. So, it is unlikely that the Strecker reaction can occur in the ISM, where radical reactions are the driving forces of molecular complexity (Rimola et al. 2010; Tielens 2013; Aponte et al. 2017).

Formamide (NH2–HC=O) is a molecule that has been observed in star-forming regions (Rubin et al. 1971; López-Sepulcre et al. 2019), as well as in comets (Bockelée-Morvan et al. 1997; Biver et al. 2014; Goesmann et al. 2015), and is thought to act as a template for peptide bond formation and RNA synthesis (López-Sepulcre et al. 2019). Therefore, formamide plays a crucial role in understanding the origins of life.

Therefore, formamide plays a crucial role in understanding the origins of life.

Despite its detection, the mechanism of formamide formation is not yet fully understood, although it is believed to originate from the reaction of formaldehyde with the NH2 radical (Barone et al. 2015). Specifically, there is ongoing debate in the scientific community regarding whether formamide is formed in the gas phase (Codella et al. 2017; Vasyunin and Herbst 2013; Barone et al. 2015; Spezia et al. 2016) or on dust surfaces (Song and Kästner 2016; Rimola et al. 2018; Kaňuchová et al. 2016). Song and Kästner (2016) studied the formation of formamide, which can occur efficiently through the hydrogenation of HNCO on water ice due to tunneling effects, while theoretical studies by Enrique-Romero et al. (2019) explored the reaction of NH2 with HCO radicals on interstellar water ice. However, this reaction competes with the H transfer of HCO to NH2, forming NH3 instead.

Kaňuchová et al. (2016) experimentally studied the desorption of formamide as a product of cosmic ray interactions with ice. While this could explain the observed formamide in comets and circumstellar environments, the study did not address the mechanistic processes of its formation. Theoretical studies by Boland et al. (2024) explored the formation of formamide from HCN and water ice surfaces through proton transfer effects. They suggest that a polar solid surface is necessary for abstracting the hydrogen atom, which requires overcoming large barriers. The need to investigate the catalytic properties of a surface in promoting formamide formation is corroborated by the experimental studies by Douglas et al. (2022), which have shown that only a negligible amount of formamide is produced from the gas-phase reaction of NH2 + CH2O due to the presence of large barriers. Therefore, surface-mediated effects warrant further investigation. While most studies of formamide formation focus on ISM conditions, comparatively little work has explored reactions mediated by metal centers or bare silicate surfaces in warm Mg-rich dust environments.

Astrochemical models of protoplanetary disks provide an important large-scale context for the fate of formamide. In particular, Quénard et al. (2018) show that formamide can be inherited from earlier evolutionary stages and released into the gas phase through thermal desorption in warm disk regions. This highlights inheritance and thermal desorption as possible contributors to gas-phase formamide in protoplanetary disks. At the same time, such models typically approximate dust grains as structurally uniform substrates governed by averaged binding energies and therefore do not resolve the elementary reaction steps occurring on specific mineral substrates. This leaves open the question of whether warm Mg-rich dust or hydrated Mg-bearing species can provide additional pathways for formamide formation or processing.

papers.title: Anisotropic g-tensor and strong spin-orbit interaction of holes in hexagonal germanium nanowires
papers.abstract: Hexagonal germanium combines direct-gap optical activity with the low-nuclear-spin environment of a group-IV material, making it a candidate platform for spin qubits and spin-photon interfaces. Using a ten-band $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$ model, we study the response of confined hole states in hexagonal germanium nanowires to magnetic and electric fields. We show that, by symmetry, the top valence band of the bulk crystal has a vanishing $g$ factor in the plane perpendicular to the $c$ axis, in analogy with the in-plane $g$ factor of heavy holes in two-dimensional hole gases. In nanowires, confinement induces only small transverse $g$-tensor components, so the $g$ tensor remains strongly anisotropic. A transverse electric field strongly reduces the nanowire band gap, providing a gate-tunable optical signature and limiting the usable field range. The same field induces a Rashba spin-orbit interaction that is markedly stronger for fields perpendicular to the $c$ axis and depends nonlinearly on the field strength. In narrow wires at strong fields, the spin-orbit length reaches a few tens of nanometers, comparable to hole devices in cubic silicon. We identify the microscopic origin of the Rashba coupling as a second-order process mediated by a few intermediate subbands with distinct symmetry selection rules. Our results provide guidance for the design of electrically controlled hole-spin qubits in hexagonal germanium nanowires.

The pursuit of scalable quantum computing has driven intensive exploration of semiconductor spin qubits, rooted in the foundational proposal by Loss and DiVincenzo to utilize electron spins in quantum dots as qubits [1]. Early implementations in GaAs heterostructures demonstrated proof-of-concept spin control, but the strong hyperfine coupling to the host nuclear spin bath led to rapid inhomogeneous dephasing, with typical T∗2{}_{2}^{\ast} values of ∼\sim 10ns~\mathrm{ns}. This limitation motivated the subsequent development of group-IV platforms with reduced nuclear-spin noise [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].

These advances establish silicon as a leading platform for high-fidelity spin qubits.

Recent breakthroughs in hexagonal Ge and SiGe alloys have begun to address this challenge. Unlike their cubic counterparts, hexagonal Ge and SiGe alloys can exhibit direct-bandgap optical emission with strong radiative recombination, enabling composition-tunable photoluminescence in the near- to mid-infrared range [25, 26, 21, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31]. This unique combination of direct-gap optical activity and a group-IV material base makes hexagonal SiGe a promising platform for integrated optoelectronic and potentially spin-photon applications [32, 29, 30]. Spin-orbit coupling and electric-field control of effective gg-factors have been extensively investigated both theoretically and experimentally in conventional semiconductor nanowires and quantum wells, including III-V materials such as InAs, InSb, and GaAs, as well as cubic group-IV heterostructures based on Si and Ge [39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45]. While these systems have served as important testbeds for spin-orbit physics, they do not simultaneously combine strong electric-field-tunable spin-orbit coupling, a group-IV material base, and efficient direct-gap optical activity, whereas III-V platforms are optically active but generally retain strong hyperfine coupling to host nuclear spins. This motivates the search for group-IV materials that can combine spin-qubit functionality with efficient optical interfaces.

Hexagonal Ge nanowires combine direct-gap optical activity with strong confinement-induced band mixing, offering a fundamentally different platform in which spin, orbital, and optical degrees of freedom can be coupled within a group-IV material system. Despite rapid progress in the growth and optoelectronic characterization of hexagonal Ge and SiGe nanostructures [25, 26, 21, 28, 30, 31], their spin-qubit-relevant properties have only begun to be explored [38, 46]. In particular, the geometry- and electric-field-dependent effective gg-tensor and Rashba spin-orbit interaction have not yet been quantitatively established for quantum-confined 2H-Ge nanowires. Beyond spin qubits, a quantitative understanding of these spin-dependent properties is also of crucial importance for engineering topological superconductivity and realizing Majorana bound states in semiconductor nanowire platforms [47, 48, 49, 50]. Here, we provide a theoretical analysis of these key spin-dependent properties, establishing a foundation for spin-qubit and spin-photon device design in this emerging material platform.

Starting from a ten-band 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} Hamiltonian [38], we construct a real-space discretized nanowire model with open boundary conditions in the transverse plane and translational invariance along the nanowire axis. This framework allows us to analyze quantum-confinement-induced subband formation, compute the anisotropic effective gg-tensor for longitudinal and transverse magnetic fields, and investigate the response of the top valence subband to transverse electric fields. We quantify the resulting Rashba spin-orbit interaction both from the electric-field-induced band splitting and through a Schrieffer-Wolff perturbative treatment, which further allows us to identify the parameter regimes where the perturbative description remains valid.

papers.title: Support in the domain of numerical algorithms in the education of future secondary school mathematics teachers
papers.abstract: This article presents web-based applets designed primarily to educate future mathematics teachers in the field of numerical algorithms and, secondarily, to serve high school students themselves. The applets allow users to explore the behaviour of basic numerical algorithms as applied to fundamental mathematical topics taught at high schools. The advantage is that no software is required, and students can intuitively test how a given method works by adjusting specific problem parameters, not only by viewing a list of approximate solutions, but especially through graphical output. Furthermore, they have access to multiple different methods for comparison.

Mathematics taught at secondary school typically includes topics such as finding roots of polynomials, computing eigenvalues of a matrix, calculating derivatives of functions, and evaluating definite integrals. These topics are practiced using examples where the solution can be determined exactly by a simple direct method. However, when it comes to finding, for example, the roots of a general polynomial of degree five or higher, an exact solution is generally not possible, and one must resort to approximate numerical methods. Such methods are not usually part of the secondary school curriculum, but we believe that secondary school teachers should be able to explain to students the fundamental ideas behind numerical algorithms, that these problems could not be solved without them.

papers.title: Spheres with transitive families of CMC hypersurfaces
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is to investigate the following question: what geometric restrictions does the existence of a transitive family of constant mean curvature hyperspheres impose on a Riemannian metric on $\mathbb S^n$? The notion of a transitive family can be made precise through the theory of Zoll families developed by Ambrozio, Marques, and Neves. Within this framework, we partially extend their local rigidity theorem for even conformal factors on $\mathbb S^3$ to every dimension $n\ge4$, assuming each hypersphere in the minimal Zoll family has the area of a round equator. Moreover, we give a partial answer to the following higher-dimensional version of a question posed by Robert Bryant: must a metric on $\mathbb S^n$, conformal to the round metric and admitting a Zoll family of hyperspheres with a common nonzero constant mean curvature, have constant sectional curvature? Finally, we also investigate inverse problems in the spirit of Hangan, asking which metrics make a fixed family of geodesic spheres have a common prescribed mean curvature.

A Riemannian metric gg on the sphere 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} is called Zoll if all its geodesics are simple, closed, and have the same length. Hilbert asked if every such metric had constant curvature. In [Zol03], Zoll disproved this conjecture by constructing explicitly examples of non-round Zoll metrics. Later, Funk [Fun13] proved the following infinitesimal rigidity, for a conformal deformation of the round metric through Zoll metrics with fixed common geodesic length, the infinitesimal conformal factor must be odd. The non obstructed case was treated by Guillemin [Gui76], who proved that every smooth odd function can be realized by the velocity of such a deformation. The complementary rigidity statement is due to Green [Gre63], and later was reproved by LeBrun and Mason [LM02], which state that, if g=e2​ρ​cang=e^{2\rho}\mathrm{can} is Zoll and ρ\rho is even, then ρ\rho is constant. Here, can\mathrm{can} denotes the canonical round metric of the sphere.

papers.title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
papers.abstract: We study composite optimization over the Bures--Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian measures. Our main observation is that a useful class of BW problems can be lifted into the Euclidean space of affine transport maps, such that the lifted problems can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal gradient methods. For objectives whose smooth and nonsmooth components admit convex smooth and convex proximable affine lifts, respectively, our algorithm BW-FISTA achieves minimax-optimal objective gap $O(k^{-2})$ after $k$ iterations. We verify these regularity conditions for potential and interaction energies together with common spectral regularizers, and we treat stochastic gradients under a suitable noise model. As a principal application, we consider Gaussian variational inference with a log-concave, log-smooth target. Here, the resulting entropy term is handled by an efficient, exact proximal step, and we improve the previous rate of $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$. We numerically verify this predicted boost with synthetic experiments.

Optimization over probability measures is a prominent paradigm in modern machine learning and statistics, with applications including generative modeling, distributionally robust optimization, and variational inference (Arjovsky et al. 2017, Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn 2017, Blei et al. 2017). Restricting to Gaussian measures yields a well-studied class of finite-dimensional yet geometrically nontrivial optimization problems (Chewi et al. 2020, Bhatia et al. 2019). In this work, we consider composite problems of the form infμ∈𝖡𝖶[ℱ(μ)≔𝒢(μ)+ℋ(μ)],\inf_{\mu\in\mathsf{BW}}\Bigl[\mathcal{F}(\mu)\coloneqq\mathcal{G}(\mu)+\mathcal{H}(\mu)\Bigr], (1) where 𝖡𝖶≔{𝒩(m,Σ):m∈ℝd,Σ∈𝕊d+}\mathsf{BW}\coloneqq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathcal{N}(m,\Sigma):m\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}^{d}_{+}}}\right\} is the Bures–Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian distributions over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Mirroring the typical assumptions for Euclidean proximal gradient methods, we require that 𝒢\mathcal{G} satisfies a suitable notion of convexity and smoothness, and that ℋ\mathcal{H} is appropriately convex and proximable (as defined shortly). Our main contribution is identifying an interesting class of BW problems that satisfy these assumptions and can thus be solved efficiently at accelerated rates, via a black-box application of Euclidean proximal gradient methods.

papers.title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations
papers.abstract: Generalisability is a central question for deep neural networks, including the cross-language generalisation of speaker embeddings. This study examined whether deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages and how such generalisation relates to human perception and acoustic structure. Using Cantonese--English bilingual speech presented in within- and cross-language conditions, we derived similarity from 18 state-of-the-art models and compared it with human ratings and acoustic features using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis. Embeddings exhibited cross-language generalisation that broadly paralleled human behaviour, reflecting accurate identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching. This generalisation relied on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting, mirroring human patterns. Together, these findings provide converging evidence for human--machine alignment in cross-language voice similarity processing.

papers.intro:
In speech and language processing, a pressing contemporary goal is to understand whether and how neural network models can generalise—namely, transfer representations, knowledge, and strategies acquired from prior experience to novel inputs [Hupkes2023, Lake2023]. One important case concerns cross-language generalisation (e.g., from English to Cantonese). In speaker modelling (typically via speaker embeddings; see [Wang2024b] for a review), this issue is particularly relevant because languages differ systematically in their phonetic and phonological structure. Such differences can modulate acoustic realisations of voice, potentially challenging downstream applications including cross-lingual speech synthesis [Zhang2024b, Zhou2023] and automatic speaker recognition [Liu2023].

In speaker modelling (typically via speaker embeddings; see [Wang2024b] for a review), this issue is particularly relevant because languages differ systematically in their phonetic and phonological structure. Such differences can modulate acoustic realisations of voice, potentially challenging downstream applications including cross-lingual speech synthesis [Zhang2024b, Zhou2023] and automatic speaker recognition [Liu2023].

By contrast, humans are widely recognised as exhibiting a remarkable capacity for generalisation [Lake2023, Taylor2021]. For example, Xu and Jiang [Xu2026] showed that listeners generalise across languages when judging voice similarity. English-speaking participants with and without Cantonese proficiency rated the voice similarity of speech pairs presented in Cantonese-only, English-only, or mixed-language conditions. Same-speaker pairs were consistently judged more similar than different-speaker pairs. Mixed-language pairs were rated as more dissimilar than Cantonese- or English-only pairs, particularly for same-speaker comparisons, suggesting that language switching disrupts vocal cue integration. Crucially, listeners’ language background did not significantly affect ratings, indicating that English monolingual listeners exhibited robust cross-language generalisation. Acoustic–perceptual correlations further identified pitch, vocal tract configuration, and harmonic/noise spectral balance as key cues whose weighting varied by language context.

Indeed, similarity judgement is a fundamental cognitive operation [Roads2024a], providing a principled testbed for human–machine alignment. Unlike tasks that rely on long-term memory for humans (e.g., recognition [Perrachione2011]), similarity evaluation can be modelled more directly in both humans and machines. Demonstrating this, Liu et al. [Liu2024] compared perceptual voice similarity with similarity derived from embeddings from seven deep neural network models using English speech. They found no significant correlations between perceptual and machine similarity under fine-grained control, whereas machine similarity correlated with acoustic similarity computed from an aggregate of 24 acoustic variables. Importantly, this study did not examine cross-linguistic generalisation. Other work has done so, but primarily using earlier models based on Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients [Gerlach2020, Gerlach2023]. For instance, Gerlach et al. Despite substantial engineering efforts to improve the cross-language robustness of speaker embeddings for downstream applications (e.g., [Zhang2024b, Zhou2023, Liu2023]), it remains underexamined whether and how deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages, particularly in relation to human perception. The present study addresses this gap by directly comparing machine, perceptual, and acoustic similarity structures across within- and cross-language conditions using Cantonese–English bilingual speech. Cantonese and English differ markedly in phonological structure, offering a stringent test of cross-language generalisation while enabling direct comparison with existing perceptual data [Xu2026]. We investigated what drives state-of-the-art speaker embeddings' capture of voice similarity using linear mixed models (LMMs). Applying representational similarity analysis (RSA), we examined how speaker embeddings relate to human listeners' representations of speaker identity and the fine-grained acoustic features underlying these representations. To ensure generalisability, the models analysed spanned a wide range of architectures, parameter scales, and pretraining corpora. Crucially, language-background effects were tested by comparing pretrained and Cantonese fine-tuned embeddings, providing a principled assessment of human–machine alignment in voice processing.

papers.title: Reading a neuron's tuning from its correlations with other neurons
papers.abstract: What a neuron represents is usually established by relating its activity to a stimulus. We ask whether the same facts are contained in the correlation matrix of a recorded population, which keeps the pairwise relations among the neurons and discards the stimulus. A transformer that sees only the correlation matrix of 512 sampled neurons, with no labels and no reference population in its input, decodes the preferred orientation of mouse visual cortex neurons from in-vivo MICrONS responses to a mean error of 25{\deg} (uninformed: 45{\deg}; best constant guess: 41{\deg}) and their receptive-field position at R^2 = 0.23; on the digital-twin substrate, 20{\deg} and 0.48. Asked whether a neuron prefers horizontal or vertical, it is right for 79% of neurons in vivo and 87% on the twin, against 56% for the majority answer; it does not resolve the obliques. The ordering is recoverable because the relations between orientation classes are close to circulant, which fixes the class structure up to rotation and reflection; the rotation of the frame is recoverable only because of a departure from that symmetry. The departure survives equal representation of every orientation and disjoint training and test stimuli, and it is an anisotropy of the signal correlations: in V1 the neurons preferring the dominant orientation have the most similar responses to one another, and a model population with only that property recovers the frame. Across 33 mice of the Allen Brain Observatory, with relations from drifting gratings, orientation transfers to unseen animals only when a sampled population mixes animals; populations drawn from one animal are not decoded measurably below the best constant, a limit of the diversity of populations one animal provides. For receptive fields, what crosses animals is where each animal's imaged patch looks on the screen, not the layout of neurons within it.

A neuron in visual cortex can be characterised by what it responds to: vertical gratings, or the upper left of the screen. This is conventionally established with the stimulus. We ask whether the same facts are contained in a description that mentions no stimulus. For a population that watched the same movie, one can compute the correlation of every pair of neurons and then discard the movie. Does the resulting matrix determine which neuron prefers which orientation, and where each neuron’s receptive field lies?

The idea that content can be read from relations is old. Shepard and Chipman proposed that a representation need not resemble what it stands for as long as the similarities among representations mirror the similarities among the things represented [1], and representational similarity analysis turned this into a method that compares brains and models through their similarity structures rather than their coordinates [2]. Structuralist accounts of experience claim that what a state represents, or how it feels, is fixed by its position in a space of relations [3]. Lässig [4] formulates the corresponding question for neural networks and gives the decoding framework we use here.

Two lines of work come close. Tsodyks et al. [5] showed that the spike-triggered average of spontaneous population activity reproduces the map of a neuron’s preferred orientation, with no stimulus present; the tuning was read from that pattern by comparison with the evoked map, a stimulus-labelled reference. Unsupervised manifold methods recover a neuron’s tuning from the structure of population activity alone, without measuring the variable it encodes [6], but the recovered coordinate is defined only up to the symmetries of the latent space, and it is related to the measured variable by aligning to it afterwards. In both cases the relations locate a neuron within the structure of the encoded variable, and something outside the relations, the evoked map or the measured behaviour, says which value that location corresponds to. We ask whether the relations among neurons fix the content of each neuron when the stimulus is discarded and there is no labelled neuron, no map and no behaviour to compare with. We also ask whether that content is readable across thousands of individually identified neurons and across animals. The nearest machine-learning work reads properties of a neuron from population activity: NuCLR learns a neuron’s identity from its population context with a permutation-equivariant transformer and transfers cell type and brain region to unseen animals [7]. It sees the activity itself. Our decoder sees only the correlation matrix, so it answers what the relations alone determine, and its target is stimulus tuning rather than cell class. This relational setting is common: recordings under natural behaviour have no controlled stimulus, and neurons from different sessions or animals share no stimulus-aligned coordinates, but they do share the structure of their correlations.

It is trained on labelled populations and scored on neurons it never saw, at two scales. Within one brain we use the MICrONS release [8, 9]: 12,894 neurons from a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex, with in-vivo responses to a shared movie, a fitted digital-twin model [10], orientation labels for 5,287 of them and receptive-field labels for 11,326 (Fig. 1). The decoder trained on half the neurons reads the other half. Across brains we use the Allen Brain Observatory [11]: 33 mice recorded under identical stimuli. The decoder trained on some animals reads neurons of animals it never saw, which succeeds only when a sampled population mixes animals, and only with grating relations.

papers.title: Capturing Membrane Dynamics and Spike Timing of Human Neurons at Scale using Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Characterizing the properties of neuronal cell types is central to understanding brain function. Yet, biophysically realistic neuron models remain difficult to scale to large populations while preserving the richness of cellular dynamics and within-cell-type variability. We present a cell-type-specific neural-operator framework for scalable neuronal population modeling. Rather than training separate surrogate models for individual neurons, the proposed framework learns a shared operator across multiple modeled neurons from the same cell type, conditioned on biologically interpretable electrophysiological features. Relative to the original single-neuron \texttt{NOBLE} setting, learning across heterogeneous neurons requires a richer electrophysiological conditioning representation and a training objective designed to preserve diverse spiking dynamics. This enables efficient generation of large ensembles of somatic voltage responses while preserving variability across cells and model configurations. We evaluate the approach using membrane dynamics metrics, action potential waveform metrics, spike timing accuracy, input-output firing relationships, and electrophysiological feature distributions. Our framework reproduces subthreshold membrane dynamics, spike waveforms, and firing-rate responses across major cortical inhibitory neuron types, while accurately preserving spike timing despite the sensitivity of threshold-crossing dynamics. The predicted electrophysiological feature distributions show strong agreement with detailed simulator outputs and human experimental recordings, including high explained variability in properties such as inter-spike intervals, firing frequency, action-potential shape, and post-spike recovery.

papers.intro:
Understanding how neural computation arises from the diversity of neuronal cell types remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Neural circuits comprise hundreds of distinct cell types with diverse gene-expression, morphological, and electrophysiological profiles [6, 7], and human neurons in particular exhibit substantial electrophysiological variability. Even identical current inputs to the same neuron can produce markedly different burstiness, adaptation, and spike-rate statistics [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Multimodal datasets now enable increasingly detailed characterization of neuronal cell types [6, 7, 8, 13, 14], but linking this diversity to computation remains poorly understood, especially in the human brain, where experimental access and monitoring capabilities are limited. The challenge is amplified for cell types defined jointly across transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological modalities, whose gene-expression signatures co-segregate with biophysical and morphological properties, and for which population-level variability makes generalization to unseen stimuli and model configurations especially difficult. How neuronal cell types organize, generate canonical computations, and contribute to neurological disorders therefore remains an open problem, and accurate single-neuron and cell-type representations are essential for developing circuit-level models of the brain.

Computational neuroscience aims to bridge this gap by linking multimodal cellular properties to functional dynamics. Biorealistic multi-compartment models integrate morphology, ion channel distributions, and electrophysiological recordings, enabling controlled perturbations that are often experimentally impossible [15, 16, 17]. These conductance-based models are deterministic, so variability is typically approximated by fitting multiple hall-of-fame (HoF) models per experiment, each reproducing a subset of experimental features [16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. Obtaining HoFs can require hundreds of thousands of CPU hours, and interpolating between them is unreliable because the dynamics of these biophysical partial differential equation (PDE) models are highly sensitive to their parameters [16, 17, 21]. Existing approaches therefore remain limited in their ability to scalably and realistically capture neuronal variability.

Neural operator surrogates offer an approach to overcoming these challenges. NOBLE [22] conditions a neural operator on current injections and interpretable neuron-model features to predict somatic voltage responses across the HoF models of a single neuron, with a speedup of several orders of magnitude over the numerical solver (Section 2). However, extending this approach to biologically defined neuronal populations requires capturing both HoF-dependent response variability and structured heterogeneity across neurons within the same transcriptomic cell type. Contributions. Using a rich human electrophysiological dataset spanning major cortical inhibitory populations, we learn a single surrogate shared across all modeled neurons of a transcriptomic cell type: • A cell-type-level biologically informed embedding. We select compact, interpretable features that capture within-cell-type variability while providing complementary information. Reverting to the original two-feature representation is found to increase the inverse interspike interval (ISI) error nearly threefold (Table 3). • A spike-weighted training objective. A sigmoid-gated relative L2\mathrm{L2} loss emphasizes spike-region errors, improving spike timing and action-potential dynamics without sacrificing subthreshold accuracy (Section 4.3). • Population-level validation against simulations and human recordings. Across three classes of inhibitory neurons, waveforms and feature distributions match PDE-based HoF simulations with smaller error than the PDE-to-experiment discrepancy, while inference is up to 3,640×3{,}640\times faster than the numerical solver (Figure 1, Section 5).

papers.title: Agnostic and efficient detection of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry-protected topological phases in projected entangled-pair states
papers.abstract: Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases are the simplest example of quantum phases that cannot be detected by local order parameters. Their classification is by now well-established from multiple perspectives, a prominent one being via tensor network states. The practical question, however, is not mere classification, but detection: given the ground state of an interacting Hamiltonian and a symmetry group $G$ along with its representation, is there an efficient way to tell if the state is in a SPT phase with respect to $G$? While there exist such practical tests in one spatial dimension (1D), methods in 2D have so far been restricted to finite-size systems or require an explicit form of virtual symmetries of the tensor networks representing the ground state. Here, we develop an agnostic and efficient method to detect interacting $\mathbb{Z}_2$ 2D SPT phases, using an infinite projected entangled-pair (PEPS) representation of the ground state. The method is agnostic to the symmetry representation in the virtual space of the PEPS tensor and applicable independent of the bond dimension of the tensors. Moreover, it is efficient as it does not require finite-size scalings: it works directly in the thermodynamic limit. We numerically demonstrate the procedure by mapping out phase boundaries away from fixed-point wavefunctions. We extract the SPT label cocycle data explicitly from the PEPS tensor.

papers.intro:
Conventional quantum phases, represented by ground states of Hamiltonians, are distinguished by a local order parameter such as magnetization in the paradigmatic Ising model. In recent decades, however, topological phases [1] have been found to evade this simple diagnostic, in that they lack a local order parameter and are not distinguished by broken symmetries. These phases are instead distinguished by topological invariants, which are robust against local perturbations, quantized, and only change at a topological phase transition. The simplest such topological phases are symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases [2], which are adiabatically connected to a trivial product state if the symmetry requirement is not enforced. Well-known non-interacting examples are topological insulators [3], for which full classification tables form a well-established part of the literature. As a natural extension, interacting SPTs have been thoroughly studied [4, 5, 6, 7] and experimentally observed [8]. In one dimension (1D), interacting SPTs have been exhaustively classified through the tools of matrix product states (MPSs) [9, 10, 11, 12]. The culminating statement is that the possible bosonic SPT phases for a symmetry group GG are classified by the second cohomology group ℋ2​(G,U​(1))\mathcal{H}^{2}(G,U(1)). A similar treatment using projected entangled-pair states (PEPS) provided a (partial) classification of bosonic SPTs in general dd dimensions [13, 10] in terms of higher-order cohomology groups ℋd+1​(G,U​(1))\mathcal{H}^{d+1}(G,U(1)). This was later generalized by more sophisticated tools such as cobordism theory [14, 15]. The focus on PEPS is natural for the 2D problem, as these constitute a systematically improvable space for short-range entangled states and underlie one of the leading numerical methods for computing ground states of interacting 2D quantum systems.

papers.title: Polynomial Lower Bounds for Steiner Shortcuts via Test Functions
papers.abstract:
The Steiner shortcut problem asks whether every directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges admits an augmentation $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+o(1)}$ edges such that $G_+$ has the same reachability structure as $G$ (i.e. for all $s,t\in V$, $s$ reaches $t$ in $G$ iff $s$ reaches $t$ in $G_+$), and the diameter of $G_{+}$ is $m^{o(1)}$. This is a core combinatorial question underlying many reachability algorithms in the dynamic, streaming, and CONGEST models, and all parallel algorithms with almost-linear work and sublinear depth.
  A sequence of works ruled out such a shortcut $G_{+}$ in the non-Steiner setting where $V_{+}=\emptyset$. However, as recently shown by Bernstein et al. [STOC '26], all known non-Steiner lower-bound constructions fail once Steiner vertices $V_{+}$ are allowed.
  This paper rules out almost-optimal Steiner shortcuts: we show an infinite family of graphs $G=(V,E)$ with the property that, for any $\varepsilon>0$, a Steiner shortcut $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+\varepsilon}$ edges must have diameter at least $n^{1/56-O(\varepsilon)}$.
  Our construction strengthens the standard non-Steiner lower-bound framework via an additional structure that allows Steiner vertices to be replaced by original vertices; we can then reduce back to the standard arguments without Steiner vertices. This new structure is achieved via a new general strategy based on test functions, which is quite flexible and can potentially be extended to applications beyond our work.
  We also generalize our lower bound to exact Steiner hopsets in undirected graphs and to depth reduction for monotone circuits. The latter significantly strengthens the classical lower bound based on Sylvester matrices.

papers.title: Eddies that ride the flow: a model of turbulence with Richardson dispersion and anomalous dissipation
papers.abstract: We construct a divergence-free velocity field $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t)$ on $\mathbb{T}^{n}$ that is a genuine function of position and carries both defining properties of turbulent transport: Richardson pair dispersion and a dissipative anomaly. No synthetic field has carried both, because the frame that gives the first destroys the field the second requires. The key is a dichotomy: deforming a spectrally localised pattern smears it across scales, whereas pushing its generating centres forward and re-convolving leaves the spectral envelope exactly invariant --- so transporting the eddy centres preserves both cascade and frame. In the field the finite-size Lyapunov exponent obeys $\zeta(R)=h(R)-1$ threshold by threshold within the scaling range, with a sweeping deficit $\Delta_{\rm sw}=+0.038\pm0.019$, consistent with zero, against $+0.091\pm0.019$ for the frozen field on the same data, a gap that doubles at Navier--Stokes intermittency. Companion papers prove that this family shows Richardson dispersion and a dissipative anomaly (Fefferman and Mayboroda 2026), and that a scalar advected by this flow obeys Yaglom's relation (De Lellis 2026), at small Kubo number. Trajectories forget their starting point as the smallest eddy is removed: the median separation of pairs released from one point with independent Brownian kicks varies as $\kappa_{p}^{0.0333\pm0.0038}$ over 22 decades of particle diffusivity, against $\kappa_{p}^{1/2}$ for a smooth control. A scalar in the same field closes the exact scale-by-scale variance budget, four independently measured terms balancing the dissipation to 15\% over 1.2 decades with no adjustable constant, and reaches its inertial--convective asymptote $S_{L}=-\chi r$ to $0.9995\pm0.0018$ once the measured diffusive transfer is restored, while under an imposed mean gradient $\chi$ changes by 14\% over a factor 5.8 in $\kappa$.

papers.title: Complex Menus in Discriminatory Pricing
papers.abstract: Advances in technology decrease the costs of offering and choosing from large menus of varieties. As these complexity costs fall, how large are the menus offered by monopolists likely to become? For the multi-product or multi-attribute case, ubiquitous in practice, we show that optimal menus are generically infinite in the absence of complexity costs. Complexity costs can decrease the menu size, but it grows without bound as these costs decrease. These results have no analogue in the single-dimensional model and do not rely on non-linearities in production costs or preferences; the extensive product differentiation is caused by screening considerations alone.

papers.intro:
Technological progress shapes how firms design and price their product lines. The shift from mass production of standardized varieties to flexible manufacturing and mass customization in the late twentieth century is one example (e.g., Milgrom & Roberts (1990)), and ongoing advancements in information technology, including the recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI), are likely to be another. Information technology can radically decrease the costs of offering large menus of product varieties, including the cost of designing and creating the production capabilities for new varieties as well as the cost of administering them, setting optimal prices, and marketing them to consumers. AI tools in particular can also reduce the buyer-side costs of evaluating large menus, costs that could otherwise induce buyers to disengage from the seller or retreat to other, simpler options. We refer to these types of costs as complexity costs.11 1 There are many recent examples of technology decreasing the costs of offering new product varieties (Babina et al. (2024); Bousquette (2024); Marrow (2026)), and AI agents are on the cusp of being able to make shopping decisions for consumers (e.g., Allouah et al. (2026)). In using the term complexity costs as an umbrella term, we follow usage in the operations management literature (e.g., Schaffer & Schleich (2008)).

Will we see substantially larger menus of varieties and contracts as complexity costs decrease? Or might optimal sales mechanisms continue to involve relatively small, simple menus even when offering many varieties is cheap? While a larger menu allows the seller to tailor varieties more finely to heterogeneous tastes and to reach buyers with lower willingness to pay through cheaper, inferior versions, each new variety also cannibalizes the sales of existing ones. How is this trade-off optimally resolved? The classic results of Stokey (1979), Myerson (1981), and Riley & Zeckhauser (1983) tell us that in single-dimensional screening models with linear costs and valuations, selling just one variety is optimal. Might an analogue of this insight continue to hold true in more realistic models that account for the multi-dimensional nature—with sellers marketing many products or products with multiple attributes—of most screening environments? An illustrative example of what might happen instead is provided by the evolution of menu complexity observed in the cloud computing industry. Amazon Web Services’ EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) went from one product (instance) type in 2006 to over four hundred in 2021 and lists over 1300 instances in just one geographical region today, as illustrated in Figure 1.22 2 See Barr (2021) for the historical data.

Our results suggest that cloud computing might well be a harbinger of things to come. We focus our discussion on the canonical model of multi-dimensional monopoly pricing, in which product varieties are differentiated along several quality or quantity dimensions, and the seller’s costs as well as buyers’ utility are linear in these dimensions (e.g., McAfee & McMillan (1988)). We study this model for several reasons. First, it is the canonical benchmark in the multi-dimensional screening literature. Second, it captures well the setting of digital goods, which is where one might expect to see the largest impact of falling complexity costs in the near future. Third, the linear model allows us also to isolate screening considerations in explaining complex menus. Indeed, in the linear model, extensive product differentiation is inefficient and can arise solely from monopoly power. Fourth, the model can be seen as a worst case for the need for differentiation, one in which we would least expect complexity, and, indeed, we show that our results extend beyond this canonical model.

The linear multi-dimensional screening model has been extensively studied in the absence of complexity costs, and we know that revenue-maximizing mechanisms are simple in some instances of the model and complex in others. Accounting for complexity costs, we further show that large menus are generically optimal if complexity costs are small. In other words, if including an additional variety on the menu has only a small cost, then optimal menus will typically be large. For seller-side costs, such as the costs of designing and marketing new product varieties, the optimal menu size increases monotonically as the costs decrease; for buyer-side costs, such as cognitive costs of choosing from the menu, convergence to large menus obtains as well but, interestingly, need not be monotonic.
