papers.title: Test-Time Self-Play: Scaling without a Verifier
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.

papers.intro:
How can a model improve on a single difficult target problem when it has no related training data and no reliable way to check its own answers? This question arises whenever a large language model’s underlying knowledge is, in principle, sufficient to solve a problem, yet the model rarely, or never, generates the correct solution. Examples of this can be found across domains, including in competitive programming (Zheng et al., 2025), theorem proving (Tsoukalas et al., 2024), and molecule generation (Gao et al., 2022).

How can a model improve on a single difficult target problem when it has no related training data and no reliable way to check its own answers? This question arises whenever a large language model’s underlying knowledge is, in principle, sufficient to solve a problem, yet the model rarely, or never, generates the correct solution. Examples of this can be found across domains, including in competitive programming (Zheng et al., 2025), theorem proving (Tsoukalas et al., 2024), and molecule generation (Gao et al., 2022).

Test-time scaling aims to close this gap, spending additional compute at deployment to improve performance on the target problem. Many test-time scaling methods, such as rejection sampling (Snell et al., 2024), rely on a verifier for the target problem that determines whether an attempt is correct. Similarly, prompt-optimization methods such as ACE (Zhang et al., 2026a) that use execution feedback for evolving prompts. Other methods rely on auxiliary data, typically similar problems retrieved from a large corpus and used to train on a neighborhood of the target problem (Hübotter et al., 2025; Hübotter et al., 2026). Another set of methods requires neither verifier nor auxiliary training data, instead aggregating a signal from the model’s own rollouts on the target problem through majority voting (Zuo et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026; Shafayat et al., 2025; Launer et al., 2026).

We propose Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), a test-time scaling method that does not rely on auxiliary training data or strong verifiers. TTSP is inspired by training-time asymmetric self-play methods such as Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2025) and R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025), which learn from self-generated synthetic problems alone. We adapt this approach to the single-target setting, concentrating the synthetic problems on a target problem rather than across a benchmark distribution. The only external requirement of TTSP is an interactive environment, such as a Python interpreter, to ground the model.

(ii) We propose TTSP, a test-time scaling method based on asymmetric self-play that is robust to weak verifiers.

papers.title: OPRD-Imp: a dataset of experimentally observed impurities and side products in multi-step pharmaceutical syntheses
papers.abstract: Predicting reaction impurities is a critical yet persistently data-limited challenge in pharmaceutical process chemistry. While machine learning models for reaction outcome prediction have advanced rapidly, benchmarking their ability to predict impurities remains impractical due to the absence of curated, publicly accessible datasets. We present OPRD-Imp, a dataset of 229 organic reactions drawn from 62 publications in Organic Process Research & Development, each annotated with experimentally observed impurities and their mechanistic origins. A total of 784 impurity entries is provided, classified into four origin categories. Reactions are represented as reaction SMILES and impurities as individual SMILES strings, with multi-step synthetic route connectivity preserved. All data were manually extracted from the source publications by trained chemists following a standardized extraction protocol, with expert chemical validation and manual structure drawing. OPRD-Imp is intended to serve as a benchmark resource for evaluating models that predict reaction impurities, providing experimentally reported impurity annotations and mechanistic origin labels that are not systematically represented in conventional reaction datasets.

papers.title: Accelerating reaction network identification via frequency-domain analysis
papers.abstract:
The identification of intracellular reaction networks from single-cell data lies at the heart of many biological studies, as it can unravel key mechanisms in living organisms and provide insights for their rational engineering.
  However, the stochastic and nonlinear nature of these reacting systems poses significant challenges for this identification problem, making the state-of-the-art methods (e.g., particle-filtering-based approaches) computationally demanding.
  This paper reports a noteworthy numerical observation that for certain systems, the Fourier transform can render the likelihood of the measurement data approximately Gaussian, therefore resulting in a substantially accelerated Bayesian inference algorithm.
  A gene transcription example is presented to illustrate this finding and demonstrate the efficiency of {the proposed Fourier-based method}.

papers.intro:
Modern biotechnologies have enabled scientists to track intracellular reaction processes at high temporal resolution (Stephens and Allan, 2003). Identifying the dynamic model of such intracellular reaction systems from these single-cell time-course data lies at the heart of many biological studies, as it provides crucial insights into living systems and lies the foundation for their control. Despite its importance, this identification problem remains challenging due to the stochastic and nonlinear nature of these systems (Browning et al., 2020; Schnoerr et al., 2017; Bronstein et al., 2015). Notably, these features suggest that the likelihood function—a key component in Bayesian statistics—often has no closed-form expression, thereby posing significant challenges for the statistical inference of the underlying system.

Modern biotechnologies have enabled scientists to track intracellular reaction processes at high temporal resolution (Stephens and Allan, 2003). Identifying the dynamic model of such intracellular reaction systems from these single-cell time-course data lies at the heart of many biological studies, as it provides crucial insights into living systems and lies the foundation for their control. Despite its importance, this identification problem remains challenging due to the stochastic and nonlinear nature of these systems (Browning et al., 2020; Schnoerr et al., 2017; Bronstein et al., 2015). Notably, these features suggest that the likelihood function—a key component in Bayesian statistics—often has no closed-form expression, thereby posing significant challenges for the statistical inference of the underlying system.

Many efforts have been devoted to this problem by employing stochastic simulations to approximate the likelihood and then combining them with established Bayesian computational methods for system identification. Representative approaches include the well-known particle Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Andrieu et al., 2010; Golightly and Wilkinson, 2011; Browning et al., 2020), approximate Bayesian computation (Toni et al., 2009), among others. Although these methods have achieved numerous successful applications in biology, they still face significant computational challenges, as the likelihood approximation requires a large number of Monte-Carlo simulations. This difficulty arises because Monte-Carlo methods are generally inefficient in estimating rare events, and the likelihood essentially represents the rare probability of observing the given data. While techniques such as the control variates (Backenköhler et al., 2022), marginalization methods (Zechner et al., 2014; Fang et al., 2024), and importance sampling (Golightly and Sherlock, 2019; Ben Hammouda et al., 2023; Wildner and Koeppl, 2019) can mitigate this issue to some extent, they still require substantial computational resources. Overall, the existing simulation-based likelihood approximation methods might not be optimal for reaction network identification.

papers.title: Richardson dispersion and anomalous dissipation for the random velocity model with controlled sweeping
papers.abstract: The present paper establishes the Richardson dispersion law, predicting the particle separation with time according to $\E R_t^2 \sim t^3$, as well as anomalous dissipation for the associated tracer, for a random H\"older continuous velocity vectorfield with controlled sweeping.

papers.intro:
The present paper establishes the Richardson dispersion law and the anomalous dissipation of a tracer for a random Hölder continuous velocity vectorfield. The construction is homogeneous in time and geometrically dense in scales. In addition, it exhibits sweeping control long conjectured to be the key to important aspects of the turbulent behavior: small eddies are materially transported by the larger ones. Its physics companion is simultaneously released as [26]. The Obukhov-Corrsin-Yaglom law for the same vectorfield is established in the simultaneously released [13].

papers.title: Hybrid integration of a SESAM with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit
papers.abstract: The realization of high-performance femtosecond lasers on photonic integrated circuits (PICs) requires robust, low-loss coupling between a saturable absorber and a photonic waveguide. In this work, we demonstrate the hybrid integration of a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) with a silicon nitride (SiN) PIC by micro-assembly. This micro-assembly strategy transfers the non-linear functionality of the absorber onto the PIC. We characterize the linear and non-linear performance of an unbonded SESAM and of a SESAM bonded to inverse-tapered SiN waveguides. At 1560~nm, the bonded device shows a waveguide-coupled modulation depth of 5.2\%, a maximum reflectivity of 37.2\%, and a saturation fluence of 47~\textmu J/cm$^2$. This work demonstrates that SESAMs can be integrated directly onto silicon nitride-based PIC platforms and provides a pathway towards fully integrated, self-starting, chip-scale ultrafast lasers.

papers.intro:
Femtosecond laser systems and optical frequency combs are essential for a wide range of applications, including dual-comb ranging [3, 5], ultra-low noise microwave generation [7, 28], dual-comb spectroscopy [10, 19], and optical atomic clocks [18, 26]. While these systems offer excellent performance, they rely on fiber or free-space optical components. This results in a relatively large footprint and cost, limiting their widespread deployment. Replacing such table-top femtosecond laser systems with photonic integrated circuits (PIC) would offer significant advantages in terms of cost, power consumption, and mechanical stability.

However, chip-scale femtosecond laser systems and optical frequency comb generators have mainly been limited to lab-scale demonstrations, with different integration approaches presenting trade-offs in performance, complexity, and scalability [4]. For example, heterogeneously and micro-transfer printed semiconductor mode-locked lasers achieve self-starting mode-locking with picosecond pulse durations [25, 6] but have limited pulse energy. Moreover, dissipative Kerr soliton microcombs can generate broadband combs with sub-picosecond pulse duration [11, 27, 1] but also provide limited pulse energies. Other approaches, such as a rare-earth doped SiN waveguide-based Mamyshev oscillator [20], have enabled high pulse energy but require a dedicated start-up procedure.

One of the main challenges in achieving stable on-chip mode-locking is the integration of a saturable absorber (SA) with low non-saturable loss, high modulation depth, and self-starting capabilities. For example, on-chip saturable absorbers have been demonstrated in the form of non-linear SiN waveguide interferometers, which have been used to demonstrate a Q-switched mode-locked laser at 1.9 µm, achieving 215 fs pulses at gigahertz repetition rates [22]. While CMOS-compatible, self-starting continuous-wave (CW) mode-locking with these non-linear interferometers has not been demonstrated to date.

In contrast, semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors (SESAMs) are a type of saturable absorbers that offer reliable self-starting [14]. These devices consist of an epitaxially grown Bragg mirror combined with a saturable absorbing layer with a short recovery time, enabling sub-picosecond pulse generation in free-space and fiber lasers [15, 12]. Moreover, direct bonding of a SESAM to a monolithic crystalline laser cavity was used to demonstrate a compact, alignment-free, ultra-low-noise mode-locked laser operating at 1550 nm [21]. Furthermore, SESAMs have enabled mode-locking in erbium-doped silica-on-silicon planar lightwave circuits, with the SESAM held against the waveguide facet by a micro-positioner [2], and more recently dispersion-managed MLLs in erbium-doped SiN waveguides [16].

An indium phosphide (InP)-based SESAM is bonded directly to the polished edge facet of a SiN PIC using a UV-curable epoxy [Fig. 1(a)]. To ensure low-loss waveguide-SESAM coupling, an inverse waveguide taper expands the waveguide mode at the facet and reduces diffraction loss in the bonding gap. We characterize the SESAM before and after bonding, using two SESAMs from the same wafer, and obtain a waveguide-coupled, unsaturated reflectivity of up to 61% at 1600 nm, and a modulation depth of 5.2% and a saturation fluence of 47 µJ/cm2 at 1560 nm. Although demonstrated at 1550 nm and 1560 nm, the integration technique is platform-agnostic and can be applied to any edge-coupled PIC platform and to other wavelengths, providing a general route to on-chip saturable absorbers.

papers.title: The polar discontinuity picture in nickelate superlattices: comparison of the insulating and metallic phases
papers.abstract: We present a first-principles study of the formal-charge polar discontinuity in superlattices of BaTiO$_3$ interfaced with SmNiO$_3$ or BiNiO$_3$, comparing the results for the insulating and metallic nickelate phases. Polar discontinuities arising from differently charged layers in perovskites are well-studied in heterostructures such as LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$, and recently, signatures consistent with such a polar discontinuity have been observed in systems where the formally charged layers would reside in a metal. We first identify signatures of the polar discontinuity in the structure and the density of states of superlattices with BaTiO$_3$ and insulating BiNiO$_3$, and find partial screening by modification of the BiNiO$_3$ charge disproportionation pattern analogous to our previous study on BaTiO$_3$/SmNiO$_3$. We then examine superlattices constructed from the corresponding metallic nickelate phases and find that, despite the presence of screening charges, the qualitative interfacial response is remarkably similar to that of the insulating counterparts. We show that the metallic screening charges have little influence on the apparent formal-charge polar discontinuity and discuss practical limitations of the polar-discontinuity picture when interpreting and quantifying screening at metallic nickelate/ferroelectric interfaces.

papers.title: Leave It Better Than Found: Value-Guided Cooperation in Sequential Tasks
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of sequential task continuation, where one robot acts in a workspace that has been affected by a previous robot. Current approaches in multi-robot cooperation rely heavily on co-training or co-optimization, assumingthat the robots have access to collective interaction data during the policy training or planning process. However, as increasingly varied robotic embodiments and policies are deployed and operate in the same real-world environment, learning policies for cooperation becomes infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of possible robot combinations that need to be accounted for. To address this challenge, this paper considers the problem of ad hoc sequential cooperation between robots that have never before operated together in a shared environment. We demonstrate that robots can explicitly communicate their environmental preferences through sharing their value functions, enabling coordination without the need for prior joint training. To ground this exchange and prevent overconfidence in out-of-distribution states, we further introduce a k-nearest neighbors (KNN)- based uncertainty filter. Our method yields an increase of up to 48.5 pp compared with naive or even selfish agents, in task success rates across simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating that value function transmission between agents is useful not merely as an internal learning tool, but as an effective basis for ad hoc coordination. Website: https://proroklab.github.io/PAVE/
papers.intro:
As robotic systems achieve greater autonomy, heterogeneous agents, e.g., cleaners, delivery bots, and security systems, will increasingly operate in the same public and domestic spaces. Robots modify these spaces to achieve their goals, leaving subsequent actors with the environments that they left behind. These workspace overlaps require spontaneous cooperation between independently developed systems. We formalize this challenge as sequential task continuation: a setting where an agent must proactively anticipate how its physical actions will alter the shared space and affect subsequent actors.

Robots modify these spaces to achieve their goals, leaving subsequent actors with the environments that they left behind. These workspace overlaps require spontaneous cooperation between independently developed systems. We formalize this challenge as sequential task continuation: a setting where an agent must proactively anticipate how its physical actions will alter the shared space and affect subsequent actors.

Currently, robot behaviors are typically designed in isolation by different parties to perform distinct tasks. When actors interact in the same shared workspace, we require methods and protocols that bridge these independent systems. For instance, delivery bots should not drop packages along common patrol routes, and cleaners should not rearrange the environment in such a way that areas become inaccessible to other robots. Because hand-crafted rules are too brittle to handle the infinite edge cases of open-world environments, learning-based coordination is required. Training a separate cooperative policy for every possible pairing of robots is unrealistic, as the possible combinations increase exponentially with the number of robot embodiments and tasks.

Instead, we turn to ad hoc coordination between agents that does not require joint training, as robots can easily share key components of their decision-making with other agents. Given the representation of other agents’ preferences, robots can adapt their behavior on the fly (ad hoc) to aid other robots in their tasks while still pursuing their own. Existing frameworks in this domain, however, rely on restrictive assumptions. Zero-shot coordination [15] trains a single robust policy, but it does not allow online adaptation. Ad Hoc teamwork, first proposed in Stone et al. [31] and implemented in PLASTIC [1] and TEAMSTER [26], adapts online but assumes a single common payoff and infers teammate behavior from observation rather than direct communication. Both approaches assume that actors act simultaneously and not sequentially.

Our approach is different: agents pursue distinct tasks and exchange compact representations of their preferences. Rather than relying on task-specific learned communication channels [9, 18], we leverage a quantity that reinforcement-learning agents already learn: the value function, which maps states to expected return. For sequential task continuation, the relevant part is the follower’s value over shared environment states. Sharing the value function tells the leader which handoff states are useful for the follower. Our method, Policy Adaptation via Value Exchange (PAVE), uses this single exchange of the value function to coordinate with the following agent without joint training, adapting the leading agent’s policy online using a receding horizon planner.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning typically relies on joint training with shared critics, as in MAPPO [36], MADDPG [20], COMA [10], and QMIX [25]. These approaches do not scale to sequential task coordination as the robots act not simultaneously but sequentially in a shared environment. Cooperative Consecutive Policies [8] instead train distinct policies acting on a shared embodiment to solve long-horizon tasks, by optimizing each current policy with respect to the next agent’s Q-function to ensure an optimal hand-off. Although distinct from our method, it assumes a shared embodiment and joint training, and it inspires one of our baselines. Dhakal et al. [5] propose a planner for rearrangement tasks that anticipates the effects of its actions on future tasks of the same agent. PAVE differs by reusing an existing value function, filtering out-of-distribution value estimates, and considering multiple agents instead of a single agent.

Other approaches similarly treat the environment as the medium of inter-agent influence. Stigmergy [14, 7, 24] is a natural process used by swarm animals such as ants to coordinate through pheromone deposits in the environment. Environment Co-Design [11, 12, 17] also considers adapting the environment to benefit the agents acting within it. PAVE defines a middle ground: agents communicate directly via their value functions, but enact that coordination indirectly. One agent manipulates the physical space via its task-constrained policy to favorably shape the state for the next agent, achieving continuation without requiring central design or shared training. papers.title: TerraMesh-Masks: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation for Earth Observation
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) enables models to segment a variety of concepts specified in natural language, removing the need for fixed label sets and fine-tuning. While recent OVS approaches have shown strong performance on natural images, they transfer poorly to Earth observation (EO) data due to differing semantics, scales, sensing modality, and geographic context. To date, large-scale EO-specific datasets and benchmarks for OVS remain scarce. We, therefore, introduce TerraMesh-Masks, a large-scale open-vocabulary segmentation dataset for EO, comprising 16 million binary masks aligned with nine million multimodal TerraMesh samples and annotated using OpenStreetMap and Overture-derived semantics. In addition, we provide an expert-reviewed evaluation set of 523 samples covering over 200 classes to enable robust evaluation. To demonstrate the impact of TerraMesh-Masks, we build an open-vocabulary version of TerraMind. Our results demonstrate significantly improved performance over general-purpose state-of-the-art models reaching 35.18% IoU versus 16.29% for DINOv3.txt and 11.33% for SAM-3. We release the dataset publicly under a permissive license at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-esa-geospatial/TerraMesh-Masks.
papers.intro:
Open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) promises more flexible and scalable interaction with Earth observation (EO) data compared to fine-tuning models for a fixed set of classes manually. Users could query models with flexible language rather than a pre-defined closed label set, and use a single model for a variety of concepts [1]. However, existing OVS models are developed primarily for natural images and transfer poorly to satellite imagery [2], where semantic concepts are expressed at lower spatial resolution, often require multispectral sensing, and vary strongly across geography and land-cover context. While previous works focused on high-resolution aerial imagery [3, 4, 5], the field currently lacks both a strong benchmark and a large-scale training resource for open-vocabulary segmentation with satellite data.

Open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) promises more flexible and scalable interaction with Earth observation (EO) data compared to fine-tuning models for a fixed set of classes manually. Users could query models with flexible language rather than a pre-defined closed label set, and use a single model for a variety of concepts [1]. However, existing OVS models are developed primarily for natural images and transfer poorly to satellite imagery [2], where semantic concepts are expressed at lower spatial resolution, often require multispectral sensing, and vary strongly across geography and land-cover context. While previous works focused on high-resolution aerial imagery [3, 4, 5], the field currently lacks both a strong benchmark and a large-scale training resource for open-vocabulary segmentation with satellite data.

We address this gap with TerraMesh-Masks, a planetary-scale semantic-mask dataset, grounded in OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps, built on top of TerraMesh [6]. We additionally provide an expert-reviewed evaluation set called TerraMesh-Masks-Eval for benchmarking future OVS models. To demonstrate the value of this dataset, we adapt TerraMind to open-vocabulary binary segmentation. Our results show that EO-specific multimodal training is substantially more effective than applying a general-purpose baseline off the shelf. As shown in Fig. 1, TerraMind-OVS models outperform the generic models SAM-3 [1] and DINOv3.txt [7] as well as many EO-specific models like GeoPixel [3] in the vast majority of categories.

papers.title: National-scale mapping of tree species composition in Switzerland from high-resolution aerial imagery and multimodal data
papers.abstract: Tree-species composition shapes forest productivity and how forests respond to climate disturbances such as drought, windthrow and insect outbreaks. Yet most national forest maps assign each pixel a single dominant species and cannot show the share of accompanying species. We mapped the basal-area shares of ten main tree species and a residual Other class across Switzerland at 30 m resolution. A deep-learning model combining 0.1 m aerial RGB imagery, airborne laser scanning (ALS), annual AlphaEarth satellite embeddings, and climate variables was trained on basal-area observations from 3,992 Swiss National Forest Inventory (NFI) sites. In spatial cross-validation, the model reached a macro-$R^2$ of 0.485 across the 11 classes. On an independent forest-reserve dataset, the map reached a macro-$R^2$ of 0.552 for individual 30 m pixels and 0.733 for plots, and identified the dominant class in 73.2% of pixels and 81.1% of plots. The map shows maple and ash as widespread minor components that dominant-class maps omit. It also reproduces the elevational sequence from broadleaved lowland stands through spruce to larch and Arolla pine near the treeline. By resolving the species mixture within each 30 m pixel, the map complements field inventory statistics with spatially continuous information that can support forest monitoring, the management of mixed stands, and climate-adaptation planning across Switzerland.

papers.intro:
Accurate, spatially explicit information on tree-species composition is essential for understanding how forests function and respond to disturbances. Tree diversity is positively associated with forest productivity (Liang et al., 2016), and species differ in their susceptibility to drought, windthrow and insect outbreaks (Anderegg et al., 2020; Senf and Seidl, 2021). Forest services need composition information to assess current forest condition and to select species for climate-adapted regeneration (Fassnacht et al., 2016; Strauss and Fischer, 2025). In mixed forests, this information goes beyond the dominant species. In other words, stands with the same dominant species can differ widely in the number and proportions of accompanying species. Large-area composition maps therefore need to quantify the shares of all species in a stand, including the accompanying ones (Bolyn et al., 2022; Klehr et al., 2025).

Large-area composition maps therefore need to quantify the shares of all species in a stand, including the accompanying ones (Bolyn et al., 2022; Klehr et al., 2025).

Remote sensing (RS) has made large-area tree-species mapping increasingly feasible by combining wall-to-wall image coverage with forest-inventory observations. Satellite time series record seasonal differences among species and provide repeated observations over large, environmentally diverse regions (Blickensdörfer et al., 2024; Breidenbach et al., 2021). Combined with national inventory data, they support products that distinguish multiple species or species groups, including a 10 m map of the dominant species in Switzerland (Koch et al., 2024). Most of these products, however, assign a single class to each pixel. At resolutions of 10–30 m, one pixel can cover several crowns and species, so a single class leaves the within-pixel composition unresolved (Fassnacht et al., 2016). More accurate classifiers make the dominant label more reliable, but they still do not quantify the shares of secondary species. Mixed stands also complicate the construction of reference data. Restricting training samples to homogeneous or nearly pure stands simplifies the link between image and label, but it underrepresents mixed conditions during model development. Evaluating on pure stands alone then gives an incomplete picture of performance where mixtures are common (Blickensdörfer et al., 2024).

Continuous composition targets avoid this simplification by describing each reference unit as a vector of species proportions. Such targets have been learned from inventory data of mixed stands with spectral–spatial deep learning (Bolyn et al., 2022), from synthetic mixtures of pure Sentinel-2 time series (Klehr et al., 2025), from airborne laser scanning (Murray et al., 2024), and from combinations of lidar, airborne spectral and satellite data (Ørka et al., 2021; Candelas Bielza et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2026). All of these studies cover a single region (Table 1), which spans a limited range of climate, elevation and species pools, so the relationship between imagery and composition is learned and tested under similar environmental conditions (Blickensdörfer et al., 2024). In contrast, Switzerland is a demanding test case: its forests extend from the lowlands of the Plateau to the treeline in the Alps, and their composition shifts from broadleaved and mixed stands at low elevations to coniferous stands at high elevations (Strauss and Fischer, 2025; Wüest et al., 2020).

Very-high-resolution aerial imagery provides evidence that freely available satellite pixels cannot. At 0.1 m resolution, individual crowns, their texture and their arrangement are visible, and such imagery has supported individual-tree detection and species identification in Swiss forests (Beloiu et al., 2023). Switzerland acquires such imagery for its entire territory on a roughly three-year cycle (Federal Office of Topography swisstopo, 2026b). Using it for composition mapping, however, poses a different learning problem. Inventory plots record the species and diameter of individual trees, but these records are not matched to crowns in the image, so a model must relate the appearance of a whole canopy patch to the plot-level composition. Self-supervised models pretrained on large unlabeled image collections provide features that transfer to forest imagery with few labels (Siméoni et al., 2025). Such features have supported canopy height mapping (Brandt et al., 2026), but they have not yet been tested for estimating species composition from inventory plots.

Species that look alike on one date can differ in their seasonal trajectories (Cloutier et al., 2024), and annual satellite embeddings summarize such trajectories from several sensors (Brown et al., 2025; Ball et al., 2026). papers.title: Coverage Hides Churn: Auditing and Preserving Conformal Decisions as VLM Label Registries Grow
papers.abstract: Vision-language classifiers can learn new labels from text alone, so the label lists they serve keep growing. We show that this growth silently changes conformal decisions about old labels. Common softmax-based conformal scores compare each label with an average over all labels; adding labels changes that average, and with it the score of every old label, even when the model, the image, and the old calibration data stay the same. Recalibrating after the update keeps the coverage guarantee, yet across eleven settings it changes at least one old decision on 53-90% of new images. Coverage cannot reveal this, because it checks only the true label: in five controlled settings that keep the old calibration, so that only the normalizer changes, old-class coverage moves by at most 0.01 while 60-67% of images change. papers.title: Dual-Arm Tabletop Rearrangement with Movable Stacking and Gap-Aware Push Transfers
papers.abstract: Object rearrangement in cluttered tabletop scenes is challenging, especially in wide workspaces where dual-arm systems improve coverage and efficiency. Limited free space often necessitates buffering, while objects near or across the shared reachability region of the manipulators must be transferred under careful coordination to avoid inter-arm collisions. Conventional inter-arm transfer typically relies on a fixed handoff configuration, which constrains where and how objects are exchanged, enforces spatiotemporal synchronization of the arms, and reduces flexibility in dense layouts. This paper presents a dual-arm rearrangement framework that combines movable stacking with Gap-Aware Push Transfer for asynchronous cross-boundary exchange. The method scans the shared boundary to identify collision-free transfer gaps, places an object near a selected crossing point, and then pushes it into the receiving workspace without requiring simultaneous interaction between the two arms. A joint Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based planner coordinates both manipulators while reasoning over buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the resulting plan. Experiments show that the proposed method shortens joint execution sequences and becomes increasingly advantageous over a fixed handoff baseline as scene density increases, achieving lower execution cost in denser scenes while remaining competitive in lighter ones.

papers.title: Transparency in Team Contracts
papers.abstract:
In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a contract, sharing part of the project's success among the agents; second, to design a (Bayesian) persuasion scheme, selectively sharing information with the agents. In this work we are interested in the optimal combination of both these tools.
  We tackle the joint problem through the prism of simplicity vs. optimality, and establish a stark dichotomy: The simple disclosure scheme of full transparency achieves a tight $4/3$-approximation to the optimal combination of information disclosure and team contract, when the team's production function is submodular. In contrast, full transparency can be arbitrarily far from optimal when production is supermodular.
  The techniques that we develop to bound the gap for submodular functions, also yield a new deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm for pure multi-agent contract design, with a significantly improved approximation ratio of $2.311$, and thus a $3.081$-approximation algorithm for the joint information and contracting problem.

papers.intro:
Algorithmic contract design is an important frontier at the intersection of economics and computation (Dütting et al., 2024b). A fundamental problem in algorithmic contract design involves a principal who delegates a project to a team of agents, and seeks to design a (near-)optimal payment scheme to incentivize their costly and unobservable efforts (Dütting et al., 2023). In contracting problems, it is often the case that the principal is more informed than the agents. For example, the principal may hold information about the difficulty of the task, the state of the market, a competing lab’s technology, etc. This information affects how the agents’ efforts translate into success or failure of the project. In such situations, in addition to designing the contract, the principal may gain from strategically revealing or withholding information. This brings us into the realm of algorithmic information design — another vibrant frontier (Dughmi, 2017; Dughmi and Xu, 2021).

The combination of contract and information design introduces an intricate design problem of jointly optimizing the information disclosure and contracting schemes — see (Castiglioni and Chen, 2025) for a recent algorithmic treatment in a single-agent environment. In general, joint optimization of two or more incentive schemes is typically complex, exhibiting all the known intricacies of multi-parameter auction design (Daskalakis, 2015) (see (Daskalakis et al., 2016) for the combination of auction and information design, and (Castiglioni et al., 2025) for auction and contract design). Beyond presenting new technical challenges, the joint design of incentive schemes brings theory closer to real-world applications, where different mechanisms interact rather than operate in isolation. The simple vs. optimal paradigm is particularly well-suited for bridging the gap between theory and practice, shedding light on why certain simple designs are ubiquitous despite their sub-optimality (see (Babaioff et al., 2020) for simple auctions, and (Dütting et al., 2019) for simple contracts).

papers.title: GINGER: Spicing Up Graph-Based Vector Search
papers.abstract:
We present \textsc{Ginger}, a state-of-the-art open-source C++ library for graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). We developed \textsc{Ginger} at Google to push the speed and memory efficiency of graph search on large and high-dimensional embedding datasets. \textsc{Ginger} surpasses existing ANNS libraries with regards to query throughput and indexing time while matching the memory footprint of the most space-efficient competitors.
  \textsc{Ginger} builds upon recent advances in proximity graph construction (PiPNN) and vector quantization (TurboQuant). We introduce Nested TurboQuant (NTQ), a two-level quantizer which supports low precision graph navigation and high precision reranking in a single code. This representation achieves near floating point precision with $2.6\times$ less memory. We also compress the size of our proximity graphs by up to $2.5\times$ without impacting query throughput. We combine graph reordering with a new lossless compression codec called AdaptiveGap, which builds upon StreamVByte. At $95\%$ recall, \textsc{Ginger} speeds up query throughput by an average of $1.8\times$ over each dataset's fastest competitor and by at least $2.3\times$ over any single library. This lead grows to $2.9\times$ over compact libraries on high-dimensional embeddings.

Proximity graphs have been shown to perform well in very high dimensions, and are thus the dominant technique for ANNS indexing whenever high recall is paramount. A proximity graph represents each entity as a vertex and connects it to nearby and further directionally diverse neighbors. Queries route through the graph via greedy beam search, which iteratively expands the closest unexplored vertices until converging to the query neighborhood. Prominent proximity-graph algorithms include HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018a), Vamana (DiskANN) (Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019), NSG (Fu et al., 2019), and PiPNN (Rubel et al., 2026b; Rubel et al., 2026a). Compared to cluster-based inverted-file (IVF) indexes such as Faiss (Douze et al., 2024) and ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023), proximity graphs achieve high recall with many fewer distance evaluations on modern embeddings.

papers.title: CAMP: Context-Aware Mapping and Placement for LLMs on 3D-IMC Arrays
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur severe memory-access overheads due to the cost of loading large weight matrices and key-value (KV) caches. Analog In-Memory Computing (AIMC) is an emerging solution that enables computation directly on static weights stored in memory, substantially reducing energy and latency. 3D-IMC further stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers, increasing capacity but revealing a new challenge: how weights are placed in memory determines which matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) can execute concurrently, affecting latency and throughput. The concurrency aspect of 3D-IMC weight-mapping remains underexplored in the literature, leading to sub-optimal utilization of compute resources on 3D-IMC chips. In this context we propose CAMP (Context-Aware Mapping and Placement), an inference-context-aware weight mapping algorithm for 3D-IMC-based LLM accelerators. CAMP captures the potential resource contention resulting from the architecture, targeted network, and runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimized weight mapping. This mapping is refined through a profiling-driven feedback loop that efficiently prunes the search space and returns optimized mappings within practical runtimes. CAMP is an offline, software-based solution requiring no hardware changes and improving 3D-IMC compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput over state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.

The mainstream hardware for llm inference is the gpu (gpu). papers.title: Credibility Clustering for Experience Rating: An Automated Approach to Risk Group Allocation in Group Life Insurance
papers.abstract: In insurance, experience rating plays a crucial role in mitigating adverse selection by adjusting premiums according to historical claims experience. A key step in this process is the classification of insured collectives into homogeneous risk groups. Within group life insurance, this classification traditionally relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds, which may lead to inefficiencies and inconsistent outcomes. This paper proposes a data-driven methodology for automating risk group allocation based on a combination of the multidimensional B\"uhlmann-Straub model and k-means clustering -- referred to as credibility clustering. By incorporating credibility weights, the method accounts for the varying statistical significance of experience data and ensuresthat risk classifications are both actuarially sound and practically implementable. Empirical results based on real-world group life insurance data from a major European insurer demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms the two k-means benchmark variants considered in the empirical application in terms of viability, temporal stability and accounting for statistical reliability.

papers.title: Zero-Point Renormalization Reshapes the Shift Current: The Role of Electron-Phonon Coupling
papers.abstract: Shift current (SC) drives the bulk photovoltaic effect, holding promise for near-instantaneous, low-dissipation photodetection and energy conversion. The current understanding of SC relies primarily on a single-particle picture, in which the SC is determined purely by band dispersion. While many-body effects from directly excited quasiparticles, such as excitons, magnons and phonons, have been explored, the renormalization of electronic states by quantum virtual-phonon coupling --- inherent in essentially all solids and particularly decisive for transport --- remains unaddressed. Here, using first-principles calculations, we identify this missing channel --- band-renormalized shift current (BRSC) --- in monolayer MoS2. We find that the zero-point renormalization alone, without any polarization-carrying photoexcited phonons and with barely any alteration of the band dispersion, dramatically reshapes the SC spectrum: emergent low-energy peaks arise from phonon-assisted optical transitions between momentum-distinct states, with a pronounced redshift of higher-energy features. A mere 1.0% strain sharply tunes the BRSC, whereas raising the temperature enhances it. Our findings overturn the band-structure-only paradigm, establishing electron-phonon coupling as an indispensable ingredient for nonlinear photocurrent and opening a strain-thermal route for engineering next-generation optoelectronic responses.

papers.title: AGN Archaeology: A Systematic Search for Fading AGN in MaNGA
papers.abstract: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) vary on broad timescales, but are primarily thought to "flicker" on and off during episodes of high and low accretion. Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) which are actively accreting material often show optical spectra dominated by AGN emission in their nuclei and beyond. In this work we develop an empirical model to quantify the fractional AGN contribution to optical spectra using the Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich (BPT) emission line diagnostic diagram. We leverage this model against integral field unit (IFU) data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey to select 34 galaxies with weak nuclear AGN activity relative to their AGN signatures at large radii; this signifies past AGN activity which is fading with time (i.e., fading-AGN). The majority of our fading-AGN reside in edge-on systems undergoing minor mergers. We construct a simple model consisting of a disk galaxy with ionization cones and find that the orientation of such a system will impact its BPT classification in both single-fiber and IFU observations. The mean distance to the extended AGN emission in our sample corresponds to a light-travel time of $1.1\times10^4$ years. We use this to set a lower-limit on the typical lifetime of the AGN phase ($t_{\text{AGN}}>1.3\times10^5$ years) which is consistent with SMBHs growing via brief accretion bursts. These fading-AGN allow us to probe the elusive period of post-AGN galaxy evolution, and they give a $\sim10^4$ year baseline for understanding the accretion history in these systems.

papers.intro:
AGN have been shown to vary on timescales ranging from hours to millions of years; this variability occurs across the entire electromagnetic spectrum [136, 168, 137, 169, 74, 156, 152, 134, e.g.,]. There are numerous causes for the short-term variability including dense gas eclipsing the AGN along the observer’s line of sight [140, e.g.,], thermal fluctuations in the accretion disk [94], or tidal disruption events [65, e.g.,] to name a few. SMBHs need a relatively stable gas supply to remain classified as an AGN using traditional techniques (see Hickox & Alexander 76 for a review of these techniques), and this nuclear fueling can occur through numerous physical processes [84, 163, 146, 5, e.g.,]. The AGN phase is a finite event meaning that AGN will turn on and off over cosmic time analogous to a “flickering” light bulb [74, 152], and this variability occurs on much longer timescales relative to the short-term variability previously discussed. However, we can observationally identify AGN which have recently turned off or on based on the spatial extent and location of the AGN emission [152, 52, 59, e.g.,].

Fading-AGN are AGN where the SMBH has halted (or substantially reduced) its accretion of material and therefore the entire system will begin to appear orders of magnitude dimmer. However, once the SMBH has exited its accretion phase, signatures of the past AGN will still be detectable at locations outside the central region of the galaxy. These signatures, which are referred to as AGN light echoes (LEs) or extended emission line regions (EELRs), persist due to gas cooling timescales and (often most significantly) light travel time (i.e., the time it takes light to travel some distance). Fading-AGN can also lend insight into the host galaxy’s large-scale gas environment and trace the history of accretion onto the SMBH. LEs and EELRs can inform us about the geometry of AGN narrow-line regions (NLRs) which allow for tests of the unified model [7, 124, e.g.,]. EELRs, in particular, are the longest tracer of AGN activity that account for ∼105\sim 10^{5} years in some cases [112, 99, e.g.,]. A blind search for fading-AGN allows us to place empirical limits on the typical lifetime of the AGN phase [59]. Such searches are challenging as spectroscopic data are frequently needed to determine the primary source of ionization, and the majority of (non-IFU) spectroscopic surveys focus their observations on galaxy nuclei where you would either not detect the EELR (due to the size on the sky) or the EELR is diluted by the host galaxy.

Perhaps the most well known example of a fading-AGN is Hanny’s Voorwerp near IC 2497 [112] which was discovered through the Galaxy Zoo project [111]. Hanny’s Voorwerp mimics a NLR with its high-ionization (>35.12>35.12 eV, Berg et al. 16) emission line ratios, despite being located ∼15−35\sim 15-35 kpc from the galaxy’s nucleus [151, 89]. Similarly, past searches for fading-AGN have focused on identifying extended [O III] λ​5007\lambda 5007 emission from photometric surveys; these are regions which are unusually luminous in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) g−g-band in the local Universe [89, 90, 164, e.g.]. Furthermore, merging systems are the ideal location to search for extended emission, as galaxy scale interactions can drive gas towards the SMBH and produce extended gas clouds to be illuminated by the central AGN [91, 92, 93, 52]. However, the reliance on merging systems may skew our understanding of fading-AGN regarding their ubiquity.

Extended AGN emission is relatively straightforward to identify in IFU data due to spatially resolved emission line diagnostic diagrams and spectroscopic redshift determinations. In Section II we discuss the MaNGA survey and the data model that we adopt. Section III discusses our AGN decomposition model, the selection algorithm used to find candidate fading-AGN, and the removal of interlopers. We investigate properties of the fading-AGN such as their luminosity and morphology in Section IV. In Section V we place a lower limit on the AGN phase lifetime in the local Universe, perform 3D modeling to test the effects of orientation, and compare our results to previous work. In Section VI we summarize our findings and their importance. When necessary we utilize the following cosmology: H0H_{0}=70 km s-1 Mpc-1, ΩM\Omega_{M}=0.3, and ΩΛ\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7.

papers.title: REST: Routing with En-route Seating Thresholds for pedestrian accessibility
papers.abstract: Public seating can support walking by providing opportunities to rest at useful positions along complete journeys. We introduce a route-based framework that assesses nearby seating, access to everyday destinations, and whether rests are well spaced along routes. One method finds the shortest route that does not exceed a chosen distance without rest; another allows longer stretches but adds a cost expressed as equivalent walking distance. We apply the framework to Mannheim, Germany. With a 1,000 m travel budget and a 500 m limit on walking without an opportunity to rest, 99.5% of older residents in Feudenheim lived within 500 m of a rest, yet only 33.5% could reach at least one destination in each of five categories (food shops, pharmacies, primary healthcare, public transport, and community services) on ordinary shortest routes meeting this limit. Finding alternative routes with sufficiently spaced rests increased this share to 61.4%; allowing longer stretches with an added cost raised it to 76.2%, compared with 89.7% when resting needs were ignored. Across Mannheim, 20.2% of older residents lost access to a reachable category when routes required a resting opportunity every 500 m, versus 7.1% when longer stretches were allowed at extra cost. Compared with the shortest physical distance, the least burdensome routes incurred extra costs from seating gaps: a median of 7.3 m of equivalent walking distance across city areas (90th percentile: 45.9 m). Better-placed seating could reduce this burden without changing street layouts. These measures help planners identify deficiencies, test improvements and guide route choices.

papers.title: Violent relaxation in hierarchical stellar systems: pathways toward massive black hole formation in the early Universe
papers.abstract: Massive stellar systems have been detected in the high-redshift Universe via the James Webb Space Telescope using gravitational lensing techniques. Such stellar systems may evolve on short dynamical timescales, despite a formally large 2-body relaxation time. If the stellar system consists of a large number of gravitationally bound clusters, a 2-body relaxation time can be defined for the star clusters in analogy to the 2-body relaxation time for stars, implying a faster evolution determined by the number of stars per cluster. At their formation, clusters will go through a process of "cold collapse" as part of their early, non-collisional, evolution. This phase enhances the mass segregation between the more massive and less massive population of stars. We derive a criteria based on the mass of the two components that determines under which conditions the massive component may even decouple from the cluster itself. Mergers of clusters and multiple mergers on average tend to produce systems with larger cluster radii. For the formation of massive black holes via dense stellar systems, the most promising pathway consists in the cold collapse of a dense massive cluster, after few mergers (or possibly none). In such a cluster with a sufficient number of massive stars, the massive population of stars will dynamically decouple in the central region and go through core collapse, leading to the formation of a central massive object. In the case of multiple mergers, massive but more spatially extended stellar systems will form.

papers.intro:
Violent relaxation is a rapid process where a collisionless system, such as a newly formed galaxy or star cluster, reaches a stable state of equilibrium. It happens through fast changes in the overall gravitational field, on timescales corresponding to only a few crossing times. It is a fundamental process in the evolution of star clusters, which may occur already at formation in case of sub-virial initial conditions (cold collapse) (Akiyama & Sugimoto, 1989, e.g., ), as well as during the evolution of star clusters particularly in the case of mergers or in case of strong external gas inflows.

It happens through fast changes in the overall gravitational field, on timescales corresponding to only a few crossing times. It is a fundamental process in the evolution of star clusters, which may occur already at formation in case of sub-virial initial conditions (cold collapse) (Akiyama & Sugimoto, 1989, e.g., ), as well as during the evolution of star clusters particularly in the case of mergers or in case of strong external gas inflows.

This makes it particularly relevant as a build-up process of observed massive stellar systems at high redshift. Observational evidence is showing a large number of even massive stellar systems at early times in the Universe. In particular, JWST has discovered massive star clusters at high redshift, such as the Cosmic Gems at redshift 10.210.2 (Adamo et al., 2024) or the Firefly Sparkle at redshift 8.38.3 (Mowla, 2024). More than 220 massive dense clusters were found by JWST via gravitational lensing at redshifts 1≤z≤41\leq z\leq 4 (Claeyssens et al., 2026). These are ideal candidates to form intermediate-mass black holes via stellar collisions (Vergara et al., 2025; Vergara et al., 2026; Rantala et al., 2025; Rantala et al., 2026; Schleicher et al., 2026; Bocchi et al., 2026; Williams et al., 2026, e.g.,). While typical models so far do not explicitly consider the process of violent relaxation, it is likely relevant in setting the initial conditions of star clusters before their subsequent evolution and before potentially going through a core collapse phase (Portegies Zwart & McMillan, 2002; Katz et al., 2015; Reinoso et al., 2018; Reinoso et al., 2020; Vergara et al., 2021, see e.g.,). Similarly, during the hierarchical assembly of star clusters in dwarf galaxies and their subsequent mergers, repeated violent relaxation events are expected and will strongly influence the subsequent evolution of these clusters (Lahén et al., 2025a; Lahén et al., 2025b).

JWST also discovered a class of objects whose properties are still more uncertainty, the so-called Little Red Dots (Matthee et al., 2024; Greene et al., 2024, e.g.,). These could be very dense and massive stellar systems (Guia et al., 2024; Escala et al., 2025; Liempi et al., 2026c, e.g.), or Active Galactic Nuclei with a quite massive black hole (Maiolino et al., 2024; Maiolino et al., 2025; Juodžbalis et al., 2026), with typical masses above those expected from the typical black hole mass - bulge mass relation (Häring & Rix, 2004; Schutte et al., 2019, e.g.). Even if the real nature and origin of these systems is still unknown, many of the scenarios for their formation involve massive star clusters and efficient stellar collisions (Kritos & Silk, 2025; Liempi et al., 2026a, e.g.,), implying that violent relaxation could be relevant both for the initial assembly of the stellar masses and to determine the resulting initial conditions. Finally, in the high-redshift Universe, the importance of this process to build up large stellar bulges at high redshift has already been demonstrated via simulations and analytical models by Bournaud et al. papers.title: The Pristine survey XXXI. A stream offset from the Stream: very metal-poor stellar debris trailing 100$^{\circ}$ from the LMC-SMC system
papers.abstract: Context: The stellar counterpart to the $200^\circ$-long HI Stream from the Clouds probes their tidally stripped stellar populations and constrains their interaction history and structure before infall into the Milky Way. Aims: We investigate the chemodynamics and possible origin of very metal-poor (VMP; [Fe/H] $<-2$) stars in the stellar Stream, targeting distant red giants selected from the Pristine--Gaia synthetic metallicity catalogue. Methods: We obtained high-resolution Gemini/GHOST spectroscopy of 33 candidate members, deriving radial velocities and metallicities. We combine these data with literature red giant members and assess their association with the Clouds using orbital integrations in a time-dependent Milky Way--LMC potential. We also compare their distribution with collisionless test particles initially placed in a diffuse LMC stellar halo. Results: We identify 12 high-confidence members based on energy and angular momentum: one intermediate metal-poor star ([Fe/H] $\sim-1.6$), ten VMP stars, and one extremely metal-poor (EMP) star ([Fe/H] $<-3$). The new VMP stars trace over $100^\circ$ of the trailing Stream, follow the Clouds' kinematics, and lie $\sim20^\circ$ from both the HI Stream and previously known, more metal-rich debris, suggesting a metallicity-dependent spatial distribution. Combined with the literature, they approximately double the known red giant sample and extend its metallicity range from [Fe/H] $\sim-0.5$ to $-4.3$. Orbital integrations support an association with the Clouds, while test particles reproduce the debris' broad spatial distribution. Conclusions: VMP and EMP stars contribute to the Clouds' tidal debris. They may originate in the extended stellar halos of the LMC or SMC, or in disrupted satellites. Their spatial and kinematic properties can constrain future simulations of the Milky Way--LMC--SMC interaction.

papers.intro:
The Clouds are one of the most remarkable laboratories for studying galaxy interactions in the nearby Universe. The large and small of these dwarf galaxies (LMC and SMC), the Bridge, the Leading Arm, and the Stream together provide a unique opportunity to investigate tidal interactions, gas accretion, circumgalactic medium (CGM) physics, and the assembly history of the Milky Way. Among these substructures of the Clouds, the gas M. Stream (MS, or the Stream) is the most prominent. It is an enormous gaseous feature extending over more than 200∘ across the southern sky and contains both neutral and ionized gas distributed far beyond the present-day extent of the Clouds (see D’Onghia and Fox, 2016; Besla and Kallivayalil, 2026, for a detailed review).

It is an enormous gaseous feature extending over more than 200∘ across the southern sky and contains both neutral and ionized gas distributed far beyond the present-day extent of the Clouds (see D’Onghia and Fox, 2016; Besla and Kallivayalil, 2026, for a detailed review).

Observations over the last five decades have revealed a complex morphology for the MS. Early H i surveys identified both a trailing stream extending behind the Clouds and a Leading Arm located ahead of their orbit (Dieter, 1965; Wannier et al., 1972; Mathewson et al., 1974; Putman et al., 1998). The trailing stream itself appears bifurcated into multiple filaments that differ in kinematics and chemical composition, suggesting contributions from both the LMC and SMC (Putman et al., 2003; Nidever et al., 2008; Fox et al., 2013; Richter et al., 2013). Despite extensive observational and theoretical efforts, the origin of the MS remains an open question. Two broad mechanisms have been proposed for the formation of the gas Stream: (i) tidal stripping during past interactions between the Clouds, which can produce both gaseous and stellar debris, and (ii) ram-pressure stripping as the Clouds move through the Milky Way’s gaseous halo, which removes gas without stripping pre-existing stars. Both processes likely play a role, but their relative contributions remain uncertain (Besla et al., 2012; Besla et al., 2013; Lucchini et al., 2020; Krishnarao et al., 2022).

papers.title: Mitigating scanning-induced systematics in Hipparcos and implications for Gaia astrometry
papers.abstract: Space-based astrometric missions such as Hipparcos and Gaia rely on one-dimensional scanning strategies that couple the measured signals with both observation times and scanning geometry. This coupling can introduce spurious periodicities and complicate their interpretation. We present a non-parametric extension of the phase-distance correlation (PDC) periodogram that quantifies and reduces dependence on scan geometry at the period-search stage. Using Hipparcos data, we identified recurrent periodicities associated with characteristic scanning-law timescales and showed that they are strongly suppressed by the scan-angle-controlled statistic. We then applied the method to Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4) prerelease epoch astrometry, where a recurrent ~54-day feature is suppressed across multiple sources while independently known orbital signals remain detectable. The method provides a diagnostic of scan-angle dependence and a way to mitigate its impact on period searches. These results are particularly relevant for Gaia DR4, where public epoch astrometry will enable large-scale searches for companions ranging from exoplanets to dormant black holes.

Space astrometry missions have transformed our view of the Galaxy, providing precise positions, parallaxes, and proper motions for an enormous number of sources. Hipparcos established the foundation of modern space astrometry (Perryman et al., 1997), and Gaia has extended it to more than a billion objects with much higher precision (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023b). Beyond its contribution to Galactic structure and stellar astrophysics studies, Gaia is also a major tool for time-domain science (Eyer et al., 2023), including the astrometric detection and characterization of stellar and substellar companions, as well as compact companions.

Astrometric measurements can broadly be divided into narrow-angle, or relative, astrometry and wide-angle, or absolute, astrometry. Narrow-angle astrometry measures the position of a target relative to nearby reference sources over a small field of view, whereas wide-angle astrometry aims to determine positions, parallaxes, and proper motions in a global reference frame over large angular scales (Lindegren and Bastian, 2010, see). Space missions such as Hipparcos and Gaia were designed for the latter purpose. Their scanning strategies allow measurements obtained at different times and in different parts of the sky to be linked into a global astrometric solution (van Leeuwen and Evans, 1998; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016).

A central feature of this observing mode is that these missions do not measure the full two-dimensional position of a source at each epoch. Instead, they repeatedly scan the sky following a complex scanning law, and each observation provides a one-dimensional positional measurement along the instantaneous scanning direction (van Leeuwen and Evans, 1998; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016). The astrometric time series of a given source therefore consists of pairs of along-scan (abscissa) measurements and scan orientations. This strategy is fundamental to the missions, but it also creates a non-trivial coupling between observation times, scan geometry, and the measured signals.

Given that the scan geometry is coupled to the temporal sampling, the periodogram of a scanning-astrometric time series reflects both the intrinsic variability of the source and the observing window imposed by the scanning law. This is analogous to the spectral-window problem in unevenly sampled time-series analysis (VanderPlas, 2018, see), with the additional complication that each measurement is a one-dimensional projection along a scan direction that changes with time. As a result, scan-angle-dependent residuals or systematics can introduce apparent periodicities, and real periodic signals may be distorted or biased.

Gaia DR3 already demonstrated the scientific potential of this transition by publishing an extensive NSS data set, including many solutions with orbital elements or acceleration parameters, and a very large sample of astrometric binary solutions (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023a; Halbwachs et al., 2023), showing both the richness of the catalog and the need for careful treatment of selection effects and spurious solutions.

papers.title: The cold substellar frontier in JWST Extragalactic surveys: a robust parallax measurement yields the most distant known ultra-cold Y dwarf
papers.abstract: We present an analysis of JADES-GS-BD-5, an extremely cold Y dwarf identified in the JADES/GOODS-South field. Using multi-epoch JWST/NIRCam imaging spanning a $\simeq2$-yr baseline, we calibrate the JWST astrometry and obtain the first robust parallax measurement for a brown dwarf discovered in a JWST extragalactic deep field. We measure a proper motion of $\mu_{\rm tot}=49.8^{+0.3}_{-0.3}$ mas yr$^{-1}$ and a parallax of $\varpi=15.7^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ mas, corresponding to a geometric distance of $d=64^{+6}_{-5}$ pc, $\sim3\times$ further than that of the previously known most distant Y dwarfs with parallax-measured distances. We hence determine a tangential velocity of $v_{\rm tan}=15.0^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ km s$^{-1}$, consistent with a Galactic thin-disk object. We find no evidence for binary acceleration, significant photometric variability, or a plausible host. The $J$-band spectral morphology of JADES-GS-BD-5 is consistent with existing Y-dwarf templates, while its extremely faint luminosity and overall near-infrared spectral profile confirm that it is one of the coldest dwarfs discovered to date. We therefore adopt a classification of $>$Y1, consistent with a NIRCam colour-based proxy of cY1.5. The robust parallax-determined distance allows us to determine its bolometric luminosity, $\log(L_{\rm bol}/L_{\odot})=-7.08^{+0.09}_{-0.09}$. Evolutionary modelling places JADES-GS-BD-5 in the planetary-mass regime and makes it a rare benchmark for the study of cold giant-planet atmospheres. Current atmospheric models fail to reproduce its SED in detail, pointing to the importance of disequilibrium chemistry and vertical mixing. Finally, we also report additional proper motion measurements for eight of the other nine known JADES Y-dwarf candidates, highlighting JWST extragalactic surveys as a powerful route to building a statistically useful, parallax-calibrated sample of Y dwarfs.

papers.intro:
Trigonometric parallax remains the only model-independent route to derive the distances of individual brown dwarfs and isolated planetary-mass objects, and such distance measurements are of crucial importance for inferring their physical properties. As such objects never reach a stable hydrogen-burning main sequence and instead cool continuously, their physical properties at any time are governed by a combination of mass, age, and composition (Burrows et al., 2001; Bowler, 2016; Dupuy and Liu, 2017; Chabrier et al., 2023). Measurements of their distances allow us to convert their observed apparent magnitudes into absolute magnitudes and ultimately luminosities. This provides an anchor for empirical spectral type–magnitude and colour–magnitude relations, which can then be used to deduce the physical properties of objects without parallaxes (Dupuy and Liu, 2012; Dupuy and Kraus, 2013; Faherty et al., 2012; Best et al., 2021; Fontanive et al., 2023; Fontanive et al., 2025; Fontanive et al., 2026, e.g.,). Substellar objects with well-constrained properties supply the valuable empirical benchmarks against which ultracool atmosphere and evolutionary models are tested (Phillips et al., 2020; Marley et al., 2021; Lacy and Burrows, 2023; Beiler et al., 2024a; Mukherjee et al., 2024; Leggett et al., 2025; Mang et al., 2026; Radcliffe et al., 2026, e.g.), and volume-complete samples further allow us to place crucial constraints on the substellar luminosity function, potentially providing further insight into the low-mass cut-off of the stellar initial mass function (IMF) (Kirkpatrick et al., 2012; Kirkpatrick et al., 2021; Best et al., 2024; Hainline et al., 2026b, e.g.). Accurate distances also allow measurements of proper motion to be converted into tangential velocities, and hence can provide valuable kinematic information (Faherty et al., 2009; Burningham et al., 2013; Fontanive et al., 2025, e.g.).

They are intrinsically fainter and predominantly radiate into the thermal near and mid-infrared (IR). Measurements of Y dwarf parallaxes have consequently required dedicated space-based campaigns with Spitzer and HST (Marsh et al., 2013; Dupuy and Kraus, 2013; Beichman et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2018; Kirkpatrick et al., 2019; Kirkpatrick et al., 2021; Fontanive et al., 2021; Fontanive et al., 2025; Marocco et al., 2026, e.g.). The result of their faintness and the consequent difficulty to measure parallaxes is that only ∼50{\sim}50 Y dwarfs are known to date, all within 20 pc of the Sun, and even fewer have a measured parallax.

Brown dwarfs of spectral types later than Y1 are known only in small numbers, essentially all within ∼15{\sim}15 pc (Kirkpatrick et al., 2021; Leggett, 2026), and the cold extreme of the sequence almost solely relies on a single object, WISE J085510.83−-071442.5 at 2.28 pc (Luhman, 2014; Skemer et al., 2016; Kirkpatrick et al., 2019, WISE 0855 for short;). papers.title: Evolution of Dust In Protoplanetary Disks With Magnetized Winds
papers.abstract: Observations and theory increasingly indicate that protoplanetary disks are weakly turbulent, implying that magnetized disk winds may dominate their angular momentum transport and long-term evolution. Yet dust evolution in wind-dominated disks remains poorly understood, despite its importance for planet formation. In particular, whether wind-dominated disk evolution can create regions with enhanced dust-to-gas mass ratios that enable planetesimal formation via the streaming instability is unclear. We build a parametric hybrid disk evolution model that includes turbulent accretion, wind-driven accretion, and wind-driven mass loss to investigate dust evolution in magnetized protoplanetary disks. We employ this model to carry out a parameter study in which the initial total accretion rate, the wind-driven mass loss rate, and the turbulence strength are varied. We find that although wind-dominated disks are more favorable to dust growth and concentration than turbulence-dominated disks, conditions suitable for the streaming instability arise only within the inner few au and only under the most extreme conditions: very weak turbulence ($\alpha_\text{turb} = 10^{-5}$) where magnetized winds drive most of the accretion ($\dot{M}_\text{acc,tot} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{wind,acc}$), and wind-driven mass loss comparable to the accretion rate ($\dot{M}_\text{wind,outflow} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{acc,wind}$). Our results therefore imply that, beyond the inner few au, the parametric wind-driven evolution models considered in the literature do not by themselves produce conditions suitable for planetesimal formation via the streaming instability, motivating more physically complete models in which spontaneous, long-lived dust traps can arise.

Protoplanetary disks (PPDs) set the initial conditions for planetary systems, via the interaction between their gas and dust reservoirs during the disk’s lifetime. Assuming that no significant dust growth occurs during cloud collapse [43, 72, 50, which is currently a matter of debate, see ], young PPDs inherit the dust properties provided by the interstellar medium (ISM), with characteristic sizes of ∼1​μ​m\sim 1\ \mu\mathrm{m} [55] and an average dust-to-gas mass ratio of ∼0.01\sim 0.01 if inherited from the Milky Way ISM [18]. ISM-like solid dust particles in PPDs require highly efficient growth to reach kilometer-sized planetesimals, from which the subsequent steps of planet formation may proceed via pebble and planetesimal accretion as well as gas accretion [44]. However, dust growth is hampered by barriers such as collisional fragmentation [16, 12] and radial drift [92, 11]. A potential way to circumvent these barriers is through the streaming instability [94, 39, 6, SI,] – one of the resonant drag instabilities [74] – in which the rapid concentration of dust into filaments can lead to gravitational collapse of clumps within them into planetesimals.

Whether the SI can operate depends sensitively on both the dust-to-gas mass ratio and the aerodynamic coupling of dust to the gas, which is expressed through the Stokes number [47, 68, 48]. Larger dust particles can trigger the SI at lower dust-to-gas mass ratios, whereas smaller particles require stronger concentration. Achieving these conditions is challenging because: (1) dust particles with Stokes numbers of order unity undergo rapid radial drift before large dust enhancements can be achieved [19, 11]; (2) Smaller dust particles remain more tightly coupled to the gas and are therefore more sensitive to turbulent diffusion, which opposes both radial and vertical concentrations [3].

MHD wind-dominated weakly turbulent PPDs may be especially important for dust evolution. Weak turbulence reduces radial and vertical dust diffusion, allowing dust to settle and concentrate more efficiently [24, 93]. MHD wind-driven accretion and mass loss can also alter the gas surface density, which can reduce radial drift, increase dust retention, and increase dust-to-gas mass ratios. For example, in the case of extreme mass loss rates exceeding the wind-driven accretion rate, inner cavities produced by outflows can generate pressure maxima in the inner few AU [78, 90], where dust can accumulate and potentially form planetesimals via the SI [83]. In addition, gas surface accretion due to magnetized disk winds, combined with dust settling onto the midplane, can allow disks to retain dust while the gas is accreted onto the central star, increasing dust-to-gas mass ratios [59].

A number of studies have begun to discern the dust response to wind-dominated disk evolution in the past decade. Multi-dimensional MHD simulations which include dust evolution have revealed MHD winds’ positive effects on dust concentration, a pre-requisite for planetesimal formation through the SI channel [65, 35]. While highly relevant for uncovering the fine details of MHD-driven gas dynamics and their knock-on effects on dust behavior, such multi-dimensional simulations are limited by computational cost, and thus cannot rigorously model collisional dust growth on timescales comparable to the disk lifetime. One-dimensional simulations can resolve these problems by sacrificing on the finer details of disk dynamics, allowing for broader studies on planet formation and evolution. A number of such studies already exist in the literature [82, 41, 91], to which we add the advantages of our model in its ability to explore a broad range of turbulence strengths, wind-driven accretion and outflow strengths, and total accretion rates over Myr-timescales in order to provide a more complete picture accounting for the diversity of observed and simulated PPDs.

papers.title: Bringing Dark States to Light after Frustrated Tunneling Ionization
papers.abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in gases is typically regarded as a sub-laser-cycle process, well described by the semiclassical three-step model. In this work, we report the extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) emission observed in an HHG experiment arising from a longer temporal process associated with dark states populated through frustrated tunneling ionization. The emission exhibits a larger spatial divergence than typical high-order harmonics, resembling the polarization decay of optically bright states. Supported by the time-frequency analysis of the theoretical calculations, we show that the emission originates from the nonradiative capture of the tunneling electrons into excited dark states of the neutral atom, followed by Floquet-like laser-dressing effects induced by the extended tail of the driving pulse. Our results reveal a largely unexplored pathway for XUV generation through laser-dressed dark states, thereby enabling the enhancement of coherent XUV emission at targeted wavelengths with high repetition rates.
