papers.title: The retirement party of GRS 1915+105: the radio fading to quiescence of the archetypal microquasar
papers.abstract: After more than 25 years of near-Eddington activity and over six years in a Compton-thick obscured phase, the black-hole X-ray binary GRS 1915+105 has begun to fade in the radio to a level lower than ever previously recorded, possibly marking the onset of its final descent towards quiescence. With the accretion flow hidden in the X-rays, the radio emission is currently the best tracer of the accretion activity. We aim to establish whether the fading marks the end of the outburst that began in 1992 or a temporary switch-off. We present the long-term MeerKAT monitoring of the source from the ThunderKAT and X-KAT programmes up to 2026 July, deep dual-band (L- and S-band) MeerKAT Director's Discretionary Time observations, and three Einstein Probe/FXT X-ray pointings bracketing them. Following a last Jy-level flare in early 2025, the 1.28 GHz flux density declined monotonically to $\sim$0.2-0.4 mJy by 2026 March, and after 2026 May 9 it was no longer formally detected in our 10-min monitoring observations. Deep MeerKAT observations in 2026 July detect the source at $\sim$150 $\mu$Jy in L band and $\sim$90 $\mu$Jy in S band, the lowest radio flux densities ever recorded from the system, corresponding to $L_{\rm R}\simeq2\times10^{28}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at 1.28 GHz, with a spectral index $\alpha=-0.67\pm0.41$ across 1.28-2.62 GHz. The radio decline is the first direct evidence that the central engine itself is fading rather than merely receding further behind the absorber. The steep spectrum is consistent with either a combination of optically thick and thin emission, or an unusual, intrinsically steep core-jet spectrum. Should this mark the onset of quiescence, disc-instability models predict it to last of order $10^4$ yr. The switch-off of the central engine may shed light on the nature of the donor star and on the origin of the very-high-energy gamma-ray emission in this system.

papers.intro:
In black-hole (BH) low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs), a stellar-mass black hole accretes matter via an accretion disc formed by gas stripped from a low-mass donor star. BH LMXBs are typically transient systems, alternating between long periods of quiescence, at luminosities of the order of L∼1030L\sim 10^{30}–103310^{33} erg s-1 (Wijnands et al., 2015, see), and relatively short outbursts (lasting months, in most cases), during which their luminosity can reach and sometimes surpass the Eddington limit, ∼1039\sim 10^{39} erg s-1. During outbursts these systems show clear repeating patterns of behaviour across various accretion states, each associated with mechanical feedback in the form of winds and relativistic jets (Fender et al., 2009; Ponti et al., 2012, e.g.). In the hard state the X-ray spectrum is dominated by Comptonisation in a hot flow close to the black hole, with the seed photons supplied either by a cool, geometrically thin accretion disc truncated at large radii or by synchrotron emission of the hot electrons themselves (Poutanen & Veledina, 2014, e.g.). Alternatively, a significant fraction of the X-ray emission may originate at the base of a compact jet (Markoff, 2010, e.g.). Fender (2001) established that black-hole X-ray binaries in their hard states typically show flat-spectrum radio emission (α∼0\alpha\sim 0, where Sν∝ναS_{\nu}\propto\nu^{\alpha}), which is regarded as the signature of partially self-absorbed compact jets, and is interpreted as synchrotron radiation from relativistic electrons in a magnetic field.

Across the hard and quiescent states of BH LMXBs a non-linear correlation is observed between the radio (LRL_{\rm R}) and X-ray (LXL_{\rm X}) luminosities, which provides a valuable tool to probe the connection between compact-jet production, traced by the radio emission, and the inner accretion flow or jet base, traced by the X-rays (Hannikainen et al., 1998; Corbel et al., 2000; Corbel et al., 2003; Gallo et al., 2003; Crook-Mansour et al., 2026). Whether quiescence is simply the low-luminosity tail of the hard state, with broadly similar spectral and physical properties, or a physically distinct regime in which compact jets need not always be produced, remains debated, as only a few systems have been detected in quiescence at radio wavelengths.

GRS 1915++105 is the archetypal Galactic microquasar, hosting a 12.4−1.8+2.0​M⊙12.4^{+2.0}_{-1.8}\,M_{\odot} black hole (Reid et al., 2014) at a parallax distance of 9.4±0.79.4\pm 0.7 kpc (Reid & Miller-Jones, 2023). It has the longest orbital period among the known XRB systems (Steeghs et al., 2013, 33.85 d,), and correspondingly the largest accretion disc of the class. Since its discovery at the onset of its 1992 outburst (Castro-Tirado et al., 1992; Castro-Tirado et al., 1994) it sustained a near-Eddington ∼\sim25-year-long activity phase, with recurrent compact jets and repeated superluminal ejections (Mirabel & Rodríguez, 1994; Fender et al., 1999; Rushton et al., 2010). Following a 2018 transition to the hard state (Negoro et al., 2018; Motta et al., 2021), in mid-2019 the soft X-ray flux dropped significantly and the source became Compton-thick (Miller et al., 2020; Koljonen & Hovatta, 2021; Motta et al., 2021; Athulya & Nandi, 2023; Miller et al., 2025, NH≳1024N_{\rm H}\gtrsim 10^{24} cm-2;), a state it has maintained ever since while remaining bright at radio wavelengths.

This prompted deep follow-up radio and X-ray observations in 2026 July, which recovered the system at the lowest radio flux density recorded since its discovery. We then place the source on the radio/X-ray and luminosity–orbital-period planes (Sects. 3.3 and 3.4), discuss the nature of the fading (Sect. 4) and summarise our conclusions (Sect. 5).

We then place the source on the radio/X-ray and luminosity–orbital-period planes (Sects. 3.3 and 3.4), discuss the nature of the fading (Sect. 4) and summarise our conclusions (Sect. 5).

papers.title: Simulation Modeling and Control of an Elastic Shaping Antagonistic Variable Stiffness Actuator
papers.abstract: Position--stiffness regulation of antagonistic variable stiffness actuators (VSAs) involves coupled nonlinear dynamics, parameter uncertainty, and feedback states that are not directly measured. This paper addresses this challenge through a simulation-based workflow that integrates elastic shaping, model verification, and layered nonlinear control. This study builds on a previously developed actuator comprising two crossed four-bar compliant transmission elastic units. Its optimized elastic mapping provides the structural basis, with an ADAMS torque-curve root mean square error (RMSE) of $2.57\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm}$ against the target. A control-oriented analytical model is implemented in Simulink and compared with the independently executed ADAMS model under matched inputs. The maximum joint-angle RMSE across the tested cases is $4.66\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}$. A layered controller combines extended Kalman filtering for state reconstruction, feedback linearization for nominal decoupling, and adaptive sliding-mode control for residual compensation. At the end of the nominal simulation, the joint-angle error is approximately $3.14\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{rad}$. The stiffness error is $3.07\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm/rad}$ relative to a target of $50\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm/rad}$. Parameter-variation and ablation tests assess tracking performance and the effects of the controller modules within the evaluated conditions. The resulting workflow links structural-response modeling, state estimation, and robust control assessment, supporting repeatable comparisons beyond nominal tracking alone.

Robotic exoskeletons for assistance and rehabilitation must provide motion support while maintaining compliant physical interaction with the wearer [1, 2]. This requirement creates a trade-off between motion performance and mechanical compliance at the actuated joints [3]. Variable stiffness actuators (VSAs) offer a way to address this trade-off by adjusting mechanical stiffness while generating motion [4]. However, stiffness adjustment changes the torque–deflection relation of the elastic transmission, linking stiffness variation to the motion response. This coupling limits independent regulation of stiffness and motion, so that stiffness adjustments can perturb the joint trajectory and may lead to tracking errors, oscillations, or instability. VSA design therefore requires the mechanical properties of the elastic mechanism to be considered alongside position–stiffness control requirements [5].

VSA design therefore requires the mechanical properties of the elastic mechanism to be considered alongside position–stiffness control requirements [5].

Mechanical stiffness can be adjusted through the elastic elements and their transmission geometry [6], for example by changing spring preload [7] or the transmission ratio [8]. Antagonistic actuation uses two opposing elastic branches, drawing inspiration from the coactivation of antagonist muscles [9]. The balance of branch torques determines the joint equilibrium position, whereas the elastic properties of both branches determine joint stiffness. English and Russell demonstrated antagonistic stiffness adjustment using nonlinear rolamite springs, illustrating the importance of branch elasticity [10]. Designing an antagonistic actuator thus requires both an appropriate branch arrangement and a torque–deflection relation compatible with position–stiffness regulation.

Control evaluation must also extend beyond nominal parameters and ideal state feedback to account for parameter mismatch and limited measurements. Feedback linearization has enabled motion–stiffness decoupling [13], and simultaneous regulation has been demonstrated for bidirectional antagonistic actuators [14]. Nonlinear disturbance observers [15] and adaptive neural-network compensation [16] have further improved robustness to model uncertainty. Robust compensation, however, does not by itself provide the feedback states required by the controller. Encoders measure angles, but direct differentiation for velocity estimation is sensitive to noise [17], while stiffness estimation depends on the transmission model [18]. Extended Kalman filtering combines model predictions with measurements to reconstruct states [19]. The effects of estimation errors on decoupling and compensation must nevertheless be assessed in closed-loop tests. Multibody modeling provides a separate response reference based on components and constraints. Previous VSA research has used ADAMS and Simulink separately to examine mechanism responses and nonlinear dynamics [21]. Virtual prototyping can reduce repeated physical testing and support design iteration without repeatedly manufacturing and assembling prototypes [22]. papers.title: Auditory and Visual Virtualization in 6DoF XR: Effects on Plausibility and Dynamic Auditory Distance Perception
papers.abstract: Extended reality (XR) enables controlled yet naturalistic multisensory experiments, but its validity depends on whether virtualized cues are perceptually plausible and lead to behavior comparable to the real world. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to perceptually evaluate a six-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) XR system that combines real-time room acoustic simulation, binaural rendering, and an audio-visually matched virtual replica of a large laboratory room in terms of both plausibility and behavior. In two experiments with 45 participants, we investigated how auditory and visual virtualization affect plausibility and dynamic auditory distance perception (ADP). A plausibility experiment compared real and virtual sound sources in audio-augmented reality (AAR) and virtual reality (VR), while a locomotion-based ADP experiment assessed distance-judgment accuracy, signed error, and task effort across four virtualization conditions. The system produced plausible binaural rendering in both AAR and VR, with higher plausibility in VR, indicating that perceptual requirements for XR audio depend on the visual reference frame. In the ADP task, any form of virtualization reduced accuracy and increased effort, although performance remained high overall. Virtual audio produced a bias toward nearer perceived source distances, whereas visual-only virtualization reduced accuracy without a significant directional bias. These effects did not add up in full VR. Overall, the findings demonstrate the strong potential of current 6DoF XR systems for interactive perceptual research, while revealing that task-specific behavioral validation may be necessary.

papers.intro:
Extended reality (XR) technologies, including augmented, mixed and virtual reality (AR, MR and VR), have had a significant impact on the design and conduct of perceptual multisensory studies and cognitive experiments Parsons (2015); Apochi et al. (2024); Bello et al. (2025). XR enables researchers to create a wide range of highly controlled yet naturalistic experimental environments that would be almost impossible to produce in traditional laboratory settings. This is particularly relevant to the fields of hearing science and psychoacoustics Picinali et al. (2023); Ramírez et al. (2024a); Ramírez et al. (2024b); Ramírez (2026), where the trade-off between experimental control and ecological validity has been recognized as a major limitation of traditional laboratory research Keidser et al. (2020); Beechey (2022). Many auditory studies rely on simplified, unimodal, and static listening conditions that do not adequately reflect the complex, multisensory, and dynamic nature of real-world hearing Picinali et al. (2023); Keidser et al. (2020); Ramírez (2026). In contrast, immersive XR systems offer the ability to simulate everyday, interactive and multisensory environments—even for moving listeners and sources—while maintaining control over sensory cues. This elicits a sense of presence, leading participants to engage with the environment as if it were real and exhibit more close-to-natural perceptual and behavioral responses Slater and Wilbur (1997); Slater (2009); Skarbez et al. (2021).

Recent advancements in XR technology, particularly in room acoustic simulation and binaural rendering—the core technologies enabling spatialized audio in XR environments Roginska and Geluso (2018); Vorländer (2020); Gupta et al. (2022)—have significantly enhanced the realism and immersion of audiovisual simulations. These developments present promising opportunities for applying XR technology to auditory and hearing research. However, before state-of-the-art systems can be reliably used in complex multisensory experiments, their perceptual quality must be evaluated. Moreover, it is necessary to understand how auditory and visual virtualization affect behavior, and whether outcomes in XR are comparable to those in the real world. In particular, systematic perceptual evaluations of six-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) systems, in which users can move freely within a virtual space while the audio and visual renderings update continuously in real time, are lacking. Furthermore, the perceptual implications of auditory and visual virtualization in such 6DoF systems on perceptual quality measures, such as plausibility, and fundamental perceptual processes, such as dynamic auditory distance perception (ADP), remain poorly understood and have yet to be investigated.

One effective, rigorous, and popular method of evaluating the perceptual quality of virtual acoustic environments and binaural rendering is to assess the plausibility of the environment using the experimental paradigm proposed by Lindau and Weinzierl Lindau and Weinzierl (2012). Effectively, such a plausibility experiment tests whether the XR audio rendering system can evoke auditory illusions, i.e., the impression that virtual sound sources rendered through headphones are actually real. In the experiment, either a real or a virtual sound source is presented, and participants decide whether the source is real or virtual using a Yes/No paradigm, thereby implicitly assessing whether the perceived sound is “in agreement with the listener’s expectation towards a corresponding real event” (Lindau and Weinzierl, 2012, p. 804). This definition of plausibility in XR audio aligns with Slater’s definition of plausibility illusion in VR, which refers to the illusion that “what is apparently happening is really happening” (Slater, 2009, p. 3553). The results of an XR audio plausibility test are usually analyzed according to signal detection theory (SDT), yielding the sensitivity parameter d′d^{\prime}, the corresponding two-alternative forced-choice detection rate (number of correct answers), and the response bias (e.g., criterion cc or likelihood ratio β\beta) per participant Hautus et al. (2022). These results provide a measure of the plausibility, and consequently, the perceptual quality of the assessed XR audio rendering, and are also assumed to offer insight into the system’s general suitability for perceptual research.

Following the strict paradigm proposed by Lindau and Weinzierl Lindau and Weinzierl (2012), various studies have assessed the plausibility of binaural audio-augmented reality (AAR) rendering based on acoustic measurements. In the experiment introducing the paradigm, Lindau and Weinzierl Lindau and Weinzierl (2012) yielded a very high degree of plausibility for binaural rendering with 1DoF, with participants mostly guessing whether a sound was real or simulated. The authors proposed that a binaural AAR system can be considered plausible if the mean d′d^{\prime} across subjects is significantly smaller than a threshold of d′=0.1777d^{\prime}=0.1777, as determined by a minimum effect test of the null hypothesis. Although this threshold was commonly used in later studies, it represents a rather conservative measure of plausibility, reflecting only a 5% deviation from chance-level performance in a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task. Therefore, other studies Brinkmann et al. (2019) have proposed more lenient thresholds, such as d′=0.9539d^{\prime}=0.9539, which corresponds to 75% correct responses in a 2AFC task and is often considered a practical definition of the just-noticeable difference (JND). Correcting the detection rate for the guessing probability shows that, at the JND level, participants are giving the correct answer in 50% of the cases. This criterion may hence better reflect the perceptual boundary at which AAR rendering begins to feel convincingly real.

papers.title: Idiosynchromatic Poetry
papers.abstract: We prove equivalences of asymmetric partition relations involving natural numbers and products of weakly compact cardinals $\kappa$, infinite cardinals $\lambda<\kappa$ and natural numbers to certain classes of finitary problems in the theory of edge-coloured digraphs. We are able to determine three classes of Ramsey numbers exactly, typical examples in these classes are $r(\omega^2 2, 3)$, $r(\kappa\lambda 2, 3)$ and $r(\kappa\lambda 3, 3)$. We moreover provide general upper bounds for $r(\omega^2 m, 3)$ and $r(\kappa\lambda m, n)$.

While the former are usually more interested in statements with consistency strength which are hence independent over ZFC\ZFC the latter are normally interested in finitary problems. In between falls a class of problems the æsthetic appeal of which is in the author’s opinion usually underestimated—partition relations between countable ordinals.

papers.title: Uniqueness and nondegeneracy for a critical Choquard equation with Hardy potential
papers.abstract: We study the critical Choquard equation \[ -\Delta u-\mu |x|^{-2}u =\bigl(|\cdot|^{2-N}*|u|^p\bigr)|u|^{p-2}u \qquad\text{in }\mathbb R^N, \] where $|\cdot|^{2-N}$ is the Newton kernel, $p=\frac{N+2}{N-2}$, and $0<\mu<\frac{(N-2)^2}{4}$. For every $N\ge3$, we prove that positive solutions in $D^{1,2}(\mathbb R^N)$ are radially symmetric about the origin, unique up to dilation, and nondegenerate. Our proof uses normalized logarithmic derivatives to obtain a cooperative system. The resulting monotonicity principle underlies both the uniqueness and nondegeneracy arguments, and remains effective in the subquadratic range $1<p<2$, corresponding to $N\ge7$. Consequently, the linearized quadratic form has Morse index one and the sharp inequality admits a global quadratic remainder estimate. The best constant is strictly concave in the Hardy parameter on $\bigl[0,\frac{(N-2)^2}{4}\bigr)$, is of class $C^2$ with strictly negative second derivative in the interior, and satisfies two-sided bounds that agree to first order at $\mu=0$.

papers.title: A globally convergent stochastic semismooth Newton method for strongly convex problems in Hilbert spaces
papers.abstract: We propose and analyze a globalized stochastic semismooth Newton method for stochastic optimization problems in Hilbert spaces where the objective is strongly convex with Lipschitz continuous, Newton differentiable gradient. Gradient and generalized Hessian information are only available through mini-batching. In each iteration, a full semismooth Newton trial step is accepted or rejected based on a stochastic residual test and rejected steps are replaced by damped steps in the same Newton direction. Throughout, we admit gradient estimators with affinely growing variance, as arises in optimization problems with random partial differential equations as constraints. We prove non-asymptotic global R-linear convergence in expectation as well as almost sure convergence. For sufficiently fast-growing batch sizes, the method transitions almost surely into a regime of pure Newton steps and converges R-superlinearly almost surely. The method is applied to the optimal control of a random elliptic equation featuring a Huber tracking term as well as a random parabolic equation with a Moreau--Yosida penalization of an almost sure state constraint.

papers.title: Structured Agentic Learning for Persistent Spatial Acquisition in RDT-TAIS-Assisted Communications
papers.abstract: Persistent TAIS operation can reduce repeated radio-information acquisition by reusing environmental knowledge across control intervals. This knowledge changes with radio-environment evolution and current communication task. This paper studies persistent spatial knowledge maintenance for TAIS control and formulates it as a sequential information-acquisition problem that maximizes effective communication performance while accounting for physical-acquisition overhead under an outage-reliability constraint. We develop structured agentic spatial intelligence (ASI), which realizes a communication-oriented agent that maintains persistent spatial knowledge, forms beliefs from radio and context observations, and adapts physical information acquisition through closed-loop interaction with the radio environment. By jointly exploiting radio-consistent context inference, temporal knowledge-sufficiency assessment, graph-structured regional reasoning, and predictive outage-risk feedback, structured ASI determines when additional acquisition is needed, where it is directed, and how much physical information is sufficient before stopping or escalating to full radio-environment reacquisition. Numerical results show that structured ASI improves the effective rate by 2.59% while reducing acquisition overhead by 25.0% at six structural changes per 100 control intervals, and achieves a 2.82% effective-rate gain with a 41.8% overhead reduction over a heterogeneous 400-interval mission.
papers.intro:
Transparent amplifying intelligent surfaces (TAISs) provide an engineered transmission path for indoor-to-outdoor communication across building facades, where direct propagation can suffer severe penetration loss [8]. Previously acquired radio information can also support robust wireless operation [5], but surface configuration still commonly relies on pilot-based acquisition under prescribed surface states [3]. Repeated probing can therefore consume substantial radio resources as the surface grows.

Wireless propagation exhibits persistent temporal and spatial structure that can be reused across communication intervals [13, 2]. In indoor-to-outdoor deployments, building geometry and dominant propagation structures typically evolve more slowly than the instantaneous channel, which creates an opportunity to reduce repeated acquisition by maintaining spatial knowledge of the radio environment.

In indoor-to-outdoor deployments, building geometry and dominant propagation structures typically evolve more slowly than the instantaneous channel, which creates an opportunity to reduce repeated acquisition by maintaining spatial knowledge of the radio environment.

The usefulness of maintained spatial knowledge nevertheless changes with both the physical environment and the communication task. Structural changes can invalidate maintained information, whereas user movement or a context change can alter which regions influence the current TAIS-assisted link. Hence, outdated information can remain task-irrelevant, while physically valid information can become newly relevant. Effective knowledge reuse must determine when the maintained knowledge is insufficient [11, 6], where fresh information is required [7], and how much physical acquisition is sufficient [14]. These coupled decisions form a WHEN–WHERE–HOW MUCH sequential information-acquisition problem.

papers.title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

papers.intro:
Drug discovery is central to addressing unmet medical needs and improving human health. In recent years, AI has been reshaping this field, with the potential to fundamentally transform how new therapeutics are discovered. A growing range of specialized models has enabled advances and improved efficiency across individual research tasks, exemplified by AlphaFold in protein structure prediction [12], RFdiffusion in de novo protein design [19], and PocketXMol in structure-based molecular design [14]. These advances strengthen individual components of drug discovery, but their contribution to the overall process depends on effective coordination across interdependent research stages. Organizing and advancing this process continues to rely on human direction and judgment. Extending these capabilities from individual tasks to autonomous research across the full discovery process remains a central challenge.

Recent advances in AI agents have opened a new avenue for autonomously conducting complex scientific research. This direction has motivated a growing body of work in scientific discovery and biomedicine. Co-Scientist generates and iteratively refines novel scientific hypotheses [7]. Biomni provides a general-purpose biomedical agent that automates diverse research tasks, reducing the burden of repetitive and fragmented research workflows [9]. The Virtual Biotech coordinates specialist agents to integrate evidence across disciplines and provide analysis and decision support for therapeutic development [22]. While these systems automate research tasks and support scientific decisions, a gap remains between these capabilities and autonomous end-to-end drug discovery, from an initial research objective to the delivery of molecular candidates ready for experimental testing.

While these systems automate research tasks and support scientific decisions, a gap remains between these capabilities and autonomous end-to-end drug discovery, from an initial research objective to the delivery of molecular candidates ready for experimental testing.

We view drug discovery as a continuous process of scientific decision making across a vast space of targets, mechanisms, molecules, and research strategies. Each decision shapes the evidence gathered and the options available at subsequent stages, so a poorly supported choice can divert an entire investigation. Advancing a research direction in depth therefore depends on maintaining decision quality throughout the process. This requires an agent to assess the available evidence, determine appropriate next steps, and revise its approach as results emerge, even when experimental feedback is delayed or incomplete. At the same time, a carefully pursued direction covers only a small part of the possible discovery space. Research breadth is therefore equally necessary: alternative hypotheses must be investigated and compared to identify promising directions that an early commitment might otherwise leave unexplored. Because each investigation can require substantial literature analysis and scientific computation, achieving this breadth calls for the capacity to extend research effort across many directions.

To address these challenges, we introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery (Figure 1). To support high-quality scientific decisions, we develop a knowledge-enhanced decision system built around a scientific decision knowledge base. This knowledge base brings together skills distilled from human expert experience and skills derived from scientific publications through Paper2Skill, a framework we develop to transform published research into transferable decision knowledge. Paper2Skill synthesizes methodologically related studies, capturing the connections between research objectives, methodological choices, and the conditions under which those choices are appropriate. The resulting skills provide reusable guidance that enables the agent to select suitable methods and adapt research procedures to the scientific problem at hand. A supporting computational platform, AIPherDD, enables the execution of scientific models and tools [6, 5, 16, 11], providing task-specific evidence that the system evaluates using its decision knowledge to determine how the investigation should proceed. To enable scientific exploration across a broad research space, we develop Self-Scaling Discovery, a framework for organizing and scaling autonomous scientific investigations. The framework structures the research space into focused questions and coordinates parallel agents to investigate them within a shared research objective. Each agent inherits the relevant research context, allowing it to pursue a focused investigation while retaining its connection to the broader discovery task. Findings across investigations are brought together to update the research space, refine priorities, and guide subsequent rounds of exploration. This organization enables systematic exploration across diverse targets, mechanisms, and discovery strategies while maintaining a coherent research direction as the scale of investigation grows. Together, these capabilities enable PharmAgents2 to advance research from an initial discovery objective to experimentally testable candidate delivery through informed scientific decisions and systematic exploration.

Recent benchmarks evaluate biomedical agents from several perspectives: BiomniBench-DA assesses the quality of biomedical analyses using expert-designed rubrics [15], DrugDiscoveryBench measures computational task accuracy in early-stage drug discovery [1], and SMDD-Bench evaluates small-molecule design capabilities [8]. However, these evaluations leave open whether an agent can autonomously carry a drug discovery objective through to experimentally testable candidate delivery. To address this gap, we introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, which evaluates scientific decision quality and end-to-end research execution at two complementary levels. The first track assesses scientific decisions through 121 questions across nine drug discovery scenarios, with reference outcomes grounded in published evidence. The second evaluates autonomous research and candidate delivery through three tasks derived from real drug discovery projects, using expert-defined criteria to assess the quality of the research process. These benchmark results demonstrate that, compared with the evaluated baselines, PharmAgents2 makes higher-quality scientific decisions and conducts end-to-end investigations that more closely align with expert-defined expectations.

papers.title: Distilling Neural Population Geometry into Transformers and GRUs for Motor Control
papers.abstract: We introduce neuro-distillation (Neuro-Dist), a technique designed to directly transfer computationally useful neural population structure from biological brains into artificial controllers. Using three macaque motor-cortical datasets as neuro-distillation teachers, we align controller internal states with cortical neural population geometry during training; controller deployment requires no neural data. We evaluate gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks and Transformers controlling a simulated arm. Neuro-Dist achieves the lowest median error among five methods, including distillation from movement kinematics, in 10 of 18 comparisons across trained, student-held-out, and new target directions. Seed-split aggregate statistical comparisons significantly favor Neuro-Dist over all six controls on trained and new targets, and five on student-held-out targets (Holm-corrected familywise p<0.05). We furthermore find that Neuro-Dist can substantially improve controller robustness to sensory feedback noise. Mechanistically, Neuro-Dist induced low tangling of trajectories in internal controller state space---a functionally important characteristic of motor cortex, demonstrating successful transfer of a known motor-cortical population geometry feature. These findings establish neuro-distillation as a complement to behavioral distillation and point to a novel class of neuro-interfaces that tap biological neural population structure as a computational resource for improving the control of goal-directed behavior in robotics and embodied AI.

papers.intro:
Behavioral control in embodied AI agents and robotic systems is typically learned from task objectives, demonstrations, or simulated experience. Examples of large-scale efforts include collecting demonstrations with 13 physical robots over 17 months (Brohan et al., 2023) and training a manipulation policy with 131,072 parallel simulated robot instances over approximately 32 hours (Handa et al., 2024). In contrast, mammalian behavioral control builds on neural circuitry shaped by hundreds of millions of years of vertebrate evolution across successive generations of global populations (Zador, 2019). As a reference point for mammalian population scale, for example the contemporary abundance of the straw-coloured fruit bat alone—a single species with dexterous flight control—is estimated at roughly one billion individuals (Greenspoon et al., 2023; O’Mara et al., 2019). Evolution shapes inherited circuit organization, while development and lifetime learning adapt these circuits to individuals and their environments (Zador, 2019). Reproducing the breadth and adaptability of biological behavior in everyday physical environments remains an open challenge for artificial systems (Zador, 2019; Tao et al., 2025). This motivates investigating biological neural systems as a source of reusable computational structure that may be difficult to engineer a priori and costly to empirically rediscover through training of artificial systems alone. As an example, neural population dynamics could supply training priors that transfer useful structure to artificial agents.

We investigate this possibility in motor control, where the mammalian central nervous system combines ancient spinal circuitry with more recently evolved cortical pathways (Jung et al., 2018; Rathelot & Strick, 2009). Two converging lines of research suggest that transferring biological representations to artificial motor controllers may be feasible. First, in the visual system, supervision derived from primate cortical recordings has improved image recognition (Federer et al., 2020; Safarani et al., 2021), with representational alignment also improving visual-model robustness (Li et al., 2019; Dapello et al., 2023). Second, studies of motor-cortical population geometry describe movement preparation and execution as low-dimensional manifolds (Churchland et al., 2012; Russo et al., 2018). Such neural population geometry provides a conceptual bridge between biological and artificial systems (Chung & Abbott, 2021); task-trained artificial recurrent networks can develop cortex-like dynamics (Sussillo et al., 2015). During reaching movements, a characteristic of population dynamics is low trajectory tangling: nearby population states tend to have similar velocity vectors. This organization distinguishes motor-cortical activity from the muscle signals it helps generate and has been linked to noise robustness: Models trained to generate the same output using less-tangled internal trajectories tolerated more state noise (Russo et al., 2018). Primate motor cortex therefore offers a biologically motivated source of neural population structure for artificial controllers.

papers.title: Exact regions for the symmetrized Blest coefficient
papers.abstract: Spearman's rho treats all ranks alike, yet in many comparisons of two rankings an agreement at the top matters more than one at the bottom. Blest's rank correlation builds this preference into Spearman's rho, and its symmetrized version $\eta$, introduced by Genest and Plante, does so without favoring either of the two rankings. How far can such a top-weighted coefficient stray from other rank correlations? We answer this question for Spearman's rho, Blomqvist's beta and Chatterjee's rank correlation $\xi$ by determining the exact set of values that $\eta$ and each of these coefficients can attain jointly. Given Spearman's rho, $\eta$ can differ from it by at most $27/128$, and the extreme values of $\eta$ are attained only when the two rankings agree perfectly on the top ranks and are completely reversed on the bottom ranks, or vice versa. Given Blomqvist's beta, $\eta$ obeys exactly the same sharp bounds as Spearman's rho. For Chatterjee's rank correlation, both boundary curves are explicit and are attained by copulas with densities. Here symmetrization has a surprising effect. Compared with Blest's original coefficient, $\eta$ has a narrower range at fixed Spearman's rho, but near independence a wider range at fixed Chatterjee's rank correlation, where $|\eta|$ can come close to $\sqrt{11\xi/5}$ while Blest's coefficient stays below $\sqrt{32\xi/15}$. The proofs combine explicit Kantorovich potentials from optimal transport with a convex relaxation that turns out to be exact.
papers.intro:
When two judges rank the same wines, or two search engines rank the same documents, a disagreement about the first places usually matters more than a disagreement about the last ones. Spearman’s rho, one of the most widely used measures of agreement between two rankings, is blind to this distinction, since it penalizes a swap of two neighboring ranks in the same way at the top and at the bottom of the list. Blest [2] proposed a variant of Spearman’s rho that weights the leading ranks of one ranking more heavily, at the price that the coefficient changes when the two rankings exchange their roles. Genest and Plante [7] therefore introduced the average of Blest’s coefficient over both orderings of the rankings. It keeps the emphasis on the leading ranks, now of both rankings, and treats the two rankings alike. As we point out below, this coefficient is also the population version of the weighted rank correlation of Pinto da Costa and Soares [15], which was designed with the same aim.

A top-weighted coefficient is useful only if it tells us something that Spearman’s rho does not. How far apart can the two coefficients be, and which patterns of agreement drive them apart? More generally, how much information does the symmetrized coefficient share with other rank coefficients? We answer these questions at the population level by computing exact regions, that is, the sets of all pairs of values that two coefficients attain jointly over all dependence structures. The boundary of an exact region contains all sharp inequalities between the two coefficients, and the dependence structures on the boundary show what drives the coefficients furthest apart.

papers.title: Results from a Stellar Occultation by (623) Chimaera
papers.abstract: We present results from a stellar occultation by the asteroid (623) Chimaera on October 21st, 2025, when it passed in front of V magnitude 13.86 star UCAC4 626-004193. Chimaera is the largest asteroid in the Chimaerid asteroid family and will be subject to a spacecraft flyby in the 2030s. Eighteen telescopes were deployed, spanning the United States from Arizona to North Carolina, incrementally spaced by $\sim4.4$\,km with respect to the cross-track of the shadow. In total, sixteen telescopes collected useful data. This multi-chord observation, when compiled into a single sky-plane plot, suggests a profile which is well-described by an elongated elliptical fit, with a semi-major axis $a=26.2\pm0.8$ km and a semi-minor axis $b=16.0\pm1.0$ km. The projected area from ellipse fitting is 1316 km$^2$, and a limb fit is calculated to enclose 1312 km$^2$. Photometry collected in the Gaia G band over a seven-month period coinciding with the occultation corresponds to a geometric albedo $p_G=0.059\pm0.005$; comparing with archival occultation observations and direct observations gives $p_G=0.051\pm0.004$ and $p_V=0.051\pm0.004$. We compare occultation sky-plane projections with 3-D modeling from inversion techniques and demonstrate that the models can accurately predict the orientation of Chimaera at the time of each occultation.

papers.intro:
Stellar occultations, which occur when Solar System bodies transit stars, have been shown repeatedly to be one of the most powerful tools to probe minor planets from the surface of the Earth (Evans and Lourens, 1961; Millis et al., 1987; Morgado et al., 2023). Precise timing (millisecond or sub-millisecond) of the ingress and egress of the occulting body’s shadow provides the most accurate astrometric measurements obtainable through atmosphere, and when combined with multiple telescopes distributed throughout the cross-track of the shadow, can be used to probe topography on the kilometer scale. Occultations have also been used to detect satellites around asteroids (Buie et al., 2022; Gault et al., 2022)

The inner main-belt asteroid (623) Chimaera (hereafter Chimaera) orbits the Sun in an orbit ∼2.47\sim 2.47 au in radius, with an eccentricity of 0.112 and a relatively high inclination of 14.1​°14.1\degree (gathered from the JPL#\#108 ephemeris, Chamberlin et al. 1997). It occupies an orbit very close to the 3:1 resonance with Jupiter at 2.5 au (known as the 3:1 Kirkwood gap). This specific mean motion resonance in the main asteroid belt, along with the v6 secular resonance, is hypothesized to be the progenitor of the majority of inner-Solar System asteroidal material, including meteors and meteorites (Yoshikawa, 1990; Morbidelli and Moons, 1995; Moons and Morbidelli, 1995).

Chimaera, for many reasons, is a unique asteroid. At ∼78​°\sim 78\degree, the spin axis obliquity of Chimaera (Sorli et al., 2024) is comparable to that of the giant planet Uranus (82​°82\degree). The asteroid has become of particular interest when it was identified as the parent of the high-inclination, eponymous Chimaerid asteroid family (Nesvorny, 2015). This family is composed of 108 identified member asteroids which are predominantly the primitive C-type in the taxonomical scheme of Tholen (1984), as suggested through a survey of twenty Chimaerids with the OSIRIS spectrometer on the 10.4 m Gran Telescopio Canarias (Morate et al., 2019). This spectral analysis demonstrates that the Chimaerid family possesses a non-negligible fraction of hydrated bodies, indicating that at some point in the history of the family, low temperature (sub-320 K) liquid water was involved in their collective chemical evolution, generating carbonates, hydroxides, oxides, phyllosilicates, sulfates, and other compounds (Fornasier et al., 2014). The existence of this large family of asteroids related to the parent Chimaera indicates a collisional event at some point in Chimaera’s history, in which large pieces of debris (the largest, (2642) Vesale, with a diameter of 7.4 km) were ejected into different heliocentric orbits. It is possible that the abnormal spin axis obliquity of Chimaera is a result of this prehistoric collision, as has long been suggested for Uranus (Safronov, 1966; Kegerreis et al., 2018). Interestingly, it has been suggested that there is a low chance that the asteroid (162173) Ryugu, visited by the Hayabusa 2 mission in 2018, may be a member of the Chimaera family (Morate et al., 2019).

Chimaera is of further interest due to its selection as a target for the upcoming Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA) spacecraft, currently under construction by the United Arab Emirates Space Agency (UAESA) and expected to launch in 2028. This spacecraft will fly by six asteroids before entering orbit around the seventh, (269) Justitia, before deploying a probe which will perform an uncontrolled descent to the surface of the asteroid (Almazmi et al., 2024; Biktimirov et al., 2026). Chimaera is the second largest of the asteroids to be surveyed by this spacecraft. Successful stellar occultation measurements have been conducted for two of the EMA target asteroids, (269) Justitia (Buie et al., 2025) and (59980) Moza (Oakey et al. in prep.), probing their size, scale, and the possibilities for small satellites around these bodies.

papers.title: IntentWeaver: Sustaining Coherence across Evolving Intents in Human-AI Co-Writing
papers.abstract: Writers hold intents at many levels, from overarching goals to concrete wording, and evolve them by periodically popping back up from the text to higher-level intents. Generative AI co-writing disrupts this practice. Dense drafts capture attention and trap writers in local editing; higher-level intents stall while lower-level ones drift from them unnoticed, a breakdown we term intent incoherence. Our formative study traced this breakdown from attention capture through silent drift to failed reconciliation. We present IntentWeaver, which supports intent evolution while sustaining coherence in human-AI co-writing. It derives an intent hierarchy from the draft and writer interactions, evaluates each intent's fulfillment and cross-level coherence at every change, and propagates consequences across intent levels. In a within-subjects study (N=24) against a baseline, participants using IntentWeaver revisited and evolved higher-level intents more often, with fewer unnoticed deviations, and produced texts better realizing them. We further discuss design implications for emergent intents.

papers.intro:
Human intent is fundamentally structured as a multi-level hierarchy, where lower-level intents dictate how an action is executed, while higher-level intents define why and to what end it is pursued (Vallacher and Wegner, 1987; Kuutti, 1996). In the context of human writing, this hierarchical organization manifests not as a static, upfront plan, but as an emergent phenomenon; intents continuously surface, sharpen, and dissolve as the writer engages with the evolving text (Flower and Hayes, 1980; Flower and Hayes, 1981). Cognitive models of writing illustrate how authors construct and maintain these nested intent layers progressively through the act of composition, spanning from overarching conceptual goals (e.g., topic, audience, and genre), through section-level purposes and effects, down to specific content and lexical choices (Bereiter and Scardamalia, 1987; DiMarco and Hirst, 1993). To prevent this highly fluid process from degenerating into undirected drift, writers must constantly govern coherence across different intent levels, keeping immediate textual outcomes aligned with their broader objectives. They achieve this through a recurrent “popping back up” mechanism (Flower and Hayes, 1981), stepping back from local execution to re-evaluate progress against higher-level intents, reaffirming or revising these goals wherever appropriate, and propagating adjustments downward to reconcile drifted intents. Navigating this continuous loop of discovery and reconciliation is cognitively demanding, requiring metacognitive regulation to monitor, evaluate, and restructure goals across levels of abstraction in real time (Hacker et al., 2009).

Large Language Models (LLMs) have catalyzed a new human-AI co-writing paradigm, shifting the writer’s primary role from manual drafting to guiding and curating AI-generated text (Reza et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2024). This collaborative mode offers tangible cognitive benefits: AI outputs alleviate the “blank page” syndrome (Clark et al., 2018; Gero et al., 2022) by rapidly generating exploratory content, while confronting these concrete drafts helps writers recognize, crystallize, and refine nascent intents they might otherwise struggle to articulate (Gero et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024). However, this same generative capacity disrupts the natural cognitive dynamics of writing. Overwhelmed by the continuous influx of dense, AI-generated text, writers are forced into a reactive cycle of evaluating and editing local passages (Bhat et al., 2026; Siddiqui et al., 2025). Such micromanagement crowds out the metacognitive regulation (Lee et al., 2025) required to periodically “pop back up” and evaluate local text against higher-level goals (Bhat et al., 2026; Umarova et al., 2025). Consequently, high-level intents stagnate while untethered lower-level intents proliferate and drift, leading to “intent incoherence” – a subtle but critical breakdown where writers feel highly productive editing AI outputs, yet invisibly decouple from or even violate their overarching purpose until the final text no longer reflects it (Bhat et al., 2026; Jakesch et al., 2023).

Recent human-computer interaction (HCI) research has attempted to mitigate intent-related challenges in co-writing with AI. One line of work externalizes intent through structured representations to guide AI generation, utilizing hierarchical goal decomposition (e.g., VISAR (Zhang et al., 2023) and IntentFlow (Kim et al., 2026)) or persistent intent specifications (e.g., Script&Shift (Siddiqui et al., 2025)). Another line supports exploration of output alternatives given intents, by better organizing AI responses (e.g., Luminate (Suh et al., 2024)) or enabling rapid comparison of outcome variations (e.g., ABScribe (Reza et al., 2024)). While these systems successfully assist in top-down formulation and articulation of intents, they tend to treat intent as a static, unidirectional constraint. There is a lack of support for the bottom-up process of writing: recognizing when local textual discoveries warrant the revision of a higher-level goal. Maintaining coherence across the intent hierarchy is thus largely left to the writer’s unaided initiative – the very capacity that reactive co-writing erodes.

To address this gap, we conducted a formative study with 12 frequent AI co-writers, which revealed their frictions in higher-level intent monitoring, cross-level drift detection, and bidirectional intent reconciliation. Guided by these insights, we designed IntentWeaver, an interactive system that supports intent evolution and sustains coherence throughout the human-AI co-writing process. Unlike prior systems that require upfront, structured intent externalization, IntentWeaver allows intent to emerge from, and evolve alongside, the AI-generated text. Concretely, the system continuously derives and maintains an intent hierarchy from the evolving texts, surfaces coherence breakdowns and fulfillment gaps, and propagates user revisions at any level across the hierarchy.

To evaluate whether IntentWeaver mitigates intent incoherence and supports the evolution of high-level intents, and how writers appropriate and experience this system, we conducted a within-subjects study with 24 participants against a baseline system that preserves the core features of current mainstream AI co-writing tools. Results of mixed-methods analyses, combining task outputs, interaction logs, post-task questionnaires, and semi-structured interviews, showed that with IntentWeaver, participants returned to their high-level intents more often and evolved them further, and far less of their drift went unnoticed. Their final texts also realized the intents better, with no cost to agency or workload. We further identified three patterns of appropriation. Based on these findings, we offered design considerations for systems that maintain intent as a live structure, and consider where this approach applies beyond writing.

papers.title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
papers.abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

papers.intro:
Liability adjudication [13, 42], as a prevalent and critical task in the real world, refers to the analysis of event descriptions based on domain-specific skills to determine whether a particular party should bear liability [17]. Such tasks exist in various real-world scenarios, including ride-hailing dispute resolution and legal liability determination. For example, in a dispute over property management fees, the property owner is adjudicated not liable for breaching the payment obligation after executing a service-verification skill demonstrating that the property management company failed to provide the agreed-upon services as stipulated in the Civil Code.

For example, in a dispute over property management fees, the property owner is adjudicated not liable for breaching the payment obligation after executing a service-verification skill demonstrating that the property management company failed to provide the agreed-upon services as stipulated in the Civil Code.

Traditional algorithms for liability adjudication have primarily relied on logic-reasoning approaches [26, 48] and semantic-analysis methods [32, 1]. Logic-reasoning approaches rely on logical structures of skills to yield deductions [2], while semantic-analysis methods predict liability through similarity computation [6] or classifiers [27]. However, these algorithms can only make adjudications based on fixed rules rather than optimizing the skills themselves, and they cannot generate interpretable reasoning trajectories. Recently, LLMs have emerged as a promising solution, offering a new paradigm for liability adjudication. Trained on vast domain-specific corpora, LLMs possess extensive embedded adjudication knowledge, which has sparked significant interest in leveraging them for this task [52, 47], particularly through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [23, 50].

These LLM-based approaches enhance the adjudication process by incorporating domain-specific priors into the reasoning pipeline, guiding evidence analysis with divergent skills that reflect varied expert perspectives, and providing interpretable reasoning trajectories that make the decision process transparent and traceable. Despite this promise, we identify three fundamental challenges that limit the effectiveness of skill-based LLM methods in liability adjudication. These challenges stem not from engineering imperfections, but from core tensions in how skills are acquired, executed, and deployed at scale, tensions that are intrinsic to the skill-based paradigm itself.

Challenge 1: Skill Coverage under Distribution Shift. Real-world liability scenarios are dynamically evolving. Emerging fraud behaviors, regulatory changes, and novel dispute patterns continually introduce decision boundaries that existing skill libraries fail to cover [8]. This creates a skill coverage gap between the static knowledge embedded in the library and the shifting data distribution of incoming cases. A natural response is to induce new skills from recent adjudication data, yet this raises a fundamental learning dilemma: inducing a skill from a single case risks capturing idiosyncratic patterns that lack statistical validity, while inducing from the full dataset is intractable due to case heterogeneity and the excessive context length required to process all instances simultaneously.

This creates a skill coverage gap between the static knowledge embedded in the library and the shifting data distribution of incoming cases. Challenge 2: Skill Execution Alignment. Even when a skill is logically comprehensible to human experts, LLMs may interpret its natural language formulation inconsistently due to divergent priors, ambiguous operator precedence, or implicit assumptions. This creates a semantic execution gap where the LLM’s actual reasoning trajectory deviates from the expert’s intended logic, even if the final label happens to be correct. Current approaches treat skills as static artifacts and do not account for the fact that LLM execution is inherently stochastic and sensitive to phrasing. Without a feedback mechanism that observes the LLM’s execution trajectories and adjusts the skill formulation accordingly, the system cannot guarantee stable or faithful skill execution.

Challenge 3: Skill Scalability under Context Budget. As the skill library grows to cover diverse scenarios, feeding the entire collection into LLM alongside a test case becomes infeasible due to finite context windows. This inevitably triggers skill omission, where relevant skills are discarded because they exceed the context budget, and attentional interference, where irrelevant skills dilute LLM’s reasoning capacity. Existing methods either present all skills indiscriminately or rely on coarse retrieval strategies that fail to respect the tight coupling between skill applicability and the structural preconditions of individual cases. This causes a scalability routing problem: how to identify the minimal yet sufficient subset of skills for a given case while strictly adhering to context constraints.

To address these three challenges, we propose KDASO. Rather than treating skill generation, refinement, and selection as isolated engineering components, KDASO frames them as interdependent solutions to the core problems of coverage, alignment, and scalability. Specifically, to close the skill coverage gap under distribution shift, we introduce Neighborhood-Conditioned Skill Induction, which leverages local manifold structure to identify representative case neighborhoods for skill generation, balancing the specificity of single-case induction with the feasibility of full-set processing. To bridge the semantic execution gap, we develop Execution-Aligned Skill Refinement, which analyzes discrepancies between LLM execution trajectories and expert reasoning paths, then restructures skill formulations to improve trajectory stability. To solve the scalability routing problem, we design Context-Budgeted Skill Routing, which trains lightweight applicability classifiers to dynamically route the most relevant skills for each case while guaranteeing context budget compliance.

papers.title: Towards Track Height Control in Additive Manufacturing on Porous Substrates: An Approach for System Identification and Controller Selection
papers.abstract: Additive manufacturing is transforming the creation of materials and parts, enabling the design and manufacturing of multifunctional parts with tailored properties. One compelling example is the combination of a porous core and a non-porous surface, which offers significant advantages in terms of weight reduction, material efficiency, strength and wear resistance. Directed Energy Deposition (DED) processes enable the transition from porous core to non-porous part surface by closing the pores. However, the surface-layer of porous substrates presents a substantial challenge to achieving consistent track heights during DED, directly impacting the final part geometry and performance. Therefore, precise control of the deposition process is crucial for realising the full potential of the multifunctional parts. In order to address this challenge, this work presents a conceptual approach for track height control during Laser-based Directed Energy Deposition (DED-LB) on porous substrates. First, the DED-LB process and the associated measurement setup are explained, along with a discussion of their limitations. The focus then shifts to the control problem, beginning with system identification to characterise the process dynamics. Subsequently, a selection of control strategies is investigated, as well as their compatibility with the process. This research provides a foundational step toward reliable additive manufacturing on porous substrates, and thus toward producing multifunctional parts.

papers.title: Discovery of the redback pulsar PSR J2053+6905 and multi-epoch optical observations of the system
papers.abstract: Using the Green Bank Telescope, we discovered the 1.68-ms binary pulsar PSR J2053+6905. The discovery resulted from a targeted search for radio pulsations from a redback candidate, previously identified through optical and X-ray observations and spatially coincident with the $\gamma$-ray source 4FGL J2054.2+6904. We report the first results from the pulsar timing, including the spin period, dispersion measure, precisely measured Keplerian binary parameters, and the pulsar mass function. We also found potential evidence of scintillation and long radio eclipses. To constrain the system parameters, we performed multi-epoch time-series photometric observations using the 2.1-m telescope at the Observatorio Astron\'omico Nacional on the Sierra San Pedro M\'artir (Mexico) and the 1.5-m telescope of the Maidanak Astronomical Observatory (Uzbekistan), complemented by time-series optical spectroscopy with the 10.4-m Gran Telescopio Canarias. The optical light curves revealed a pronounced asymmetry, as well as significant long-term variations. From the spectra, we derived a radial velocity curve semi-amplitude $K = 337(4)$ km s$^{-1}$. Combining it with the pulsar mass function, we constrained the ratio of pulsar and companion masses to $M_{\rm p}/M_{\rm c} = 7.05(8)$. By fitting the stable segments of the light curves with a symmetric direct heating model, we derived constraints on the component masses ($M_{\rm p} \approx 2.1\ {\rm M}_\odot$ and $M_{\rm c} \approx 0.3\ {\rm M}_\odot$), the Roche lobe filling factor, and the companion's day- and night-side temperatures. The long-term evolution of the light curve profiles is likely driven by the dissipation or migration of a cold stellar spot.

papers.intro:
Redback (RB) pulsars are a subclass of the so-called ‘spider’ pulsar systems – close binaries with orbital periods of ≲1\lesssim 1 d, each comprising a millisecond pulsar (MSP) and a low-mass (0.1–1 M⊙) stellar secondary (Roberts, 2013, e.g.). The latter is ablated by the pulsar wind, and the evaporated material can cause eclipses of the pulsar radio emission for a substantial part of the orbit. RBs are distinguished from another spider subclass, the black widows (BWs), which have very light, ≲\lesssim0.05 M⊙, substellar companions. While spiders in the radio pulsar state are non-accreting, the pulsars can attain masses exceeding 2 M⊙ as a result of an earlier evolutionary phase of mass transfer from their companions. Consequently, these systems, as part of the wider recycled neutron star population (Kiziltan et al., 2013, e.g.,), can provide important constraints on the equation of state of matter above the nuclear saturation density (Kumar et al., 2023; Romani et al., 2026, e.g.).

In recent years, the population of spiders has grown significantly thanks to the Fermi γ\gamma-ray space telescope and targeted follow-up of unassociated sources with radio, X-ray and optical telescopes (Clark et al., 2023; Bangale et al., 2024; Thongmeearkom et al., 2026, e.g.). papers.title: When Molecular Dimerization Induces Magnetic Bi-Stability at the Metal-Organic Interface
papers.abstract: We present a method to create metal-organic dimer complexes by on-surface assembly on a metal substrate using low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS). We demonstrate that a dimer of Mn-Phthalocyanine (MnPc)2 on a Ag(111) surface can be switched between two stable configurations upon a small conformational change controlled by STM manipulation. By means of density-functional theory calculations, it is found that the two conformations correspond to an antiferromagnetic (AFM) and a ferromagnetic (FM) state respectively. Directly coordinated Mn atoms of the dimer lead to an AFM-coupling whereas indirectly coordinated (shifted) Mn atoms lead to a FM-coupling. Rarely seen in a molecular- dimers with transition-metal atoms, the FM-AFM-FM transition is thus readily on-surface accessible. Furthermore, the two configurations of the switch are easily identified by their Kondo states, opening interesting routes in terms of both, writing (FM versus AFM states) and reading. These results pave the experimental route toward dimer-based materials with complex magnetic structures of potential interest for application in spintronics, logics and computing.

papers.title: Detecting Weather Fronts from Satellite Observations: What Does Reanalysis Add?
papers.abstract: Weather fronts are transition regions between air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties and are associated with mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather. We investigate machine learning (ML) methods for detecting weather fronts and quantify the contribution of reanalysis data to performance. We compare two configurations of the same ML model for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe: (1) using only geostationary infrared satellite observations, and (2) additionally using 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields. The satellite-only model achieves a neighbourhood critical success index at a 150 km tolerance (CSI@150) of $0.402$, which lies within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services. The satellite$+$ERA5 model achieves $0.575$, an improvement of $0.173$. Our analysis shows that low-level winds are the least predictable from the satellite representation ($R^2 = 0.23$, compared with $0.88$ for temperature), while removing winds or moisture causes the largest decreases in detection performance.

papers.intro:
Weather fronts are narrow transition regions where air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties meet, causing sharp changes in temperature, humidity, wind, and pressure (Hewson, 1998; Biard and Kunkel, 2019). Detecting fronts matters for both weather forecasting and climate analysis, because a substantial fraction of extreme mid-latitude precipitation occurs near them (Catto and Pfahl, 2013). Operational forecasters identify fronts manually (Biard and Kunkel, 2019; Justin et al., 2025) from surface observations, satellite imagery, and numerical weather prediction (NWP) output. Independent meteorological services often analyse the same synoptic situation differently, because their local information, analysis conventions, and regional priorities differ. Automated methods, from thermodynamic diagnostics on gridded fields (Hewson, 1998; Schemm et al., 2015) to deep learning models (Biard and Kunkel, 2019; Lagerquist et al., 2019; Niebler et al., 2022; Justin et al., 2025), offer objective and reproducible alternatives. Most rely on reanalysis, which combines historical observations with an NWP model to reconstruct past atmospheric states. We study the automated pixel-wise classification of cold, warm, and occluded fronts over the North Atlantic and Europe.

Detectors that rely on reanalysis or NWP fields lag behind the latest observations. Reanalyses such as ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020) become available after several days and operational NWP analyses typically after a few hours, while real-time forecasts contain no observations made after their initialisation. Geostationary satellites, in contrast, observe the atmosphere several times per hour, so a satellite-only detector can run in near real time. However, infrared radiances do not directly measure the temperature, humidity, and wind fields that characterise frontal zones. Reanalyses estimate these fields by data assimilation. This trade-off motivates our question: what does reanalysis add beyond satellite observations for frontal detection? We answer it by comparing satellite-only and satellite++ERA5 detectors through cross-modal probing, variable-group ablation, and single-group addition.

papers.title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
papers.abstract: Skills let language agents reuse experience across tasks as natural-language documents. Recent work evolves skills from interaction, but existing methods have limitations when skills evolve online. Prior methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories collected over many tasks. Some then adopt the new skill without any check, which can degrade the skill over time. Others keep it only if it improves performance on a held-out validation set, which is too slow and costly to run after every update. We introduce EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that mitigates skill degradation at low latency and cost. We first run the agent iteratively to build pools of skills and score each skill on a private test set to obtain utility labels. We pair the skills and use rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector is trained on the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill. At deployment it decides in a single forward pass, which is significantly faster than evaluation on the private test set. Compared with adopting every new skill, EvoGuard improves success by 11.0% on ALFWorld, 5.9% on ScienceWorld, and 2.7% on LiveCodeBench.

Gap 1: Offline multi-trajectory evolution does not match deployment. Most methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories (Xia et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). The update runs in a training phase before deployment. It analyzes trajectories from many tasks at once. A deployed agent rarely works this way. Each task arrives once and is attempted once. The next task is usually a different one. The skill must therefore be revised from a single trajectory and then reused by later tasks. SkillRise carries a skill across tasks in this way (Yao et al., 2026). However, it trains the executor jointly with skill curation and does not check individual updates.

This decision only requires the relative order of the two skills, not their absolute utilities. We therefore cast it as a pairwise preference problem. EvoGuard works in three stages (Figure 2). (1) Multi-source skill pool construction. We run the rewrite loop on training tasks with a base generator and an expert generator, and collect the generated skills into a pool. (2) Utility-grounded pairwise preference learning. We estimate the utility of every skill on a private test set of its family. Rejection sampling keeps pairs from the same family with a clear utility gap. We then train a pairwise selector to predict which skill in a pair has the higher utility. (3) Online skill selection. After every task, the frozen selector reads the family description and the two skills. It keeps the skill it predicts to be better. This takes one forward pass and runs no extra rollouts in the environment.

We then train a pairwise selector to predict which skill in a pair has the higher utility. (3) Online skill selection. papers.title: IDPrior: Decoupling Identity Generation from Facial Image Synthesis
papers.abstract: Large-scale identity-labeled face datasets are essential for training modern face recognition models, yet collecting and annotating such data is costly and raises privacy and ethical concerns. Existing synthetic face generation methods typically derive identities from predefined class labels, unconditional image generation, or predefined latent sampling strategies, without explicitly modeling the underlying distribution of facial identities. In this paper, we propose IDPrior, a two-stage framework that decouples identity generation from image synthesis. We first learn a diffusion prior in the embedding space of a pretrained face recognition model to model the distribution of facial identities and generate novel identity embeddings. These embeddings are then used to condition a pretrained identity-conditioned diffusion model (DM), enabling the synthesis of multiple images of the same identity. This modular design provides a scalable approach to identity generation while remaining compatible with existing and future identity-conditioned DMs. Experiments indicate that IDPrior generates diverse and well-separated identities while maintaining a closer correspondence to the distribution of authentic identities. Face recognition models trained on datasets generated using IDPrior-generated identities achieve competitive or improved performance compared with existing synthetic-data-based methods across multiple face verification benchmarks. Code and generated datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/fdbtrs/IDperturb.

papers.title: Rain Beyond Streaks: Cascaded Realistic Rain and Wet Surface Synthesis via Scene Priors
papers.abstract: Realistic rain synthesis is a persistent challenge for vision systems operating in adverse weather. Existing methods primarily focus on generating rain streaks, often neglecting consequent surface effects such as reflections and puddles, which are critical for perceptual realism and robustness of downstream vision tasks. We introduce CascadeRS, a rain synthesis framework that leverages depth and segmentation priors to render scene-consistent rain and surface effects. In addition to rain streaks, CascadeRS produces reflections and puddles aligned with scene semantics through a physics-inspired zero-shot, controllable generative pipeline. It produces photorealistic rainy urban scenes, with high perceptual realism, which we validate qualitatively with an extensive user study and quantitatively. We produce the Cityscapes-CascadeRS dataset, to study downstream task performance under real rainy conditions. Our results establish CascadeRS as a scalable and realistic rain-generation framework for evaluating and enhancing the robustness of vision in adverse rainy weather. Code and dataset are available via https://github.com/nis-research/CascadeRainSynthesis
