papers.intro:
Rain is a common environmental factor that degrades image quality and challenges outdoor vision tasks such as autonomous driving and traffic surveillance [41, 16, 35, 37]. It introduces visual distortions (streaks, blur, reduced contrast) and surface reflections that obscure details, reduce visibility, and alter object appearance (see Figure 1).

Rain is a common environmental factor that degrades image quality and challenges outdoor vision tasks such as autonomous driving and traffic surveillance [41, 16, 35, 37]. It introduces visual distortions (streaks, blur, reduced contrast) and surface reflections that obscure details, reduce visibility, and alter object appearance (see Figure 1).

Common strategies to address model prediction robustness under rain include de-raining [61, 3] and rain synthesis [12]. On one side, de-raining methods aim to recover a clean image from a rainy input. However, as supervised approaches, they require paired rainy–clean data, which are not available under real-world conditions. Despite good results [50, 13, 42, 45, 62], they often overfit to specific rain types due to the use of non-realistic synthetic training data with limited rain patterns, and may overcorrect by removing fine background details [7, 2, 43]. On the other side, synthesizing rain effects enables the training of vision models with rain-affected images and systematic evaluation of performance under adverse rain conditions. It is a less costly approach compared to collecting real-world rain image data. Existing methods [28, 8, 56, 58] oversimplify the modeling of rain using uniform streak patterns. Because they lack depth-based variability, realistic fog, proper interaction with lighting, and occlusion by scene objects, the generated rain exhibits low perceptual realism. Wet reflective surfaces and puddles also affect image perception, but are often not considered and modeled in existing methods [42, 45, 13]. Examples are shown in Figure 1, where methods like PBR [11] and Cityscapes-Rain [13] do not account for rain-related surface effects. Generative AI models for rain synthesis require large amounts of training data (often created with rendering engines [37, 4, 39]) and might overfit to certain rain types. They lack controllable and principled generation, resulting in issues with retaining fine-grained details or misalignment between prompts and generated images. We show examples in Appendix D. Moreover, real rain datasets are scarce [57, 63] and evaluations mostly rely on synthetic data.

In this paper, we address the generation of perceptually realistic rain images with a principled approach that is grounded in scene depth and semantics priors, and further uses physics-inspired priors. We propose Cascade Rain Synthesis (CascadeRS), a framework with a learning-free rain synthesis module that produces realistic and physics-inspired puddles, wet-surfaces, and reflections guided by the depth and semantics scene priors to ensure perspective coherence. CascadeRS only receives inputs from pre-trained depth-estimation and semantic segmentation models, while not requiring training data and learning itself, decomposes the scene into depth-aware layers, and generates rain and fog consistently with the scene geometry. We design it as a modular pipeline, enabling a controllable generation process. We generate the CityScape-CascadeRS dataset of rain-affected urban scenes integrating depth-guided atmospheric and surface rain synthesis, which we use to benchmark perceptual realism (quantitatively, with FID scores and qualitatively, with a user study) and impact on downstream segmentation and object detection robustness, in comparison to existing generative methods and datasets.

papers.title: Asymptotic advantage of quantum one-way and SMP communication for total functions
papers.abstract: We exhibit a total Boolean function on n input bits whose bounded-error quantum simultaneous-message (and hence one-way) communication complexity is in O(\sqrt n), whereas its randomised one-way (and hence simultaneous-message) communication complexity is in \Omega(n). The same function admits a classical simultaneous-message protocol of cost O(\sqrt n) when the players share O(\sqrt n) EPR pairs.

papers.title: GPWM: Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion
papers.abstract: We introduce GPWM, a Generative Particle World Model that predicts how 3D scenes evolve by generating the motion of particles and rigid bodies over time. Unlike video world models that generate scene appearance, GPWM operates directly in 3D physical space. A single representation and architecture cover rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction. GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines flow matching with diffusion forcing to generate coherent physical trajectories far beyond its training horizon. We train and evaluate GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments. GPWM outperforms the best prior learned-dynamics baseline in each of six physical domains, reducing prediction error by 31% on average. Breaking from the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single Unified GPWM models these heterogeneous regimes with one set of weights, largely outperforming per-domain baselines and even surpassing our own specialist models in two domains. GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties, object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables contact-rich planning by learning a generative prior over joint actuator-object motion. Instead of searching over unconstrained actions, planning searches the model's latent noise for interactions that achieve a desired object-space goal. With the same world model, noise-space planning substantially outperforms action-space search on pushing and picking, where complex contact sequences are hard to discover. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans achieve goal-directed manipulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific policies.

papers.intro:
A general-purpose physical world model should predict how a 3D scene evolves and how to act to bring it toward a desired state. This requires modeling diverse objects and materials, maintaining coherent dynamics over long horizons, and reasoning through physical contact. Recent generative video world models capture rich and multimodal scene evolution (NVIDIA, 2026; Wan et al., 2025; Bruce et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026), but generate visual appearance rather than explicitly representing the motion and interactions of physical objects in 3D. Particle- and point-based models instead represent physical state directly in 3D (Li et al., 2019; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Pfaff et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2025a; Duisterhof et al., 2026). However, existing learned 3D dynamics models are typically limited by deterministic prediction, short generation horizons, or specialization to particular materials and interactions (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2026). We ask: can a generative model of 3D particle motion capture diverse physical dynamics, predict over long horizons, and support planning through contact?

We introduce GPWM, a generative world model that represents 3D scenes as particles and rigid bodies and predicts their motion over time (Figure 1). Deformable objects are modeled through particle displacements and rigid bodies through body-level transformations, providing a common representation for rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular dynamics. GPWM conditions on observed 3D scene history and, when available, physical properties and future actuator motion. Actuators share the same geometric representation as other scene components, allowing their trajectories to either condition physical prediction or be generated jointly with object motion for planning.

Learning generative particle dynamics at scale presents two challenges: scenes may contain thousands of particles across interacting objects, and prediction errors accumulate over long rollouts. GPWM addresses the first with object-aware multi-resolution tokenization and spatio-temporal attention in relative 3D coordinates. To address the second, we combine flow matching with diffusion forcing, independently varying noise levels across future frames. This enables streaming generation, where near-future states are progressively resolved and committed while farther-future states remain uncertain and revisable, allowing generation far beyond the training horizon.

Conventional action-space planning searches actuator commands and predicts their consequences, but can struggle to discover complex contact sequences or exploit world-model errors through out-of-distribution actions. The resulting actuator trajectories execute successfully in simulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific policies.

papers.title: Viable Phantom Crossing in Softly Broken Shift Symmetric Gravity
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a viable fit to current cosmological data from a simple Horndeski modified gravity theory that softly breaks shift symmetry. This SBSS model crosses the phantom divide $w=-1$ at $z\approx0.5$ and fits observational data (baryon acoustic oscillations and supernova distances, and cosmic microwave background power spectra) better than $w_0w_a$CDM, by $\Delta\chi^2\approx-3$ for the same number of effective parameters, while providing a physical foundation for cosmic acceleration. The theory is healthy, has no cosmological constant or potential, and has substantial protection against high energy quantum loop corrections.

papers.title: Goal Revelation as a Bridge Between Information-Theoretic Empowerment and Capability-Based Human Power
papers.abstract: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). As we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. Two such measures in the context of Markov games are information-theoretic empowerment, the capacity of the channel from an agent's actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, a measure of goal attainment built from the probabilities that a human would attain each goal in a family of candidates were they pursuing it. We show where the two meet. From individual power, Fano's inequality yields a floor $B(s)$. This floor is a lower bound on what we term goal revelation, the mutual information $\mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s)$ between the human's latent goal and the realised trajectory. Empowerment caps revelation from above, so that $B(s) \le \mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s) \le \mathbb{I}(\mathbf{A}_h \to \xi \mid s) \le \mathfrak{E}_h(s)$. Each quantity can be large while the one below it stays at zero, highlighting the following failure modes. An assistant maximising empowerment can prefer an interface offering broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom to one that lets the human attain every goal they might hold. An assistant maximising revelation cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome, since relabelling goals leaves mutual information unchanged while zeroing every attainment probability. Positive guarantees therefore come only from the attainment end of the chain. A satisfaction floor, computable from two statistics of interaction logs, offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system, and simulations in random environments show the three quantities are correlated but far from interchangeable.

papers.title: Ultrahomogeneous hypertournaments
papers.abstract: A $k$-hypertournament is a higher-arity generalisation of a tournament, consisting of a set together with an irreflexive $k$-ary relation such that the automorphism group of each substructure of size $k$ is the alternating group $\mathrm{A}_k$. We show that, for each $k \geq 3$, there are continuum-many non-isomorphic countable ultrahomogeneous $k$-hypertournaments, answering a question of Cherlin.

papers.title: Goal-Branching LaCAM: Temporary Goals as Search Branches in Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
papers.abstract: LaCAM is a search-based solver for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) that runs a depth-first search over joint configurations, using PIBT to generate successors and lazily adding single-agent constraints to explore alternatives. Although LaCAM is complete, it can struggle on dense, corridor-heavy instances because extracting blocking agents from deadlocks requires coordinated moves of several agents, often away from their goals, which PIBT's greedy one-step successors rarely propose and which LaCAM can only reach by enumerating constraints one agent at a time. This paper proposes Goal-Branching, where blocking agents are given temporary goals, each tried as an additional branch of LaCAM's search. We examine random and corridor-aware rules for choosing these temporary goals and show that completeness is preserved for any such rule. On dense instances (60-90% of free cells occupied) of three maze and room maps, Goal-Branching solves 89% of instances against 44% for LaCAM*, and, on instances both solve, it finds a first solution 10-14x faster on maze-32-32-2 and room-32-32-4, and nearly 200x faster in median time at 75% density on room-32-32-4. Solution cost increases by 15-22% on instances both solve, while on open maps and the full MovingAI benchmark its solutions cost no more than those of LaCAM* and it is at most 3% slower.
papers.intro:
Multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) asks for collision-free paths that move a team of agents from their start locations to their goals on a shared graph (Stern et al. 2019). It underpins applications such as automated warehouses, where hundreds of robots share narrow aisles (Wurman et al. 2008), and it is NP-hard to solve optimally (Yu and LaValle 2013). Many of the practically hard instances are dense ones, in which agents occupy a large fraction of the free space and must repeatedly make room for one another.

It underpins applications such as automated warehouses, where hundreds of robots share narrow aisles (Wurman et al. 2008), and it is NP-hard to solve optimally (Yu and LaValle 2013). Many of the practically hard instances are dense ones, in which agents occupy a large fraction of the free space and must repeatedly make room for one another.

Optimal and bounded-suboptimal solvers such as CBS (Sharon et al. 2015) and EECBS (Li et al. 2021) provide quality guarantees but do not scale to large, dense instances. Scalable solvers trade these guarantees for speed, with different strengths. Rule-based planners such as PIBT (Okumura et al. 2022) compute one step at a time and handle thousands of agents, but are incomplete. Repair-based methods built on large neighbourhood search, such as MAPF-LNS2 (Li et al. 2022) and its extensions (Wang et al. 2025), iteratively remove collisions from an initial plan and are among the strongest solvers on dense instances, often with better solution quality, but are also incomplete. LaCAM (Okumura 2023b) takes a third route, a search over joint configurations that uses PIBT to generate successors; it is complete and finds first solutions quickly at scale, though these are often costly.

LaCAM (Okumura 2023b) takes a third route, a search over joint configurations that uses PIBT to generate successors; it is complete and finds first solutions quickly at scale, though these are often costly.

LaCAM is complete, and LaCAM∗, its anytime extension, is proven to converge to an optimal solution given sufficient time. However, both can struggle to solve dense instances with dead-end corridors and other bottlenecks in a reasonable time. This is because PIBT, the configuration generator underlying both solvers, often deadlocks or livelocks in such settings, and the search is then reduced to a systematic but uninformed enumeration of successors, one agent constraint at a time. Some work has augmented the configuration generator for these situations, such as the swap technique (Okumura 2023a), which resolves livelocks between pairs of agents by pulling one of them towards a branching vertex where the two can exchange places, and tie-breaking heuristics that discourage agents from blocking each other’s routes (Okumura and Nagai 2025). However, these extensions only change how agents rank their moves towards fixed goals, and the swap technique handles one pair of agents at a time. Jams that require several agents to move away from their goals at once therefore still fall to the constraint search. In this paper we introduce Goal-Branching, a novel extension to LaCAM that resolves such jams directly. When PIBT’s step jams, Goal-Branching uses the agents that PIBT failed to move to propose temporary goals for those blocking the way, and tries each choice as a separate branch of the search before LaCAM’s own constraints. Temporary goals change where agents are heading, not the problem being solved, so the search keeps its guarantees, and the branches are cheap to generate from information PIBT already computes. Our contributions are: • Goal-Branching, an extension of LaCAM∗ that turns PIBT jams into temporary-goal branches of the search (Section 3); • proofs that Goal-Branching preserves completeness and eventual optimality, and leaves LaCAM∗ unchanged on runs without jams (Section 3.7); • an evaluation showing that on dense maze and room instances Goal-Branching solves 89% of instances against 44% for LaCAM∗ and finds first solutions up to 14×\times faster on average, and in some settings over 200×\times faster. On open maps and the full MovingAI benchmark it is never more than 3% slower, its solutions cost no more, and it solves 41 more runs than LaCAM∗ (Section 4).

papers.title: Mass loss in AF supergiants: At the verge of the Eddington limit and still with weak line-driven winds
papers.abstract: We study global atmosphere models of AF supergiants. In agreement with previous studies, we found super-Eddington layers in the photospheres of these stars, which lead to density inversions. Our tests showed that the super-Eddington layers are caused by hydrogen ionization. The analysis of radial perturbations has not revealed any instability of such layers, but we show that super-Eddington layers in an optically thick environment are prone to instabilities due to nonradial perturbations. We predict the wind parameters of AF supergiants from our global wind code with a comoving-frame radiative force. Despite the existence of density inversions, the predicted mass-loss rates are significantly lower than those estimated from observations. Theoretical values approach the observational estimates only for the most luminous supergiants, which are close to the Eddington limit due to light scattering on free electrons. Part of the discrepancy between the mass-loss rates could be attributed to the influence of the clumping on the observational properties. Low mass-loss rates imply that the winds of AF supergiants may be strongly influenced by the magnetic fields, suggesting an explanation for the observed spectral variability of these stars.

This means that most of the initial mass is lost during massive star evolution. While a part of the mass could be lost during the supernova explosion, mass estimates of Wolf-Rayet stars (Shenar et al., 2019) indicate that strong outflows take place even before the supernova explosion. However, we are not sure when this happens and how.

Traditionally, it is assumed that most of the mass loss occurs continuously via stellar winds (Georgy et al., 2013; Groh et al., 2013). However, advances in the field of wind modeling indicate that both theoretical and observational mass-loss rates are lower then it was previously assumed. In the case of theoretical predictions, lower mass-loss rates are connected with introduction of global wind models with comoving frame line force (Krtička & Kubát, 2017; Sander et al., 2017; Sundqvist et al., 2019). On the other hand, lower mass-loss rates derived from observations stem from inclusion of small-scale wind structure (clumping) into modeling (Sundqvist et al., 2010; Šurlan et al., 2012; Šurlan et al., 2013).

Evolved supergiants may experience density inversion in their atmospheres, which, albeit not directly responsible for the acceleration of the wind (Achmad et al., 1997; Asplund, 1998), may still moderate mass loss. The density inversion appears as a result of a strong radiative force, which may overcome the gravity (exceeding the Eddington limit). The presence of a density inversion could possibly cause the strong variability of the outflow observed in some of these stars (Richardson et al., 2011; Magerramov et al., 2017; Maryeva et al., 2022). Wind variability is also manifested spectroscopically via so-called high-velocity absorption events (Kaufer et al., 1996; Markova et al., 2008; Corliss et al., 2015; Pivoňková et al., 2022). Although these events were suspected to be connected with the presence of magnetic fields, the absence of strong large-scale fields in many of these stars (Shultz et al., 2014) does not seem to support this concept. Detectable fields appear only in a fraction of these stars (Martin et al., 2018).

In AF supergiants, the Eddington limit, where the continuum radiative force balances the gravity, is exceeded just locally in the photosphere due to hydrogen ionization (Sanyal et al., 2015; Sanyal et al., 2017). This differs from the super-Eddington winds (van Marle et al., 2008; Owocki et al., 2017), where the continuum radiative force is supposed to drive the wind. According to the degree to which the wind-driving region approaches the Eddington limit, hot-star winds are classified into Wolf-Rayet-type winds and OB-type winds (Sander, 2023, e.g.,). While acceleration of Wolf-Rayet-type winds starts deep in the atmosphere in the optically thick region of the so-called iron bump (Sander & Vink, 2020), the wind driving in OB stars is initiated in optically thin parts of the photosphere. Locally, the radiative force in OB stars may also overcome the gravity in the optically thick parts of the photosphere, but this just initiates turbulence and not mass loss (Debnath et al., 2024).

We start with description of stationary gray atmosphere models (Section 2), which allow us to better understand the density inversions due to hydrogen ionization and their stability (Appendix 3). papers.title: First-order condensation and meniscus pinning in finite open wedges
papers.abstract: We study first-order condensation in finite open wedges using classical density functional theory (DFT) and compare the resulting microscopic phase behaviour with recent macroscopic predictions. Two geometries are considered: a symmetric wedge formed by two identical inclined walls and an asymmetric wedge formed by a vertical and an inclined wall. The DFT calculations confirm the two condensed morphologies predicted for the symmetric wedge and the three morphologies predicted for the asymmetric wedge and their emergence depending on the wedge size, opening angle, and wall contact angle. Under partial-wetting conditions, the microscopic phase boundaries are in nearly perfect quantitative agreement with the macroscopic predictions, including reentrant changes between pinned and depinned meniscus configurations and the appearance of the semi-double-pinned state in the asymmetric wedge. Under complete-wetting conditions, the DFT phase diagrams retain the topology predicted by the macroscopic theory, but the single-pinned region is systematically enlarged. This shift is attributed to adsorbed liquid films, which reduce the effective width available to the gas and thereby increase the effective aspect ratio of the confinement.

The wedge has narrow and wide openings, and the condensed phase is bounded by two menisci. This construction provides a transparent geometrical interpretation of the condensation mechanisms and yields explicit or implicit predictions for the phase boundaries. At the same time, it neglects molecular-scale effects such as density oscillations near the walls, diffuse liquid–gas interfaces, adsorption films, and microscopic structure near edges and corners. These effects are expected to be particularly important under complete-wetting conditions, where liquid films form on the walls before condensation and reduce the effective space available to the gas.

We study the same symmetric and asymmetric open wedges and determine both the condensation point and the resulting morphology from the equilibrium density profiles. papers.title: Torsion points in families of elliptic curves
papers.abstract: We study the specialization of torsion points in one-parameter degenerations of elliptic curves with singular fibers of Kodaira type. We describe the resulting torsion curves, their ramifications, intersection multiplicities, and irreducible and connected components.

papers.title: Finite-element reconstruction of molten-zone dynamics and chemical segregation in optical floating-zone grown Ni--Mn--Ga
papers.abstract: Homogeneous single-crystal growth of Ni--Mn--Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys is limited by incongruent melting, Mn reactivity, and longitudinal composition segregation. We report a modified optical floating-zone method in which growth is performed inside a transparent sapphire crucible, stabilising the molten zone while preserving optical heating and visual monitoring. The resulting crystals show improved growth reproducibility and controlled macroscopic geometry. To interpret the measured segregation profiles, a transient finite-element heat-transfer model in COMSOL Multiphysics was coupled to an effective molten-zone mass-balance calculation. The model reveals that the local solidification velocity is not fixed by the imposed translation speed but varies strongly as the molten-zone geometry evolves. The calculated solidification-front geometry is independently supported by EBSD analysis of a quenched growth interface, while the coupled mass-balance calculation reproduces the dominant features of the measured composition profiles. These results show that deviations from ideal Scheil--Pfann behaviour arise from the evolving molten-zone geometry and solidification conditions. The experimentally constrained model therefore provides a practical means of reconstructing otherwise inaccessible growth conditions and a basis for optimisation of sapphire-confined floating-zone growth of incongruently melting alloys.

papers.intro:
Incongruently melting materials, where the composition of the solid differs from that of the melt during solidification, present a challenge for crystal growers. Floating zone techniques where only a portion of the charge volume is molten at a given moment of the growth process are known to help mitigate the effects, but macroscopic chemical segregation - concentration gradients - are still typically observed. This problem is particularly important in functional alloys such as Ni–Mn–Ga, where relatively small composition variations can strongly affect the phase transformation temperatures and resulting functional properties.

Magnetic shape memory (MSM) smart materials are of significant interest for technological applications. Since their first experimental demonstration in 1996 [45], the Ni–Mn–Ga Heusler alloys have been extensively studied [31, 25, 41, 12, 43, 19, 36, 44]. The initially observed strains of 0.2% were rapidly improved upon, with the highest observed strain currently at 12% [40]. They are being investigated for industrial applications ranging from microfluidic pumps [38], vibrational energy harvesters [35, 10], and actuators [13], to incorporation in kinetic energy absorbing polymers [21, 11]. Whilst several polycrystalline forms, including wires [47], printed structures and foams are being trialled [5, 48, 22], single crystalline Ni–Mn–Ga material is required to maximise the MSM effect [23].

Moreover, the stoichiometric alloy exhibits MSM effect only below 200 K (its martensite transformation temperature), and to increase the working temperature a composition modified from the ideal Heusler 2-1-1 stoichiometry is needed. Minor composition changes result in dramatic shifts of the onset of the martensitic transformation, ∼\sim 28 K/at.%Mn{}_{\text{Mn}} in the Ni50Mn25+xGa25-x system [16]. The ability to easily tune the structural transition is an important feature of the Ni–Mn–Ga family. Bulk Ni–Mn–Ga single crystals have been grown using several directional-solidification approaches. Early studies employed the conventional Bridgman method, demonstrating bulk single-crystal growth but also revealing pronounced longitudinal chemical segregation associated with the incongruent solidification of Ni–Mn–Ga [37]. Modified Bridgman and Bridgman–Stockbarger (BS) techniques, including seeded growth, were subsequently developed to improve crystallographic orientation and growth stability and have been used to produce high-quality crystals for magnetic-shape-memory studies [2, 17]. Nevertheless, such compositional variation, while useful for scientific studies spanning a broad range of Ni–Mn–Ga compositions, is undesirable for technological applications, where reproducible functional behaviour requires tight compositional control [9]. Zone-melting methods offer a means of reducing these longitudinal composition gradients by restricting the volume of molten material and allowing the melt composition to approach a quasi-steady segregation state during translation [32, 15, 29]. Optical floating-zone (OFZ) growth was explored as a crucible-free implementation of this approach, avoiding direct contact between the molten alloy and a conventional crucible while providing control over the molten-zone geometry, although segregation and the stability and shape of the solid–liquid interfaces remain important limitations [46, 27, 26, 3]. A stable and well-defined solidification front for OFZ is particularly important because its geometry and local velocity govern the direction of crystal growth, grain selection, and the development of defects and sub-grain boundaries.

In the present work, we present the results of growth experiments in a sapphire-confined modified optical floating-zone geometry, overcoming several limitations of the standard optical floating-zone growth. We complement this modified growth method with a time-dependent finite element heat-transfer model, coupled with an effective molten-zone mass-balance calculation. Using the measured post-growth composition profile together with the initial compositions of the seed crystal and feed rod, the model reconstructs the evolving molten-zone shape and local solidification velocity during growth, rather than assuming a constant molten-zone length and equating solidification velocity with the imposed crucible translation rate, as in classic Scheil–Pfann descriptions.

papers.title: $p$-parity conjecture for Panchishkin Galois representations
papers.abstract: Let $p$ be an odd prime, and let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be symplectic self-dual $p$-adic de Rham representations of $G_{\mathbb{Q}}$ that are pure (of weight $-1$) and satisfy the Panchishkin condition at $p$. Suppose that $V_1$ and $V_2$ are residually isomorphic, compatibly with their Panchishkin filtrations. We prove the relative $p$-parity conjecture relating the ratio of the global root numbers of $V_1$ and $V_2$ to the difference of their Bloch-Kato Selmer dimensions. We have no restriction on the dimension of the Galois representation, the Hodge-Tate weights or the monodromy operator at $p$, and the residual isomorphism need not be symplectic. The proof expresses ratios of local root numbers in terms of local invariants over the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension: a new invariant introduced at $p$, and local Iwasawa $\lambda$-invariants at $\ell\neq p$. Both are compatible with the arithmetic local constants of Mazur-Rubin and Nekov\'a\v{r}. A key input, proved using Sen theory, is that the Bloch-Kato and strict local conditions at $p$ coincide over the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension, generalising results of Coates-Greenberg and Nekov\'a\v{r}. As applications, we obtain new cases of the $p$-parity conjecture, including cases of rank greater than two: Artin twists of CM Hida families, orthogonal Artin twists of ordinary modular forms, symmetric cubes along Hida families, and families of abelian surfaces, together with unconditional numerical examples.

papers.title: New results on cyclic and ordered Ramsey numbers
papers.abstract: Inspired by the work of Poljak, Ba\v{s}i\'c, Damnjanovi\'c, Stevanovi\'c, and Sto\v{s}i\'c used the Kissat SAT solver in a recent paper to systematically determine the small cyclic and ordered Ramsey numbers of several families of graphs. By studying the patterns in their data, Ba\v{s}i\'c et al. formulated 15 conjectures on cyclic and ordered Ramsey numbers. In this paper, we confirm 9 of their conjectures, trace confirmations of 2 more to existing literature, and, perhaps surprisingly, disprove another one.

papers.title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion
papers.abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.

papers.intro:
Many questions in interpretability reduce to understanding some direction in the residual stream of a language model (LM) – such as an SAE feature (Bricken et al., 2023), a linear probe’s weights (Alain and Bengio, 2016), a steering vector (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024), or a direction derived from a fine-tuning weight diff (Zhong and Raghunathan, 2025; De Schamphelaere et al., 2026). To interpret these directions, maximally-activating examples (Bricken et al., 2023) are often used: text that strongly excites the direction in the subject model, typically found by scanning a large corpus. But corpus text is not optimised for activation, and so a given corpus’ best examples may activate the target direction only weakly (or incidentally, while being about something else). Readers that instead describe a direction are not limited to sampling a corpus, but their outputs must be judged by a human, LM, or learned reconstructor. This motivates our question: given only a residual stream direction vv, can a model write text xx that the subject model itself maps to vv? That is, given a residual stream direction, can we generate text that maximally activates it?

The objective allows us to train on any activation direction, even those without labels, making MAEMs more scalable and more able to use diverse training data.

papers.title: DART: Domain-Agnostic Residual Transfer for Generalist Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) aims to detect anomalies in unseen domains using only a few reference samples. Recent normal-abnormal guided methods improve this setting by exploiting abnormal references, but their residuals often mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific appearance factors such as texture, geometry, and acquisition conditions. This residual domain entanglement limits cross-domain transfer and may produce spurious activations on novel domains. We propose DART, a plug-in framework for normal-abnormal guided GAD that learns to separate residuals into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components. DART combines a Residual Disentanglement Module, which preserves anomaly-discriminative information while suppressing domain information, with Cross-Domain Meta-Training, which forms episodes across source domains to make the separation effective. The method is architecture-agnostic and can be inserted between residual computation and the detection head of existing GAD pipelines. Experiments on MVTec AD, VisA, and BraTS show consistent improvements over multiple base methods, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts. https://github.com/aqeeelmirza/DART

papers.intro:
Visual anomaly detection is central to industrial inspection [1, 2], medical diagnosis [3], and safety-critical monitoring [4]. Most existing methods [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] train separate models for individual domains, which becomes impractical when new categories appear frequently, labeled data is scarce, or target-domain training is restricted. Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) addresses this limitation by training a unified model on source domains and deploying it on unseen target domains without fine-tuning [10, 11]. At inference, the model detects anomalies in a query image by comparing it with a few target-domain references. Early GAD methods, such as InCTRL [10] and ResAD [11], rely only on normal references, assuming that anomalies induce larger residuals relative to normal prototypes.

Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) addresses this limitation by training a unified model on source domains and deploying it on unseen target domains without fine-tuning [10, 11]. At inference, the model detects anomalies in a query image by comparing it with a few target-domain references. Early GAD methods, such as InCTRL [10] and ResAD [11], rely only on normal references, assuming that anomalies induce larger residuals relative to normal prototypes.

Recent normal-abnormal guided GAD methods further exploit a small number of abnormal references, which are often available in practical settings. NAGL [12], for instance, uses residual mining and anomaly feature learning to transfer abnormal cues from references to queries, improving over normal-only prompting. However, we show that the residuals driving this transfer are often domain-entangled: they mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific factors such as texture, object geometry, and acquisition conditions. For example, a cracked-bottle residual encodes both the crack pattern and bottle-specific appearance; when transferred to leather or transistors, such domain-specific information can trigger false activations or suppress genuine anomalies. We call this phenomenon residual domain entanglement and identify it as a key bottleneck for cross-domain normal-abnormal guided GAD (see Figure 1).

papers.title: Multi-Probe Cosmological Constraints on Clustering DBI Dark Energy Scenario
papers.abstract: We present a multi-probe observational analysis of a clustering tachyonic Dirac-Born-Infeld~(DBI) dark energy model. Its noncanonical kinetic term gives a subluminal sound speed, so dark energy perturbations can grow on subhorizon scales. Working in a multifluid framework that tracks both the background expansion and linear perturbations, we constrain the model with nested sampling, using Planck 2018 compressed CMB distance priors, DESI DR2 BAO, cosmic chronometers, $f\sigma_8$ growth data, and three Type Ia supernova compilations: Pantheon$+$, DES-SN5YR, and Union3. The standard cosmological parameters agree with $\Lambda$CDM within $2\sigma$, with DBI preferring a slightly lower $H_0$ and higher $\Omega_{m0}$, with the largest shift being $\simeq1.8\sigma$ in $H_0$ for Pantheon$+$. The Bayesian evidence favours DBI in every compilation, moderately for Pantheon$+$ ($\Delta\ln\mathcal{Z}\simeq3.4$) and inconclusively for DES-SN5YR and Union3 ($\Delta\ln\mathcal{Z}\simeq0.6$-$0.7$). The field thaws naturally. Dark energy perturbations stay several orders of magnitude below matter perturbations, yet the noncanonical sound speed still alters the Hubble friction term, raising $S_8$ by only $\approx0.5\sigma$ relative to $\Lambda$CDM. Four independent diagnostics, namely the CPL parametrization, $Om(z)$, the statefinder hierarchy, and the growth index, all point to genuinely evolving dark energy rather than a cosmological constant. The thermal history is left intact, with negligible early dark energy. However, one limitation remains. Because $w_\phi=\dot\phi^2-1\geq-1$, the phantom regime is out of reach, which is in line with the no-go theorem for a single minimally coupled scalar field, so the model cannot follow the DESI DR2 preference for an effective equation of state crossing $w=-1$.

The late-time accelerated expansion of the Universe, established through Type Ia supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), and the cosmic microwave background (CMB) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], remains one of the most compelling unsolved problems in modern cosmology. Within the standard Λ\LambdaCDM framework, this phenomenon is attributed to a cosmological constant, but the associated fine-tuning and coincidence problems motivate dynamical alternatives in which an evolving field describes the dark sector. Among the many possibilities in the dynamical dark-energy sector, a particularly well-studied class of candidates is provided by noncanonical scalar fields (kk-essence) [7, 8], where the kinetic structure can lead to rich background dynamics and provide a distinctive signature in the growth of cosmic structures.

Among the many possibilities in the dynamical dark-energy sector, a particularly well-studied class of candidates is provided by noncanonical scalar fields (kk-essence) [7, 8], where the kinetic structure can lead to rich background dynamics and provide a distinctive signature in the growth of cosmic structures.

Among kk-essence theories, the Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) model [9, 10] offers a theoretically motivated framework, originally arising from the effective description of D-branes in string theory [11, 12]. In particular, the tachyonic DBI scalar field, arising from the effective action of a non-BPS D-brane, provides a natural dark-energy candidate with a bounded kinetic term and a well-defined pressure. In cosmology, DBI fields can behave as dark energy or unify dark matter and dark energy, depending on the choice of Lagrangian. An important phenomenological feature of DBI-type Lagrangians is the emergence of a nontrivial effective sound speed (cs2c_{s}^{2}) [13], which typically depends on time. Since the sound speed controls the propagation of perturbations, it determines whether the dark component remains smooth on subhorizon scales or clusters with matter.

papers.title: Gradient higher integrability for a general class of degenerate parabolic double phase systems
papers.abstract: We establish quantitative local higher integrability estimates for weak solutions of degenerate parabolic systems with generalized double phase growth, whose prototype is $$u_t-\operatorname{div}\left(\frac{G'(|Du|)}{|Du|}Du+a(x,t)\frac{H'(|Du|)}{|Du|}Du\right)=0\qquad\text{in }\Omega_T.$$ Here $G$ and $H$ are Young functions satisfying suitable structural assumptions. The nonnegative coefficient $a$ is allowed to vanish and has a concave modulus of continuity $\omega$ with respect to the parabolic distance. For $\Psi(z,\varkappa)=G(\varkappa)+a(z)H(\varkappa)$, we prove that solutions in $L^\infty(0,T;L^s(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^N))$, $2\le s<\infty$, satisfy $\Psi(\cdot,|Du|)\in L^{1+\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, provided $$\limsup_{\rho \to 0+}\omega(\rho)\frac{H(\rho^{-\frac{n+s}{s}})}{G(\rho^{-\frac{n+s}{s}})}<\infty.$$ For bounded solutions, the corresponding condition involves $H(\rho^{-1})/G(\rho^{-1})$. These conditions extend the known interpolative gap bounds from power growth to general growth functions and continuity moduli. In particular, for $G(\varkappa)=\varkappa^p$, $H(\varkappa)=\varkappa^q$, and $\omega(\rho)\simeq\rho^\alpha$, they recover $q\le p+s\alpha/(n+s)$ and $q\le p+\alpha$, respectively. The proof combines an intrinsic stopping-time argument with inverse-function estimates to derive Poincar\'e and reverse H\"older inequalities adapted to the general growth phases.

papers.title: Construction and performance evaluation of a meter-scale monolithic scintillator tracker with embedded scatterers
papers.abstract: A meter-scale Fiber-Readout mOnolithic and Scatterer-embedded scintillator Tracker (FROST) was constructed and operated in the NINJA experiment to enable muon-track matching between the nuclear emulsion detectors and the downstream muon detector. The detector consists of a 1.32 m $\times$ 1.40 m plastic scintillator plate assembled from optically bonded scatterer-embedded plates, with wavelength-shifting fibers arranged at a pitch of 10 mm. During J-PARC neutrino-beam operation, FROST achieved a data acquisition efficiency of 99.59% and a detection efficiency of 99.946$\pm$0.006% for selected neutrino-induced muons well within the active area. A position reconstruction method based on the light-yield distribution was developed for both single- and multi-particle events. In a neutrino-interaction simulation, muon position resolutions of 1.77 mm and 1.61 mm were achieved in the two orthogonal readout directions, assuming correct muon identification. Using a beam-data sample dominated by single-muon events, upper limits on the position resolution of 2.20 mm and 2.03 mm were obtained for track angles below 20{\deg}. These results demonstrate that the FROST concept can be scaled up to a meter-scale active area while maintaining high detection efficiency and a position resolution well below the readout pitch under actual experimental conditions.

papers.intro:
Plastic scintillators are widely used in tracking detectors because they provide fast response times and can be fabricated in various sizes to cover large active areas. In conventional plastic scintillator trackers, the detector is typically divided into discrete scintillator elements, and the hit position is determined from the elements that are hit. Using smaller segments improves the position resolution but increases the number of scintillator elements and readout channels. This increase becomes particularly significant for large-area trackers, where it leads to higher cost and greater complexity of the readout system. It is therefore important to achieve a position resolution finer than the readout pitch without requiring a corresponding increase in the number of readout channels when scaling scintillator trackers to large active areas.

To address this challenge, the Fiber-Readout mOnolithic and Scatterer-embedded scintillator Tracker (FROST) concept was proposed in a previous study [1]. FROST consists of a monolithic plastic scintillator plate with embedded scatterers and wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers arranged in two orthogonal directions. The scintillation light is collected by the WLS fibers and detected by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). The collected light yield tends to be larger in channels whose fibers are closer to the charged-particle crossing position. The embedded scatterers localize the scintillation light around the crossing position and further strengthen this tendency. The crossing position is reconstructed from the channel-to-channel light-yield distribution with a position resolution well below the readout pitch. The monolithic design also avoids inactive gaps associated with conventional scintillator segmentation, allowing near-100% detection efficiency in principle.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning of Local Predictive Directions as a Neural Computation
papers.abstract: Natural sensory dynamics are globally nonlinear but often exhibit simple local geometry, with nearby trajectories evolving preferentially along a small number of predictive directions. We ask how neural circuits could discover this geometry directly from temporal experience. We introduce Local Predictive Directions (LPD), a self-supervised framework that learns local directions whose projections maximally predict near-future trajectory evolution. LPD applies past-future canonical correlation analysis to temporal differences, making the learned representation invariant to translations of the underlying state while avoiding estimation of equilibria or a global dynamical model. To represent systems with multiple predictive regimes, we introduce a non-negative similarity-matching objective, with offline and online algorithms, that partitions trajectory segments into predictive domains, each associated with a distinct local predictive direction. The online algorithm admits a natural neural-network interpretation: the resulting activities provide soft domain assignments, while synaptic weights encode the corresponding local predictive filters. On stochastic nonlinear dynamical systems, LPD recovers the local predictive geometry and partitions trajectories into distinct dynamical regimes. On naturalistic sensory streams, the online algorithm produces center-surround spatial receptive fields and ON/OFF sustained and transient temporal filters resembling those of early visual neurons. Our results suggest that predictive learning can provide a self-supervised mechanism by which neural circuits discover the local geometry of environmental dynamics and represent it in receptive fields.

papers.intro:
High-dimensional time series from physical, biological, and neural systems often evolve on structured nonlinear manifolds. Global dynamics may be complex, yet short-time evolution is typically low-dimensional: within a small neighborhood, state changes are captured by a few tangent directions — the local-linear view underlying classical nonlinear dynamical systems theory (Strogatz, 1994), Koopman and dynamic mode decomposition (Schmid, 2010; Brunton et al., 2021), and local models of nonlinear time series (Farmer and Sidorowich, 1987; Casdagli, 1991). Some tangent directions are more predictive than others: perturbations along them set the system’s evolution over the next few steps, while orthogonal ones decay, fluctuate, or say little about the future. This suggests a self-supervised problem: from an unlabeled trajectory alone, can one discover tangent directions that vary slowly along it and whose projections predict future evolution?

Near a saddle point, for instance, unstable manifolds organize future trajectories: projecting the state, relative to the saddle, onto an unstable direction determines which branch is followed (Strogatz, 1994). Such saddle-organized dynamics are central to stable heteroclinic channels, winnerless competition, and transient neural dynamics (Rabinovich et al., 2001; Rabinovich et al., 2006; Rabinovich et al., 2008; Cvitanović and Lippolis, 2012). Away from fixed points, short trajectory segments still sample a local linearization, so the predictive objects are not global coordinates but local tangent-space directions varying across state space.

Existing approaches fall into three families (details in Appendix A). Switching linear dynamical systems and spectral HMM methods (Ackerson and Fu, 1970; Fox et al., 2009; Linderman et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2012) require explicit inference over latent discrete states under a generative model. Koopman operator theory, dynamic mode decomposition and VAMP (Brunton et al., 2021; Schmid, 2010; Wu and Noé, 2020), and their deep variants (Lusch et al., 2018; Otto and Rowley, 2019; Takeishi et al., 2017), seek a globally linearizing feature space whose leading modes span broad regions of state space and may not resolve local saddle-to-saddle geometry. Deep predictive objectives (Mardt et al., 2018; Oord et al., 2018; Zerveas et al., 2021) learn global embeddings, but are heavily parameterized and less interpretable.

Past–future correlation offers a principled definition of such predictive directions. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) finds projections of paired variables with maximal correlation (Hotelling, 1936); related past–future covariance methods underlie subspace system identification and balanced stochastic realization (Arun and Kung, 1990; Katayama, 2005), and connect to predictive information and the Gaussian information bottleneck (Bialek et al., 2001; Chechik et al., 2005). Applied to past and future observations, it finds projections of the present maximally informative about subsequent evolution, recovering dominant predictive modes in locally linear dynamics. This motivates the Rectified Spectral Unit (ReSU), a biologically inspired self-supervised rule combining past–future CCA with rectification to learn predictive features from dynamical data (Pughe-Sanford et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026). Existing CCA- and ReSU-based methods are nonetheless global or single-regime: they assume one predictive structure dominates, or that local neighborhoods are supplied externally, and so do not discover multiple local predictive directions whose locations and domains are unknown.

Applied to past and future observations, it finds projections of the present maximally informative about subsequent evolution, recovering dominant predictive modes in locally linear dynamics. This motivates the Rectified Spectral Unit (ReSU), a biologically inspired self-supervised rule combining past–future CCA with rectification to learn predictive features from dynamical data (Pughe-Sanford et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2026). Existing CCA- and ReSU-based methods are nonetheless global or single-regime: they assume one predictive structure dominates, or that local neighborhoods are supplied externally, and so do not discover multiple local predictive directions whose locations and domains are unknown.

We introduce a self-supervised objective and algorithm for learning such local predictive directions (LPDs) directly from trajectories, Fig. 1. Temporal differences give access to local tangent-space information: applying past–future CCA to finite differences rather than absolute states makes the method invariant to translations of the local coordinate system, such as a saddle’s unknown location, so predictive directions are learned from trajectory increments without estimating equilibria or fitting a global dynamical model. To discover multiple local predictive regimes, we replace canonical projection followed by rectification with a non-negative similarity-matching formulation. Similarity matching provides a normative route from similarity-preserving objectives to online neural learning algorithms (Pehlevan et al., 2015; Pehlevan and Chklovskii, 2019; Pehlevan et al., 2020; Lipshutz et al., 2021), while non-negativity promotes localized, parts-based, and clustering-like representations (Lee and Seung, 1999; Pehlevan and Chklovskii, 2014; Sengupta et al., 2018). Here, similarity matching preserves the predictive correlation structure of the data while non-negativity induces competition and locality, Fig. 1b; output units therefore specialize to different regions of state space, learning distinct local predictive directions, Fig. 1c, and their non-negative activities act as soft domain assignments, Fig. 1d. Unlike clustering by geometric proximity or variance (Reynolds and others, 2009), the proposed objective clusters trajectory segments by short-time predictive structure. The resulting algorithm admits offline and online implementations, the online one having a natural neural interpretation in terms of feedforward weights, lateral competition, and rectified activity.

papers.title: An Agent-Driven, Cross-Validated Inverse-Design Pipeline for Dielectric Metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Inverse design of dielectric metasurfaces is powerful but labour-intensive: each new target requires choosing a parameterization and a figure of merit, managing compute resources, and critically assessing results that may be numerically unconverged, sensitive to fabrication errors or trapped in local optima. Here we present an open-source pipeline in which an artificial intelligence (AI) coding agent turns a plain-language specification into metasurface optimization runs, executes them, analyses every run with a fixed checklist and proposes the next iteration. Designs are optimized with differentiable three-dimensional rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA), including robustness to fabrication tolerances, and every reported design is independently verified with finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations. We demonstrate the workflow at 1550 nm on a freeform silicon metagrating, on a polarization-independent meta-atom library assembled into beam-deflecting supercells, and on metalenses built from the same library. In the metagrating case, the independent FDTD verification revealed a 5\% overestimate of the efficiency by the optimization model that a conventional convergence test had not detected, and the robust design retained most of its efficiency under $\pm$10~nm fabrication errors. In the other cases, instead, the obtained RCWA results are confirmed by full-wave simulations.

papers.title: Hardness of integer linear feasibility with cyclic support
papers.abstract: We prove that integer linear feasibility is strongly $NP$-complete even when the constraint matrix has exactly two nonzero entries in every row and column, with its support forming a single cycle. This holds already for monotone systems (one positive and one negative coefficient in each inequality) with nonzero coefficients of absolute value $2$ or $3$ and right-hand sides in $\{-1,0,1,2\}$. No variable bounds are supplied separately from the system. For systems in which each inequality involves at most two variables, this strengthens known hardness results by restricting all numerical data to fixed finite sets. For systems in which each variable occurs in at most two inequalities, this establishes, to the best of our knowledge, the first $NP$-hardness result for feasibility. We also give negative answers, unless $P=NP$, to questions on polynomial-time solvability of integer programs with bounded coefficients and bounded totally $\Delta$-modular treewidth, and on fixed-parameter tractability of integer bound propagation with respect to coefficient and right-hand-side magnitudes.

papers.title: dsp: An R Package for Bayesian Time Series Modeling with the Dynamic Shrinkage Process
papers.abstract: dsp provides a unified state-space framework for modeling nonstationary time series using the Dynamic Shrinkage Process (DSP), a class of global-local shrinkage priors. DSP adaptively regularizes time-varying parameters to shrink noise while preserving abrupt changes and other local structure. The package supports Gaussian and count-data smoothing, changepoint detection, time-varying parameter regression, and volatility estimation, with posterior predictive draws available for missing-value imputation and forecasting. Nonstationary time series often contain periods of relative stability punctuated by abrupt changes in mean or variance. dsp offers a common interface for model specification, posterior computation, summarization, and visualization across models that were previously developed separately in the literature. Core functionality is implemented in C++ via Rcpp for computational efficiency. We describe the underlying models, package design, and the main functions for fitting, summarizing, and plotting posterior results.

papers.title: Goos-H\"anchen Shifts at 458 nm from DUV Dichroic Laser Mirrors
papers.abstract: We report polarization- and angle-dependent lateral beam shifts observed at 458~nm upon reflection from a deep-ultraviolet (DUV) dichroic multilayer mirror. These Goos--H\"anchen (GH) shifts originate from the phase of the complex Fresnel reflection coefficient and are quantitatively reproduced using a transfer-matrix model. Simultaneous reflectance (R), transmittance (T), and GH shift measurements provide complementary constraints on the coating's amplitude and phase response. The analysis is extended to transmission, predicting analogous phase-induced lateral shifts. In frequency-doubling cavities using dichroic mirrors, these phase effects can accumulate over multiple reflections, leading to deviations from ray-optics predictions that may affect cavity mode structure and resonance conditions. Our results show a GH shift of as much as 2~\textmu m (\bm{$\approx 4.4\lambda$}), which, combined with RT data, enables improved characterization of the phase response of the multilayer coating. The p-polarized reflectance is minimized at a pseudo-Brewster angle of \bm{$\theta_B \approx 46^\circ$} at 458~nm, providing a natural reference point around which the GH shift is enhanced.

papers.intro:
The Goos–Hänchen (GH) shift is a lateral displacement of an optical beam upon reflection at an interface, arising from the angular dependence of the phase of the complex reflection coefficient. First observed experimentally by Goos and Hänchen in 1947 for transverse electric (s) polarization [7], the effect was later extended to transverse magnetic (p) polarization [8]. The effect was theoretically described by Artmann using the stationary-phase approximation which related the shift to the angular derivative of the reflection phase. [2]. Beyond total internal reflection, GH shifts have been investigated in partial reflection and transmission regimes, and are referred to as net GH shift or lateral shift.

First observed experimentally by Goos and Hänchen in 1947 for transverse electric (s) polarization [7], the effect was later extended to transverse magnetic (p) polarization [8]. The effect was theoretically described by Artmann using the stationary-phase approximation which related the shift to the angular derivative of the reflection phase. [2]. Beyond total internal reflection, GH shifts have been investigated in partial reflection and transmission regimes, and are referred to as net GH shift or lateral shift.

Significant effort has been devoted to enhancing and controlling GH shifts through engineered optical phase responses in structured and resonant systems, including photonic crystals [15], metasurfaces [10], graphene-based systems [19], and absorbing media [5]. Related beam-shift effects have also been observed in atomic and hybrid atom-optomechanical systems, including Bose–Einstein-condensate-based platforms, where quantum coherence, detuning, and interference provide additional mechanisms to manipulate reflected and transmitted beam shifts [1, 4]. In all cases, the underlying mechanism is the angular dependence of the complex reflection or transmission phase. Weak measurement techniques [9, 13, 14] have further enabled amplification of otherwise small beam shifts through interference between slightly displaced optical beams. Beyond fundamental interest, GH shifts can influence precision optical systems by affecting beam propagation and mode behavior in optical waveguides [16] and optical microcavities [17]. In optical implementations, these effects are relevant in dielectric multilayer coatings, where thin-film interference generates strong angular and polarization dependencies in reflectance, transmittance, and phase. Although GH shifts in idealized multilayer systems have been studied theoretically, experimental investigation in realistic coating systems under partial reflection and transmission conditions relevant to cavity optics remains limited. Bridging this gap is crucial for dichroic mirrors in frequency-conversion and deep-ultraviolet systems, where coatings simultaneously separate harmonic wavelengths and define beam propagation paths. Here, small phase gradients translate into measurable beam shifts missed by ray-optic models, affecting alignment sensitivity and mode propagation. In this work, we experimentally investigate polarization- and angle-dependent GH shifts in a dielectric multilayer mirror at 458 nm under partial reflection. By combining beam-shift measurements with angular reflectance and transmittance data, we constrain the phase response of the complex reflection coefficient and extend the analysis to transmission-induced beam shifts for application-relevant coatings, as for example, those used in frequency-doubling cavities.

papers.title: VINO: Revisiting 3D Representation Learning with Volume Transformers
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning has given rise to vision foundation models that learn general-purpose image representations transferable across downstream tasks, yet representation learning for 3D scenes has not achieved comparable success. Motivated by this, we identify key limitations of current 3D representation learning approaches and revisit their core design choices. We first replace the commonly used hierarchical PTv3 backbone with the Volume Transformer, a ViT-like architecture for 3D scenes. We then redesign two core objectives of modern approaches built around student-teacher networks: matching representations across views and predicting masked content from visible context. For the first objective, we separate the roles of teacher and student: the teacher provides clean, consistent targets while the student learns invariance to stronger perturbations. For the second objective, we prevent the student from accessing the masked geometry and instead require it to infer missing representations from visible context only. Finally, we redesign 2D-to-3D knowledge distillation, replacing direct regression of view-dependent image features with view-consistent supervision. Together, these changes form VINO, a framework that learns semantic representations of 3D scenes without labels. VINO substantially improves dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks and transfers strongly to out-of-domain settings.

This asymmetry also motivates a reconsideration of how the teacher should construct targets. Conventionally, the teacher’s projection head is obtained as an EMA copy of the student’s. In sparse 3D scenes, however, the occupancy of voxels itself encodes geometry. Retaining masked locations therefore reveals the structure that the student should infer (see Fig. 2). Instead, as in object-level 3D methods (??), we remove masked tokens entirely before the student encoder and use a lightweight cross-attention predictor to reconstruct their representations from visible context. We supervise these predictions with the same targets introduced above, providing a unified supervision signal across both objectives.

papers.title: A Complete Equational Theory for Quantum Circuits with Generalized Control
papers.abstract: Controlled subcircuits are commonplace in quantum algorithms as they represent the quantum analogue of branching statements (if then). We introduce a generalization of controlled subcircuits in the form of a binary operation which sends pairs of unitary quantum circuits to a generalized controlled operation, whose semantics are based on matrix exponentials and logarithms. The family of quantum circuits with generalized controlled operations and circuit exponentiation is denoted HQC for Hierarchical Quantum Circuits. We formalize HQC as a modified prop category using a novel category-theoretic construction, and provide a sound and complete equational theory for diagrammatic reasoning in HQC.

papers.intro:
As quantum computing hardware continues to advance, so too does its software. While quantum circuits remain the de facto standard language for low-level quantum programming, they are cumbersome when designing large-scale programs with tens of thousands of gates. Higher-level abstractions of quantum circuits are on the horizon. Diagrammatic reasoning [9] is a natural fit for reasoning about such abstractions since quantum circuits are diagrams. Diagrammatic reasoning has already been applied to a variety of circuit-related tasks, including optimization [21], simulation [36, 37], equivalence checking [28], and error correction [20, 22, 32]. Equational theories are collections of equations that serve as toolboxes for performing diagrammatic reasoning.

Control is one such ubiquitous abstraction in quantum algorithm design. Controlled subcircuits appear in essentially every powerful quantum algorithm (e.g., [23, 35, 14, 16]). We generalize the existing notion of control by allowing a subcircuit to be controlled not just by one qubit in a particular basis, but by an arbitrary basis on any number of qubits. This notion of control is captured by a new binary operation (⊙)(\odot) called the control product which joins two subcircuits together to create a generalized controlled operation. The simplest example is the CNOT, which is created by joining the Pauli ZZ and XX gates together as Z⊙X=CNOTZ\odot X=\textsf{CNOT}. However unlike the normal notion of control, the control product allows any two subcircuits UU and VV of arbitrary sizes to control each other as U⊙VU\odot V. Examples of how such a product can aid in circuit design and verification are found in [13] and [33], respectively.

Related work. The first complete equational theory for uncontrolled quantum circuits was presented in [8] and improved in [6, 5]. Two recent works have provided equational theories for standard controlled quantum circuits using controlled props [11] and rig categories [17]. Another recent work introduced a related methodology for constructing controlled unitaries via subspace selection and phasing [18]. The control product we introduce here can be seen as a way to efficiently package exponentially many such selection-and-phasing statements together into one circuit object. Controlled operations have also recently been studied in the context of quantum control flow [41, 39] for its applications to quantum computer architectures with a quantum program counter.

papers.title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
papers.abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

papers.intro:
On 6 October 2026, OpenAI published more than seven hundred mathematical manuscripts, all produced by an unreleased internal model [22]. A substantial number, though fewer than half, of the released results come with a formal proof checked by Lean [12, 13]. Formal proof used to be very expensive. In 2008, Georges Gonthier wrote on the four color theorem that formalizing the infamously large case analysis in its proof was the easy part, done in a few part-time months, while certain graph-theoretic arguments “took a few years to sort out” [15]. According to OpenAI, an average result took about three hours of computation. The numbers cannot be compared directly. Not every result of OpenAI was formalized, but the three hours also include finding the proof, which is usually the harder task. Even with these caveats, the cost of a formal proof has fallen by orders of magnitude.

Even with these caveats, the cost of a formal proof has fallen by orders of magnitude.

Appel and Haken’s original proof of the four color theorem in 1976 is often viewed as the first major theorem whose proof no human could verify by hand. It is a reduction to almost two thousand configurations that were checked by a computer program [2, 3]. At the time, philosophers asked whether such an argument was a proof at all [30]. Accepting the original proof of the four color theorem meant trusting a custom program written for that one purpose. Formal proof offers a way around this. The idea goes back to John McCarthy in 1962 [19]: write the proof in a language precise enough that a single, small, general-purpose program can check every step. A number of systems followed, including Automath (1967) [10, 11], LCF (1972) [20], and later Coq [9] and Lean, among others.

The correctness of a formal proof does not depend on any code written specifically for that proof. All trust rests on the proof checker, which is shared by all its users and has been examined by them for years. In other words, trust is moved out of each individual proof and into one piece of common infrastructure, and the correctness of a proof does not require a review. What still requires review is the statement: the checker certifies that a proof establishes its formal statement, not that the formal statement expresses the intended mathematics. This is the main subject of the present paper.

The current technology-driven crisis in mathematics appears more profound than the controversy around Appel and Haken’s proof in the 70s. AI systems now produce results at a volume that human refereeing cannot match, and the question of trust that the four color theorem raised for a single proof now arises for whole bodies of work. Nonetheless, we expect that formalization will become an increasingly important tool, since its cost has collapsed. Agents based on openly available frontier models can already formalize mathematics automatically with relative ease [4]. Such automatic formalization is often called autoformalization [31, 32].

While it is unknown according to which principles OpenAI decided what to formalize, a potential deciding factor could have been the size of the gap between already formalized theory and that required by a result. In the present paper we address this gap within the field of inverse problems. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library of autoformalized results in linear regularization theory. Shared libraries not only speed up the formalization process but also save computational resources by eliminating overlapping work. Inverse problems are a natural field for such a library. The classical theory rests on functional analysis that is largely available in Mathlib, and it is now being extended rapidly by learned and data-driven regularization methods. Convergence guarantees for such methods are new and less scrutinized theory, where we would expect formalization to find more issues of the kind we report in Section 5.4 in the settled classical theory.

Cheap formalization may change how applied mathematics is done. An applied inverse problem is usually studied piece by piece: uniqueness and stability, regularization, discretization, convergence of the numerical method and the model of the noise are treated in separate papers, often under assumptions that do not quite fit together. A formal library can hold such pieces in one place and check that the conclusions of one match the assumptions of the next. This makes large projects feasible that follow an applied problem from its mathematical model to guarantees for the algorithm that solves it. Much of the work such projects require, for example tracking constants, checking that every case is covered, or verifying that a known result carries over to a slightly different setting, is tedious and often simply not done. This is the kind of work that can now be delegated to AI agents, while people decide what should be proved and check that it was.

papers.title: Energy-Based Anisotropic Hysteresis Modeling for Permanent Magnets
papers.abstract: Modeling the anisotropic hysteresis behaviour of permanent magnets requires vector hysteresis models capable of representing preferred (easy) magnetization directions. This work extends the energy-based vector play model to anisotropic materials by replacing the spherical pinning region of each particle with an ellipsoid, whose semi-axes represent direction-dependent pinning forces. Special attention is paid to the geometrically consistent adaptation of the update formula for the vector play model. The anhysteretic part of the model is also given an angular dependency. The model is compared to measurements taken from a NdFeB magnet and reproduces the measured loops for field inclinations of up to 30{\deg} from the easy axis.

papers.intro:
Permanent magnets (PMs) are essential components of electrical machines, actuators, and sensors. Designing these devices requires finite element (FE) simulations to predict operating points and irreversible demagnetization under overload, short-circuit, or magnetizing conditions. Commercial FE tools typically model PMs using the linear relationship 𝒃=𝒃r+μ0​μr​𝒉\bm{{b}}=\bm{{b}}_{\mathrm{r}}+\mu_{0}\mu_{\mathrm{r}}\bm{{h}} and nonlinear demagnetization models have been developed on this basis [1, 2]. Most of these nonlinear models, however, are scalar along the easy axis. The transverse direction is either treated as linear or via lookup tables, and recoil follows ad hoc rules. Even the most comprehensive anisotropic nonlinear models developed for AlNiCo are formulated in two dimensions (2D) [3, 4].

Most of these nonlinear models, however, are scalar along the easy axis. The transverse direction is either treated as linear or via lookup tables, and recoil follows ad hoc rules. Even the most comprehensive anisotropic nonlinear models developed for AlNiCo are formulated in two dimensions (2D) [3, 4].

Since most PM materials are highly anisotropic, neglecting the full vector character of the material response is a serious limitation. Due to their uniaxial texture, the remanence, coercivity, and permeability differ significantly between the easy axis and the transverse plane. The switching field also depends on the angle between the applied field and the easy axis. The angular dependence of the switching field varies depending on the material and microstructure. It ranges from pinning-dominated switching to coherent rotation, which is described by the Stoner–Wohlfarth model [2, 5]. Fields inclined to the easy axis are particularly harmful because the higher transverse permeability provides a flux path for the external field. In addition, magnetization along the transverse direction reduces the easy-axis magnetization [4].
