papers.title: The $q$-Poincar\'e sum and separability in a Coxeter group
papers.abstract: Given a finite Coxeter group $W$ and an element $q$ of a commutative ring $\mathbf{k}$, we define the element $\mathbf{L}_{q} :=\sum_{w\in W}q^{\ell\left( w\right) }w$ of its group algebra $\mathbf{k}\left[ W\right] $. We say that an element $w\in W$ is $W$\emph{-length-symmetric} if its coefficient in the commutator $\left[ \mathbf{L}_{a},\mathbf{L}_{b}\right] $ is $0$ for all $\mathbf{k}$ and all $a,b\in\mathbf{k}$. We prove several sufficient criteria for elements to be $W$-length-symmetric. In particular, we show that any separable permutation (i.e., permutation avoiding the patterns $2413$ and $3142$) in the symmetric group $S_{n}$ is $S_{n}$-length-symmetric. More generally, we construct a notion of separable elements of a finite Coxeter group $W$ (which, for finite Weyl groups, agrees with the eponymous notion introduced by Gaetz and Gao), and show that all such elements are $W$-length-symmetric. This is only a sufficient condition; other $W$-length-symmetric elements include (twisted) involutions and elements of dihedral parabolic subgroups.

papers.title: Sparse Bayesian Sensing for Antenna Arrays with Per-Element Gain, Phase, and Position Errors
papers.abstract: The sensing capabilities of 6G wireless communication systems rely on accurate models of phased-array antennas. However, hardware imperfections can introduce a mismatch between the assumed and the actual array response, leading to performance degradations. To prevent these, we propose a parametric, model-based sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) channel estimation algorithm with integrated self-calibration, which accounts for antenna-position deviations as well as gain and phase offsets. The algorithm learns channel parameters such as delay and direction-of-arrival (DoA), together with per-antenna complex weights and position deviations based on fast variational SBL with dictionary refinement. We derive a marginal-likelihood-based cost function for the antenna position update. The sensing performance is evaluated in terms of the optimal subpattern-assignment (OSPA) metric of the delay and DoA. The proposed method approaches a benchmark based on the derived hybrid Cram\'er--Rao lower bound (HCRLB) in the considered single-snapshot sensing scenarios. Finally, we investigate the influence of the detection threshold using synthetic and measurement data. On single-snapshot measurements, our algorithm reduces the position OSPA from about 6 m to 0.2 m for an appropriately chosen threshold.

papers.intro:
Array-based sensing is widely used in applications such as radar, sonar, acoustic source localization, and channel estimation for wireless communications, where direction-of-arrival (DoA) and delay are estimated from incoming signals. With the emergence of 6G wireless systems, array-based sensing is becoming a key technology for integrated sensing and communications (ISAC). The accuracy and performance of such sensing systems depend on the knowledge of their current array response. Array-based sensing is widely used in applications such as radar, sonar, acoustic source localization, and channel estimation for wireless communications, where direction-of-arrival (DoA) and delay are estimated from incoming signals. Hardware deviations are known to distort the array beampattern, causing mismatches in parametric signal models [1],[2]. The main consequence for channel parameter estimation is the detection of additional spurious components, which degrade the sensing performance [3], [4]. Common antenna array calibration models account for complex gain impairments, effective antenna position deviations, and mutual coupling. Methods that jointly estimate these calibration parameters and the channel parameters can broadly be classified into model-based, learning-based, and hybrid approaches. Model-based approaches extend conventional estimation methods, such as maximum likelihood (ML) or multiple signal classification (MUSIC), to incorporate self-calibration. These variants have predominantly focused on narrowband signal models, deterministic calibration parameters, and DoA estimation [5], [6]. Model-based sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) offers advantages, including super-resolution, model-order estimation, and the ability to handle coherent sources [7, 8, 9, 10]. In contrast, supervised learning-based methods require substantial amounts of labeled training data [11]. More recently, there is a trend to use hybrid variants, where parts of the physical model are learned by gradient-based optimization in an unsupervised fashion. For example, [12] reformulates MUSIC in a differentiable form to enable gradient-based optimization. In [13], a learning-based approach is developed to optimize sensing performance in the presence of antenna-position and complex gain deviations, using a loss function based on the residual of the orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) algorithm. Despite avoiding the need for labeled training data, such hybrid model-based learning methods still rely on training with thousands of snapshots. This motivates self-calibration methods that exploit the signal model directly.

papers.title: Survey of Surveys Data Release 3. Homogenised stellar parameters across nine spectroscopic surveys
papers.abstract: Large spectroscopic surveys have measured atmospheric parameters for millions of Milky Way stars, but differences in instruments, wavelength ranges, analysis methods, and assumptions introduce survey-dependent systematics that complicate their joint use. We aim to place effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity estimates from major spectroscopic surveys onto a common, externally validated scale, and to provide a homogenised catalogue for large-scale Galactic studies. We construct the calibration hierarchically. We first define an internal reference scale from the best-populated and best-overlapped surveys (APOGEE, GALAH, and LAMOST LRS), and model survey-to-reference corrections and their uncertainties with machine-learning regression. The scale is then extended to LAMOST MRS, Gaia RVS, RAVE, DESI, Gaia-ESO, and SEGUE, and anchored to high-quality measurements from the PASTEL database. The calibration reduces survey-to-survey offsets and improves consistency in independent overlap samples: independent calibration of GALAH and LAMOST LRS temperatures onto the APOGEE scale reduces their median offset from 44.5 K to 6.2 K. The final catalogue contains about 10.13 million stars, including 6.10 million in the recommended high-quality subset and 3.69 million in the metallicity-optimised subset. For the high-quality subset, Gaia benchmark stars give median residuals of 30 K in $T_{\rm eff}$, 0.03 dex in $\log g$, and $-0.02$ dex in [Fe/H]. The [Fe/H]-optimised subset gives median residuals of 0.003 dex against Gaia benchmark stars, 0.05 dex for globular clusters, and $-0.02$ dex for open clusters. As an example application, we confirm the presence of metal-poor stars on thin-disc-like orbits, including stars with [Fe/H] $< -2$, showing that the catalogue can be used to study rare Galactic populations on a consistent multi-survey scale.

These surveys probe complementary magnitude ranges, Galactic components, and evolutionary stages, providing an unprecedented view of the structure and chemical evolution of our Galaxy. However, fully benefiting from the scientific potential of these surveys is difficult when their parameter scales are used together without explicit calibration. Differences in wavelength coverage, spectral resolution, target selection, analysis methods, and underlying assumptions introduce survey-dependent zero-points and parameter-dependent trends in the reported effective temperatures (TeffT_{\rm eff}), surface gravities (log⁡g\log g), and metallicities ([Fe/H]). These effects can propagate into the inferred structure and chemo-dynamical properties of the Milky Way, especially when studies rely on stars drawn from several surveys or focus on sparsely populated regions of parameter space. A homogeneous parameter scale is therefore needed not only for catalogue-level consistency, but also for robust comparisons of Galactic populations across different observational regimes.

Several works have addressed cross-survey calibration, increasingly using data-driven “label transfer” trained on overlap samples to place different surveys on one common scale, including The Cannon (Ness et al., 2015; Casey et al., 2016; Ho et al., 2017), The Payne (Ting et al., 2019), and StarNet (Fabbro et al., 2018; Bialek et al., 2020), with further multi-survey examples discussed in the same context (Xiang et al., 2019; Wheeler et al., 2020; Nandakumar et al., 2022, e.g.). In this wider literature, Thomas et al. (2024) proposed a neural-network method that translates pipeline outputs from one survey base to another (e.g., GALAH to APOGEE), treating the differences as a multi-parameter, non-linear transformation instead of a single global offset, and stressing that the method is most reliable where the overlap sample provides good coverage. Guiglion and others (2024) provided a complementary example in which stellar parameters and abundances for Gaia RVS are inferred using Gaia (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016) spectra together with additional Gaia information, and the results are placed on the APOGEE reference scale, showing how anchoring to an external reference can be built directly into the inference workflow. Finally, large collaborations highlight that it is also important to control internal differences within a survey before comparing to others, as shown by the Gaia-ESO strategy for homogenisation and calibration across analysis pipelines (Pancino et al., 2017).

In SoS-I (Tsantaki et al., 2022), we constructed the largest homogenised radial velocity (RV) catalogue available at the time, placing Gaia and major ground-based spectroscopic surveys onto a common reference scale. SoS-II (Turchi et al., 2025) represented a major extension of SoS-I in two aspects. First, the homogenisation framework was extended from RVs to spectroscopically derived stellar atmospheric parameters (TeffT_{\rm eff}, log⁡g\log g, and [Fe/H]). Five spectroscopic surveys were internally and externally calibrated onto a common scale anchored to high-resolution reference data. Second, this calibrated spectroscopic scale was used as a training reference to infer atmospheric parameters from large photometric surveys Sloan Digital Sky Survey (Abazajian et al., 2003, SDSS;), the SkyMapper Southern Sky Survey (Keller et al., 2007, SM;) with machine-learning methods. This second step produced homogenised stellar parameters for about 23 million stars and demonstrated substantial improvements over previous similar works, particularly in the metal-poor regime ([Fe/H]<-1).

Our approach combines empirical error re-normalisation, data-driven regression models, and uncertainty calibration techniques to ensure both accuracy and statistical consistency. papers.title: BeAR: The Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code - A GPU-accelerated framework for low-resolution, high-resolution, and joint retrievals of exoplanet atmospheres
papers.abstract: We present BeAR, the Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code and successor of Helios-r, and its new high-resolution cross-correlation framework for emission and transmission spectra. BeAR performs joint retrievals by adding the log-likelihoods of high- and low-resolution data computed from the same model atmosphere. The framework implements established cross-correlation log-likelihoods, with the line-depth scaling either fitted analytically or sampled as a free parameter, their per-pixel generalization, fast model filtering, and model re-injection adapted to this filtering. The forward model and likelihood run entirely on a graphics processing unit (GPU). One forward model takes about 1 ms on an NVIDIA GH200, allowing millions of models per minute on a GPU cluster. In separate retrievals of Gemini South/IGRINS and JWST/NIRSpec dayside spectra of the hot Jupiter WASP-77Ab, BeAR reproduces published abundances, C/O ratios, and metallicities to within 1.5 sigma, the preference for 13CO, and the thermal structure and line contrast to within 1 sigma. The joint retrieval confirms a sub-solar metallicity and a near-solar C/O ratio. A full IGRINS retrieval with 17 free parameters takes 27 to 42 minutes on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 or about 14 minutes on eight RTX 4090 GPUs. Injection--recovery tests show that the posteriors underestimate the uncertainties of abundance ratios by about a factor of two.

The changing Doppler shift of the planet’s lines during the observation separates them from the nearly stationary telluric and stellar lines, and cross-correlation with a model template combines the many lines that individually lie below the noise (Snellen et al., 2010; Brogi et al., 2012; Birkby et al., 2013). The distinct line patterns separate species with overlapping bands (Brogi et al., 2017; Line et al., 2021), and lines of different strength probe different pressures (Brogi & Line, 2019). Measuring abundances and temperature structures from such data can be done with a Bayesian atmospheric retrieval using a parametric forward model (Madhusudhan & Seager, 2009; Line et al., 2013; MacDonald & Batalha, 2023), and at high resolution such retrievals need two additional ingredients. The first is a mapping from cross-correlation to likelihood (Zucker, 2003; Brogi & Line, 2019), which Gibson et al. (2020) generalized to per-pixel uncertainties. The second is a consistent treatment of the detrending. SysRem (Tamuz et al., 2005; Birkby et al., 2013) and principal component analysis (de Kok et al., 2013, PCA;) remove part of the planetary signal together with the telluric and stellar lines, so every trial model must be distorted in the same way. Repeating the detrending for each model (Brogi & Line, 2019; Line et al., 2021; Pelletier et al., 2021) is slow and can dominate the cost of a retrieval. For example, a retrieval of the IGRINS data of WASP-77A b took about three days on 24 central processing unit (CPU) cores and one graphics processing unit (GPU) (Line et al., 2021). Gibson et al. (2022) replaced this step by filtering each model with a fixed linear projection derived once from the data, which they found to be orders of magnitude faster than repeating SysRem and substantially faster than repeating PCA for every model. Fitting high- and low-resolution data with one atmosphere can break degeneracies that neither resolves alone. The low-resolution spectrum retains the absolute flux and, in emission, the flux difference between strongly absorbing bands and the windows between them, which probe different pressures. It therefore constrains the absolute abundance scale and the temperature gradient, whereas resolved lines separate species whose bands overlap and also give access to Doppler shifts caused by the planet’s orbital motion, rotation, and winds (Brogi et al., 2017; Brogi & Line, 2019). Smith et al. (2024a) performed the first such joint retrieval with JWST data, combining IGRINS and NIRSpec/G395H dayside spectra of WASP-77A b, and obtained tighter constraints than from either instrument alone; earlier joint fits used Hubble and Spitzer data (Brogi et al., 2017; Gandhi et al., 2019; Kasper et al., 2023; Boucher et al., 2023). As JWST and ground-based spectra accumulate for the same planets, such analyses are likely to become more numerous.

Smith et al. (2024a) find that their post-eclipse IGRINS constraints depend strongly on the number of removed components, and Wang et al. papers.title: Adapt the Object to the Subject: Representative Study Material for Empirical Software Engineering
papers.abstract: External validity is a central concern in empirical software engineering, yet the debate has largely focused on whether study participants are representative. How well the study objects they reason about - code, models, or requirements - are representative of each participant's own work is often overlooked. Practitioners' own artifacts would be ideal, but are often out of reach, so researchers sample from public datasets or construct objects artificially. Whether this lack of subject-object fit affects participants' ability to act on the material remains unknown. We take a first step toward answering this question for requirements. We propose an approach that uses an LLM to generate context-adapted synthetic requirements just-in-time during an online survey from a short, participant-supplied context description, optionally injecting requirements smells as controlled stimuli. To validate the approach, we conducted a controlled experiment with 31 industry practitioners in a 2x2 design that crosses stimulus generation (static vs. synthetic) with quality (clean vs. smelly). Each participant rated the perceived representativeness and assessability of 20 requirements. Using Bayesian data analysis within a statistical causal-inference framework, we find that perceived representativeness has a strong positive effect on assessability. Synthetic requirements are rated as more representative and, primarily due to this gain, more assessable than static ones sourced from public datasets; smell injection leaves both perceptions unchanged. Our results support treating a lack of study-object representativeness as a first-class validity threat and position context-adapted synthetic study objects as a practical addition to the empirical methodology toolbox.

papers.title: Secure Formal Raising: Protecting the Development of AI through Executable Properties
papers.abstract: Model raising revisits Turing's developmental view of machine intelligence. Formal Raising (FR) has recently been proposed to complement this view with explicit behavioral properties. This paper extends that proposal to the security of the raising environment. Secure Formal Raising (SFR) models policy integrity, authorization, and confidential data flow using four-valued evidence that preserves unknown and inconsistent assessments. We prove six security invariants and show that they force admission to accept only confirmed evidence. A plain-C reference implementation satisfies the invariants in a bounded exhaustive exploration, which also exposes a confused-deputy gap for tool calls that a provenance requirement closes.

How should an intelligent machine acquire its behavior? In 1950, Turing proposed educating a comparatively simple “child machine” instead of directly programming an adult-like intelligence [1]. He distinguished its initial construction from the education through which it develops. This developmental perspective makes interaction with teachers part of the system’s design, rather than merely a source of test inputs.

Aydin et al. recently revived this perspective for contemporary AI through model raising [2]. They propose shaping values with capabilities early on, using first-person experience, social interaction, and a scaffolded curriculum. Their proposal motivates bringing behavioral commitments into development instead of relying on later alignment. It does not itself provide an executable specification of those commitments.

Formal Raising (FR) is a newly proposed complement to this developmental view [3]. It represents selected requirements as explicit, machine-checkable properties that participate in evaluation and action selection. Hard rules exclude inadmissible alternatives, while declared priorities rank competing preferences. The preceding FR work primarily develops ethical examples; it is a starting point for further investigation rather than an established account of AI development.

This paper builds on that proposal by addressing the integrity of the raising environment. A teaching message may change a curriculum, a retrieved document may influence an action, and a tool call may disclose information. Who may change the policy, and which operations may a developing system execute? Ethical evaluation alone does not establish teacher authenticity or authorization. The proposed Secure Formal Raising (SFR) model therefore enforces protection against unauthorized modification, execution, and disclosure at explicit transition boundaries.

papers.title: Newton Steps are Faster for Linear Complementarity Problems
papers.abstract:
Linear Complementarity Problems (LCPs) with sufficient matrices form a well-studied class of problems, dating back from the foundational works of Cottle and Dantzig (1968). LCPs capture convex quadratic programs, and admit reductions from problems such as discounted stochastic games or mean-payoff games. While the original approach for solving these problems was based on pivoting methods, in their 1991 book, Kojima, Megiddo, Noma, and Yoshise introduced an interior point method (IPM) with running time that is polynomial in the input size, but which depends linearly on a certain parameter called the handicap number of the matrix. Despite the ensuing rich literature on sufficient LCP IPMs, the linear dependence on the handicap number has not been improved since then.
  We present an IPM whose running time depends on the square root of the handicap number. The algorithm can decrease the duality gap by a constant factor in $O\left(\min\left\{\sqrt{n} (1+\kappa),n^{9/8}\sqrt{1+\kappa}\right\}\right)$ iterations. Curiously, this can already be achieved using standard Newton updates. We analyze the IPM in a norm defined by a local weighting, where centralizing Newton steps quadratically converge to the central path, without any dependence on the handicap number. The weights arise from a characterization by Rump (Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 1997, 1998, 2003) of the sign-real spectral radius and its relation to sufficiency; another ingredient of our proof is a new operator norm characterization of the handicap number.
  Moreover, the connection to Rump's work also enables us to show coNP-completeness of testing sufficiency, and approximation hardness of the handicap number.

papers.intro:
Interior point methods (IPMs) are among the most powerful algorithmic tools for continuous optimization. Their success is closely tied to convexity, which provides the structure needed to control Newton steps and guarantee rapid convergence. A longstanding question is how far these methods can be extended beyond convex optimization, and what properties can replace convexity in their convergence analysis.

papers.title: Energy-conserving scheme for a shallow-water model with capillary effects
papers.abstract: We consider numerical approximations of shallow-water and thin-film flow models with capillary effects. These models lead to third-order differential equations, and we work with an augmented model with second-order derivatives. For a wide class of such models, which includes the classical shallow-water model and thin-film flow models, we develop a fully discrete energy-conserving scheme for both the quadratic and fully nonlinear capillary models. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme is stable and conserves total energy in the absence of dissipative effects.

Here we develop numerical approximations of free-surface flows in the thin-film limit, accounting for capillary surface tension while neglecting the magnetic field. In the shallow-water approximation, long-wave scaling of the vertical momentum equation yields a balance between the vertical pressure gradient and gravity. Integrating this balance over the depth gives a pressure composed of a hydrostatic part and a free-surface contribution. The standard assumption that the pressure at the free surface equals the ambient pressure is valid only when surface-tension effects are negligible or the interface is flat. For liquid metals, capillary effects are not negligible, so the approximation must retain the pressure jump induced by capillary forces at the free surface. This jump is naturally incorporated through Hamilton’s principle; the resulting Euler-Lagrange equations [27, 5] contain third-order spatial derivatives. Discretizing third-order operators is challenging and often produces severe instabilities and spurious grid-scale oscillations [4, 23, 11]; preserving the total-energy balance at the discrete level is equally difficult [4]. Energy conservation is important in this setting because it prevents spurious energy growth in long-time integrations and allows dispersive capillary waves to be resolved without relying on artificial dissipation. A common remedy is to reformulate the model with lower-order derivatives. Bresch et al. [4] introduce a scaled depth gradient as an auxiliary variable and obtain a second-order augmented system, while Dhaouadi et al. [9] use hyperbolic relaxation to obtain a first-order formulation.

In the formulation of [4], the scaled depth gradient makes the capillary energy quadratic and yields an augmented system that conserves total energy. Dhaouadi et al. [9] instead use an extended Lagrangian to express capillarity through lower-order derivatives, resulting in a first-order nonlinear system with a stiff source term and relaxation parameters that must be chosen by the user. We adopt the formulation of [4] because its quadratic energy is amenable to entropy-stable discretization and its conservative form admits a discrete energy balance. The total energy plays the role of a convex entropy for the augmented system, which allows us to use the entropy-stability framework of Tadmor [31]. papers.title: Key role of orbital exchange in CoO magnetism
papers.abstract: Co ions in the antiferromagnetic phase of CoO are known to possess a substantial orbital moment, making this material promising for orbitronic applications. However, intersite exchange interactions involving these orbital degrees of freedom remain poorly quantified, and their role in CoO magnetism is unclear. Here, we derive a full low-energy effective Hamiltonian for CoO, including orbital exchange terms, using an ab initio force-theorem approach based on DFT+dynamical mean-field theory. We find sizable orbital interactions, with quadrupolar orbital exchange emerging as the dominant nearest-neighbor term. The collinear antiferromagnetic order obtained from the effective Hamiltonian features magnetic moments tilted away from the pseudocubic <001> direction and an orbital contribution amounting to about one-third of the total moment, in agreement with experimental estimates. We show that the moment tilting originates from the combined effect of orbital and spin-orbital exchange interactions. The same interactions also produce a prominent splitting of the lowest excitation band. By directly modeling the inelastic neutron scattering (INS) intensity, we further show that the characteristic column-like structures previously observed in CoO INS provide a clear fingerprint of orbital exchange. We also discuss possible impact of our findings for further advances in the field of complex collective excitations, their transport properties and applications in the realm of orbitronics.

papers.title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
papers.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
papers.intro:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level brains for physical AI systems, interpreting visual observations and task instructions to guide behavior in robotics and autonomous driving (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025; Tian et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025). Their reasoning need not be expressed solely in language. VLMs can formulate intermediate predictions as visual plans: points and bounding boxes identify relevant locations or objects (Yuan et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025), while trajectories describe intended motion or forecast how a scene will evolve (Gu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a). Recent work uses spatial traces and visual primitives to guide action generation (Li et al., 2025a; Lee et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026). These plans make spatial goals and anticipated motion explicit before action. Each visual primitive has identifiable boundaries and an organized coordinate layout.

Recent work uses spatial traces and visual primitives to guide action generation (Li et al., 2025a; Lee et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026). These plans make spatial goals and anticipated motion explicit before action. Each visual primitive has identifiable boundaries and an organized coordinate layout.

Generating such plans efficiently becomes increasingly important as their spatial detail grows. Longer trajectories, additional objects, and joint 2D image and 3D predictions require more coordinate tokens, which autoregressive VLMs decode sequentially (Chen et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025). For physical agents that update their plans as new observations arrive, sequential decoding limits spatial detail and update frequency under a fixed latency budget. This motivates decoding methods that can generate complete visual plans with fewer sequential forward passes while preserving their spatial accuracy.

In this work, we introduce VFlash, a generalist decoding framework for physical AI (Figure 1) that accommodates both text (e.g., sub-task plans) and diverse visual primitives, such as bounding boxes, variable-length trajectories, and dense 3D motion predictions. Our study reveals an interesting observation: a lightweight diffusion drafter can even surpass its autoregressive target in spatial accuracy of the visual plans while decoding much faster. The structure of visual primitives helps explain this finding: once a primitive’s type, dimensionality, and length are specified, its boundaries and coordinate layout are known. Aligning draft blocks with these boundaries allows an entire geometric object to be predicted jointly, with tens to hundreds of tokens decoded in a single forward pass. These observations motivate aligning training and decoding with complete primitive boundaries and directly accepting structurally valid drafts without requiring token-level agreement with the target, while retaining verified decoding for text.

At the center of VFlash is Flash Primitive Decoding (FPD), which uses the requested output structure to organize both drafter training and inference. A tool call specifies the size of a variable-length prediction, while the primitive type determines its coordinate layout. Conditioned on features from a frozen target VLM, a lightweight diffusion drafter learns to predict complete primitives from annotated spatial data. At inference, the decoder applies layout-specific constraints (Willard and Louf, 2023; Geng et al., 2023) and accepts valid primitives in full. The target VLM supplies context for subsequent predictions, and ordinary text retains speculative decoding with target verification.

VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to its autoregressive target across the evaluated robot trajectory tasks. In the downstream robot manipulation pipeline shown in Figure 1, it reduces inference latency by about 80% on both Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. These visual plans also provide useful conditioning for action models: on MolmoSpaces (Kim et al., 2026b), a world action model (Ye et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026c) conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

Beyond acceleration, our work suggests a broader role for parallel decoding in multimodal systems. Lossless speculative decoding preserves the autoregressive target’s output distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a), whereas structured visual planning instead permits predictions to be judged by their spatial accuracy and usefulness for action, in the spirit of relaxed acceptance criteria (Bachmann et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c). VFlash enables a System-1 mode (Kahneman, 2011) of visual planning in VLMs, producing fast, structured spatial predictions through joint coordinate decoding. This perspective interestingly connects to recent System-1 models such as Jev, which emphasize fast, typed decisions (Almeida, 2026; Yu and Yao, 2026). VFlash brings this perspective to complete geometric predictions, exploiting structure within each primitive. The resulting gains in both speed and spatial accuracy suggest that autoregressive decoding need not define the quality ceiling for visual outputs.

papers.title: On generalized token graphs with tokens of different colors
papers.abstract: We generalize the concept of token graphs, and we call them supertoken graphs. In this work, we consider the variant in which tokens are distinguishable (for instance, by color) and at most one token is allowed on each vertex. We formally define this kind of supertoken graphs and present their basic properties. We study their diameter, in which cases they are Cayley graphs, and their spectra. Moreover, we provide bounds or exact values for the independence, the vertex cover, the clique, and the chromatic numbers of these graphs. Finally, we characterize the cases in which the supertoken graphs of complete graphs are planar.

papers.title: Sudden disappearance of a bright exciton in solid helium
papers.abstract: Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, are investigated extensively in optical spectra, where their wave vector is considered to be vanishing. Excitonic spectra as a function of wave vector are much less explored, both theoretically and with measurements of the loss function. Here, we uncover a striking angular dependence of excitonic spectra for the prototypical case of solid helium, where a prominent excitonic peak is completely suppressed for a momentum transfer in certain directions. The effect is entirely due to the electron-hole exchange interaction. This phenomenon leads to a counter-intuitive effect close to Bragg points, where an infinitesimal change of direction of wave vector is sufficient to change the spectrum dramatically. We explain in which way the nature of excitons makes such a scenario possible. We discuss the pressure dependence, point to experimental evidence for our findings, and predict under which circumstances dramatic angular dependencies may also be found in other materials.

In the absorption spectra of semiconductors and insulators, sharp features found inside the fundamental gap are often due to excitons, bound electron-hole (e-h) pairs [40, 10]. Excitons are studied extensively at vanishing wave vector, both theoretically and experimentally [12, 52]. Much less effort has been devoted to non-vanishing wave vector 𝐪\mathbf{q}, not least because this parameter range is inaccessible in optical spectroscopies. With progress in scattering experiments, such as electron energy loss spectroscopy [27, 26] (EELS) and inelastic x-ray scattering [61, 7] (IXS), information concerning non-vanishing 𝐪\mathbf{q} is increasingly available and attracts attention [41, 63, 44, 2, 32, 46, 30, 28, 62, 38, 59, 55, 56, 66, 65, 23, 31, 34, 71, 48]. Recent studies in different classes of materials have demonstrated that the investigation of the exciton dispersion as a function of 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a very efficient strategy to identify the exciton character [33, 14, 18, 19, 43]. The knowledge of exciton dispersion is also important to interpret emission experiments such as luminescence [51, 74, 45, 21, 54, 49, 47], to provide insight into exciton dynamics and lifetimes [5, 69, 64], and to detect excitonic insulating phases [39, 42, 70].

The simplest assumption would be that the exciton dispersion is due to the dispersion of band-to-band transitions. This is predicted by the Wannier model [72], which is typically used for semiconductors and small-gap insulators, and the dominance of band structure effects on the exciton dispersion has even been observed in wide-gap materials such as LiF [33, 46]. In large gap materials with flat bands the Frenkel model is more appropriate [29]. In the Frenkel model, the exciton is a localized excitation that can hop through the crystal thanks to the e-h exchange (ehX) interaction, whereas the strong direct e-h interaction (ehD) is responsible for the large exciton binding energy, but not for dispersion. In molecular crystals, for example, the dispersion can be often explained by the ehX interaction [22, 4]. In all those cases, changing the absolute value or angle of momentum transfer are expected to lead to smooth changes of the spectra.

Helium has the highest atomic ionization energy among all elements. In the solid state, it has a huge band gap, beyond 20 eV. In this extreme insulating regime, the weak dielectric screening leads to strong electron-electron and electron-hole effective interactions with very large exciton binding energies.. Therefore, solid helium offers an ideal playground for discovering intriguing exciton physics. Helium is also the only element that does not solidify at ambient pressure, even at very low temperatures, becoming instead superfluid. papers.title: Systematic Study of Cosmic Rays in Star-Forming and Starburst Galaxies using Fermi-LAT and Multiwavelength Data
papers.abstract: The majority of $\gamma$ rays from star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and starburst galaxies (SBGs) are expected to originate from interactions between high-energy cosmic rays (CRs) and the interstellar medium, making $\gamma$-ray observations a powerful tool for probing CR populations and interstellar environments. Using 15 years of Fermi-LAT data, we conducted a systematic study of seven sources. The $\gamma$-ray spectra of the bright SBGs M82 and NGC~253 exhibit a decrease in energy flux below a few hundred MeV, suggesting a substantially smaller contribution from CR electrons than previously inferred. Detailed fits of the spectral energy distribution, which combine our GeV $\gamma$-ray measurements with reported radio and TeV $\gamma$-ray results, indicate that the electron-to-proton ratios in M82 and NGC~253 are comparable to that of the Milky Way. In contrast, energy densities of CRs in these two SBGs are 2.5--8 times lower than that of the magnetic field, unlike the Milky Way. For the nearby Local Group galaxy M31, we decomposed the $\gamma$-ray emission into two components, revealing a central source with a soft spectrum and a compact size of less than 0.33 degree, which indicates a considerable contribution from unresolved sources. Our new analysis also reduces the $\gamma$-ray fluxes of several SBGs, bringing all SBG sample members to levels comparable to or below the calorimetric limit, with calorimetric efficiencies ranging from 0.33 to 1.20. In contrast, all SFG sample members exhibit low efficiencies at the 10\% level. We developed a theoretical model of interstellar $\gamma$-ray emission that successfully reproduces the observed calorimetric efficiencies, providing a robust framework for interpreting and predicting $\gamma$-ray emission from SFGs and SBGs.

papers.intro:
Cosmic rays (CRs) in the Milky Way Galaxy are believed to originate from supernova remnants and other star-formation processes, such as the winds of massive stars and pulsars (e.g., [30, 20]). Similarly, galaxies with high star-formation rates are expected to exhibit CR densities comparable to or greater than those of the Milky Way. In these external galaxies, CRs generate electromagnetic radiation through mechanisms analogous to those in the Milky Way. Specifically, CR electrons produce synchrotron radiation via interactions with interstellar magnetic fields and non-thermal Bremsstrahlung radiation via interactions with interstellar gas. They also upscatter the interstellar radiation field (ISRF) via inverse Compton (IC) scattering. CR protons produce γ\gamma rays through nuclear–nuclear collisions with interstellar gas. Multiwavelength observations of external galaxies therefore provides insights into both CR populations and the properties of their interstellar environments, including magnetic fields, the ISRF, and gas content, thereby advancing understanding of the underlying astrophysical processes.

The γ\gamma-ray band is particularly important because it is sensitive to CR protons within galaxies. CR protons produce intense GeV and TeV γ\gamma rays through the decay of neutral pions, which are generated by nuclear–nuclear interactions with ambient interstellar gas. This process typically results in γ\gamma-ray emission that dominates over that from CR electrons in typical interstellar environments. Fermi-LAT (W. B. Atwood et al., 2009) detected GeV γ\gamma-rays from the nearest star-forming galaxies (SFGs), specifically the LMC, SMC, and M31 (A. A. Abdo et al., 2010a; A. A. Abdo et al., 2010b; A. A. Abdo et al., 2010c), shortly after its launch. The instrument also identified significant GeV γ\gamma-ray emission from the nearby starburst galaxies (SBGs) M82 and NGC 253 (A. A. Abdo et al., 2010d). Concurrently, ground-based Cherenkov telescopes observed significant TeV γ\gamma-rays from these two galaxies (VERITAS Collaboration et al., 2009; F. Acero et al., 2009), thereby establishing SBGs as γ\gamma-ray sources. A strong correlation between observed GeV γ\gamma-ray luminosities and total infrared luminosities (M. Ackermann et al., 2012a) suggests that the majority of γ\gamma rays originate from interstellar CRs produced by star-formation activity, rather than from the nuclear supermassive black hole. The hard spectrum observed in SBGs (photon index Γ∼2.2\Gamma\sim 2.2) indicates that these galaxies act as CR calorimeters, in contrast to the Milky Way, which is escape-dominated (M. Ackermann et al., 2012b). These observations have prompted theoretical investigations into CR transport in both SBGs and the Milky Way. For example, M. R. Krumholz et al. (2020) proposed that CR diffusion in SBGs is nearly energy-independent up to about 1 TeV. The observed flux exceeds the expected starburst component in a proton-dominated scenario, leading the authors to attribute the emission to MeV radiation from the corona surrounding the Seyfert nucleus.

(2018)), together with more than 15 years of accumulated observations, now make it possible to study γ\gamma-ray emission from SFGs, SBGs, and Seyferts with unprecedented accuracy and uniformity. papers.title: FALCON (FERMI-ALMA Calibrator ObservatioN): Cross-matching ALMA Calibrators with Fermi-LAT Blazars
papers.abstract: Blazars are active galactic nuclei with relativistic jets closely aligned with our line of sight, producing Doppler-boosted emission from radio to gamma rays. Millimeter emission near the synchrotron self-absorption turnover probes compact regions at the jet base, yet large statistical studies in this regime remain limited. We construct the FALCON (FERMI--ALMA Calibrator ObservatioN) catalogue, a millimeter-selected blazar sample by cross-matching the ALMA Calibrator Source Catalogue with the Third Data Release of the Fourth LAT AGN Catalog (4LAC-DR3). After removing duplicates, we obtain 949 unique gamma-ray-associated sources, corresponding to approximately 25 % of the 4LAC-DR3 blazar population. For the subset with available redshift measurements, we compute millimeter and gamma-ray luminosities and find a strong, statistically significant correlation that remains robust after accounting for redshift effects. Fermi-detected blazars exhibit systematically flatter millimeter spectral indices than gamma-ray non-detected ALMA calibrators, while the redshift-controlled luminosity correlation becomes progressively weaker from high-synchrotron-peaked BL Lacs toward flat-spectrum radio quasars. These results indicate an intrinsic connection between millimeter and gamma-ray emission, consistent with a common origin in relativistic jets governed by Doppler boosting and time-averaged jet power.

papers.intro:
Blazars are radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN) whose relativistic jets are oriented close to the line of sight, so that their Doppler-boosted, non-thermal emission dominates the observed spectrum from radio to gamma rays [46]. Their broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) shows two characteristic humps: a low-energy component produced by synchrotron radiation from relativistic electrons in the jet, and a high-energy component, peaking in the gamma-ray band, generally attributed to inverse-Compton (IC) scattering. A central open question in jet physics is how these two components are physically connected, and why the gamma-ray output varies so widely across the population, with many radio-bright blazars remaining comparatively faint in gamma rays [25, 18]. The detectability of a blazar in gamma rays has been linked to a range of global jet properties, including faster jet speeds and brightness [22, 29], smaller viewing angles [26], larger apparent jet opening angles [40, 30], stronger variability [41], and the presence of multiple inverse-Compton components [1, 45]. Enhanced gamma-ray activity has also been associated with dynamical events within the jet, such as the ejection of superluminal components [4] and high-frequency radio flares [24]. These diverse connections underscore the need to characterize the relationship between the synchrotron and IC components across a large and uniformly selected sample.

Among the accessible wavebands, the millimeter regime offers a particularly clean view of the innermost jet. At these frequencies the emission lies near the synchrotron self-absorption turnover and samples the optically thin synchrotron spectrum of the most compact regions at the jet base, where contamination from thermal emission associated with the accretion flow and its host galaxy and from extended radio lobes is minimal [17]. Millimeter measurements therefore probe the synchrotron emission from precisely the regions where particle acceleration is expected to feed the high-energy output, making the millimeter spectral properties of blazars a direct diagnostic of the physical conditions underlying their gamma-ray emission. Compact, parsec-scale radio cores of blazars have furthermore been statistically associated with the arrival directions of high-energy neutrinos [39, 19]. Because the millimeter band probes these same innermost jet regions, characterizing the millimeter properties of the blazar population would be also of multi-messenger interest.

[23] reported a significant correlation between (sub-)millimeter and gamma-ray luminosities spanning several orders of magnitude, and found that gamma-ray–bright blazars tend to show flat or rising millimeter spectra, interpreted as a newly emerging, self-absorbed synchrotron component associated with activity in the inner jet. Cross-correlation analyses of radio-to-submillimeter and gamma-ray light curves for 5454 sources have likewise revealed correlated variability, with the bulk of the gamma-ray production located within or upstream of the millimeter core on (sub-)parsec scales [13]. Detailed studies of individual sources of o​n​eone sources place the gamma-ray emission at parsec-scale distances along the jet, in some cases beyond the broad-line region [42], and resolved monitoring of objects such as the broad-line radio galaxy 3C 120 has linked enhanced millimeter activity to gamma-ray dissipation at sub-parsec distances from the central engine [43]. Together these results suggest that the disturbances in the inner jet responsible for millimeter flares are closely tied to episodes of enhanced gamma-ray emission.

Despite these advances, existing statistical samples remain limited. The correlation studies above rest on relatively small samples with a substantial fraction of upper limits, which restricts their statistical robustness and may bias the inferred relations. Wide-field surveys face complementary difficulties. The Planck mission provided the first blind, all-sky samples selected at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths [35, 37], but its arcminute-scale positional uncertainties, photometric errors, and contamination from Galactic dust and dusty star-forming galaxies complicate the identification of the relatively rare blazars among far more numerous dusty star-forming galaxies, and constructing clean blazar samples from these data remains challenging even with dedicated mitigation [38]. Deeper surveys with the South Pole Telescope and Herschel reached fainter flux densities and recovered radio/millimeter–gamma correlations [47, 27], but cover limited sky areas (∼2500​deg2\sim 2500~\mathrm{deg}^{2} for SPT and ∼642​deg2\sim 642~\mathrm{deg}^{2} for Herschel) and therefore yield samples much smaller than the all-sky Fermi-LAT survey. Previous statistical studies have thus generally been constrained by modest sample sizes and by selection effects such as flux limits and redshift dependence.

These limitations can be largely overcome using the ALMA Calibrator Source Catalogue 11 1 https://almascience.nao.ac.jp/sc/. Over the past decade, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) has repeatedly observed thousands of compact, bright radio sources as calibration targets. These calibrators consist predominantly of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) and BL Lac objects and therefore form one of the largest and most homogeneous millimeter-selected samples of blazars currently available [8]. Using the ALMA calibrator archive, [32] demonstrated that the calibrator population is overwhelmingly dominated by blazars and constructed one of the largest millimeter-selected blazar samples through cross-matching with the Roma-BZCAT catalogue [28]. In fact, the ALMA Calibrator Source Catalogue contains several thousand compact radio sources observed across multiple millimeter bands, making it effectively the largest millimeter-selected blazar sample assembled to date. Owing to ALMA’s sub-arcsecond angular resolution, source confusion and contamination from dusty star-forming galaxies are negligible compared with wide-beam surveys. Although calibration data have recently been exploited for blind continuum and spectral-line searches [7, e.g.,], and the calibrator population itself has been characterized at radio and millimeter wavelengths [7, 32], these studies have primarily focused on identifying and characterizing the blazar population contained in the ALMA calibrator archive. In contrast, its physical connection to gamma-ray emission has not yet been systematically investigated.

papers.title: Diameter bounds for complexes that are close to flag or close to normal
papers.abstract: The Hirsch problem asks how large the diameter of the dual graph of a simplicial complex can be, in terms of its number of vertices. For normal complexes, the classical bounds are the Larman-Barnette bound, which is linear for fixed dimension, the Kalai-Kleitman bound, which is quasi-polynomial, and the Adiprasito-Benedetti bound n-d, which however holds only for flag complexes. After sharpening the Larman-Barnette and the Kalai-Kleitman bounds, we study how the three bounds deteriorate when flagness or normality is weakened. We give three ways to quantify the distance from flagness, and in each case we bound the diameter in a way that interpolates between the Adiprasito-Benedetti and the Larman-Barnette bounds. We also quantify the distance from normality by a parameter q, and obtain a bound that is a polynomial of degree q in n. Finally, we conjecture a statement on flag layered families that would imply an interpolation between the Adiprasito-Benedetti and the Kalai-Kleitman bounds.

papers.title: Dynamical Keldysh model for colored noise and finite relaxation rate
papers.abstract: The Keldysh model describes quantum dots subjected to Gaussian noise with infinite correlation time. For multi-component noise coupled through non-commuting matrices, the spectrum exhibits a pseudogap. We solve the model for coloured noise with any correlation time, $1/ \gamma$. Finite memory leads to the pseudogap being filled, its peaks merging and the line narrowing.

papers.title: Non-Perturbative Resolution of Luttinger's Theorem Violations in Strongly Correlated Systems
papers.abstract: Many-body physics faces an apparent paradox concerning violations of Luttinger's theorem in strongly correlated systems. The theorem relates the electron number to the Luttinger count -- the monodromy of the logarithm of the imaginary-frequency Green's function $G(i\epsilon)$ -- and, at finite magnetic field, connects the Hall conductivity to the magnetic-field derivative of the Luttinger count via the Streda formula. Here, we provide a non-perturbative solution to this paradox. We demonstrate that the reported violations of Luttinger's theorem do not require a breakdown of the skeleton diagram representation of physical quantities, thereby resolving a long-standing point of contention in many-body theory. Furthermore, we show that the Luttinger integral, which accounts for the mismatch between the particle number and the Luttinger count, is itself a genuine topological invariant directly tied to the Luttinger-Ward functional $\Phi[G]$ rather than to the Green's function alone. We demonstrate that this invariant, like the monodromy of $\ln G(i\epsilon)$ itself, stems exclusively from the zero-frequency discontinuity of the Matsubara trajectory.

papers.intro:
Luttinger’s theorem [1] is a fundamental concept in modern theories of interacting electrons. Initially derived as a straightforward consequence of self-consistent many-body perturbation theory [1], its significance has evolved over time, with a growing emphasis on its topological nature [2, 3, 4], thereby transcending its perturbative origins. Indeed, it is related to one of the simplest topological quantities that can be constructed from the fully interacting single-particle Green’s function. It also has a profound connection to another celebrated topological response, the quantum Hall conductivity, through the Streda formula, as recently pointed out by Gavensky, Sachdev and Goldman [5].

papers.title: Which Signals of Code Correctness Survive Distribution Shift? Hidden-State and Causal Predictors of Program and Verdict Correctness
papers.abstract:
Large language models increasingly judge code, yet without external feedback such judgments are unreliable, and verifying them by executing tests or by extended reasoning is costly. Instead, execution-free correctness predictors use signals from the model's output probabilities, sampled solutions, or hidden states to identify judgments that warrant further verification. However, these predictors may degrade under distribution shifts when generalizing across projects and languages.
  We compare six execution-free predictors from four families on Qwen3-Coder-30B and gpt-oss-20b under benchmark shift between LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench and language shift across Python, C++ and Java. We evaluate two targets: whether the model's own verdict on a program can be trusted, and whether the program itself is correct. Besides established approaches, we adapt two novel causal localization methods to code, which have been shown to be more robust out-of-distribution on natural language tasks. For verdict correctness, causal localization improves robustness to language shift. For Qwen3-Coder a probe on the causally localized subspace stays 0.09 AUROC ahead of output confidence under language shift (0.11 in distribution), significantly outperforming the best non-causal predictor by 0.04 AUROC on average. This advantage, however, does not generalize consistently to gpt-oss or to benchmark shift. For program correctness, predictors transfer more successfully between benchmarks, largely by identifying problems on which the model tends to fail. However, their ability to rank candidates within the same problem is limited.

LLMs are increasingly used to judge code, including their own. They determine whether a candidate solves its task, whether a change is safe to accept, and which of several candidates to keep. Without external feedback, such judgments are unreliable. Models rarely improve by verifying their own outputs [18, 26], favor their own generations [37], and remain inconsistent as code judges [23]. Reliable verification is costly: executing tests requires an environment and a test suite [41], and reasoning about a candidate involves generating many additional tokens. A cheap signal indicating when a judgment can be trusted could gate these costlier checks rather than replace them [42, 24]. Execution-free correctness predictors provide such a signal from the model itself, such as the probability of its answer [48, 4], the agreement among sampled solutions [5, 47, 2], or its hidden states [3, 51, 45]. Probes on hidden states are particularly cheap, since they reuse activations the model computes anyway, and are already deployed as first-stage monitors [33, 27]. Such a predictor serves two purposes: it can estimate whether a program is correct, and whether the model’s own verdict on it can be trusted.

Instead, prior work on code has considered only a subset of predictor families and shift settings, and has largely focused on predicting program correctness [44, 15, 20, 12]. papers.title: Interpretable Multimodal MRI-Clinical Fusion for Functional Outcome Prediction After Acute Ischemic Stroke
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the added prognostic value of day-1 multimodal MRI for predicting three-month functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Sixty-six AIS patients with ADC, DWI, FLAIR, and clinical data were analyzed. Three-dimensional pretrained ResNet embeddings were extracted from each MRI modality, reduced using fold-isolated principal component analysis, and combined with structured clinical variables and ADC-derived lesion biomarkers. Linear support vector machines were evaluated using eight-fold stratified group cross-validation across MRI modality combinations. Clinical-only modeling achieved strong performance (AUC = $0.899 \pm 0.151$), while MRI-only models showed limited discrimination (AUC $\approx$ $0.67$-$0.73$). Among multimodal configurations, FLAIR-clinical fusion achieved the highest mean cross-validated performance (AUC = $0.948 \pm 0.061$), followed by ADC-clinical fusion (AUC = $0.941 \pm 0.094$). Full ADC-DWI-FLAIR fusion did not consistently outperform single-modality clinical fusion. Feature-importance analysis identified age, NIHSS subscores, ADC lesion burden, and learned FLAIR representations as key contributors, while qualitative FLAIR activation maps showed responses over lesion-like regions. These findings suggest that compact day-1 FLAIR and ADC representations provide complementary prognostic information beyond clinical variables and support interpretable, data-efficient outcome prediction in AIS.

papers.intro:
Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) remains a major cause of adult disability and long-term functional dependence worldwide [7]. Early prediction of three-month functional outcome is clinically important because it can support treatment planning, rehabilitation allocation, patient counseling, and trial stratification. The modified Rankin Scale (mRS) is widely used as the standard functional outcome endpoint after stroke, with poor outcome commonly defined as mRS >> 1 or mRS >> 2 depending on the clinical setting [1]. However, accurate individualized prognosis remains challenging because recovery depends on complex interactions between baseline neurological severity, age, vascular risk factors, lesion burden, treatment response, and early tissue evolution.

However, accurate individualized prognosis remains challenging because recovery depends on complex interactions between baseline neurological severity, age, vascular risk factors, lesion burden, treatment response, and early tissue evolution.

Clinical variables such as age, pre-stroke disability, and the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) are among the strongest predictors of post-stroke outcome [15, 8]. Nevertheless, clinical scores alone do not directly capture lesion location, infarct extent, or tissue-level changes after reperfusion. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), especially diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, provides sensitive markers of acute ischemic injury [13]. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging can provide complementary information related to lesion visibility, edema, and subacute tissue changes. Together, these modalities may improve outcome prediction by representing different aspects of ischemic tissue damage.

Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging can provide complementary information related to lesion visibility, edema, and subacute tissue changes. Together, these modalities may improve outcome prediction by representing different aspects of ischemic tissue damage.

Recent machine learning and deep learning methods have shown promise for combining imaging and clinical data in stroke prognosis [11, 4, 10]. Three-dimensional convolutional neural networks can extract volumetric representations from MRI without requiring handcrafted radiomic features, while linear classifiers can provide more transparent decision boundaries in small clinical cohorts [9, 2, 6]. However, many studies either focus on a single imaging modality, use imaging as a black-box input, or do not explicitly separate the contribution of clinical variables, MRI modality choice, and lesion-derived biomarkers. This makes it difficult to determine whether performance gains come from deep image representations, structured clinical predictors, or explicit lesion burden measures.

This makes it difficult to determine whether performance gains come from deep image representations, structured clinical predictors, or explicit lesion burden measures.

A further challenge is data efficiency. Stroke imaging datasets with complete longitudinal clinical outcomes are often small, making end-to-end deep learning prone to overfitting. Hybrid approaches that use pretrained 3D networks as feature extractors, followed by fold-isolated dimensionality reduction and linear classification, may offer a practical compromise between representation learning and interpretability [14, 3, 5]. In this setting, systematic evaluation of MRI modality combinations is important: adding more modalities does not necessarily improve generalization, especially when sample size is limited and modality-specific features are redundant or noisy. Our previous work showed that day-1 ADC-based multimodal modeling improved three-month mRS prediction compared with baseline ADC imaging, highlighting the prognostic value of early post-treatment diffusion changes [12]. However, that study focused primarily on ADC and did not systematically evaluate the relative contribution of ADC, DWI, and FLAIR modality combinations or explicitly separate the effect of ADC-derived lesion biomarkers from MRI image inputs.

In this work, we evaluate day-1 multimodal MRI fusion for predicting three-month functional outcome after AIS in a quality-controlled cohort of 66 patients. We compare ADC, DWI, and FLAIR representations individually and in combination, with and without structured clinical variables and ADC-derived lesion biomarkers. We use pretrained 3D ResNet feature extraction, fold-isolated principal component analysis, and class-balanced linear support vector machines under eight-fold stratified group cross-validation. In addition to predictive performance, we provide interpretability through filtered linear coefficient analysis and qualitative FLAIR CNN activation maps. Our goal is to identify which imaging modalities and lesion-derived features add prognostic value beyond clinical variables, while maintaining a data-efficient and interpretable modeling framework.

papers.title: Singular values of iterated Aluthge transforms of compact operators
papers.abstract: Yamazaki proved that the norms of the iterated Aluthge transforms of an operator converge to its spectral radius, and Ando showed that for matrices the singular values of the iterates converge to the moduli of the eigenvalues. We prove that the latter holds for every compact operator on a Hilbert space and every generalized Aluthge transform $\Delta_t$ with $0<t<1$: for every $j$, the $j$-th singular value of the $n$-th iterate converges to $|\lambda_j(T)|$, and the products of the $k$ largest singular values, as well as the Ky Fan norms, decrease monotonically to their limits. This is the Aluthge counterpart of the Yamamoto--Davis theorem. We also determine the limit in the Schatten $p$-norm whenever $T$ belongs to a strictly smaller Schatten class.

papers.title: VocabulARy 2.0: A Generative AR System Enabling Personalised 3D Mnemonics for Vocabulary Learning in Context
papers.abstract: Mnemonics support vocabulary learning by linking unfamiliar words to familiar concepts through memorable verbal and visual associations. We present a generative AR system that enables learners to create personalised 3D mnemonics by transforming familiar objects in their surroundings into situated mnemonic anchors. The system scans the environment, detects visible objects, and generates bilingual flashcards. After selecting a word, the learner describes a personal association. The system combines this description with an image of the selected object to generate a textured 3D model using generative AI. Learners can then place the model relative to the real object, transforming it into a situated mnemonic anchor.

papers.title: Subspace Learning with Outlier Exposure for Out-of-Distribution Detection
papers.abstract: Out-of-Distribution (OoD) detection is pivotal for reliable deployments of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), aiming to distinguish anomalous samples from the In-Distribution (InD) data in training. By introducing outliers as surrogate OoD data to finetune DNNs, Outlier Exposure (OE) has greatly advanced OoD detection in recent years. Existing OE-based research remains predominantly logit-centric, either by generating diverse outliers or by regularizing them with objectives operating at the prediction-output level. Nonetheless, these approaches leave much of the rich information in feature spaces untapped. In this work, we propose an OE-based detection framework, named RecOE, that learns appropriate feature subspaces from InD data and auxiliary outliers, such that the InD-OoD discrepancy can be effectively characterized through the learned feature subspaces. Specifically, the feature subspaces are optimized to capture the dominant variations of InD and outliers by minimizing reconstruction errors therein. Besides, a sample-level objective discourages reconstruction in the opposing subspace, while an orthogonality regularizer reduces subspace overlap, further promoting discriminative subspaces. At inference, the difference in reconstruction errors between the learned subspaces serves as the OoD detection score. Extensive experiments show the superiority of RecOE on multiple benchmarks, in which significant performance gains are achieved over recent strong baselines with only slight extra overhead from two small-size matrices of subspace bases. The source code is available at https://github.com/shenhongxu123/RecOE.

Such behavior poses substantial risks in safety-critical scenarios, including autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, and financial systems [30], making OoD detection a crucial research problem.

Such behavior poses substantial risks in safety-critical scenarios, including autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, and financial systems [30], making OoD detection a crucial research problem.

Existing OoD detection methods can be broadly categorized according to whether they require finetuning of a DNN. A series of post-hoc methods [16, 23, 21, 33, 11, 26, 10, 31] have been proposed with the main idea of leveraging the responses from a pretrained model to devise detection scores that capture the InD-OoD discrepancy. Another line of research introduces outliers as surrogate OoD data to finetune the DNN with regularization terms, which effectively promotes detection performance, known as Outlier Exposure (OE) [17]. OE-based methods advance OoD detection in two main aspects: outlier construction and outlier regularization. The former improves auxiliary outliers to provide surrogate OoD supervision through boundary-aware mining [2, 25], ID-outlier mixing [43], and informative extrapolation [45]. The latter develops regularization objectives to finetune the DNN for enhanced InD-outlier separation via energy-based margin regularization [23], gradient regularization of the OoD score function [32], or feature-based geometric constraints [37, 38]. Our work falls into the outlier-regularization category.

papers.title: Funnel MPC for port-Hamiltonian systems
papers.abstract: Port-Hamiltonian systems are an energy-based modelling formalism, that has strong ties to the physical models and allows interconnection of systems. Funnel MPC, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme, allows for output tracking with prescribed error bounds. Earlier works focused on systems with stable internal dynamics, which typically excludes port-Hamiltonian systems. We introduce a modified stage cost design that takes into account the port-Hamiltonian structure of the system and allows deactivation of the funnel cost. We show initial and recursive feasibility for a class of port-Hamiltonian systems with relative degree one including unstable internal dynamics.

The port-Hamiltonian systems formalism is a well-established framework for modelling and control of physical systems. For a comprehensive overview, we refer the reader to [1, 2].

The port-Hamiltonian systems formalism is a well-established framework for modelling and control of physical systems. For a comprehensive overview, we refer the reader to [1, 2].

One appealing feature of port-Hamiltonian systems is that the formalism is intrinsically based on power-flow between the (virtual ideal) components of the system; e.g., a real-existing spring is virtually decomposed into an ideal spring, modelled as an energy storage component which stores and releases potential energy, and a damper, where energy is dissipated due to internal friction of the spring. In particular, the energy supplied to the system appears naturally as product of the external port variables. This property has prompted [3, 4] to propose this quantity as the natural cost function for port-Hamiltonian optimal control problems.

papers.title: NutriVisRAG: Multimodal Exemplar Grounding for Nutrient Estimation with Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Diet is a major determinant of health, yet accurate dietary assessment from free-living meal images remains challenging. Existing retrieval-based Vision-Language Model (VLM) approaches to nutrient estimation typically rely on textual food representations, while, to our knowledge, direct grounding on visually similar annotated meals has not been investigated. We present NutriVisRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a vision encoder to retrieve similar meals with known nutritional annotations and provide them as multimodal in-context exemplars for VLM nutrient estimation at inference time, without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate NutriVisRAG across four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies, including free-living meals from adults with insulin-treated diabetes, where carbohydrate estimates are compared against two dietitians' annotations. Across all 96 configurations (4 datasets x 4 VLMs x 3 retrieval encoders x 2 prompting strategies), NutriVisRAG reduced the primary estimation error in 56, with improvements more frequent under whole-meal (35/48) than per-item prompting (21/48). Across the evaluated configurations, the lowest NutriVisRAG error was below the best Vanilla error in 13 of 16 VLM--dataset pairs. For GPT-5.4-mini, under whole-meal prompting, the best-performing retrieval encoder for each dataset reduced the primary error on all four datasets relative to Vanilla, with reductions of 1.7--35.7%. Overall, our results show that grounding in multimodal exemplars comprising images and respective annotations can improve nutrient estimation at inference time without task-specific fine-tuning, although the benefits remain configuration-dependent.

papers.intro:
Accurate dietary assessment is central to nutritional monitoring and the prevention and management of diet-related chronic diseases, yet conventional self-reported approaches remain burdensome and prone to measurement errors [17]. Advances in computer vision and smartphone technologies have enabled automated dietary assessment from meal images through multi-stage pipelines combining food segmentation, recognition, portion estimation, and nutrient calculation, alongside integrated models that directly predict food quantity and nutritional composition [29, 28, 51, 43, 44]. These approaches have benefited from increasingly large food segmentation and recognition datasets [11, 30, 31, 46]. Errors in either segmentation or recognition can propagate to downstream portion and nutrient estimation, and recognition remains particularly vulnerable to distributions not represented during training [4]. Even when food regions and identities are correctly determined, estimating physical quantity remains a separate challenge, as portion estimation typically relies on depth, geometric reconstruction, or reference cues that require additional acquisition information [29, 28, 51, 43, 2]. End-to-end models instead bypass this by predicting food weight, energy, or macronutrients from visual representations. However, these approaches require large training datasets with quantitative dietary annotations [51, 44, 50].

Large Language Models, pretrained on large-scale text corpora, have demonstrated strong few-shot and in-context learning capabilities across diverse language tasks without task-specific fine-tuning [13, 10]. Extending this foundation-model paradigm to visual inputs, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) combine language modelling with visual representations to support multimodal understanding and generation [45, 6]. Recent studies have evaluated VLMs for food recognition, meal decomposition, portion and weight estimation, calorie estimation, and macronutrient prediction, with performance varying substantially across models and prompting strategies [1, 47, 58, 39, 50, 34, 53, 49]. Task-specific fine-tuning, specialised prediction components, and parameter-efficient adaptation can improve performance, but require additional dietary training data and model adaptation [1, 58, 50]. Nevertheless, quantitative dietary estimation remains challenging because food quantity and nutritional content must still be inferred from limited visual information [39, 50, 34, 53, 55, 8, 49]. Explicitly supplied nutritional information can nevertheless improve nutrient estimation [34, 50].

papers.title: Liouville systems I: Blow-up analysis and orthogonal decomposition
papers.abstract:
We study blow-up solutions of generalized Liouville systems on a closed surface at and near critical parameter hypersurfaces. Under a Morse assumption on the reduced functional, we establish the following results.
  First, we introduce amplitude variables in the approximate manifold and prove that every sequence of blow-up solutions at a fixed critical parameter, or along an admissible sequence from the lower side, admits a unique minimizing decomposition up to permutation. The remainder converges to zero and is orthogonal to the center, scale, and amplitude directions. The concentration scales are comparable, the limiting configuration satisfies the scale balance conditions, and the amplitudes vanish after multiplication by the logarithmic scale. Second, we determine the leading parameter defect in both critical decay regimes and prove that, along each fixed admissible path, all sufficiently large solutions lie in finitely many disjoint bubbling neighborhoods. Finally, assuming the leading coefficient is nonzero at every balanced critical configuration, the solution set at the fixed critical parameter is compact.
  These results provide the analytic foundation for studying the resonant degree via critical points at infinity.
