papers.title: The Popular Get More Popular: Auditing Brand Bias in Generative Search
papers.abstract: The shift from traditional to generative search has fundamentally transformed online product discovery. Because conversational recommendations synthesize choices into a few direct answers, subtle systemic preferences toward specific providers can exert profound commercial impacts. In this work, we audit this phenomenon through two distinct dimensions: (i) brand popularity bias, the systematic preference for market-dominant entities over long-tail alternatives, and (ii) brand familiarity bias, the ranking advantage an entity encoded in an LLM's parametric memory holds over an unfamiliar competitor. First, evaluating commercial queries across major engines, we observe persistent brand popularity bias: dominant brands in the top quintile are cited 1.4x to 2.8x more frequently than the average brand within a sample of 1,176 top market players, already present in parametric memory that external web retrieval fails to mitigate. Second, through controlled in-context experiments holding product attributes constant, we find that substituting authentic brand signatures with unfamiliar ones significantly degrades recommendation rank. Conversely, fact-preserving content rewrites yield negligible ranking gains. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that generative search engines reinforce a ``rich-get-richer'' dynamic by favoring established market leaders and imposing a parametric barrier to entry that standard content optimization cannot overcome.
papers.intro:
Chatbots and search engines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have shifted consumer product discovery from static URL ranking to conversational, fine-grained recommendations with synthesized justifications. Because users ascribe high credibility to these outputs and increasingly rely on them for everyday decisions (Spatharioti et al., 2025), generative search exerts substantial influence over consumer choice and market exposure. Auditing the mechanisms governing LLM-driven product recommendations is therefore of paramount importance.

Chatbots and search engines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have shifted consumer product discovery from static URL ranking to conversational, fine-grained recommendations with synthesized justifications. Because users ascribe high credibility to these outputs and increasingly rely on them for everyday decisions (Spatharioti et al., 2025), generative search exerts substantial influence over consumer choice and market exposure. Auditing the mechanisms governing LLM-driven product recommendations is therefore of paramount importance.

Because these instruments operate at a global scale, minor systematic biases in their generation logic can produce profound market effects, as brands prioritized by generative search engines might gain distinct commercial advantages. While model preferences may sometimes reflect genuine product superiority, it is critical to disentangle meritocratic selection from systemic model bias. Trained on massive Web corpora, LLMs inevitably inherit and amplify pre-existing statistical biases (Gallegos et al., 2024). While recent literature has audited LLMs for sociodemographic biases—including gender (Armstrong et al., 2024), ethnicity (Salinas et al., 2024), and social group (Kondapally et al., 2026)—as well as prompting biases like persona (Jack et al., 2026) and cognitive biases (Filandrianos et al., 2025), brand-level economic biases remain underexplored.

In this study, we formalize and audit two distinct dimensions of brand bias: (1) Brand Popularity Bias: The systematic preference of LLMs toward highly popular, high-market-share brands over long-tail or niche alternatives. Overrepresented in pre-training corpora, popular brands might enjoy a structural head start in user recommendations, which may create a “rich-get-richer” (or Matthew) effect (Merton, 1968). This could reduce the visibility of local or specialized competitors (Klimashevskaia et al., 2024; Mansoury et al., 2020). (2) Brand Familiarity Bias: The advantage a brand recognized within an LLM’s parametric memory holds, at equal content, over an unfamiliar or novel entrant. This dimension evaluates the algorithmic barrier to entry for newly emerging brands that lack pre-existing weight representations in frozen models.

On one hand, fair recommendation engines should evaluate product merit independently of brand prominence, benefiting both niche vendors through equal exposure and consumers through increased diversity. On the other hand, established brands often correlate with higher consumer trust, quality control, and widespread user satisfaction. papers.title: The obscured nucleus of NGC3256 S. I. Anisotropic AGN near-IR radiation field traced by CO v=1-0 with JWST/NIRSpec
papers.abstract: The southern nucleus of NGC3256, a nearby luminous infrared (IR) interacting system (d=40 Mpc; L(IR)=10^11.6 Lsun), hosts a deeply obscured low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) associated with a massive and fast bipolar collimated molecular outflow. JWST/NIRSpec observations revealed bright spatially resolved ro-vibrational CO v=1-0 4.67um emission at the base of this molecular outflow extending out to ~300pc, which is excited by the ~4.7um IR radiation from the southern dusty core. Using Monte Carlo radiative transfer (MCRT) models, we analyzed the CO v=1-0 band emission to determine the intensity of the ~4.7um IR radiation field across the outflow base. We find that the core spectral luminosity density at ~4.7um, as seen by the material in the outflow base, is ~2-4 times higher than that inferred along our line of sight, indicating an anisotropic near-IR radiation field. Moreover, the slower than d^-2 decrease of the near-IR flux density across the outflow base suggests a collimated radiation field, for which we estimate a small half-opening angle (15-20deg) and a diameter of the collimating structure of 15 +- 5 pc. This is slightly smaller than the diameter of the obscuring envelope (25 +- 5 pc). Combined with the expansion of this obscuring envelope, traced by the blueshifted CO v=1-0 absorption toward the nucleus, this suggests that the AGN is beginning to clear its environment. We estimate N_H~10^22-23 cm^-2 for NGC 3256 S, which is similar to that of Type 2 AGN. papers.intro:
Mergers of gas-rich galaxies funnel large quantities of gas and dust into their central regions, triggering intense star formation and active galactic nuclei (AGNs; e.g., Sanders & Mirabel 1996; Hopkins et al. 2013; Rodríguez Montero et al. 2019). This activity initially occurs in heavily dust-obscured environments, where ultraviolet and optical emission from young stars and the AGN is absorbed by dust and is re-emitted in the infrared (IR), leading to IR-bright galaxies with LIR>L_{\rm IR}>1011-12 L⊙L_{\rm\odot}, i.e., luminous and ultraluminous IR galaxies (LIRGs and ULIRGs). Among the most deeply embedded systems are compact obscured nuclei (CONs), with NHN_{\rm H}>1024-25 cm-2. CONs are characterized by their exceptionally compact and strong mid-IR radiation densities, which are capable of exciting submillimeter HCN-vib emission (Falstad et al. 2021; García-Bernete et al. 2025; González-Alfonso et al. 2026). As star formation- and AGN-driven feedback clears the obscuring dust and gas, ULIRGs, the most luminous systems, are thought to transition into quasars (e.g., Snyder et al. 2013; Kawaguchi et al. 2020). This clearing is consistent with the ubiquitous detection of massive molecular outflows in ULIRGs (Sturm et al. 2011; Veilleux et al. 2013; Cicone et al. 2014; González-Alfonso et al. 2017; Pereira-Santaella et al. 2018; Lutz et al. 2020; Lamperti et al. 2022).

The NGC 3256 system is an advanced merger (projected nuclear separation of <<1 kpc). The northern component is dominated by a strong starburst with a star formation rate of ∼\sim15 M⊙M_{\odot} yr-1 (Lira et al. 2008), which is not investigated in this paper. Similar to CONs, no high-ionization transitions or direct X-ray emission are detected in NGC 3256 S from the AGN (e.g., Lira et al. 2002; Alonso-Herrero et al. 2012; Pereira-Santaella et al. 2011; Pereira-Santaella et al. 2024a; García-Bernete et al. 2025). papers.title: Optimal Learning in Games with Arbitrary Delays: Best-of-Both-Worlds for Self-Play and Adversarial Opponents
papers.abstract: We study learning in zero-sum games with delayed feedback. We introduce Multi-Anchor Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (MAO-OMD), a single algorithm which obtains optimal fast rates in self-play on smooth games, while simultaneously maintaining minimax optimal guarantees against arbitrary opponents. In particular, in smooth zero-sum games with arbitrary and unknown feedback delays, MAO-OMD obtains $O(\sigma_{\max}+1)$ social and individual regrets when used by both players, where $\sigma_{\max}$ denotes the maximum number of outstanding gradients, while also guaranteeing minimax optimal $O(\sqrt{T+d_{\mathrm{tot}}})$ individual regret against arbitrary opponents, where $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total delay. Moreover, we show that these optimal rates cannot be obtained simultaneously using the standard black-box reduction to the undelayed setting. We also extend our results to multi-player games, and to games with player-dependent delay sequences.

Formally, let f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} be a smooth convex–concave function on nonempty, compact, convex action sets 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. We measure each player’s performance by its individual (external) regret, the difference between its cumulative loss and that of the best fixed action chosen in hindsight against the opponent’s realized actions. We also consider social regret, defined as the sum of the players’ individual regrets.

In the absence of delays, individual and social regret have been studied extensively [17, 7, 41, 56]. A classical result linking regret minimization to equilibrium computation shows that, in a two-player zero-sum game, a social regret bound of RTR_{T} guarantees that the players’ averaged strategies form an (RT/T)(R_{T}/T)-approximate Nash equilibrium [16]. Thus, standard no-regret algorithms with O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}) regret automatically yield an O⁡(1/T)O(1/\sqrt{T}) convergence rate. However, it is known that significantly faster rates can be achieved in self-play, where both players employ the same learning algorithm. In particular, when both players employ optimistic algorithms, which use a prediction of the forthcoming gradient when choosing the next action, the resulting dynamics can induce significantly faster convergence to equilibrium [9, 50, 51, 58]. In zero-sum matrix games, [51] established an O⁡((log⁡T)/T)O((\log T)/T) equilibrium convergence rate for optimistic mirror descent, while [58] further showed that optimistic algorithms achieve O⁡(1)O(1) social regret in general-sum games, yielding an O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) convergence rate in the zero-sum case. In general-sum games, [8] obtained improved bounds on external and swap regret, while [10, 2] proved bounds that depend only polylogarithmically on TT. Recent preprints have further established individual or swap regret bounds that are independent of TT in finite general-sum games [35, 1, 57, 36].

The key challenge in extending existing optimistic methods to delayed feedback is that delays break the mechanism behind their fast rates. Without delays, the prediction error of each round is controlled by the movement between consecutive actions; the stability term of the update, which regularizes toward the previous action, pays for exactly that movement. Under delays, however, a newly observed gradient may have been generated at an action played many rounds earlier, so its prediction error is controlled by the movement from that past action to the current one, which the stability term toward the previous action does not cover. papers.title: Sharp moderate deviations and uniform Berry--Esseen bounds for Hotelling's $T^2$-statistic via Stein's method
papers.abstract:
Let $\mathbf X_1,\ldots,\mathbf X_n$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ with common mean $\boldsymbol\mu_n$, where $d\ge2$ is a fixed integer. Let $\bar{\mathbf X}_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf X_i$ denote the sample mean and let \[ \widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (\mathbf X_i-\bar{\mathbf X}_n) (\mathbf X_i-\bar{\mathbf X}_n)^\top \] denote the sample covariance matrix. Assume that the average covariance matrix is positive definite and that $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is nonsingular almost surely. For testing $H_0:\boldsymbol\mu_n=\boldsymbol\mu_0$, the Hotelling statistic is \[ T^2_{H,n} =n(\bar{\mathbf X}_n-\boldsymbol\mu_0)^\top \widehat\Sigma_n^{-1} (\bar{\mathbf X}_n-\boldsymbol\mu_0). \] Under $H_0$, we establish finite-sample Cram\'er-type moderate deviation results and uniform Berry--Esseen bounds under finite $p$th moments for $2<p\le3$. The moderate deviation error order is optimal over independent triangular arrays, as shown by explicit constructions. For identically distributed observations with a fixed distribution, we obtain \[ \sup_{0\le x\le b_n} \left| \frac{\mathbb P(T^2_{H,n}\ge x^2)} {\mathbb P(\chi_d^2\ge x^2)}-1 \right| =
O\!\left((1+b_n)^p n^{-(p-2)/2}\right) \] for every nonnegative sequence $b_n=o(n^{(p-2)/(2p)})$. The uniform Berry--Esseen bound is $O(n^{-(p-2)/2})$. The proof uses a radial Stein identity and a recursive error estimate. We apply the results to chi-squared calibration in simultaneous testing.
papers.intro:
Hotelling’s T2T^{2}-statistic is a standard tool for inference on a multivariate mean. It combines the sample mean and sample covariance matrix into an affine-invariant statistic and is commonly calibrated by a chi-squared distribution in fixed dimension. The accuracy of this calibration determines the accuracy of the resulting critical values, confidence regions, and pp-values. When many hypotheses are tested, the relevant tail probabilities can be very small. An approximation that is accurate in absolute terms may then give a substantial error in the ratio of the true and approximating tail probabilities. This distinction motivates both Berry–Esseen bounds, which control the difference between distribution functions, and Cramér-type moderate deviation results, which control the ratio of tail probabilities; see Fan et al. (2007) and Liu and Shao (2013) for their role in simultaneous testing.

The scalar theory provides a natural starting point. Shao (1999) established a Cramér-type moderate deviation result for Student’s statistic under a finite third absolute moment. Jing et al. (2003) obtained quantitative results for self-normalized sums of independent random variables under finite (2+δ)(2+\delta)th moments, 0<δ≤10<\delta\leq 1. A systematic account is given by de la Peña et al. (2009). papers.title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for the self-normalized central limit theorem for independent triangular arrays
papers.abstract: For a rowwise independent triangular array $\{X_{n,i}:1\le i\le n\}$, put $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i}$ and $V_n^2=\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i}^2$. We prove that $S_n/V_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm d}{\mathrm N}(0,1)$ implies $\max_{i\le n}|X_{n,i}|/V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0$. The same assumption gives $V_n^2/b_n^2\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}1$ for any choice of medians $b_n^2$ of $V_n^2$. Combined with the results of Shao (2018), this yields necessary and sufficient conditions for the self-normalized central limit theorem and resolves his conjecture for independent sequences. The proof identifies the joint limits of the sum and its sum of squares, then uses the standard normal ratio to remove every non-Gaussian component.

papers.title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines
papers.abstract: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.

papers.title: When Less is More: Emerging Network-Wide Use Cases for Hollow-Core Fibers in Optical Networks [Invited]
papers.abstract: Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF) is emerging as a disruptive technology for next-generation optical networks, offering 30\% lower propagation latency than standard Single-Mode Fiber (SMF), record-low attenuation (0.05-0.1 dB/km), and nonlinearities reduced by three to four orders of magnitude. While the physical-layer benefits of HCF have been extensively demonstrated, recent industrial commitments by hyperscalers (e.g., Microsoft, Amazon) and the rapid maturation of nested antiresonant nodeless fibers (NANF) call for a systematic assessment of the impact of HCF at the network level. Building on a series of prior contributions, we overview four emerging network-wide use cases for the selective deployment of HCF in hybrid SMF/HCF networks: (i) latency-constrained Edge Data Center (edgeDC) consolidation; (ii) energy-efficient high-power amplification; (iii) capacity scaling via single-fiber bidirectional (BiDi) transmission; and (iv) coexistence of classical and quantum (QKD) channels. Consolidated results across realistic metro, national, and continental topologies convey a unifying message: in each use case, a selective HCF upgrade captures a significant share of the achievable benefit compared to a network overhaul. The required HCF budget is use-case-specific, i.e., 6-24\% of the total network fiber length for edgeDC consolidation (up to 50\% fewer edgeDCs), 40\% of the network links for QKD/classical coexistence (up to 38\% fewer quantum modules), and 40-60\% of the network links for energy-efficient capacity scaling via BiDi-HCF (up to 28\% lower network power per Tbps and 70\% more served traffic, at half the HCF strand count of a unidirectional HCF upgrade), whereas for energy-efficient high-power amplification the gain keeps growing with the HCF budget (up to 60\% lower network power per Tbps at the national scale) and what saturates is the benefit of increasing the EDFA output power.
papers.intro:
Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF) represents a paradigm shift in optical communications, overcoming the fundamental limits of solid-core silica fibers. While the concept of guiding light in an air core was demonstrated in the late 1990s [33], the recent advances in Nested Antiresonant Nodeless Fibers (NANF) have allowed HCF to surpass the long-standing attenuation records of standard Single-Mode Fibers (SMF), reaching values between 0.05 and 0.1 dB/km [41, 10, 13]. Beyond the hero transmission loss, HCF offers additional distinctive characteristics: (i) a propagation latency that is 30% lower than SMF (because light propagates in air rather than silica), and (ii) nonlinearity that is reduced by three to four orders of magnitude with respect to SMF [43].

Beyond the hero transmission loss, HCF offers additional distinctive characteristics: (i) a propagation latency that is 30% lower than SMF (because light propagates in air rather than silica), and (ii) nonlinearity that is reduced by three to four orders of magnitude with respect to SMF [43].

These properties have moved HCF from a laboratory curiosity to a strategic technology in industrial roadmaps. In 2022, Microsoft acquired Lumenisity, a pioneer in HCF manufacturing, and in 2025 announced plans to scale production through partnerships with Corning and Heraeus [3, 4]. In parallel, Amazon Web Services has outlined a roadmap for the integration of HCF in key Availability Zones to support latency-sensitive workloads, in particular AI-driven traffic [8], and China Mobile has demonstrated HCF deployment for Data Center Interconnects (DCI) [56]. The wave of industrial interest is matched by increased academic activity, with HCF-related contributions at top optical-communication venues such as OFC and ECOC, and an emerging set of network-wide studies [43, 30, 2, 39, 12, 11, 59, 60].

The wave of industrial interest is matched by increased academic activity, with HCF-related contributions at top optical-communication venues such as OFC and ECOC, and an emerging set of network-wide studies [43, 30, 2, 39, 12, 11, 59, 60].

While fiber design, fabrication processes, and physical-layer transmission experiments have been demonstrated [41], the focus is now shifting towards the complete network ecosystem, raising the question: how and where should HCF be deployed in optical networks? This is a non-trivial question because: 1) HCF is unlikely to fully replace SMF in the medium term, due to the limited production capacity, the immaturity of the supply chain, and the still-high (and uncertain) cost per km. Therefore, hybrid SMF/HCF networks, where HCF is used selectively on a subset of links, are the most plausible deployment scenario; 2) The selection of which links to upgrade may depend on the targeted use case: minimizing the number of edge data centers (edgeDCs) under latency constraints may lead to upgrade patterns that are different from those that minimize energy per bit or maximize served traffic; and 3) Different use cases may benefit from different HCF types (e.g., low-attenuation HCF for capacity scaling, low-noise/wideband HCF for QKD coexistence, low-backscatter HCF for bidirectional transmission), suggesting that, unlike SMF (where ITU-T G.652 dominates), HCF deployment may be intrinsically segment- and use-case-specific.

papers.title: Heat Transport Mechanisms in MOF-5
papers.abstract: We find that MOF-5 supports both long-lived phonons and linker vibrations whose split spectra signal a breakdown of the phonon quasiparticle approximation. Combining mode-projected molecular dynamics spectra with spectral Wigner heat transport, we resolve two contrasting transport channels: low-frequency particle-like phonon propagation decreases strongly from 200 to 500 K, whereas wave-like phonon coherence remains nearly constant and supplies about half the intrinsic conductivity at 500 K. A phenomenological extrinsic scattering model provides a plausible explanation for the discrepancy between calculated and measured conductivities in terms of both its magnitude and temperature dependence. We also identify signatures of phonon quasiparticle breakdown in the linker vibrations of ZIF-8 and HKUST-1, indicating that this feature extends to other metal-organic frameworks.

papers.title: Connectivity in a New Bounded-Space Dynamic Model
papers.abstract:
We introduce a new model for dynamic algorithms in which the algorithm has read-only oracle access to a dynamically changing input and random access to its own bounded workspace. It is a dynamic analogue of the time-space tradeoffs for static inputs studied in complexity theory, where only writable memory counts as space. We study dynamic undirected $s$-$t$ connectivity: after every edge update to an $n$-vertex graph, an algorithm with $S$ words of workspace must report whether $s$ and $t$ are connected. The graph is accessed via adjacency list queries (degree, $j$-th neighbor) or adjacency matrix queries.
  Our algorithms are randomized; our lower bounds hold for randomized algorithms with $cn$ bits of workspace, $c>0$ a small constant ($cn/\log n$ for the worst-case matrix bound). We prove: (1) With adjacency lists, worst-case time $\tilde\Theta(n^2/S^2)$ per insertion is necessary and sufficient for incremental algorithms. (2) With an adjacency matrix, worst-case time $\tilde\Omega(n^2/S)$ per insertion is necessary for incremental algorithms, and sufficient for $S\ge\sqrt{n}$. (3) With amortization, incremental algorithms achieve $\tilde O(n/S)$ time per insertion with adjacency lists and $\tilde O(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, while $\tilde\Omega(\sqrt{n/S})$ and $\tilde\Omega(n\sqrt{n/S})$, respectively, are necessary. (4) Fully dynamic algorithms need amortized time $\tilde\Omega(n/S)$ per update with adjacency lists and $\tilde\Omega(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, even on forests, where both bounds are tight (lists: under bounded degree).
  Conventional dynamic connectivity admits polylogarithmic update time with $\Omega(n)$ words of space. In contrast, our lower bounds show that polynomial update time is necessary whenever $S\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$, even for a single pair of vertices and even for incremental algorithms with amortized guarantees.

Undirected ss–tt connectivity, the problem of deciding whether two given vertices of a graph lie in the same connected component, is one of the most basic problems in both algorithms and complexity theory. In complexity theory, it has long been the main problem in the study of deterministic logarithmic space. Aleliunas et al. [4] use random walks to solve it in randomized logarithmic space, and Lewis and Papadimitriou [57] showed that it is complete for symmetric logarithmic space (𝖲𝖫\mathsf{SL}). A long sequence of deterministic algorithms using ever less space [79, 68, 67, 7, 86] culminated in Reingold’s celebrated theorem [77] that undirected ss–tt connectivity can be solved in deterministic logarithmic space, and 𝖲𝖫=𝖫\mathsf{SL}=\mathsf{L}.

This combination arises when a graph is owned by one system and monitored by another. The owner stores and maintains the graph as part of an application’s data, while a separate monitor with limited private memory is notified of each update and can inspect the graph, but may not annotate it or build an unrestricted auxiliary index: the graph is read-only to the monitor, even though its owner keeps modifying it. For example, a network-management system maintains a topology of bidirectional links that changes as links fail and recover, and a monitoring task with a small memory allocation must track whether two designated sites are connected. Similarly, a data-integration pipeline accepts links asserting that two records describe the same entity, and an auditor must raise an alarm as soon as a chain of accepted links joins two records known to describe different entities; this problem is incremental unless links can later be withdrawn. In both cases the relation is symmetric, so the graph is undirected, the pair to monitor is fixed in advance, and the monitor is responsible for a single bit, whereas conventional connectivity data structures maintain the entire partition into components. Appendix A discusses such scenarios in more detail.

Our setting restricts the monitor’s memory in two ways: it limits both the information the monitor can retain between updates and the scratch space it can use while processing a single update. All persistent summaries, random seeds, caches, and temporary computation count toward the budget; in particular, any information about past updates, such as component labels or a log of the updates, must be kept in this memory. What the monitor can do is reread the graph, exactly as the static small-space algorithms do. The difference is that a static algorithm answers a single query about a single graph, whereas the monitor must answer after every update and cannot afford to start from scratch each time. The tension between retaining and recovering information is the time–space tradeoff we study: How much time per update is needed to maintain ss–tt connectivity in a changing graph with S≪nS\ll n words of writable memory, given read access to the current graph? The answer depends on the interface through which the graph can be inspected. We consider the two standard ones. In the adjacency-matrix model (the matrix model for short), the algorithm can ask whether two given vertices are adjacent. In the adjacency-list model (the list model), it can instead ask for the degree of a vertex and for its jjth neighbor. A system that supports only pairwise edge tests need not support neighbor enumeration, and comparing the two models asks how trading pairwise tests for neighbor enumeration changes the private memory needed for efficient dynamic algorithms in our model. Each such query is an input probe and costs unit time. Section 1.1 defines the model precisely, and Figure 1 illustrates it.

papers.title: Adversarially Robust Streaming Algorithms for $(k, z)$-Clustering
papers.abstract: We design adversarially robust algorithms for dynamic geometric streams that $(1 + \epsilon)$-approximate $k$-Median and $k$-Means in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, using $\tilde{O}(kd \mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1}))$ space. This result significantly improves a recent $O(d\log n)$-approximation for $k$-Median [Gribelyuk, Lin, Woodruff, Yu, and Zhou, FOCS 2026], and is furthermore the first algorithm whose space is linear in $kd$, even in the oblivious (non-adaptive) setting. We develop several new techniques which may be of independent interest, including a new data-oblivious Euclidean primitive called hierarchical Lipschitz assignment, a robust dimensionality reduction for clustering, and a robust streaming algorithm for inner-product queries.

In the model of dynamic geometric streams, introduced by Indyk [Ind04], the input PP is presented as a stream of point insertions and deletions from the integer grid [Δ]d[\Delta]^{d}, and the algorithm has to produce an output after each update. As usual, we denote n=|P|n=|P| and assume for simplicity that Δ=poly⁡(n)\Delta=\operatorname{poly}(n), and our primary goal is to design space-efficient algorithms. In the clustering literature, the output of a streaming algorithm is usually an ε\varepsilon-coreset [HM04], which is actually stronger than reporting a solution. A coreset is a (reweighted) subset P′⊆PP^{\prime}\subseteq P, such that the cost of every center set CC evaluated on P′P^{\prime} is a (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon)-approximation to that on the dataset PP. Such a summary often provides a stronger guarantee than reporting a single approximate solution, since a coreset can be used to evaluate arbitrary center sets and recover an approximately optimal one.

In this work, we focus on streaming algorithms for (k,z)(k,z)-Clustering that are adversarially robust, meaning that each stream update can depend on the algorithm’s outputs so far, i.e., an adversary can choose the input to be adaptive to the output stream. This is in contrast to the classical model of an oblivious adversary that chooses the entire input stream before the algorithm is run. The adaptive-adversary setting is important in applications where decisions based on the algorithmic outputs influence how future data is generated or collected. For example, placing temporary facilities at the reported cluster centers can influence future customer demand, making the input stream adaptive. This setting was introduced to the streaming model by [BY20, BJWY22], and is known to have fundamental importance in other computational models, such as dynamic algorithms [Waj20, BKM+22, BDP+25] and data structures [CN20, CLN+22, CSW+23, AC24].

Designing adversarially robust streaming algorithms is a central challenge that has attracted substantial attention [MBN+17, AMYZ19, BY20, BHM+21, ABJ+22, BJWY22, BEO22, BKM+22, CGS22, ACGS23, PR23, WZZ23, FJW24, WZ24, BOS26, GKSY26, LSW+26]; see [WZ26] for a survey. A major obstacle is that linear sketching, a powerful technique for dynamic streams, faces fundamental limitations against adaptive adversaries, even for basic estimation problems [HW13, GLW+24, GLW+25]. Consequently, the problem of frequency moment estimation, which is foundational to the area of streaming algorithms, has been a long-standing open question until a recent breakthrough mitigated it via a novel non-linear sketching approach [GLW+26b, GLW+26a]. Our work on clustering, which is a geometric optimization problem, can be viewed as a natural next step of going beyond frequency statistics.

These streaming algorithms output an ε\varepsilon-coresets using space that is comparable to the coreset size, which is nearly optimal. For oblivious adversaries, the rich line of results on coresets [HM04, HK07, Che09, FL11, FSS20, CSS21, CLSS22, BCP+24, HLW24] readily implies algorithms for insertion-only streams via the merge-and-reduce framework [HM04]. These streaming algorithms output an ε\varepsilon-coresets using space that is comparable to the coreset size, which is nearly optimal. For dynamic streams (which include deletion of points), the merge-and-reduce framework is inapplicable, yet both kk-Median and kk-Means have algorithms, via more ad-hoc methods, that output ε\varepsilon-coresets using O⁡(k​poly⁡(ε−1​d​log⁡Δ))O(k\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon^{-1}d\log\Delta)) space [BFL+17, SYZ18]. For the adaptive-adversary setting there is only one known algorithm, that achieves a much larger approximation ratio O⁡(d​log⁡Δ)O(d\log\Delta) using poly⁡(k​d​log⁡Δ)\operatorname{poly}(kd\log\Delta) space, works only for kk-Median, and only finds a solution rather than a coreset [GLW+26a].

Bridging this gap between oblivious and adaptive adversaries introduces significant technical difficulties. Previous clustering algorithms for oblivious-adversary streaming return not only a center set but also a coreset [BFL+17, SYZ18]. This is not possible with an adaptive adversary, as it can delete the coreset points and force the algorithm to eventually report all the data points, which clearly requires linear (in nn) space, and therefore we must seek an alternative to the coreset approach. Furthermore, existing methods for clustering in dynamic streams are based on linear sketches and sampling, which usually cannot work with adaptive adversary. Hence, we need fundamentally new techniques.

This guarantee follows immediately from our main result (Theorem 1.3), which gives an adversarially robust streaming algorithm for maintaining a cost oracle. Informally, a cost oracle is a data structure that estimates the clustering cost of any center set CC given as a query; see Definition 1.2 for the formal definition. A cost oracle is clearly stronger than an approximate solution (a center set), as achieved in Theorem 1.1, because one can enumerate all feasible solutions, query the oracle for their cost, and report the one of minimum cost. papers.title: Counting over Unbreakable Decompositions: A Single-Exponential Parameterized Algorithm for Minimum Bisection
papers.abstract: The Minimum Bisection problem asks whether an $n$-vertex graph can be split into two halves with at most $k$ edges between them. We give a single exponential time algorithm for minimum bisection, running in time $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$. This improves the previous bound of $2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}$ due to Cygan, Komosa, Lokshtanov, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, Saurabh, and Wahlstr\"om (TALG 2021). Our algorithm counts solutions instead of only finding if one exists. We show that our dynamic program can be implemented on top of an unbreakable decomposition using algebraic techniques. Along the way, we compute in time $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$ a tree decomposition with adhesions of size at most $2k$ whose bags are $(3k,k)$-edge-unbreakable inside their own subtrees.

papers.intro:
Graph partitioning problems ask to cut a graph into parts with few edges between them, subject to a constraint on the parts. When the constraint is local, such as separating given terminals, parameterized algorithms are well understood. Important separators of Marx [25] and their refinements give fast algorithms for Multiway Cut [25, 8] and for a whole family of related problems [10, Chapter 8]. Global constraints are less well understood. The most prominent example is Minimum Bisection: given a graph GG on nn vertices and an integer kk, can V⁡(G)V(G) be split into two sets of sizes ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor and ⌈n/2⌉\lceil n/2\rceil with at most kk edges between them?

Feige and Krauthgamer gave the first polylogarithmic approximation [14, 15], Räcke obtained an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-approximation [28], and Khot showed that there is no PTAS unless NP⊆⋂ε>0BPTIME⁡(2nε)\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\mathrm{BPTIME}(2^{n^{\varepsilon}}) [21].

Parameterized by the cut size kk, the complexity of Minimum Bisection remained open for a long time, and the reason is precisely the global constraint. Recursive understanding, developed by Grohe, Kawarabayashi, Marx, and Wollan [17] and by Kawarabayashi and Thorup [20], and the randomized contractions of Chitnis, Cygan, Hajiaghayi, Pilipczuk, and Pilipczuk [9] solve many cut problems by recursion. They find a part of the graph with a small boundary, solve the problem inside it, and replace it by a small equivalent gadget. What remains is highly connected, in the sense that every cut of size at most kk has a small side, and there color coding [1] finishes the job. For Minimum Bisection the recursive step fails: whether a part can be replaced depends on the sizes of all other parts. Cygan, Lokshtanov, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, and Saurabh [12] circumvented this with unbreakable tree decompositions, tree decompositions with small adhesions whose bags are highly connected in the above sense. A dynamic program over such a decomposition handles the global constraint by indexing its tables with sizes. Unbreakable decompositions have since become a standard tool, for example for Min kk-Cut [24] and Fair Bisection [19], and they can now be even computed in linear time [2, 22].

papers.title: Combinatorics of noncommutative harmonic oscillator determinant
papers.abstract: We obtain an explicit evaluation of the determinants that appear in the denominators of the integrands for the iterated integrals expressing special values of the spectral zeta function of the noncommutative harmonic oscillator at integers greater than 1. The determinants in question are those of cyclic tridiagonal matrices; their explicit evaluation is carried out, in addition to the inclusion-exclusion principle, conceptionally using combinatorial arguments based on monomer-dimer systems. This explicit evaluation serves as a core component in the study of arithmetic properties such as the modularity of the special values of the spectral zeta function.

Originally defined by Isidor Rabi in 1936, the model’s integrability was finally demonstrated in 2011 by D. Braak [1]. papers.title: The Short Pulse equation on the half lines: a Riemann--Hilbert approach
papers.abstract: In this work, we analyze the initial boundary value (IBV) problems for the Short Pulse (SP) equation $u_{xt}=u+\frac{1}{6}(u^3)_{xx}$ (classical solutions) on the half-lines $x\ge 0$ and $x\le 0$ under the condition of sufficient decay as $x\to +\infty$ or as $x\to -\infty$. Using the Riemann--Hilbert (RH) problem approach, we show that these two IBV problems differ substantially regarding the boundary values required for problems to be well-posed. Namely, the solution of the ``right problem'' ($x\ge 0$) is uniquely determined by the initial data $u(x,0)$, $x\ge 0$ alone, whereas for the ``left problem'' ($x\le 0$), two boundary functions $u(0,t)$ and $u_x(0,t)$ have to be prescribed, together with the initial data, for a well-posed problem.

Introduced approximately fifty years ago, the Inverse Scattering Transform (IST) provides a rigorous analytic framework for solving a distinguished class of one-dimensional nonlinear evolution equations, often referred to as integrable equations. The IST method is fundamentally built on the analysis of an associated Lax pair, a pair of linear operators that typically depend on a spectral parameter and whose compatibility condition yields the nonlinear equation [13, 27, 2, 1]. Originally developed for initial-value problems on the real line with rapidly decaying data, the method reduces the direct spectral analysis to a classical scattering problem, while the inverse step, addressing the reconstruction of the solution from scattering data, is traditionally formulated via the Gelfand–Levitan–Marchenko (GLM) integral equations [20] or, alternatively, as a Riemann–Hilbert (RH) factorization problem in the complex spectral plane [26].

Extending the IST to nonlinear evolution equations posed on domains with boundaries, such as the half-line or finite intervals, introduces substantial analytical challenges stemming from the incorporation of boundary conditions. These difficulties were effectively addressed by the development of the Unified Transform Method (UTM), also known as the Fokas Method, introduced by Fokas in [10] and subsequently advanced by many authors [11, 5, 9, 6, 14]. The UTM generalizes the IST by simultaneously analyzing both equations of the Lax pair, and a central component of the method is the global relation, which links the spectral functions associated with the initial and boundary data.

In such contexts, spatial boundaries represent physical interfaces, where wave profiles are generated or prescribed. papers.title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Dependent Graph Classes
papers.abstract: Monadically dependent graph classes are those in which first-order logic cannot encode all graphs. They include all nowhere dense classes and all classes of bounded twin-width. We show that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically dependent graph class. Together with the known hardness result for hereditary classes that are not monadically dependent, this gives a complete characterization of the hereditary graph classes with fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking. This resolves a central open problem in algorithmic model theory. Our proof combines ideas from structural graph theory (graph decompositions), finite model theory (locality of first-order logic), and model theory (counting types). In particular, we show that in monadically dependent classes, tuples of fixed length have only $|U|^{O(1)}$ types of fixed quantifier rank over any set of parameters $U$.

papers.title: Domain-specific information retrieval
papers.abstract: Information Retrieval (IR) is much more than ad hoc web search: a large portion of the information seeking activities takes place in specific domains, often addressing work-related tasks. Examples are lawyers finding relevant prior cases for a legal case and academic researchers studying the background material for a paper. In Chapter 2 we outline the most common domain-specific tasks, datasets and applications. Domain-specific IR has a number of challenges that make set it apart from simple web search tasks: they often deal with long documents, long queries and long sessions with specific user needs. We discuss these in Chapter 3. We also address issues related to bias and fairness of models. In Chapter 4, we describe the models and methods developed for domain-specific tasks and data, addressing the specific challenges, including user aspects related to domain-specific IR tasks, dealing with queries, user models, and user interactions. We show that many of the methodological advances in domain-specific IR are transferable to other domains and even to open-domain web search. We conclude with the main takeaways and propose research directions for the near future.

papers.title: A centroaffine perspective on improved Brascamp--Lieb and dimensional Brunn--Minkowski inequalities
papers.abstract: We study dimensional concavity properties of even log-concave measures within the framework of weighted centroaffine differential geometry. We express the relevant local concavity inequalities in terms of a weighted Hilbert--Brunn--Minkowski operator and establish an anisotropic Poincar\'e inequality for odd functions and a strengthened Brascamp--Lieb inequality for even functions. As applications, we obtain quantitative dimensional concavity estimates for a class of geometric measures and measures with pinched Hessian, extending results of Cordero-Erausquin and Rotem for rotationally invariant measures and Eskenazis and Moschidis for the Gaussian measure.

papers.title: Cubic Optimization over Three Nonnegative Integers Is NP-hard
papers.abstract: We prove that deciding whether an integer cubic polynomial takes a value at most one over three nonnegative integers is NP-hard. Hardness holds even when every feasible objective value is a positive integer, so every constructed instance has a finite, attained minimum. This establishes a sharp dimension boundary for the tractability of cubic integer optimization in fixed dimension. Our reduction from positive 1-in-3 satisfiability encodes Boolean constraints as modular conditions and uses an algebraic norm to construct a cubic objective whose minimum is one exactly for satisfiable formulas. The resulting six-parameter threshold language is NP-complete and admits short exponent certificates.

papers.intro:
The complexity of integer polynomial optimization depends on both the degree of the objective and the number of variables. Lenstra [5] proved that integer linear optimization over rational polyhedra is polynomial-time solvable in every fixed dimension. For quadratic objectives, recent preprints by Wei [10] and by Ari and Hildebrand [1, Theorem 1.1] independently establish polynomial-time solvability in every fixed dimension. Their algorithms allow indefinite rational objectives and unbounded rational polyhedra.

papers.title: Modular Parameterized Model Checking of Threshold-Based Distributed Algorithms
papers.abstract: We present a novel approach for model checking fault-tolerant distributed algorithms: instead of building large, monolithic algorithm models, we propose a modular approach where the user decomposes the algorithm into modules, verifies them individually, and replaces them with a synchronous abstraction. To enable our technique, we introduce a new system model that combines aspects of threshold automata and global synchronization protocols. We investigate the expressiveness of our new model, and present a (bounded) model checking procedure as well as a method for checking the correctness of the abstraction step. We implemented the technique and report on promising experimental results on a case study

papers.intro:
Large-scale distributed systems, such as cloud platforms or blockchain systems, increasingly form the backbone of much of our industry and society. Bugs or failures in these systems can lead to significant harm, which encouraged a wide range of efforts to formally verify their correctness [29, 31, 43, 48, 56, 47, 46].

Bugs or failures in these systems can lead to significant harm, which encouraged a wide range of efforts to formally verify their correctness [29, 31, 43, 48, 56, 47, 46].

However, the task remains challenging because of the intrinsic complexity of the setting. Distributed systems and their underlying algorithms are usually required to scale to an arbitrary number of participants. Since the probability of a failure in such a system increases with the number of components, to be practical, distributed algorithms also need to be fault-tolerant. In settings like blockchain protocols, where arbitrary untrusted nodes can join, the algorithms need to withstand arbitrary failures referred to as Byzantine failures [42].

In settings like blockchain protocols, where arbitrary untrusted nodes can join, the algorithms need to withstand arbitrary failures referred to as Byzantine failures [42].

One of the main techniques for verifying the correctness of distributed algorithms is parameterized model checking [23, 8, 1], where the number of participants is treated as a parameter and verification is conducted for any parameter value. Even though the parameterized model checking problem (PMCP) is undecidable in general [2], even for very restricted classes of systems [53], many system classes for which the problem is decidable have been identified [26, 22, 18, 19]. In particular, threshold automata (TA) [37, 38, 36] provide a framework for the modeling and verification of (threshold-based) distributed algorithms with Byzantine fault-tolerance, where processes communicate via shared variables to model message-passing, and decisions can depend on these shared variables meeting certain (parametric) threshold values. TA have been used to verify correctness of a wide range of consensus and broadcast algorithms [11, 45, 10, 34, 6, 12, 35].

A major challenge of parameterized model checking is the requirement to create a faithful model of the algorithm under consideration. Since distributed algorithms can be very complex, the resulting models can become so large that they are effectively impossible to understand or mechanically verify, even in a decidable fragment. A potential solution to this problem is to model such systems at different levels of granularity in order to keep the verification problem manageable at every separate level.

Global synchronization protocols (GSPs) [30, 31, 32] are a suitable high-level model for (applications built on) distributed algorithms, abstracting from individual message passing between processes by summarizing the result as a synchronous global step.11 1 Note that this is different from synchronous threshold automata [50, 51, 52], where processes execute in lock-step, but the algorithm is still modeled on the level of individual message passing. However, modeling an application as a GSP requires hard trade-offs in precision. In particular, the effects of Byzantine failures are not modeled explicitly, but are assumed to be completely encapsulated in synchronous steps. Moreover, modeling on different levels of precision requires additional correctness arguments connecting the different levels, which may be hard to obtain.

To facilitate truly modular parameterized model checking, this work proposes a system model that supports both fine-grained modeling of individual process steps and high-level synchronous steps, with explicit support of Byzantine faults. This enables the modeling of complex applications at different levels of abstraction within the same framework, using synchronous module abstraction to replace multiple asynchronous steps by one synchronous step. We determine conditions under which parameterized model checking problems in our setting are decidable, and show how to automatically verify the correctness of a synchronous module abstraction. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first modular parameterized model checking approach that directly supports different levels of abstraction, and automatically produces a correctness argument for the abstraction.

In this paper, we introduce the model of threshold automata with synchronous actions, which is an extension of TA with global steps that are inspired by GSPs, but adapted to a setting with shared variables and Byzantine fault-tolerance (Section 3). We argue that this will be the case for many of our intended applications.

papers.title: Should We Pay This Much for Robustness? Efficient Proxy Certificates with Marginal Guarantees
papers.abstract: Modern classifiers remain sensitive to small input perturbations, while strong model-agnostic robustness certificates such as randomized smoothing are often too expensive for deployment, requiring an extensive number (e.g. 2000) of model forward passes per input. We propose a framework that delegates certification to a cheap proxy function while statistically controlling its deviation from the original sound certificate. Given an exchangeable unlabeled calibration set, we tune the proxy via robust conformal risk control to guarantee a bounded marginal (rather than pointwise) false-approval rate: the probability, over future inputs, that the proxy accepts an input whose prediction is flipped due to perturbation. The resulting proxy certificate can be used either as a standalone marginal certificate or as a fallback mechanism that invokes the expensive certificate only when the proxy rejects. We provide both single-sample and sample-heavy calibration recipes. Empirically, as a standalone certificate our method reduces the test-time certification cost to a single model forward while retaining much of the certified performance of randomized smoothing at small radii, and as a fallback it recovers the certified ratio of randomized smoothing at a more modest speedup. This enables cheap yet effective robustness guarantees for larger architectures such as vision transformers and language models.

papers.intro:
High accuracy alone is not sufficient for reliability in machine learning. Although modern neural networks achieve strong empirical performance, their predictions can be highly sensitive to small, often imperceptible, input perturbations (Goodfellow et al., 2014). This sensitivity can be exploited by adversaries to easily degrade the model’s performance. There are many empirical, and heuristic defenses proposed in the literature which have been circumvented by stronger or adaptive attacks (Athalye et al., 2018). A principled way to address this issue is to use robustness certificates, which provide formal guarantees that the model prediction remains invariant within a predefined perturbation set. Certificates can be viewed as binary decision rules: when they certify an input at a sufficiently large radius, they signal that the prediction can be trusted with respect to the specified threat model, whether the input is clean or even if adversarially perturbed, the perturbation is not effective.

Existing robustness certificates typically obtain such guarantees through architecture-specific verification methods, such as convex relaxations, or mixed-integer programming (Wong and Kolter, 2018; Katz et al., 2017; Tjeng et al., 2019). While powerful, these methods require white-box access to the model, and often need to be adapted when new architectures or layers are introduced. Alternatively, randomized smoothing (RS) (Cohen et al., 2019) wraps around any black-box classifier, and convolves it with a noise augmentation. The resulting smoothed classifier changes slowly with local perturbations. Hence, one can derive closed-form model-agnostic bounds on its change. This black-box nature is a major practical advantage, allowing it to easily apply to large modern networks, and even to API-accessible systems (Carlini et al., 2022). However, randomized smoothing-based certificates require a large number of model forward passes (e.g. 2×1032\times 10^{3}) to estimate the smoothed class probabilities with high confidence, which can be prohibitively expensive especially with limited resources, or when the model itself is expensive to evaluate.

papers.title: Overview of the NTCIR-19 SciClaimEval Task: Cross-modal Claim Verification in Scientific Papers
papers.abstract: This paper presents an overview of \emph{SciClaimEval}, a pilot task at NTCIR-19 on verifying scientific claims against the tables and figures of the papers in which they appear. Our dataset pairs authentic claims from 180 papers in machine learning, natural language processing, and medicine with contrastive versions of their tables and figures, one supporting the claim and one minimally modified so that it does not. The task comprises two subtasks: deciding whether a piece of evidence supports a claim, and selecting which of two evidence versions does. Twenty-two teams registered, the highest number among NTCIR-19 tasks, and 14 submitted 177 runs. Most systems built on multimodal large language models, relying on prompting and multi-stage inference rather than task-specific fine-tuning. On the first subtask, the best systems reached 98.1\% pair accuracy, but all six top-ranked systems relied on the contrastive pairs; the best system that judged each claim-evidence pair on its own scored 24.3 points lower. Open-weight models, embedded in carefully designed pipelines, matched proprietary ones. Yet verifying a single claim against its evidence, the setting that matters in practice, remains an open problem.

papers.intro:
Scientific papers make claims that should be supported by the evidence they present, typically results reported in tables and figures. Scientific claim verification asks whether a claim is adequately supported by this evidence (Wadden et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2023). Unlike general fact-checking (Thorne et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020), which verifies claims against external knowledge, it focuses on the internal consistency between a paper’s claims and its own evidence. Checking this consistency is a fundamental part of peer review, yet it is time-consuming and increasingly difficult as submission volumes grow. Automatic verification could assist reviewers, help authors find unsupported claims before submission, and ultimately improve the reliability of published research.

Scientific claim verification asks whether a claim is adequately supported by this evidence (Wadden et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2023). Unlike general fact-checking (Thorne et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020), which verifies claims against external knowledge, it focuses on the internal consistency between a paper’s claims and its own evidence. Checking this consistency is a fundamental part of peer review, yet it is time-consuming and increasingly difficult as submission volumes grow. Automatic verification could assist reviewers, help authors find unsupported claims before submission, and ultimately improve the reliability of published research.

Existing datasets for scientific claim verification differ mainly in the evidence they consider. Tables are the most common, either in structured formats such as JSON or XML, as in SciTab (Lu et al., 2023), SEM-TAB-FACTs (Wang et al., 2021), and SciAtomicBench (Zhang et al., 2025), or as images, as in MMSci-Eval (Yang et al., 2025). Others turn to figures, such as MuSciClaims (Lal et al., 2025), whose figures often contain complex subplots and embedded tables, while SciVer (Wang et al., 2025) considers multiple charts, tables, and text paragraphs as evidence. Despite this progress, three limitations remain. Refuted examples are usually created by editing the claim, for instance by flipping its meaning, which can leave surface cues that models exploit instead of reasoning over the evidence. Many datasets also rely on claims that are not taken directly from scientific papers. Finally, tables are typically available in a single format, so it remains unclear how well models handle the same content across different representations.

Others turn to figures, such as MuSciClaims (Lal et al., 2025), whose figures often contain complex subplots and embedded tables, while SciVer (Wang et al., 2025) considers multiple charts, tables, and text paragraphs as evidence. Despite this progress, three limitations remain. Refuted examples are usually created by editing the claim, for instance by flipping its meaning, which can leave surface cues that models exploit instead of reasoning over the evidence. Many datasets also rely on claims that are not taken directly from scientific papers. Finally, tables are typically available in a single format, so it remains unclear how well models handle the same content across different representations.

With these limitations in mind, we organized SciClaimEval, a pilot task at NTCIR-19 on verifying scientific claims against the tables and figures of the papers in which they appear. It complements earlier shared tasks on scientific claim verification, which used tables (SemEval-2021 Task 9 (Wang et al., 2021)), abstracts (SCIVER (Wadden and Lo, 2021)), or social media posts linked to their source papers (CheckThat! (Schellhammer et al., 2026)). Rather than editing claims, we create refuted examples by having annotators modify the evidence. Each claim is thus paired with two versions of its evidence, one that supports it and one that does not, so the wording of the claim carries no cue about the label. All claims are authentic sentences taken from published papers, and tables are released in four formats: images, LaTeX, HTML, and JSON.

From each paper, we extract the text, tables, and figures. In Subtask 2, systems receive a claim with its two evidence versions and must select the one that supports it. Most systems built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs). For Subtask 1, they followed two broad strategies. Some verified each claim-evidence pair independently, often with claim decomposition, structured extraction of evidence from images, or executable checks. Others exploited the paired structure of the data by comparing the two evidence versions of the same claim. For Subtask 2, systems primarily adopted direct candidate comparison, independent verification followed by selection, or hybrid approaches combining both strategies. Common techniques included ensembles, multi-agent debate, evidence extraction, and consistency checks under reversed candidate order.

We draw the following lessons from this pilot task: • High scores rely on paired evidence. On Subtask 1, the best systems reached 98.1% pair accuracy on the test set by comparing the two evidence versions of each claim. Teams that also evaluated their systems without this information observed substantial performance drops. On the development set, for instance, removing paired information cost the two top systems 12 and 21 points of pair accuracy. • Open-weight models can match proprietary ones. papers.title: PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining LLM judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closedloop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaaJ) systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate LLM judges and recover performance after controlled shifts in the referencescore distribution. However, effective maintenance is inherently contextdependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.

As reliance on these systems grows, scalable and trustworthy evaluation of their outputs becomes increasingly important. LLM-as-a-Judge systems address this need by using one or more large language models to score, rank, or critique model outputs according to natural-language criteria [15, 8]. This flexibility is particularly useful for behavioral and safety evaluation, where judges must recognize subtle forms of toxicity, bias, inappropriate personalization, and other undesirable behavior. A judge that is well aligned with human evaluations at one point in time may lose this agreement as the stream of evaluated interactions changes. We refer to this phenomenon as judge drift: a loss of agreement between a fixed judge and the intended human evaluation policy under a changing evaluation stream. Judge drift may arise from changes in user behavior, application policies, or the distribution of encountered cases. Importantly, this notion of drift does not require the judge model itself to change; drift can emerge solely from changes in the stream of cases being evaluated. Maintaining judge alignment under such changes turns prompt design from a one-time configuration task into a continuing maintenance problem.

papers.title: Compositional Loop Invariant Inference for Multiphase Programs via Structured Neurosymbolic Reasoning
papers.abstract: Loop invariants are essential for deductive program verification, yet automatically inferring them for {multiphase programs}, whose loops contain conditional branches that induce multiple execution phases with distinct behaviors, remains an open problem. Existing LLM-based methods either reason about loops as a whole or use explicit branch information to generate atomic assertions jointly across branches, without maintaining complete candidate sub-invariants for independent generation and targeted repair. We present CLOVER, a structured neurosymbolic reasoning framework for multiphase invariant inference built on two interlinked mechanisms. First, compositional inference: CLOVER statically decomposes a loop into symbolic {loop branch sequences}, conjunctions of the loop guard and branch conditions that characterize distinct execution scenarios, and guides the LLM to generate candidate sub-invariants for each one independently, so that each LLM query focuses on a single execution scenario rather than the entire loop. Second, counterexample-guided localized refinement: when SMT verification rejects a composed disjunctive invariant, CLOVER traces the counterexample back through the branch structure to identify which specific loop branch sequence caused the failure and repairs only that sub-invariant, preserving all correct components. Both mechanisms are unified by a shared symbolic structure derived from the loop's branch semantics, which guides what the LLM generates, how candidates are composed, and where refinement is directed. We evaluate CLOVER on 316 linear arithmetic, 50 nonlinear arithmetic, and 54 multiphase benchmarks. CLOVER solves 35 of 54 multiphase benchmarks, outperforming the best LLM-based baseline (29) by 20.7\% and the best traditional method (22) by 59.1\%. On linear/nonlinear benchmarks, CLOVER remains competitive, solving 355 of 366 programs overall.

Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising approach to automatic invariant inference, overcoming the scalability limitations of traditional symbolic methods [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10] and the generalization difficulties of earlier learning-based methods [11, 12, 13, 14]. Recent LLM-based approaches [15, 16, 17, 18] follow a guess-and-check paradigm: the LLM guesses candidate invariants or clauses, an SMT solver checks them, and counterexample feedback guides the next round of guessing. These methods show good performance on standard linear/non-linear benchmarks.

Recent LLM-based approaches [15, 16, 17, 18] follow a guess-and-check paradigm: the LLM guesses candidate invariants or clauses, an SMT solver checks them, and counterexample feedback guides the next round of guessing. These methods show good performance on standard linear/non-linear benchmarks.

However, real-world loops often contain conditional branches that cause different iterations to follow different execution paths, each updating variables in its own way. Such programs are called multiphase programs [19] and arise naturally whenever loop variables cross domain boundaries that activate different branches (e.g., a loop that increments a counter ii and executes one branch while i<ni<n but switches to another once i≥ni\geq n, so that the invariant must capture both phases). Generating correct invariants for multiphase programs is a recognized challenge [20, 21]: the correct invariant is inherently a disjunction of phase-specific invariants, one per execution phase, whose complexity grows combinatorially with the number of branches. Despite long-standing interest, multiphase programs expose a critical blind spot in current LLM-based loop invariant inference techniques.

Many LLM-based methods struggle on multiphase loops because they are blind to the structure of the guess space: in a multiphase loop, the program’s branch structure induces a natural decomposition of the guess space into separate dimensions, one per execution phase, and the correct invariant is a disjunction of phase-specific clauses, one drawn from each dimension. These methods ignore this structure and collapse the multi-dimensional guess space into a flat, unstructured one, prompting the LLM with the entire program and producing candidates without distinguishing which dimension each belongs to. The resulting clauses are then combined without branch awareness: LaM4Inv [15] combines clauses exclusively via conjunction, unable to represent disjunctive invariants, while Clause2Inv [16] enumerates both conjunctions and disjunctions, causing the candidate pool to grow exponentially with the number of phases. When verification fails, the counterexample feedback is exploited only coarsely at program level, unable to localize which phase dimension caused the failure. Even approaches that improve feedback quality, such as LORIS [18], which detects local reasoning errors in the LLM’s proof steps, still operate on the loop as a whole and cannot attribute failures to specific phases.

PAL2Inv [22] is a recent path-sensitive exception. It applies abstract interpretation to obtain initial invariants, prompts an LLM to generate atomic assertions for every enumerated loop path, and uses counterexample-guided clause combination to assemble disjunctions of path-level conjunctions. This design makes path information explicit, but its generation step still asks the LLM to reason about all paths in one request, and its search state consists of path-indexed pools of atomic clauses rather than multiple alternative, complete sub-invariants for each path. Refinement therefore enriches and recombines clause pools instead of maintaining competing global compositions in which one selected phase component can be replaced while all other choices remain fixed. Thus, path sensitivity alone does not eliminate the simultaneous-reasoning and candidate-composition burdens of multiphase invariant inference.

These failures point to two core challenges. First, the LLM must reason about all phases simultaneously, yet the joint reasoning complexity overwhelms its capacity and the resulting candidate space grows combinatorially. Second, when verification fails, whole-loop feedback is too coarse to identify which phase is responsible, wasting repair effort on phases that are already correct. Our key insight is that the branch structure of a multiphase loop enables two interlinked mechanisms that address both challenges. First, compositional inference: the distinct branch-condition combinations decompose the invariant synthesis task so that the LLM generates sub-invariants for each combination independently, reducing per-step reasoning complexity from the full loop to a single execution scenario. This decomposition also naturally admits multiple candidates per combination, providing candidate diversity that prevents premature commitment. Second, counterexample-guided localized refinement: because these combinations partition the state space, any counterexample can be uniquely mapped to the responsible combination, so the framework repairs only the failed phase’s sub-invariant while preserving all other phases.

We realize this architecture in Clover, a framework that tightly integrates neural generation and symbolic verification through a shared symbolic structure derived from the program’s branch semantics. Clover statically analyzes the loop’s control flow to extract loop branch sequences, distinct combinations of branch conditions that partition the loop’s execution space. This symbolic structure guides LLM reasoning at every stage: it determines what the LLM generates (one sub-invariant per loop branch sequence), how candidates are composed (root-to-leaf disjunctions), and where refinement is directed (the specific loop branch sequence that caused the failure). Through this structure, the framework realizes both contributions. For compositional inference, each loop branch sequence becomes a level in a search tree, and the LLM generates multiple candidate sub-invariants for each level independently, maintaining candidate diversity across levels. For localized refinement, when the solver rejects a composed invariant, Clover traces the counterexample back through the loop branch sequence partition to identify the responsible loop branch sequence and restricts repair to that loop branch sequence alone, preserving all other sub-invariants.

papers.title: P-curvature from a TQFT viewpoint
papers.abstract: This paper is motivated by the recent discovery, in symplectic topology, of a relation (partly proved, partly conjectural) between quantum connection and quantum Steenrod operations. We introduce an abstract TQFT framework, based on certain features of the definition of deformed symplectic cohomology, in which such a relation holds generally.
papers.intro:
PP-curvature is an invariant of algebraic connections (first order linear differential operators) over fields of characteristic p>0p>0. It is not related to the ordinary notion of curvature, but it plays a similar role: vanishing of the pp-curvature ensures the existence of “sufficiently many” covariantly constant local sections [7, Theorem 5.1]. More recently, pp-curvature has been considered for the quantum connection from Gromov-Witten theory. The guiding conjecture, introduced by J.-H. Lee with input from Etingof, can be stated informally as follows: Take the quantum connection, which differentiates in the direction of some degree 22 cohomology class. Its pp-curvature agrees with the quantum Steenrod endomorphism associated to that class. The groundbreaking paper [8] proves it in an important instance involving equivariant quantum cohomology, namely the cotangent bundle of a flag variety [8, Corollary 5.2]. This was motivated by the appearance of that particular instance of pp-curvature in representation theory [6]. For Fano varieties, a weaker version of the conjecture (agreement up to a nilpotent error) was used in [4] to prove that the quantum connection has a singularity of exponential type at ∞\infty; in the same situation, the argument was improved to a full proof of the conjecture in [13, Proposition 1.7]. A proof for Calabi-Yau threefolds was obtained in [2, Theorem 1.5]. The paper [16] proves it for Calabi-Yau’s of any dimension, under a number of assumptions on the Fukaya category, and assuming that the prime pp is large. Conjecturally, there are potential generalizations to a relative situation involving a smooth ample divisor [13, Remark 1.15], and to the fixed point Floer cohomology of pp-th iterates of symplectic automorphisms.

Because the conjecture addresses a number of different contexts, there is not necessarily a unique answer. This paper argues in favor of the “closed string TQFT” view. We introduce an abstract framework of operations parametrized by cylinders with marked points. Within that framework, one can define versions of the quantum connection and quantum Steenrod operations, and their relation is indeed as predicted by the guiding conjecture. The general result is Theorem 5.5, which is then transformed into two versions closer to the traditional statement (Corollaries 5.10 and 6.10).

(A negative answer could mean that the conjecture only holds in the presence of a much richer “open string” categorical context, as in [16]; or, that it is a truly geometric insight depending on a sophisticated analysis of pseudo-holomorphic curves, as in [2].) Because the conjecture addresses a number of different contexts, there is not necessarily a unique answer. This paper argues in favor of the “closed string TQFT” view. We introduce an abstract framework of operations parametrized by cylinders with marked points. Within that framework, one can define versions of the quantum connection and quantum Steenrod operations, and their relation is indeed as predicted by the guiding conjecture. The general result is Theorem 5.5, which is then transformed into two versions closer to the traditional statement (Corollaries 5.10 and 6.10).

The approach here is motivated by the approach to quantum cohomology relative to a smooth ample divisor, or more technically deformed symplectic cohomology, in [15]. That approach involves counting solutions of Floer-type equations on cylinders with marked points, where the marked points dictate the intersection points with an ample divisor in the target manifold. Cylinders with mm marked points are counted with qmq^{m}, where qq is the quantum or Novikov variable. The marked points are not numbered, and can collide freely, so that the parameter spaces are symmetric products of the cylinder. Our setup has the same formal structure, starting with a qq-deformed differential. In fact, we will consider two versions of the theory. • The first version corresponds to S1S^{1}-equivariant Floer cohomology (even though, for technical reasons, we replace S1S^{1} by an infinite discrete subgroup); this is constructed in Section 4. (It would have been possible to carry out the construction of the connection and the pp-curvature computation entirely in ℤ/p{\mathbb{Z}}/p-equivariant terms, see Remark 6.6; but that is not particularly natural when thinking of the quantum connection.) The abstract nature of the argument allows us to formulate it in elementary terms, using only basic algebraic topology (singular chains and the chain level cross product) and homological algebra (qq-filtration arguments).
