authors.institution: Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Isomorphisms and automorphisms of minimal comaximal hypergraphs of commutative rings
papers.abstract: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with exactly $n\ge 2$ maximal ideals and let $k\ge 2$. We study the minimal $k$-uniform comaximal hypergraph $\mathcal{H}_k(R)$, whose vertices are the nonunits outside the Jacobson radical and whose edges are the irredundant $k$-element comaximal families. For $2\le k\le n$ we show that $\mathcal{H}_k(R)$ is a blow-up of the hypergraph of irredundant $k$-coverings of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, and that its reduced form reconstructs the maximal ideals up to permutation; for $k>n$ there are no edges. We obtain a general description of $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{H}_k(R))$ and characterize isomorphisms of such hypergraphs. For $3\le k\le n$ its automorphism group properly contains that of the comaximal graph, and for finite rings with $n\ge 3$ and every $2\le k\le n$, $\mathcal{H}_k(R)$ has the same isomorphism invariants as the comaximal graph, namely $|J(R)|$ and $R/J(R)$. The case $k=2$ recovers and extends the automorphism results for comaximal graphs obtained previously. We also compare the minimal and non-minimal comaximal hypergraphs and identify a condition under which the latter has the same automorphism group and isomorphism invariants as the comaximal graph. The same method determines the vertex set and the automorphism group of the $k$-zero-divisor hypergraph of a product of integral domains, and shows that for finite products of finite fields this hypergraph determines the ring.

papers.title: Domination and maximal intersecting families in comaximal graphs of commutative rings
papers.abstract: The comaximal graph $\mathcal{G}(R)$ of a commutative ring $R$ has as vertices the nonunits outside the Jacobson radical, two being adjacent if they generate $R$ as an ideal. For rings with $k\ge 4$ maximal ideals, only the bounds $2\le\gamma(\mathcal{G}(R))\le k$ were known, to our knowledge. We prove $\gamma=\gamma_t=\gamma_c=k$ whenever $3\le k<\infty$, without finiteness or Artinian hypotheses, classify the minimum dominating sets, and determine the domatic number. Independent dominating sets correspond to maximal intersecting families of subsets of $\{1,\dots,k\}$; we obtain a closed formula for the independent domination number of every finite non-local ring, which can be exponentially larger than the domination number. The proofs rest on the class sizes of the blow-up description of $\mathcal{G}(R)$ due to Moconja and Petrovi\'c, which we determine for every ring with finitely many maximal ideals, finite or infinite; with them, domination problems on $\mathcal{G}(R)$ become weighted extremal problems on subsets of $\{1,\dots,k\}$, and the formula for the independent domination number follows from the multiplicative form of these sizes. We also treat rings with infinitely many maximal ideals, graph polynomials, and lattices whose maximal ideals are prime.

papers.title: dynamicalnodes: Block Diagrams to ROS2 Graphs
papers.abstract: Here we introduce dynamicalnodes, a framework for rapid iterative prototyping of control and estimation algorithms within the Robot Operating System, or ROS. The framework leverages the theory of discrete-time dynamical systems to encode each component of a feedback system (e.g. reference generator, controller, plant, observer) as a pair of functions, denoted $(f,\,h) $, where $f$ is an evolution function and $h$ is an output function. With appropriate choice of domain and codomain, the $ (f,\,h) $ pairs can be composed to form feedback systems of arbitrary complexity. Moving from theory to practice, the user implements each $(f,\,h)$ pair in Python and encapsulates them in objects that facilitate composition and simulation. ROS executables are generated from these objects via rclpy, where relevant metadata such as network topology and publishing frequency are written automatically. The final result is a collection of rclpy files from which validated feedback systems can be spun up as live ROS graphs. We discuss the relevant theory behind the framework and then demonstrate the prototyping workflow applied to a canonical controls problem, a car with cruise control.

papers.title: On explicit units in a family of cubic fields and the arithmetic of curves arising from powers of these units
papers.abstract: For an integer $b\neq0,1$ let $K_b$ be the cubic field generated by the unique real root of $x^3-3bx-b^3$, let $\eta_0$ be its fundamental unit, and let $\eta_b$ be the explicit unit studied in the companion paper (arXiv:2609.37389). Write $\eta_b=\eta_0^{n(b)}$. Deciding whether $n(b)$ is divisible by $q$ amounts to finding the integral points of a plane curve $C_q$ of degree $2q$. We prove that for every integer $q\ge1$ the curve $C_q$ is irreducible with $g(C_q)=\binom{q-1}{2}$, the genus of a smooth plane curve of degree $q$ rather than of degree $2q$. The proof is not a genus computation but a structural one: $C_q$ is the inverse image, under the $q$-power map of a two-dimensional torus, of the curve traced by the minimal polynomial of $\eta_b$ as $b$ varies, and the formula falls out of two applications of Riemann-Hurwitz in the resulting tower. As a consequence the problem splits into exactly three regimes: $q=2$ rational, $q=3$ elliptic, and $q\ge4$ of general type. In particular only finitely many $b$ have $q\mid n(b)$ for each $q\ge4$. A lower bound for linear forms in two logarithms gives $n(b)<6082138$ for every $b$, so $n(b)\in\{1,2\}$ for all but finitely many $b$, though not effectively. We add two computations: $n(b)$ is determined outright for $|b|\le10^{30}$, and the rational points of $C_4$ are determined by quadratic Chabauty, giving $4\mid n(b)\iff b\in\{-75,-3,5,96\}$. We state precisely which parts of the latter rest on certified arithmetic and which do not. Finally, we show that $K_b\cong K_{b'}$ with $b\neq b'$ holds for $\{b,b'\}=\{-1,5\}$, and otherwise only if one of the two parameters, $c$ say, satisfies $|c|>10^{30}$ and $n(c)$ is divisible by a prime $q\ge5$. There are only finitely many such pairs.

papers.title: The singular Gaussian scaling limit for a tagged particle in the infinite-dimensional Dyson model at $\beta=2$
papers.abstract: We prove a logarithmic central limit theorem for a tagged particle in infinite-dimensional Dyson Brownian motion at inverse temperature $\beta=2$, starting from the sine$_2$ point process. The fluctuation is of order $\sqrt{\log t}$, which is subdiffusive and substantially slower than the polynomial fluctuations of classical short-range interacting particle systems, reflecting the rigidity induced by long-range logarithmic repulsion. We further identify the scaling limit as the singular Gaussian field corresponding to the zero-Hurst parameter, which provides a realisation of the singular Gaussian field as a scaling limit of a tagged particle raised by D\"urr, Goldstein and Lebowitz (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 38 (1985)).

papers.title: All minimum cuts of symmetric submodular functions
papers.abstract: We compute Cunningham's canonical decomposition of a symmetric submodular function on $n$ elements in $O(n^3)$ time. The decomposition represents all minimum cuts in linear space. For the pair $s,t$ produced by Queyranne's algorithm, we construct in $O(n^2)$ time a digraph representing exactly the minimum $st$-cuts of the function. Using this construction in Chekuri and Xu's decomposition algorithm gives the cubic bound.

papers.title: FREE-LIVO: Physically Decoupled Yet Tightly Coupled LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry
papers.abstract: LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry (LIVO) integrates complementary LiDAR, camera, and IMU measurements to achieve robust state estimation. However, most existing methods assume a fixed relative pose and accurate time synchronization between sensors. Toward modular and heterogeneous robotic systems, this paper presents FREE-LIVO, a tightly coupled odometry method that requires neither a rigid LiDAR-camera rig nor LiDAR-camera time synchronization. The proposed method uses a pretrained image feature matcher to establish correspondences between a camera image and a dense LiDAR intensity image generated from a single LiDAR scan using a generative model. From the resulting 3D point-to-pixel correspondences, we construct reprojection factors that directly constrain LiDAR and camera poses at different acquisition times. These factors are jointly optimized in a single factor graph together with constraints from point cloud registration, visual feature tracking, and the IMU measurements associated with each sensor. On six sequences from the public M3DGR dataset, FREE-LIVO achieves an average absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE of 0.45 m without provided LiDAR-camera extrinsic parameters and exhibits minimal accuracy degradation under time synchronization errors of up to 0.5 s. Furthermore, experiments with the LiDAR and camera mounted on separate robots demonstrate that the method can jointly estimate the trajectories of independently moving sensors.

papers.title: Information-Spectrum General Formulas for the Capacity Region of Classical-Quantum Multiple Access Channels
papers.abstract: For classical-quantum multiple access channels (cq-MACs) with two senders, we give several general expressions for the capacity region, valid for arbitrary sequences of channels. In the case of asymptotically vanishing error ($\varepsilon=0$), the capacity region is expressed in terms of spectral inf-mutual information rates. For every $0\le\varepsilon<1$, the $\varepsilon$-capacity region is expressed in terms of a quantity defined through a linear combination of three alternative hypotheses. In particular, the outer bound of Kubo and Nagaoka (2015) is tight. Our results include the quantum counterpart of the general formula of Han (1998) for the classical MAC. The most important ingredient is the one-shot inner bound of Sen (2021), which we apply to each member of an arbitrary channel sequence.

papers.title: Towards Real-Time Full-Waveform LiDAR Transformers via Intensity-Guided Token Reduction and Physics-Aware Augmentation
papers.abstract: LiDAR is a critical sensor for autonomous driving and robotics, yet it remains vulnerable to adverse conditions such as fog, rain, transparent objects, and low-reflectance surfaces. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL) addresses these limitations by capturing the complete return waveform as a histogram, preserving rich reflection characteristics including multi-path echoes and weak signals. While recent Transformer-based approaches have demonstrated promise on FWL data, two fundamental bottlenecks remain: high computational cost from redundant tokens in low-intensity background regions, and limited generalization due to scarce annotated training data. We address both bottlenecks by exploiting the physical structure inherent to FWL data. First, we propose FWL-ToPM, a token pruning and merging mechanism that leverages intensity distributions to selectively reduce tokens while retaining critical waveform content. Second, we introduce FWLAug, a data augmentation framework designed as a regularization method that preserves waveform structure, retaining the Time-of-Flight waveform of each ray and the frustum geometry, to improve generalization to unseen scenes. Evaluated on the Ghost-FWL benchmark, FWL-ToPM achieves over 8 times speedup at real-time throughput alongside a nearly 9-point F1 gain over the prior state of the art, establishing the first real-time FWL Transformer that simultaneously improves accuracy. FWLAug further improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution test set of unseen scenes. Together, these methods push FWL-based perception toward practical deployment. The code and the OOD dataset are publicly available and can be accessed via the project page: https://keio-csg.github.io/FWL-ToPM

authors.name: Ryosei Hara
authors.institution: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

authors.name: Mariko Isogawa

papers.title: Accelerating Long-Context Decoding in Large-Scale Hybrid LLMs Without Retraining
papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.

papers.title: Cores of $3$-distant convex games
papers.abstract: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. We study the core of $3$-distant convex games, which permit violations of convexity only between closely related coalitions. Although the core of such a game may be empty, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition for its nonemptiness. We also develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for finding a core allocation whenever one exists. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the framework to oligopolistic competition with merger synergies and profit allocation of joint production with complementary inputs.

papers.title: No Significant Rotation of the Spiral Structure in the IM Lup Protoplanetary Disk
papers.abstract: Spiral structures are often observed in protoplanetary disks, but their origins remain uncertain. Yoshida et al. (2025) reported a pattern speed consistent with local Keplerian rotation for the $m=2$ spiral in the dusty disk around IM Lup using multi-epoch ALMA observations, supporting a gravitational instability (GI)-driven origin. However, recent studies revise the disk geometry of IM Lup, motivating a reassessment of its spiral pattern speed. In this study, we reanalyze the disk geometry of the same multi-epoch data using visibility-based continuum emission modeling. The inferred disk geometries differ from those adopted in previous studies by a few degrees but are consistent across epochs and with recent independent estimates based on gas emission analyses. The revised geometries yield weaker residuals and more physically plausible radial spiral phase profiles. Unlike previous studies, our remeasured spiral pattern speeds are consistent with zero rotation within the uncertainties. We conclude that the previously reported Keplerian-like motion can be explained by a mismatch in the adopted disk geometry, which affects the spiral phases measured in Band 6 (2017, 2019) and Band 7 (2024) differently. In addition, we identify a tentative large-scale one-armed spiral-like structure extending beyond the known $m=2$ spiral, which may provide clues to additional perturbations, such as an embedded planet or late-stage infall. Future high-resolution Band~6 observations with a longer time baseline will be essential for more accurately determining the spiral pattern speed.

papers.title: Replay Is a Family of Assertions: Fork-Safety in Event-Sourced Agent Runtimes
papers.abstract:
Event-sourced agent runtimes commonly claim deterministic replay, cheap forking, and lineage. These are families of assertions, not one guarantee. A fixed-log fold may be deterministic while reactive settlement remains schedule-sensitive; a recorded oracle result can enable zero-call replay while the original interaction still changed cost or world state; and a prefix copy cannot undo an action in a discarded suffix.
  We present an executable F# contract that separates facts from effect requests, makes scheduling explicit, and assesses a cut relative to projection, strict execution replay, external continuation, or a declared counterfactual-world observation. Preserved counterexamples show that general settlement is neither terminating nor confluent and that disjoint declared writes do not prevent read/trigger interference. Against 5,540 public runtime logs, all 317,296 projection cuts satisfy the stated observation, while 36,251 cuts split a model request and do not license continuation; another 120,969 are Conditional because a committed oracle result must be served from the record without re-execution. In 121 observed forks, 16,625 retained-prefix events have zero structural mismatches, but none crosses an external-effect boundary. A separate public offline conformance fork crosses a committed, recorded oracle boundary. Its generator observes that the inherited result is served without a second fixture-oracle call; its verifier checks receipt/log consistency and a fork-bound HMAC assertion under a public conformance key. The result reframes cheap forking as a property-indexed semantic contract with explicit evidence and environment preconditions.

papers.title: Rewrite, Then Veto: Rewriter-Agnostic Edit Gating for LLM-Based Post-OCR Correction
papers.abstract: LLMs can repair noisy OCR transcripts of historical documents, but they also change text that was already correct. We propose EditVeto, a veto gate placed after a full-context LLM rewrite. The rewrite is character-aligned to the OCR input, its differences are split into blocks, and a 0.6B-parameter gate keeps or reverts each block. An oracle analysis motivates the design: given the true error locations, per-span generation is worse than no correction, whereas vetoing a full rewrite's edits helps. Trained on rewrites by two Qwen3 models and evaluated, frozen, on the eight HIPE-OCRepair-2026 test sets, the gate improves all five rewriters tested, two of them unseen in training: weighted cMER falls by 0.0026-0.0044 and the preference score rises by 0.15-0.25 (paired bootstrap, p ~ 0.0002 each). On published competition outputs it lowers cMER for three of four teams but raises it for the winning run (0.0050 to 0.0065). In a second, disclosed test look, a retrained gate still improves LoRA-tuned rewriters (cMER -0.0011 to -0.0021), and an ensemble of their gated edits reaches a cMER of 0.0069 and a preference score of 0.928, mostly through fine-tuning and pooling rather than gating. Built only on public models and data, it is behind the winner (0.0050) and tied with the second-ranked run (0.0071), both from the only team using domain pre-training, and ahead of all other published runs. A third, secondary look shows the unchanged gate improving zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B (cMER 0.0114 to 0.0108) but only the preference score of its LoRA-tuned version.

papers.title: Ferroelectric control of magnetic coupling in a Cr dimer adsorbed on $\alpha$-In$_2$Se$_3$
papers.abstract: Ferroelectric substrates offer a route to controlling magnetic interactions in low-dimensional systems through polarization-dependent changes in local bonding and electronic structure. Here, using first-principles calculations, we investigate the adsorption of 3$d$ transition-metal atoms and dimers on monolayer $\alpha$-In$_2$Se$_3$ and identify Cr as a stable dimer configuration on both polar surfaces. Reversing the ferroelectric polarization drives a pronounced change in its magnetic coupling: the AFM state is favored for one polarization, whereas the FM and AFM configurations become nearly degenerate for the opposite one. Analysis of the spin density, projected electronic states, and Wannier Hamiltonians reveals concomitant changes in the direct Cr-Cr hopping and in the interaction with the bridging Se atom. In particular, enhanced Cr-Se hybridization and Se spin polarization, together with a strong reduction of the direct two-center Cr-Cr hopping, point to a polarization-dependent balance between direct and substrate-mediated exchange contributions. These results show how ferroelectric polarization can tune magnetic interactions in an atomically defined 2D hybrid system.

authors.name: S. Di Napoli
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

papers.title: Category differences in similarity between fixation density maps and psychological potential fields for sketches
papers.abstract: When an object comes into view, humans can instantaneously recognize it if known to them. However, assessing how this recognition takes place remains challenging. A few studies using simple sketches have reported varying degrees of image similarity between the fixation density map (FDM), which visualizes eye movements and durations, and the psychological potential field (PPF), which visualizes part of the visual cognition process, depending on the object category. This study reports how the similarity behaves across three categories---animal, non-animal, and meaningless shape---and under rotated presentation, which is known to increase cognitive load during object recognition. The similarity was quantified through area under the curve (AUC) measures, including a baseline-adjusted AUC that isolates the early rise in similarity from stimulus-dependent baseline levels. A variability score was introduced to assess individual differences, and linear mixed models were used to evaluate category and orientation effects. Results indicated that the baseline-adjusted AUC yielded significant differences among all three categories with large effect sizes, whereas the raw AUC did not distinguish between the animal and non-animal categories due to the influence of sketch representation. No significant Category $\times$ Orientation interaction was observed, indicating that rotated presentation did not produce a category-specific effect. The meaningless shape stimuli yielded consistently low similarity and variability scores, clearly separating them from the two meaningful object categories. These results characterize the behavior of the FDM--PPF similarity under free viewing and indicate that baseline adjustment is necessary to separate category-related variation from stimulus-dependent baseline levels.

papers.title: The index of mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators: I
papers.abstract: This is the first of a series of papers which will be devoted to a study of the index of mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators on closed Riemannian manifolds. The aim of the series is to discretise the index of the Dirac operator. On flat tori, this is achieved by the Wilson--Dirac operator of lattice gauge theory on a regular lattice. On a general closed Riemannian manifold, however, no regular lattice is available. As an intermediate step between the continuum Dirac operator and its discretisations, we introduce mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators on any closed Riemannian manifold, defined by integrating covariant differences over distances comparable to a fixed length scale. In this paper, we define the index of the mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators via spectral flow and prove that it agrees with that of the continuum Dirac operator at all sufficiently small scales. The proof rests on an elliptic estimate uniform in the scale and a Rellich-type compactness theorem. In the second paper, we shall pass from mesoscopic operators to discrete Wilson--Dirac operators.

papers.title: Uniform Three-Fold Product Expansion of Algebraic-Geometry Codes over a Fixed Field
papers.abstract:
A collection of classical codes $C_1,\dots,C_m$ has product expansion if every low-weight word in the sum of their extensions to the product space can be written as a sum of words supported on few lines, each line being a codeword of the corresponding $C_i$. For $m=2$ product expansion is equivalent to robust testability of the tensor code, while for $m\ge 3$ it is strictly stronger; it is the hypothesis on the local codes behind recent constructions of good quantum LDPC codes, good quantum locally testable codes, and quantum codes with transversal non-Clifford gates. No explicit family over a fixed field was previously known to achieve constant rate, linear distance for both the code and its dual, and 3-fold product expansion at growing length.
  We prove that for the one-point evaluation codes $C_i$ of length $N_i=728\cdot27^{\,i-1}$ and pole order $\lfloor N_i/5\rfloor$ on the Garcia--Stichtenoth tower over $\mathbb{F}_{729}$, the triple $(C_i,C_i,C_i)$ has product expansion with a constant independent of $i$. The dual codes $C_i^\perp$ then form an explicit fixed-field family of rate tending to $109/130$ and relative distance at least $8/65$. The proof is geometric: we view the words of the sum code as arrays on the product of three copies of the $i$-th curve of the tower, where the parity checks are sections of a line bundle. An exact generation theorem describes the sum-code words supported on the grid footprint of a suitable divisor. A support-localisation argument then shows that every low-weight array lies on such a divisor, after deleting a small number of coordinates. We also give a sufficient criterion for three-fold product expansion in terms of degree and genus ratios, yielding explicit families over every non-prime finite field of order at least $512$. The principal conclusions have been formally verified in Lean 4.

papers.title: Where Do Reported Long-Video QA Gains Come From? A Controlled Audit of Frame Selection, Evidence Injection, and Expert Routing
papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is usually studied as frame selection: which few frames should a vision-language model see? We introduce VideoRouteAudit, a controlled audit that separates this choice from two alternatives, injecting non-visual evidence and routing to another answering model. It holds the backbone, frame budget, decoding, prompt and grader fixed while varying one decision at a time. On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling. The largest selection-only estimate is +1.9 pt (95% CI [-1.2,+5.0]) and our cascade is +1.2 pt [-1.7,+4.1]; all are equivalent to uniform within +/-5 pt. The same contrasts are unstable at the n=200 subset scale commonly used: three of four are up to 3.8x larger, one reverses sign, and resampled 200-item subsets reverse the full-bucket effect's sign in 35.8% of draws. The audit also corrects our own first results. The anomaly-domain "+ASR" arms injected no text, so the pooled +4.7 pt gain was selection plus a development prefix. With transcripts, ASR lowers XD-Violence accuracy by 10.0 pt when appended after the question and not at all when placed before it, and lowers UCF-Crime by 13.0 pt either way; on Video-MME, placing it first adds about 4 pt (7 on Qwen2-VL) to uniform sampling and to the cascade alike (post hoc, unadjusted). Swapping the answering model gives the largest contrast (+15.1 pt on MUSIC-AVQA, +33.3 pt on its worst type), but the same audio-visual expert with its soundtrack silenced keeps 92% of the gain (69% with a mismatched soundtrack), so the contrast is mostly a model swap. Code, per-item predictions and scripts that recompute every statistic are available at https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/long-video-qa-audit.

authors.name: Shih-Yao Lin
authors.institution: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics-Aware Industrial Anomaly Detection and Reasoning
papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is a long-established problem that aims to detect defects in industrial products during manufacturing for quality control. Most existing studies focus on static visual patterns as the basis for detection. However, in real manufacturing environments, many anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that cannot be perceived from static cues alone. We observe that even recent Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based approaches fall short in identifying such dynamic anomalies due to limited temporal modeling capability. To address this, we introduce MUSTARD: MUltimodal SpatioTemporal Anomaly Reasoning and Detection, a framework that equips MLLMs with fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting and reasoning about dynamics-based defects. MUSTARD introduces optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to capture critical motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. Its normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline requires only a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates. This enables efficient adaptation across various products and provides high decision interpretability. MUSTARD is the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based IAD. Experiments demonstrate its superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and providing plausible explanations. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Post-Quantum Authentication of IoT Data on Ethereum: Signatures, the Calldata Floor, and Device-Signed Merkle Roots
papers.abstract: Field devices deployed today will still be producing records when quantum computers may break their signatures, so systems that anchor IoT data on blockchains need a post-quantum (PQ) authentication path now. We measure its cost on Ethereum under the current execution rules, including the EIP-7623 calldata floor and the EIP-7825 transaction cap, and under the calldata repricing scheduled for the Glamsterdam upgrade. We combine device-side measurements of ML-DSA, Falcon, SLH-DSA, LMS and XMSS, reproduced costs of open-source Solidity verifiers, a new standard-compliant LMS/HSS verifier for SHA-256 and SHA-256/192, and complete transactions on an Osaka-rule EVM, priced with today's verifiers and with proposed precompiles. Three results stand out. Signing every record costs 8.7 times as much as ECDSA even with an ML-DSA precompile, because the calldata floor rather than verification sets the price. When each device signs a Merkle root over 100 records, a standard LMS verifier available today costs about 3,350 gas per record, against 245 gas for ECDSA in the same design, and it is unaffected by the scheduled repricing, which raises floor-bound designs by up to 1.9 times. With the proposed precompiles, ML-DSA-44 costs 1,031 gas per record, and a hybrid ECDSA and ML-DSA signature adds only 2.5%. Post-quantum device authentication is therefore deployable on Ethereum without protocol changes, provided that the latency of batching and the data-availability properties of the chosen variant fit the application.

papers.title: SM4RT: Cascaded Feed-forward Model for 4D Reconstruction
papers.abstract: We introduce SM4RT, a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction from RGB videos. While existing feed-forward approaches typically address geometry reconstruction and motion estimation separately--and often predict motions in a single coordinate frame that must account for camera movement--SM4RT solves these tasks sequentially by first reconstructing 3D geometry and then bootstrapping motion estimation from the predicted structure. By expressing each pixel's 3D motion in its corresponding camera frame, SM4RT reduces ambiguity arising from camera motion. To address the sparsity of real-world motion labels, SM4RT further incorporates a weakly supervised loss that regularizes unlabeled point motions using labeled point positions at the other time step. We evaluate motion estimation on three dynamic-scene datasets--Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey--and SM4RT achieves the best performance on most metrics compared with prior baselines. We additionally benchmark geometry reconstruction on five dynamic scene datasets and show that SM4RT achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Overall, our unified framework demonstrates that combining geometry reconstruction and motion estimation in a cascade not only avoids performance trade-offs but also enhances motion estimation through improved geometric reasoning.

papers.title: ControlAnything: Generative UI and On-Demand Device Integration for Mixed-Reality Hand Interaction by a Coding Agent
papers.abstract: Connecting hand input in mixed reality (MR) to a nearby physical device typically requires an integration written in advance for that device, its transport and the mapping. ControlAnything defers this integration to the moment of use and assigns it to a coding agent. On a Meta Quest 3, the wearer selects an object outlined by SAM 3.1 and states what their hands should control. An agent built on Meta's Muse Spark model then writes a connector program on the wearer's laptop, tests it against the live device through hand-written MIDI, Bluetooth and key-press transports, and returns augmented-reality (AR) controls, a per-frame hand program, or both. These outputs are a form of generative UI, interfaces created by an AI model; here, the agent also generates and tests the code that binds the interface to a physical device. In a single-session technical evaluation with the author as the only wearer, nine of ten requests addressing five targets reached a ready state, and the wearer stopped one. The median time to ready was 32.5 s (range 24.9-57.8 s, excluding speech transcription); sequential model calls accounted for a median of 89.9% of this time, and 91.7% of input tokens came from the prompt cache. The system's evidence of success extends to transport acknowledgements but not to physical effects. These findings point to connector reuse and the observation of effects through the headset's own sensors as next steps for on-demand device integration in MR. A user study with first-time wearers is planned.

papers.title: Structure of adjacency algebras of thin Jordan schemes
papers.abstract: We prove that adjacency algebras of Jordan schemes over fields of characteristic zero are semisimple. We then classify the adjacency algebras of thin Jordan schemes over the fields of real numbers or complex numbers. The simple summands of the adjacency algebras over these fields are restricted to specific types of simple Jordan algebras.

papers.title: Tilting bundles and modifying modules in relative dimension one
papers.abstract:
For projective morphisms $\pi:Y\to X=\operatorname{Spec}R$ over noetherian complete local rings, with fibres of dimension at most one and $\mathbf{R}\pi_*\mathcal{O}_Y\cong\mathcal{O}_X$, we construct a tilting fan from cones of pretilting bundles. Maximal cones parametrize tilting bundles, and facet adjacency encodes irreducible mutation. Completeness in positive rank is equivalent to finiteness of tilting bundles modulo line-bundle twists. For closed fibres that are split ADE highest-root cycles or their Stein contractions, we identify tilting bundles with chambers of restricted affine Tits cones and determine the fan.
  Over normal Gorenstein complete local domains, reflexive pushforward takes pretilting bundles on normal projective birational models with fibres of dimension at most one and $\pi^!\mathcal{O}_X\cong\mathcal{O}_Y$ to modifying modules. Pushforwards of canonical tilting bundles recover models as module blowups and detect contractions by additive containment, yielding an Auslander--McKay embedding.
  The hypersurfaces $R=S[[u,v]]/(uv-f)$, with $S$ a regular complete local ring and $f\in S$ a nonzero nonunit, generalize type $A$ Du Val surfaces and $cA_n$ threefolds to arbitrary dimension. We classify modifying modules by divisor flags and rank-one reflexive twists; flag blowups turn the embedding into an equivalence. If $f$ has $r\ge2$ prime factors counted with multiplicity, reflexive pushforward on any maximal-flag model gives a mutation-preserving surjection from tilting bundles, parametrized by chambers of affine type $\widetilde{A}_{r-1}$, to maximal modifying modules. Its fibres are affine Weyl group orbits determined by repeated factors. All maximal-flag models and maximal modification algebras are derived equivalent. These algebras are noncommutative crepant resolutions exactly when $S/(p)$ is regular for every prime factor $p$ of $f$.

papers.title: From Connection Loss to Collision: Closed-Loop Fault Assessment of a Fly-Connectome SNN
papers.abstract: The public release of the complete adult fruit-fly brain connectome enables brain-scale spiking-network studies, motivating closed-loop assessment of connection loss. We test a connectome-derived controller in synthetic pursuit-escape and check record consistency. Across 576 test episodes in paired campaigns, the baseline mapping at 50% connection-row deletion yields 11/48 proportional and 0/48 relay collisions by 1 s, despite paired P/R trigger/burst schedules. The prespecified secondary relay-minus-proportional net-loss difference is -22.9 percentage points (95% seed-cluster CI [-33.3, -12.5]). Two separately recalibrated mappings yield smaller, uncertain point estimates; unequal healthy clearance, recalibration and different test cohorts limit attribution. A frozen command-rate warning detects only 2/13 baseline collisions across all tested deletion levels. In a separate author-designed fly/delayed-tank catalogue, checks plus model-specific replay detect 81/87 corruptions versus 36/87 for trusted headers, accepting all 20 distinct valid inputs (six misses). These results quantify finite-horizon collisions and the gains and limits of record checks.

papers.title: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target
papers.abstract: Animals and humans often do not maximize; they act relative to goals (aspiration levels) that are frequently not yet met. How can a goal that is not (yet) realized organize choice? Deacon (2012) calls such absence-referenced organization \emph{ententional}, and Garc\'{i}a-Valdecasas and Deacon (2024) argue that ends are best understood as constraints rather than as particular states. We examine this idea in a minimal formal setting: Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS), a bandit learning rule that values each action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. We show that RS can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence can override it. Two consequences follow. First, actions that are no longer sampled are partially overridden by the goal rather than by past observations: their estimates relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded. This ``pseudo-forgetting'' distinguishes ACB from models with an explicit forgetting rate. Second, when the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle; in Bernoulli bandit simulations, adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret (expected loss). ACB offers an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behavior, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.

papers.title: Flux as a Codec: Zero-Shot Lossy Compression with Flux
papers.abstract: We propose FluxC, a zero-shot codec that uses Flux as a compression prior. Although DiffC has shown that pretrained diffusion models can serve as zero-shot codecs, we ask how the choice of coding path and reconstruction method affects rate--distortion--perception behavior. We analyze FluxC along three axes: coding cost and bit allocation, reconstruction method, and low rate distortion. At matched signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), we show that the path choice does not affect the ideal information rate, but changes how bits are allocated across time steps. For reconstruction, we compare ancestral sampling, one-step ODE reconstruction, and many-step ODE reconstruction. Our analysis shows that ODE-based reconstruction can achieve lower distortion than ancestral sampling, especially in the low rate regime. Experiments on Gaussian sources and natural images support this prediction. Moreover, FluxC performs competitively with, and in some cases outperforms, recent neural image compression methods, suggesting that Flux can serve as a principled zero-shot codec.

papers.title: Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning
papers.abstract: Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations. The project page is available at https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/.

papers.title: Reliability of Fisher-information bounds for dielectric metalenses: a site-resolved RCWA audit
papers.abstract: We assess the reliability of localization precision predicted for a 1716-nanopillar dielectric metalens using a site-resolved complex RCWA library and a vectorial Poisson Fisher model. An independent calculation reproduces the archived local axial Cramer-Rao bound of 20.7738 nm to within 0.0044 nm, yielding 20.7695 nm under the same ideal detector and 3000 detected signal photons. High-order periodic-cell calculations reveal a 0.1335 rad phase difference at a selected diameter; different substrate-index assumptions prevent attributing this difference solely to modal truncation. Replacing the recalculated coefficients at 39 actual sites changes the bound to 20.7522 nm. Restricted phase-mask benchmarks and pixel-integration checks further distinguish a stable statistical prediction from electromagnetic convergence. We provide a reproducible, model-conditional benchmark, not a physical-device performance claim.

papers.title: Limits of Generalized Magnitudes of Dissimilarity Spaces
papers.abstract: For a finite symmetric nonnegative dissimilarity matrix $D=(d_{ij})$ with zero diagonal, we study the high-resolution limit ($t\to \infty$) of $\mathbf{1}^T(e^{-td_{ij}})^+\mathbf{1}$. We prove that this limit always exists in the extended real line and is rational whenever finite, without weightability or invertibility assumptions. At fixed cardinality, a finite rational polyhedral fan governs rank and leading asymptotics. Consequently, only finitely many finite limits occur, and every limit admits an integer-data realization at the same cardinality. In contrast, allowing cardinality to vary, every rational pair of zero-pattern magnitude and high-resolution limit is realized using dissimilarities in $\{0,1,2\}$; adding the level $3$ permits either infinite limit with any rational zero-pattern magnitude. We also classify all limits on at most four points. Moreover, we derive an exact Schur decomposition valid under persistent singularity. Finally, it is shown that positive semidefiniteness at some positive scale is equivalent to equality of dissimilarity rows for every zero-distance pair, in which case the limit counts the zero-distance classes.

papers.title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers
papers.abstract: Short mode-evolution couplers have been designed with several seemingly different approaches, including fast quasi-adiabatic dynamics (FAQUAD), counter-diabatic (CD) driving realized by tailoring waveguide widths and spacing, CD driving realized by axis bending, and numerical optimization of the coupler geometry. Using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers--Henneberger frame of the bent coupler, we show that these approaches belong to the same design space. The three geometric parameters, width difference, spacing, and axis tilt, act on the light through two functions only: the coupling strength, set by the spacing, and an effective detuning, set by the width difference and the axis curvature. The gauge, bent, and mixed realizations of a CD coupler are therefore the same device and have the same bandwidth. The bandwidth is set by the angle $\chi$ between the light and the field that steers it on the Bloch sphere, integrated along the device as $\int\sin^2\chi dz$, and for a CD coupler this integral is set by the reference alone. This leads to a lithography-aware design rule: make the reference as adiabatic as the minimum gap allows, by narrowing its spacing at the anticrossing, and let exact CD suppress the remaining nonadiabatic coupling. In beam propagation method (BPM) simulations on a polymer platform, a 500\um{} coupler designed this way, without numerical optimization, maintains ${>}99\%$ transfer over 274~nm at a minimum edge gap of 1.05\um, compared with 150~nm for the CD coupler of a fixed-spacing reference at nearly the same gap. Particle swarm optimization of the geometry with BPM in the loop does not exceed the design rule. Three-dimensional BPM of the BCB channel waveguides also confirms these conclusions.

papers.title: Convection in the interior of Cepheid variable stars
papers.abstract: This paper is associated with a poster winner of a 2025 American Physical Society's Division of Fluid Dynamics (DFD) Gallery of Fluid Motion Award for work presented at the DFD Gallery of Fluid Motion. The original poster is available online at the Gallery of Fluid Motion, https://doi.org/10.1103/APS.DFD.2025.GFM.P005.

papers.title: Web bases for the Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$
papers.abstract: Queffelec--Sartori and Tubbenhauer--Vaz--Wedrich give a diagrammatic web category via generators and relations to describe the subcategory of Rep($\mathfrak{gl}(m|n)$) generated by tensor products of exterior powers of the defining representation. We construct the first explicit bases for homomorphism spaces in the web category for $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$, giving an alternative diagrammatic presentation of this web category, and explore connections to the combinatorics of planar networks. Our basis comes equipped with an algorithm to decompose any web into a linear combination of basis webs, giving an effective way to compute in the $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$-skein theory.

papers.title: Estimating Distribution Grid Upgrade Costs based on County-level Building Electrification Projections
papers.abstract: Building electrification projections are typically developed at aggregated geographic levels to support bulk power system analysis, even though a significant portion of the infrastructure investments required to accommodate electrification occurs within distribution systems. Existing methodologies to disaggregate load growth projections onto distribution networks are based on context-specific analyses that require detailed data on building electricity consumption, distribution feeders, and geographic parcels, which are often proprietary and unavailable for policy and economic impact studies. This paper presents a methodology to disaggregate county-level building electrification projections onto representative distribution feeders and evaluate their impact on distribution upgrade costs. The proposed approach combines bulk system end-use electrification projections with representative feeder sets to generate building-level electrification measures. These measures are then used to create load profiles that are consistent with county-level projections while preserving the spatial diversity of electrification demand required for distribution infrastructure analysis. Using a case study of Genesee County, in Michigan, the results show that the proposed methodology is able to capture a diversity of feeder-level responses to electrification and represent the different realities that building electrification produces within the distribution system. This allows to represent localized load variations and capture more realistic distribution system upgrade costs driven by electrification.

papers.title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution
papers.abstract: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which summarizes evidence against independence but does not describe where the conditional law changes. We propose QRCIT, a quantile-resolution conditional independence test that compares P(X|Z) and P(X|Y,Z) through a quantile deformation learned by a shared model. A lightweight residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then learns the additional deformation induced by Y, yielding a global predictive-gain statistic with conditional-randomization calibration and an inspectable deformation field over context and quantile level. We also introduce the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB), which evaluates dependence structures motivated by real applications, such as context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge, and mean-neutral patterns. Across synthetic post-nonlinear (PNL) and SDB benchmarks, QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives, with empirical Type-I behavior evaluated across settings. Higher quantile resolution improves merged-SDB power at moderate sample sizes, while diagnostics restricted to known affected regions improve detection of localized dependence. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer, and CCLE/PLX4720, QRCIT provides competitive real-data performance and interpretable deformation patterns. These results support quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.

papers.title: Should You Split Decode? Disaggregation Across Future Models and Accelerators
papers.abstract: For large language model (LLM) inference, prefill/decode disaggregation (P/D) is deployed in production to isolate phases with different resource demands. Attention/feed-forward network disaggregation (AFD) splits decode again, but adds communication, placement constraints, and another provisioned pool. We ask whether role-specific placement repays this cost as models and accelerator roadmaps change. Infrastructure is committed before future models and hardware can be benchmarked. We present SiliconForge, a calibrated model that varies the serving decomposition and hardware assignment independently. We compare P/D and P/D+AFD across four model directions, four accelerator classes anchored to current and announced parts, and two fabrics. We co-optimize each design using the same rules for pipeline overlap and the same power budget. Our main comparisons show no robust deployment-level AFD advantage in service-level objective (SLO) goodput per kW. Most nominal estimates favor P/D. The largest AFD lead comes from fitting one more prefill replica, not from a more efficient decode pool. AFD has a nominal lead in the KV-heavy (key-value) model direction when the co-located expert pool spans several small scale-up domains. Larger domains or a fast fabric for both designs weaken that lead. We therefore find that prefill provisioning, decode memory bandwidth, links, and pool granularity decide deployments more than the split alone. A fixed hardware assignment can lose its advantage as models, fabrics, hardware assumptions, and objectives change. Re-optimizing mappings and pool sizes on the same hardware cuts early commitment's median normalized goodput loss from 36% to 9%. We recommend adjustable mappings and pool sizes to let boundary and hardware choices follow model demands.

papers.title: Patch-Based Generalized Neural Texture Upscaling
papers.abstract: We propose a lightweight neural texture upscaling method. A single generalized MLP is trained on a diverse collection of texture patches and integrated into the texture sampling stage, upscaling low-resolution textures on-the-fly at rendering time. Because the model is generalized rather than overfit to specific content, no per-asset training is required - the same model applies to any existing scene without modifying texture data or the asset pipeline. Storing lower-resolution base textures reduces disk footprint, upscaling at sampling time eliminates the need to store high-resolution textures in VRAM, and sharing a single set of model weights across all textures ensures non-divergent GPU execution. We evaluate our method across multiple texture classes, demonstrating consistent improvement over analytic upscaling methods in perceptual quality.

papers.title: Balancing broomsticks to a t!
papers.abstract: A classic question from rotational mechanics asks, "Is it easier to balance a broomstick heavy side up or heavy side down?" Measuring the time a student can balance an asymmetrically weighted meter stick in two orientations is a straightforward exercise that can be used to introduce or review the t' framework, which guides lab students in comparisons of results and iterative improvement of their measurements. As a two-year college physics program, many of our students attend from other institutions, so while t' is taught in the introductory mechanics labs, there is no guarantee that a student in a following lab course will be familiar with the material. To address this, the t' concepts are reviewed in the first session of subsequent lab courses. The broomstick experiment is a quick and fun implementation.

papers.title: Getting the picture - Subtractive color mixing with an inkjet printer
papers.abstract: When teaching colors, physics teachers ask their students to ignore what is taught in art classes and embrace a primary color system of red, green, and blue. This scheme is additive and all colors can be generated by combining light of these three colors with varying intensities. There have been a number of demonstrations and tools to help students understand additive color mixing, using LEDs, color monitors, or similar technologies. However, the subtractive primaries of cyan, magenta, and yellow have received far less attention, if students have previous knowledge it is from printer ink cartridges. This gap may exist because as pigments it can be harder to vary their intensities in real time. Fortunately, our colleagues in the art department are well-versed in subtractive color mixing, and have taught this topic for many years through the lens of color printing. We steal a page from their book and describe how to create a color image using cyan, magenta, yellow, and black layers (CMYK). Black is used as an additional layer due to mixing issues concerning the imperfections of the CMY pigments. With imaging software, an inkjet printer, and some transparencies, physics instructors are just a few keystrokes away from being able to demonstrate subtractive color mixing.

papers.title: Monus vs. Interpretations in Semiring Semantics
papers.abstract: Interpretations have been widely used in the study of provenance of queries on semiring-annotated databases. Here, we consider two different interpretation-based semantics for first-order formulas in negation normal form, namely, the canonical-interpretation semantics and the compatible-interpretation semantics. We show that the resulting query languages cannot express the monus operation on semiring-annotated relations, when the annotations come from the bag semiring or the tropical semiring or the fuzzy semiring. Consequently, the semantics of SQL cannot be captured using the interpretation-based semantics considered here.

papers.title: Orbital stability and instability of standing waves for an inhomogeneous logarithmic Schr\"odinger equation
papers.abstract: We study the inhomogeneous logarithmic Schr\"odinger equation \[ i\partial_tu+\Delta u+|x|^{-1}u\log|u|^2=0, \qquad (t,x)\in\R\times\R^N,\quad N\ge2. \] For every initial datum in $H^1(\R^N)$, we establish global existence of weak solutions. We also construct explicit positive stationary solutions and solve the associated Nehari minimization problem. For $\omega\ge0$, the minimizer is unique up to {a constant} phase and is given by \[ e^{\frac{N-1}{2}(1+\sqrt{1+\omega})} e^{-(1+\sqrt{1+\omega})|x|}, \] whereas for $\omega<0$ the infimum is zero and is not attained. Finally, we prove that the standing waves associated with these profiles are orbitally stable for $\omega>0$ by a variational argument, and orbitally unstable for $-1<\omega<-1+(N-1)^{-2}$ by combining spectral analysis, localized energy and mass estimates, and phase modulation.

papers.title: Discourse Analysis of Legislative Bill Discussions
papers.abstract: Legislative hearings are distinct communication events with their own human recognizable structure and logic, yet they have been analyzed as distinct phenomena beyond their transcripts. Understanding legislative hearings at a deeper level is a major step in analyzing the work and power relationships within democratic bodies. In this work, we present a novel end-to-end pipeline for parsing rhetorical structures from legislative committee hearings with the goal of improving legislative discourse analysis and democratic accountability. We also propose a rhetorical structure grammar and find that 55.21% of California state bill discussions in our dataset can be parsed with this grammar. We evaluate our pipeline with two utterance section classifiers on a random subset of over 2,000 annotated utterances corresponding to 100 hearings. We find that a logistic regression-based classifier with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing outperforms more complex models, achieving an F1 score of 52.8% against our ground truth discourse section labels.

papers.title: The Calkin--Wilf problems on $\ell$-ary partition functions
papers.abstract: In their 1998 precursor to their celebrated paper ``Recounting the rationals,'' Calkin and Wilf listed nine open problems related to the function $b_{k,\ell}(n)$, the number of partitions of $n$ into powers of $\ell$ with each part appearing at most $k$ times. In this short paper, we answer five of their eight remaining open problems. As a consequence of our results, we extend and generalise results of both Carlitz and Reznick, and answer an open question of Reznick.

papers.title: Extensions of the Haldane gap proof: higher dimensions, near degeneracy, fermions and tensor-network states
papers.abstract: A recent remarkable paper by OpenAI showed that the spin-one Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions has a spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit. The proof elegantly deduces this gap from the Hamiltonian's spectrum on a finite system. This basic idea is an inequality involving the purity of the original Gibbs state and a dual Gibbs state that is defined via space-time rotation. Here we consider a few generalizations of this purity bootstrap argument. We first extend it to arbitrary spatial dimensions. Our main result uses the space-time duality between symmetry generators and symmetry twists to obtain upper bounds on the splitting of nearly degenerate low-energy states, together with a nonzero gap above them, from finite-system information. As applications, we show that finite-system calculations for the 2+1-D toric code in a field and the 2+1-D transverse-field Ising model establish parameter regimes with four and two low-lying states whose splittings are bounded from above by $e^{-cL}$ and $e^{-cL^2}$ respectively for arbitrarily large system size $L$, while the gap above these states remains nonzero in the thermodynamic limit. Next, we extend it to fermionic systems and use a finite calculation to establish a symmetric mass generation phase in a $2+1$-D fermionic model. Finally, we apply the bootstrap to tensor-network states and establish exponential decay of connected correlations of all local operators in the symmetric square-lattice spin-one state introduced by Jian and Zaletel.

papers.title: The Higman-Sims graph and a geometric construction of the Steiner system $S(3,6,22)$
papers.abstract: The Higman-Sims graph is the unique strongly regular graph with parameters $(100,22,0,6)$. In this paper, we show that the only distance-regular antipodal double cover of the Higman-Sims graph is its bipartite double cover. Our main tool is a geometric construction of the Steiner system $S(3,6,22)$.

papers.title: ManimCode: Learning Visual Self-Correction for Educational Animation
papers.abstract: Manim supports precise, programmatic video generation, but a successfully rendered educational animation can still have visual defects, missing explanations, or incorrect content. Rendering does not directly identify the code changes needed to correct these visual failures, so feedback-driven revision is needed. Existing agentic frameworks use iterative rendering and revision but typically rely on large models, often proprietary. Existing Manim datasets primarily contain final programs and often lack quality verification and the trajectories of feedback and revisions needed to learn this refinement process. We introduce ManimData and ManimCode, a data and training framework for feedback-driven educational animation generation. We construct ManimData through a render-guided pipeline that iteratively generates, executes, reviews, and revises Manim programs with retrieved API documentation. Its 24,034 render-verified, quality-filtered records preserve intermediate programs, execution errors, visual critiques, and corrective revisions. We use role-conditioned supervised fine-tuning on these trajectories to train ManimCode, a single 4B model, to write, review, and revise animation programs. To improve correction of errors that differ from those in the collected trajectories, we then train the Reviser with reinforcement learning on self-generated states, using rendering outcomes and reference-free quality feedback. ManimCode achieves 96.6% and 97.0% render success on ManimData-test and ManimBench, compared with 52.6% and 82.0% for the untrained 4B model under the same inference setup, while also improving video quality scores from 2.48 to 2.94 and from 3.00 to 3.44. Integrating ManimCode into two long-form educational video generation systems increases completed videos from 19/117 to 107/117 and from 53/239 to 239/239, alongside improvements in educational effectiveness and visual quality.

papers.title: Values of differentials of plane branches: block decomposition and semiroots
papers.abstract: We study the passage of special gaps from a Zariski semiroot to a plane branch. A decomposition into rectangular blocks allows us to compute the maximal valuations of the coefficients of differentials and describe the image of the transition map. We treat vertical and horizontal decompositions, as well as decompositions with alternations, obtaining criteria for the preservation of special gaps. For towers whose ramification indices after the first are all equal to two, the value semigroup of the branch and the special gaps of the first semiroot determine the special gaps of the branch.

papers.title: Mahler's Problem on Liouville Numbers II. Rational Maps
papers.abstract: In 1984, Mahler asked which analytic functions map the set $\mathscr L$ of Liouville numbers into itself. In the first paper of this series, we proved that every real-analytic solution on an open interval is the restriction of a real rational function. We now identify a canonical subfield $\mathbb L$ of $\mathbb R$ such that, for every nonconstant $R\in\mathbb R(X)$ and every nonempty open interval $I$ in its domain, $R(I\cap\mathscr L)\subseteq\mathscr L$ if and only if $R$ is defined over $\mathbb L$ and $R^{-1}(\mathbb Q)\cap I\cap\mathscr L=\varnothing$. The weaker inclusion $R(I\cap\mathscr L)\subseteq\mathbb Q\cup\mathscr L$ holds if and only if $R$ is defined over $\mathbb L$. If $R$ is not defined over $\mathbb L$, every such interval contains a Cantor set of Liouville numbers whose images under $R$ are irrational and have irrationality exponents bounded by a constant depending only on $R$. We also construct continuum many positive strong Liouville numbers $\sigma$ for which $\sigma X^m$ preserves $\mathscr L$ for every $m\geq2$, with all nonzero rational fibers consisting of $U_m$-numbers.

authors.name: Diego Marques
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

papers.title: A Theory of Partial Truth for Scientific Statements
papers.abstract: Scientific representations often combine accurate and inaccurate components, which a single bivalent classification does not distinguish. This paper develops a restricted formal framework for estimating partial factual truth. For fixed content and valuation criteria, the target is adequacy to the facts, independent of the available evidence; its numerical assessment through evidence remains fallible. Quantitative claims are evaluated by normalized discrepancies between asserted and empirically supported values. Admissible finite conjunctions are assessed over a fixed basis of distinct elementary claims using arithmetic or relevance-weighted means. The resulting valuations preserve the contributions from accurate components and are independent of grouping when component counts or total weights are retained. Zero-relevance additions leave the contextual valuation unchanged, but compensation remains possible among components with positive relevance. Worked examples examine admissibility, changes of granularity, measurement indeterminacy, and sensitivity of comparisons to discrepancy scales and relevance weights. An astrophysical application connects the assessment to published observations. The framework applies to selected testable consequences of models and theories, without providing a numerical calculus for arbitrary formulas or a unique method for choosing scales and weights. It permits conditional comparisons of factual adequacy while distinguishing them from confidence, empirical coverage, and convergence toward a complete truth.

authors.name: Gustavo E. Romero
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

papers.title: Pattern selection and biomass shifts in a vegetation model with nonlocal competition and Allee activation
papers.abstract: We study a single-species vegetation model in which a strong Allee effect acts locally and competition acts through a nonlocal kernel, and we describe the kernel with the one-parameter family of q-Gaussians, which goes from compact support to power-law tails. The local activation introduced by the Allee effect allows a finite-wavelength instability even when the Fourier transform of the kernel is positive, so Gaussian and heavy-tailed kernels can produce patterns. We derive in closed form the coefficients of the hexagonal amplitude equations and verify them against independent numerical steady states. The quadratic coefficient $Q$ results from the balance between the curvature of the local growth and the competitive inhibition at the pattern scale, and at onset its sign depends only on the fraction of the local activation that diffusion removes at the critical wavenumber. The same coefficient controls the morphology, since spots, labyrinths and gaps appear with pairwise competition only as $Q$ changes sign, and the amplitude equations predict the choice between hexagons and stripes in every simulated state in which the cubic truncation holds. It also controls the total biomass, which increases for spots and decreases for gaps.

papers.intro:
Vegetation in arid and semiarid regions often organizes in regular patterns of spots, labyrinths, stripes, or gaps in a vegetated matrix [1, 2, 3]. The usual interpretation of these structures is a finite-wavelength instability in which short-range facilitation acts as an activator and long-range competition for water acts as an inhibitor [4, 5]. A minimal description considers a single biomass field and represents the interaction through a kernel GG that weights the density in a neighborhood of each point. Fuentes, Kuperman and Kenkre showed that nonlocal competition in a Fisher-type equation produces spatial structures [6, 7], and Pigolotti, López and Hernández-García showed that, in this class of models, patterns require the Fourier transform G^​(k)\hat{G}(k) of the kernel to take negative values [8]. The same condition governs the vegetation model of Martínez-García et al. [9, 10]. Gaussian and exponential kernels have G^>0\hat{G}>0, and the same happens with kernels with power-law tails, so none of them can produce patterns in competition-only models. This is a strong restriction, if we consider that fat tails are common in dispersal kernels [11] and that there is no reason to expect a sharp cutoff in interactions mediated by water and roots.

Previous works showed that an Allee effect in the growth function relaxes this restriction [12, 13, 14, 15]. By making the per-capita growth increase with density, the Allee effect supplies a positive local feedback that can compete with the nonlocal inhibition, and van der Voort, Martínez-García and Doelman identified a general mechanism in which local growth outpaces the susceptibility to competition, which allows patterns with kernels of non-negative transform [15]. Their analysis is linear and one-dimensional, it considers kernels with compact support, and it leaves the amplitude equations and the two-dimensional morphologies for future work. The linear analysis, however, says nothing about the symmetry of the pattern. For the two-dimensional nonlocal Fisher–Kolmogorov equation, numerical studies report almost exclusively hexagonal arrays of spots [16], and Pinto-Ramos, Surendran and Martínez-García showed, through amplitude equations, that for linear local growth pairwise competition restricts the stable patterns to spots, so that stripes and gaps require higher-order competition [17]. Amplitude equations for related nonlocal models appear in Ref. [18].

The linear analysis, however, says nothing about the symmetry of the pattern. For the two-dimensional nonlocal Fisher–Kolmogorov equation, numerical studies report almost exclusively hexagonal arrays of spots [16], and Pinto-Ramos, Surendran and Martínez-García showed, through amplitude equations, that for linear local growth pairwise competition restricts the stable patterns to spots, so that stripes and gaps require higher-order competition [17]. Amplitude equations for related nonlocal models appear in Ref. [18].

In the present work we consider a minimal vegetation model with local cooperative growth and nonlocal competition, and we follow the consequences of the local activation from the linear instability to the selected pattern and to the total biomass. It is not our intention to describe a particular ecosystem, and we do not claim that real competition kernels belong to the family that we use. Our more modest goal is to show that a single quantity, the quadratic coefficient QQ of the amplitude equations, organizes both the morphology of the patterns and the change of the total biomass. We use the qq-Gaussian family because one parameter takes the kernel from compact support through the Gaussian to power-law tails, and because its Fourier transform has a closed form.

IV we derive the amplitude equations and the condition that selects the morphology, and in Sec. V we relate the total biomass to the same coefficient. papers.title: Inertial sub-range detection and characterization for ground-layer turbulence at new extremely large telescope sites in Chile
papers.abstract: The atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) presents turbulence regimes that diverge from the classical Kolmogorov 1941 (K41) power-law spectrum widely assumed in optical atmospheric profiling, yet turbulence characterization for astronomical applications remains predominantly based on K41 assumptions. Using high-frequency sonic anemometer data from site-testing campaigns at the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) and Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) sites in Chile, we apply detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA)---a technique from fractal time-series analysis---to identify the inertial sub-range and evaluate statistical isotropy in the ABL, comparing our approach with the Fourier-based algorithm for robust identification of the inertial subrange (ARIIS). Strict Kolmogorov conditions---simultaneous isotropy and $k^{-5/3}$ scaling across all fields---are satisfied in fewer than 7 per cent of observations. Temperature fields systematically decouple from velocity components under stable stratification, exhibiting Bolgiano-Obukhov scaling ($k^{-7/5}$) during nighttime hours, indicating active rather than passive scalar behaviour. DFA-detected regime transitions correlate with characteristic turbulence scales, providing objective, model-free boundaries for the inertial subrange. Comparative $C_n^2$ estimation reveals that structure function methods assuming K41 scaling diverge significantly from flux-based parameterizations under stable conditions. The rarity of true Kolmogorov conditions at these sites necessitates stratification-aware methodologies for accurate optical turbulence characterization at next-generation extremely large telescope facilities.

papers.title: Metallic Circles: Concyclic Tangency Points of Ford Circles over $k$-Fibonacci Quotients
papers.abstract: Extending a result of Kocik, we show that the tangency points of the Ford circles built over quotients of $k$-Fibonacci numbers are concyclic: they lie on a circle centred on the horizontal axis, of radius $\sqrt{k^2+4}/2$, meeting it at the reciprocal of the metallic ratio $\sigma_k$ and at $-\sigma_k$. Concyclicity turns out to be a quadratic identity of the sequence read in coordinates. In the Poincar\'e half-plane, this circle is a geodesic along which the tangency points advance with constant step $2\ln\sigma_k$.
